10049-old-lady-mary-a-story-of-the-seen-:
Margaret Oliphant's story opens with a striking claim: Old Lady Mary was very old, and therefore found it very hard to make up her mind to die. Youth, Oliphant argues, stands near the unseen world it came from, while middle life often wishes for the door that stands ajar.

The tale follows Mary through the seen and unseen, as death approaches and the veil between worlds thins. Oliphant writes with quiet sympathy and a ghostly touch, never quite explaining what Mary sees. Readers get a gentle, moving meditation on age, death, and the life beyond, from a master of Victorian supernatural fiction.
10050-a-little-pilgrim-stories-of-the-se:
Margaret Oliphant's Little Pilgrim is a Victorian tale of death as passage into another world. The evening before, the pilgrim had talked with a friend about dying. After a long illness that brought her close to death, she felt no pain, only a slow sinking through the bed, as though nothing beneath her could hold her up.

Another friend who had also neared death described drifting on a summer sea, free of pain, in a lovely sheltered corner of the unseen world. Oliphant's story follows the pilgrim into that world. Readers get a gentle, luminous tale of death as a passage, not an end, from a Victorian master of the supernatural.
10129-excellent-women:
Various writers joined to make this book of short lives of notable Christian women, from the seventeenth century to Victorian times. Each sketch is written by a different hand, so tone and detail shift from chapter to chapter. The shared aim is praise for faith shown in work, suffering, and service.

Elizabeth Fry's prison reform, Hannah More's writing, Susanna Wesley's home teaching, and Ann Judson's mission work stand beside queens, countesses, and nurses. Cairo streets, mission fields, and sick wards all appear as scenes of duty. Readers get twelve compact, admiring portraits of women whose faith shaped public and private life.
1044-extract-from-captain-stormfield-s-v:
Mark Twain sends Captain Stormfield, an old sea captain, to heaven, where he finds not harps and rest but crowds, red tape, and a vast bureaucracy. Saints queue, angels file reports, and the famous dead turn out far less grand than their fame promised. Twain wrote the skit late in life and held it back for years.

The humor bites at pious cant and human pride: heaven, in Twain's hands, looks much like earth, only larger. Stormfield's plain talk punctures each wonder in turn. The piece is short, sharp, and very Twain, and it suits readers who like their satire aimed at the skies.
10469-johnny-crow-s-garden:
L. Leslie Brooke drew and wrote this picture book in 1903, first told to him by his father and now set down for his own boys. Johnny Crow digs and sows until he makes a little garden, and animals come to visit in fine dress. The verses are short, rhymed, and full of animal jokes.

A lion wears a green and yellow tie, a rat wears a feather in his hat, a bear has nothing to wear, and an ape takes his measure with a tape. A crane and other guests join the fun. Readers get a classic, charming picture book, beloved for its rhymes and drawings.
10533-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-07:
John Lord published this seventh volume of Beacon Lights of History, on great women, opening with Heloise and love. Lord treats love as the flower of Eden, then follows Heloise from birth and education, through her gifts and aspirations, to her famous love for Peter Abelard. The tone is earnest, romantic, and moral.

Abelard's genius, wit, skepticism, and triumphs at Paris lead to mad infatuation, secret marriage, scandal, and retirement to separate convents. Letters, persecution, and a blameless later life close the tale. Readers get a classic, old-style portrait of a great woman of the Middle Ages.
10640-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-09:
John Lord, an American lecturer on history, built his Beacon Lights of History from popular lectures, and this ninth volume treats European statesmen. Its long central lecture follows Mirabeau through the French Revolution: the failure of royal finances, the Assembly of Notables, the States-General, the fall of the Bastille, and the Reign of Terror.

Lord tells the Revolution as a drama of great speakers and fateful choices, weighing what it achieved and what it might have done without violence. Other lectures in the volume take up further statesmen in the same vivid style. Readers get an old-fashioned but lively introduction to the men who shaped modern Europe.
10707-a-christmas-mystery-the-story-of-t:
William J. Locke published A Christmas Mystery in 1910, a modern retelling of the story of the three wise men. Three men famed and honored through the world meet unexpectedly before a bookstall, and the tale that follows reworks the ancient journey in present-day dress. Illustrations by Blendon Campbell, including a frontispiece of beating wings, add to the mystery.

Locke writes with warmth and a touch of the uncanny, as his travelers kneel and carry an inalienable joy back into the great world. The book suits Christmas reading, short and full of feeling. Readers get a gentle fantasy on the Magi theme, by a popular novelist of his day.
1096-the-faith-of-men:
Jack London gathers stories of the North in The Faith of Men, tales of prospectors, dogs, and the harsh code of the Yukon. Men test each other and themselves against cold, hunger, and gold fever. London wrote the stories after his Klondike years, when gold fever still filled his mind.

London writes of loyalty, betrayal, and endurance, with the force that made his Klondike stories famous. The collection suits readers who know Call of the Wild and want more of London's frozen world. The faith of the title is the trust men place in each other when law and comfort fail.
11060-the-aspirations-of-jean-servien:
Anatole France wrote this novel about Jean Servien, born in a bookbinder's back shop in the Rue Notre-Dame des Champs in Paris. Jean's father bound books for religious houses, and his mother, nursing him as she sewed sheets with a curved needle, slipped on paste-wet boards and struck her breast on an iron press. A fever followed, and in long evenings she sang lullabies picturing Jean as general, lawyer, or priest.

Jean grows into a weak, dreaming youth, chasing ideals of love, art, and glory, and following a woman through bramble lanes by moonlight, only to be met with a cry of terror. France writes with irony about maternal ambition and youthful aspiration. The novel suits readers of French literary fiction, tender toward its hero and sharp about his illusions.
11149-little-folded-hands-prayers-for-ch:
Little Folded Hands gathers prayers for children, compiled from various sources in a revised edition. Morning prayers open the book: Now I awake and see the light, Lord, Thou hast kept me through the night, and a prayer for the morning bright with rosy light.

Later prayers cover bedtime, meals, sickness, and trust: a sick child prays, Dear Father, Thy child is sick, look upon me in tender mercy. Short verses, simple language, and repeated Amens make the book fit for family prayer and Sunday-school use, teaching children to pray morning and night.
11283-plays-of-gods-and-men:
Lord Dunsany's Plays of Gods and Men, prepared from the 1917 Unwin edition, collects fantasy dramas in which gods, kings, and prophets contend in invented ancient cities. The Laughter of the Gods, a tragedy in three acts, sets King Karnos and his court in the jungle city of Thek during Babylon's decadence. where queens dispute lineage and swords while prophets speak for unseen powers. Other plays extend the same mythic world.

Dunsany's dialogue is ornate and deliberate, closer to poetry than to realistic speech. His gods are not benevolent; they laugh at human plans. The volume appeals to readers who enjoy high fantasy before the genre had a name, and it shows Dunsany's influence on later writers of invented worlds.
113-the-secret-garden:
Mary Lennox, spoiled and lonely after her parents die in India, arrives at a gloomy Yorkshire manor. Frances Hodgson Burnett's Secret Garden follows Mary as she finds a locked garden and a hidden cousin. Martha the maid and Dickon, who talks to animals, guide her.

Mary and Dickon revive the garden in secret, and Colin, long kept indoors, learns to walk and hope. The robin, the key, and the seasons mark their growth. Magic here means fresh air, work, and kindness rather than spells. The novel became a beloved children's classic.
11673-stickeen:
John Muir's Stickeen tells of a dog in Alaska in the summer of 1880. Muir set out from Fort Wrangel in a canoe to explore the icy region of the south-east, a task begun in the fall of 1879.

Provisions, blankets, and an Indian crew were stowed, while relatives on the wharf bade farewell. On the return, far spent in the day, Muir turned back from a grand view, hoping to see it again. The party then met a hard network of crevasses, with mist and snow flying thick and fast. Stickeen, the small dog at Muir's side, gives the storm story its heart and its name.
12051-dick-sand-a-captain-at-fifteen:
Jules Verne's Dick Sand, or A Captain at Fifteen, appeared in a translation first published by George Munro in New York in 1878. It was reprinted many times in the United States, and it is a different translation from Ellen E. Frewer's version. The redactor's note identifies it as number V018 in the T and M listing of Verne's works, a translation of Un capitaine de quinze ans, also from 1878.

Dick Sand, a fifteen-year-old cabin boy, must take command of a ship when its officers are lost, and navigate passengers, cargo, and danger across the sea. Verne's adventure, written for young readers, tests a boy's seamanship, courage, and judgment, and it became one of his most popular tales of youthful responsibility.
12313-pictures-of-sweden:
Hans Christian Andersen published Pictures of Sweden in London in 1851 with Richard Bentley. Andersen, author of The Improvisatore, traveled Sweden and wrote sketches of towns, people, and legends.

Contents list Trollhatta, the Bird Phoenix, Kinnakulla, Grandmother, prison cells, beggar boys, Vadstene, the puppet showman, the Skjargaards, Stockholm, and Upsala. A mid-book vision passes through rich halls and poor chambers, where voluptuousness and envy stride past a recording angel. Andersen mixes travel fact with fairy-tale fancy, as in his stories. The book gives a romantic Dane view of Sweden, before railways and industry remade it.
12358-preliminary-announcement-list-of-m:
Issued at Oxford in October 1919, this short tract relaunches a society founded in 1913 and paused by the First World War. The Society for Pure English sets out its name, its finances and its aims, then prints a list of its members. War had delayed its first issues until after the Armistice.

Its opening sections argue that pure does not mean purging foreign words from English. Instead the society wants clear, sound usage, and it plans short tracts on points of language. Profits, not subscriptions, were meant to pay an unsalaried staff, with donations invited in place of dues. The pamphlet thus captures a post-war bid to guide English by persuasion, not by rule-book.
12429-the-last-leaf-observations-during-:
James Kendall Hosmer's 1912 observations span seventy-five years of men and events in America and Europe. Hosmer, a member of historical societies in Minnesota and Massachusetts, had written lives of Samuel Adams, Jefferson and others. Here he looks back as a last leaf, a figure younger men shoulder aside, murmuring in green and rattling, dry, in winter.

The book mixes memoir, history and portraiture, from American politics to European scenes. Hosmer writes with humour about age, and with knowledge about the long nineteenth century he lived through. The volume offers a veteran historian's rear view, personal where a formal history would be distant, and rich in first-hand encounter.
1270-in-defense-of-women:
H. L. Mencken, America's sharpest critic of his day, defends women against both chivalry and feminism in these essays. He argues that women are shrewder, tougher, and more realistic than men, and that marriage, as men made it, wastes their gifts. The essays range over suffrage, morals, and the war between the sexes.

Mencken writes with his usual bite and paradox, praising women by scorning the men who rule them. The book shocked both camps in 1918. It remains a bracing, if dated, piece of contrarian wit, and it draws readers who like argument with sting.
1294-the-firm-of-nucingen:
Honoré de Balzac tells of the house of Nucingen, a great Paris bank, and of its founder, a financier who rises by speculation, bankruptcy, and cunning. The tale follows Nucingen's schemes through salons and stock exchanges, where fortunes are made and ruined on paper.

Balzac writes high finance with the detail of a man who knew its tricks, and his bankers are comic and ruthless at once. The novel is a sharp study of money power. It suits readers who like Balzac on business and the comedy of capital. Balzac's bankers are comic and ruthless, and the satire still bites.
13103-great-britain-and-her-queen:
Anne E. Keeling's history, in a revised second edition of 1897, tells the story of Britain under Queen Victoria for general readers. Chapters run from the girl queen and her kingdom through storm and sunshine, France and England, the Crimean War, India, and the colonies. Keeling writes as a loyal Victorian, proud of progress and empire.

The book also notes reform at home, such as Lord Ashley's fight that ended the work of women and children in mines in 1842. It follows the growth of Australia from a convict shore fed on imports to a land of vast flocks. Read now, it shows both the facts Victorians prized and the pride with which they told their own story.
13238-six-women:
Victoria Cross's Six Women, published in New York by Mitchell Kennerley, is dedicated to H. M. G. and E. F. C. and to memories of the East. Its hero, Hamilton, opens listless and despondent in a hot eastern town, walking under yellow awnings while bullocks draw creaking carts through dust. Cross sets her tales of love and loss in that heat and light.

Hamilton finds love with Saidie, and Saturdays become their great days, with picnics in the desert and a fat brown camel for the ride. A later scene shows a boat on a river, with Sudanese boys in white turbans standing silent at stem and stern. The book is a set of linked romances, frank about desire and set firmly in eastern color.
13254-the-dollar-hen:
Milo M. Hastings's 1911 Dollar Hen, from the National Poultry Magazine, argues that poultry farming can pay, if run on business lines. Hastings, formerly of the Kansas Experiment Station and later in charge of the USDA's commercial poultry investigation, opens by noting that doctors once ignored outdoor life as a cure for consumption. The book is practical, plain, and full of figures.

He warns farmers to drive sand points and pump water by hand on sand lands, since community systems cost more than they return. Later, he explains shipping dressed birds in refrigerator cars, and counts live poultry cars out of Iowa, Missouri, and Illinois. The Dollar Hen is a handbook for farmers who want eggs and meat to pay.
1327-elizabeth-and-her-german-garden:
First published in 1898 and signed only Elizabeth, this garden journal follows an Englishwoman newly settled on a German estate. Through the months she learns the soil, the seasons, and the habits of a household far from her old life. Her voice is frank, funny, and fond of solitude, and the garden soon becomes the centre of her days.

Month by month she plants, prunes, reads, and receives guests, while the garden changes around her. Small setbacks and small triumphs fill the entries, and her notes on flowers, books, and neighbours build a picture of a woman making a home on her own terms. The charm lies in that plain daily record, kept with wit and a keen eye.
13302-the-curly-haired-hen:
A. Vimar's Curly-Haired Hen, translated by Nora K. Hills, is a children's tale in text and pictures about Mother Etienne's farm. Chapters run from a mother's devotion and Yollande's trousseau to Father Gusson's secret, Sir Booum's circus, and the triumph of the ointment. The frame is a grandfather telling three children a story on a bad-weather day.

Yollande, a hen, wakes first at dawn and cackles vigorously after a day of fatigue, eating corn greedily from Germaine's hand. Her keepers worry over a costume, since cool mornings might bring cold or rheumatism. Later, Mother Etienne, in tears, begs Sir Booum to care for Yollande and send news. The tale is whimsical, tender, and full of farmyard charm.
13375-the-rival-heirs-being-the-third-an:
The Rev. A. D. Crake closes his Aescendune chronicle with rival heirs in the days of the Norman Conquest. An Anglo-Saxon hall, a black and dark night, a wedding of hawk and dove, and Norman pages set the contest between English and Norman claims. A fray in the greenwood, a revelation, and a hunt in the woods sharpen it.

Fire, half-told news, and a burnt monastery raise the question of who set the blaze, while an abbot in soft robes and slippers contrasts with stern monastic rule. The English heir at last takes possession, meets the Conqueror at Abingdon, and finds retribution and restoration. Crake writes a boys' tale of loyalty, faith, and the passing of Saxon England.
13539-dr-scudder-s-tales-for-little-read:
Dr. Scudder's Tales for Little Readers About the Heathen, 1849, compiled largely from Duff, Dubois, and others, teaches Christian children about Hindu life and calls them to missionary work. Parents are urged to dedicate sons, daughters, money, effort, and prayer to that cause, in hope of a moral revolution of the world.

Temples crowd every village and stand in woods, rivers, mountains, and steep rocks, following an ancient practice of mountain worship. Ascetics hold up arms until muscles grow rigid and limbs shrivel, wear great square irons round their necks, or lie on beds of iron spikes, with nails grown through hand and arm. Scudder writes with missionary zeal and the prejudices of his age.
13665-war-in-the-garden-of-eden:
Kermit Roosevelt served in Mesopotamia during the First World War, first with British forces and later with American artillery. This 1919 memoir recounts his campaign along the Tigris. He describes the march from Basra, patrols among the ruins of Babylon, and fighting in heat, dust, and flood. Photographs taken by the author illustrate the text.

Roosevelt writes as a junior officer learning war on the job. He praises the skill of British and Indian troops and notes the hardship of supply lines. Sketches of Arab tribesmen, river boats, and desert camps fill the gaps between battles. The tone stays modest and direct, with humour in hard places. The book remains a clear first-hand account of a little-known front.
13724-the-frontiersmen:
Charles Egbert Craddock's 1904 collection of frontier stories, set among the stockades and mountains of the Tennessee country in the days of Cherokee warfare. The tales follow settlers, captives, and interpreters caught between white settlements and Native towns, with titles such as The Linguister, A Victor at Chungke, and The Captive of the Ada-Wehi.

One hero, raised by Cherokees after his English father and Scotch mother were killed in a massacre, was trained in woodcraft and war by the chief Colannah Gigagei. Craddock writes with close attention to speech, landscape, and custom, and her Tennessee mountains glow in storm light over the river. The stories preserve a romantic view of the frontier, told by a writer who knew the region well.
13751-characters-from-the-histories-memo:
David Nichol Smith assembled this 1918 anthology of seventeenth-century character sketches. An opening essay traces the character as a literary form, from early models to Clarendon. Then come portraits drawn from histories and memoirs of the period. James I, the Duke of Buckingham, Sir Francis Bacon, and many others appear in turn.

Each sketch judges a public figure in a few sharp paragraphs. Writers praise, blame, and anatomise ambition, wit, and folly. Clarendon supplies several of the best pieces, while Jonson and Wilson add others. Notes explain names and events for modern readers. The book serves both literary history and Stuart politics. It shows how early modern writers sized up power.
13758-gerda-in-sweden:
Etta Blaisdell McDonald and Julia Dalrymple wrote Gerda in Sweden in 1910 for young readers. It belongs to the Little People Everywhere series, which set stories in many countries. Gerda and her brother Birger travel through Sweden, from home to Lapland and beyond. A surprise box, a ship called the North Star, and new friends start the journey.

Chapters cross the polar circle, watch the midnight sun, and visit Erik's home in Lapland. Skansen, canal locks, a winter carnival, and midsummer festival follow. Swedish customs, food, and daily life appear in story form. The tone stays gentle and instructive. Children learn geography through Gerda's eyes.
13784-mr-dooley-in-the-hearts-of-his-cou:
Finley Peter Dunne gathered Mr. Dooley pieces in this 1899 volume. Dooley, an Irish-American saloon keeper, comments on politics, war, and American life in broad dialect. He talks of Aguinaldo, the Philippines war, and heroes turned magazine writers. Cousin George and other voices join the talk.

Dunne uses humour to puncture pomposity and to defend ordinary people. Dooley's plain speech makes complex events easy to grasp. The book went through three editions of ten thousand copies in its first month. It made Dooley a national figure. Readers today get both laughs and a sharp view of 1890s America.
13883-the-tree-of-heaven:
May Sinclair published The Tree of Heaven in 1918, following one English family from peace to war. Frances Harrison sits under the tree her husband calls an ash and neighbours call a tree of heaven. Children Dorothy, Michael, Nicholas, and baby John fill the house with noise and parties. Old Nanna and young Mary-Nanna keep the nursery running.

War breaks the peace and tests each child in turn. Sinclair follows love, loss, and duty across the war years. Anthony, tall and handsome, embodies a generation sent to fight. The tree stands as an image of shelter and endurance. Sinclair's prose mixes realism with quiet symbolism. The novel offers a family view of the Great War.
13913-the-port-of-missing-men:
Meredith Nicholson published The Port of Missing Men in 1907, a romance of adventure and mystery. Shirley Claiborne fronts the volume in illustration. A quotation from Malory sets the tone: Sir Pellinore hears a horse at midnight and awaits adventure. The hero rides beyond city bounds seeking pleasant lands across distant hills.

A lost document drives the plot, with an indictment that makes its holder uneasy. He asks for it back to keep safe in his own hands, but it has vanished. Love, honour, and conspiracy intertwine through Indianapolis and beyond. Nicholson writes in the popular romantic manner of his day. The novel suits readers of early twentieth-century adventure romance.
13934-inferences-from-haunted-houses-and:
The Honourable John Harris published Inferences from Haunted Houses and Haunted Men in 1901. Harris notes surprising lack of interest in psychical matters, yet hopes science may clarify them. He cites Sir William Crookes on thought transfer without recognised organs of sense. Knowledge, Crookes held, may enter mind by unknown ways.

Harris studies pressures, pattering like water drops in a sensitive ear, and double or treble intermissions. Haunted houses and haunted men become cases for inference, not mere ghost tales. His tone is sober and curious. The book suits readers of psychical research history. It shows Edwardian science at the edge of the unknown.
13971-the-fifteen-comforts-of-matrimony-:
This volume collects men's responses to The Fifteen Comforts of Matrimony, in verse and prose. Transcribers note battered type, faded scans, and missing margins, with guesses marked where letters failed. The pieces answer women's complaints with husbands' laments and praises. A fifteenth comfort recalls a dear kind husband who never left in a morning without a parting kiss and breakfast.

Now, the speaker says, her days are spent in misery without him. The satires belong to Augustan print debate over marriage, sex, and domestic life. Their humour is plain and of its time. The volume pairs with the women's responses in the same series. It suits students of popular satire and social history.
13972-the-fifteen-comforts-of-matrimony-:
This small volume collects satirical responses to The Fifteen Comforts of Matrimony, in verse from women's voices. Transcribers note battered type, archaic spelling, and faded scans, with best guesses marked where letters failed. The pieces answer male complaints about marriage with sharp, bawdy wit. Plagues, lovers, and maids' laments fill the pages.

One speaker begs a skilful man's bleeding hand to end her maiden name. Another watches an amorous youth swear truth by all that is holy. The satires belong to Restoration and Augustan print wars over sex and marriage. Their humour is coarse and of its time. The volume suits students of popular satire and gender debate.
14070-english-grammar-in-familiar-lectur:
Samuel Kirkham published English Grammar in Familiar Lectures, in a stereotype edition from Robert B. Collins, New York. The volume adds a compendium of parsing, punctuation, false syntax exercises, and philosophical grammar, with appendix and key. Copyright deposit on August 22, 1829, marks the Southern District of New York. Kirkham designed the book for schools and private learners.

A notice praises Kirkham's proposed lecture course on grammar for genuine merit. Familiar lectures explain rules in plain talk, with exercises to correct. The system suits nineteenth-century schoolrooms. Modern readers gain a view of how grammar was taught. The book remains a landmark of American English teaching.
14081-the-three-jovial-huntsmen:
Randolph Caldecott's picture book sets a short rhymed hunting tale to bold, lively images. Three cheerful huntsmen ride out with horns sounding, keen to follow scent and sight. Their day takes a comic turn when the first creature they find is a ragged boggart in a field. They leave it alone and press on, undaunted.

Doggerel verse and pictures share the work evenly. Each stanza ends with a call to look, and each scene leans on gesture, costume, and countryside detail. Young readers meet dialect speech, brisk rhythm, and gentle nonsense rather than a stern moral. The book survives as a small classic of Victorian nursery art, meant to be read aloud and looked at together.
14082-le-corbeau-the-raven:
Paris published this bilingual Raven in 1875, pairing Edgar Poe's English poem with Stéphane Mallarmé's French translation and illustrations by Édouard Manet. A weary student, pondering forgotten lore at midnight, hears a tapping at his chamber door. A stately raven enters, perches on a bust of Pallas, and answers every question with one word.

French and English face each other across the pages, so readers can watch Mallarmé remake Poe's music. Midnight dreary becomes minuit lugubre, and the bird's grave decorum survives in both tongues. Manet's stark plates deepen the gloom without explaining it. Short but rich, the volume stands as a landmark of translation: an American nightmare rendered by a French symbolist, with art to match its shadows.
14100-eighteen-hundred-and-eleven:
Anna Laetitia Barbauld's poem of 1812 confronts Britain in the middle of the Napoleonic wars. War drums sound across vexed nations while Britain feeds a strife it cannot win, propping one sinking state after another. Colossal power bears down each fort of freedom, and hushed peoples curse the despot they obey. Nature still pours out harvests, but men call famine down instead.

Prophecy gives the poem its edge. Barbauld warns that empires fall and arts decay when genius flees a favored shore, and she imagines future youths sailing from American lakes to walk among England's ruins. Yet hope survives in the rise of new lands across the Atlantic, where commerce, learning, and free institutions may carry the light westward. Few poems of the war years spoke so plainly, and the backlash it drew shows how sharp its warning felt.
14339-music-talks-with-children:
Thomas Tapper wrote Music Talks with Children in 1898, a set of short talks for young players. Tapper speaks to children at home, urging them to live by music, not to idle. Chapters cover listening, tone, the classics, and the lesson itself. He asks why music should be studied, and what the face and hands tell. The book is warm, plain, and full of pictures from daily life.

Tapper warns against showy playing, where brilliance hides thin thought and the player shows himself, not the music. True players seek pure thought and truthful expression, after the manner the composer called for. A later talk likens a young soul to a seedling plant, beaten by rain and wind yet holding firmer roots each day. The plant grows in danger by one rule: never let go. The book trains ears, hands, and character together.
14523-sister-carmen:
M. Corvus wrote this German romance, translated by Kate Dykers and published in New York in 1891, opening on an Easter Sunday morning in a small Moravian village. A lark sings over fields as the community wakes.

Carmen, known as Sister Carmen, moves among pupils, widows, and estates such as Wollmershain, where Frau von Trautenau and her stepson share a trusting bond. Agatha teaches her pupils and accepts invitations that draw the household together. The novel is sentimental and pious, in the manner of popular German fiction of its day, with nature as moral backdrop.
14605-the-devil-s-garden:
W. B. Maxwell's 1914 novel takes its title from an image of the devil playing in a man's mind like a wanton child in a garden, choking paths and trampling buds. The story opens with a village postmaster staring at an official envelope.

Wills, bequests, and family squabbles among the Petherick clan drive the plot, as a beautiful will promises to settle claims and stir envy. Maxwell writes with Edwardian moral seriousness about temptation and duty. The novel is a solid domestic drama, less known than his earlier successes but rich in village character.
14706-greybeards-at-play-literature-and-:
Gilbert Keith Chesterton's Greybeards at Play, published in London in 1900 by R. Brimley Johnson, offers rhymes and sketches meant for old gentlemen. Chesterton dedicates the verses to E. C. B., his closest boyhood friend.

The pieces play with high themes in low spirits: a philosopher at one with nature, altruism on the high seas, and aestheticism spreading through all classes. A slug, an octopus, a vulture, and a shark all get fond verses, along with snow, fog, and rain in Baker Street. The book is early Chesterton, comic and absurd, already fond of paradox.
14717-twelve-men:
Theodore Dreiser's Twelve Men, published in 1919, gathers twelve portraits of men the novelist knew, from a free-spirited friend to a mayor and his people. Dreiser called the book a study of character rather than appearance.

Peter opens the set, an oasis of real freedom in what Dreiser calls American intellectual dreariness. Later sketches follow a doer of the word, a country doctor, Culhane the solid man, a true patriarch, village feudists, and the mighty Rourke. One doctor's tale turns on a servant sent for a buffalo robe before his patient has died. The portraits are vivid, opinionated, and humane.
14837-the-tale-of-tom-kitten:
Beatrix Potter's 1907 tale follows three little kittens: Mittens, Tom Kitten and Moppet, who tumble about the doorstep and play in the dust in their dear little fur coats. Their mother, Mrs. Tabitha Twitchit, expects friends to tea and fetches them indoors to be washed and dressed.

First she scrubs their faces, then she brushes their fur, but kittens will not stay clean and fine for long. Potter's pictures and short sentences carry the comedy of small disobedience and a mother's patience. Dedicated to all pickles, especially those that get upon her garden wall, the book remains a perfect first story about getting ready and coming undone.
14875-elsie-s-children:
Martha Finley's Elsie's Children, a sequel to Elsie's Motherhood, brings the story of Elsie and her children down to the present time and closes the series. Its preface says the volumes were written not at friends' request but in answer to public demand, from readers loath to part with Elsie.

As child, young girl, wife and mother, Elsie has gathered many friends, and Finley hopes they will find neither her nor her children less lovable here. The complete authorised edition, published by arrangement with Dodd, Mead, keeps the family's moral world intact: faith, home, duty and affection. For series readers, it is a farewell visit to a much-loved household.
1506-the-two-noble-kinsmen:
Presented on its title page as the work of John Fletcher and William Shakespeare, this late romance opens before the gates of Athens. Two noble kinsmen, Palamon and Arcite, swear eternal friendship. Captured in war against Thebes, they fall in love with the same woman, Emilia, and friendship gives way to rivalry.

Imprisoned, escaped, and at last set to fight a tournament for Emilia's hand, the cousins pursue honour to a bitter, ironic close. The play blends romance with tragedy and ends with a twist of fate. It is a rich, uneven work, long debated, and a fascinating last flower of Jacobean drama.
15218-the-woman-who-toils-being-the-expe:
Bessie and Marie Van Vorst, two gentlewomen, went to work as factory girls and wrote this 1903 account of what they found. Bessie, as Esther Kelly, wore pickle factory dress, while Marie, as Bell Ballard, worked in a shoe factory. A prefatory letter from Theodore Roosevelt, after reading a serial chapter, fronts the book.

Their chapters describe wages, hours, heat, and the daily grind of women who toil, with a dedication to Mark Twain for his human sympathy. The book shocked polite readers and fed reform debate. Labor historians still cite it as a vivid, firsthand record of women's factory life.
15257-the-curious-case-of-lady-purbeck-a:
This 1909 study tells the curious case of Lady Purbeck, a seventeenth-century scandal built on the feud of Coke and Bacon. Chapters open with Sir Edward Coke, Lady Elizabeth Hatton, and their daughter's birth, then trace rivalry, a forced match to Sir John Villiers, and a mother's flight with her child. Sieges and lawsuits follow.

The author, known for lives of Digby and James II, writes with an antiquary's delight in court gossip and legal war. Lady Purbeck's story shows how family, rank, and royal favor collided in Stuart England. History readers will find the case strange, vivid, and well told.
15269-the-empire-of-russia-from-the-remo:
John Abbott's 1859 history of Russia, in a series on continental monarchies, traces the empire from remotest periods to his present time. He says busy readers no longer want endless battles and court intrigues, so he follows Russia's path plainly, from infancy to greatness. Karamsin, historian under Alexander I, backs his tale.

Abbott writes without notes, trusting a wild and wonderful career to carry itself, with fancy unneeded. The volume covers tsars, wars, and growth in brisk narrative. Readers of nineteenth-century popular history will find it readable, confident, and very much a product of its American moment.
15410-a-little-pilgrim-in-the-unseen:
Margaret Oliphant wrote this short tale of death and the life beyond it, issued by Macmillan in 1899. It opens with a woman who has talked calmly of dying after a long illness, then wakes free of pain. A short prefatory note frames the story as an attempt to follow a gentle, trusting soul into the unseen world.

The tale stays close to that one woman as she takes her first steps in a new place, meeting what comes with simple faith rather than fear or doubt. Nothing here turns on plot twists or grand visions. Its pull lies in quiet comfort: death pictured as a soft waking. It suits readers who had just lost someone close. The book is dedicated in memory to a friend who died in 1882.
1542-the-two-noble-kinsmen:
This edition of The Two Noble Kinsmen follows C. F. Tucker Brooke's 1908 text of the Shakespeare Apocrypha, presenting the play as the work of John Fletcher and William Shakespeare. Palamon and Arcite, kinsmen and sworn friends, are taken prisoner before Athens and both fall in love with Emilia, the sister of Hippolyta.

Their friendship breaks under love's pressure, and a tournament is set to decide who shall marry Emilia, with fate reserving a final irony for the victor. The play's poetry is rich and its ending is strange. It is a valuable text for readers tracing the border between Shakespeare and his fellows.
15552-christmas-outside-of-eden:
Coningsby Dawson, author of The Garden Without Walls and Carry On, published this Christmas fantasy in New York in 1922, with Dodd, Mead, illustrated by Eugene Francis Savage. A cover picture shows a man and woman at a cave entrance, after Eden's golden gates were locked against them forever. God, the tale says, gave them no time to pack.

The story itself is one robins tell, huddled beneath holly on Christmas Eve, every year since the world started, long before Christ was born, for robin memory runs further back than men's. Their Christmas began just outside Eden, within sight of its gold-locked doors. Dawson retells the fall as a tender, wistful fable, where exile, weariness, and a first Christmas outside paradise meet in a short, poetic tale.
15570-paradise-garden-the-satirical-narr:
George Gibbs, author of The Yellow Dove, published this satirical novel with Grosset and Dunlap in New York, illustrated by William A. Hottinger. The epigraph, from Two Gentlemen of Verona, says a man cannot be perfect unless tried and tutored in the world. Twenty-seven chapters run from the great experiment and Jerry to Eve, the minx, the cabin, and Jack Ballard taking charge.

Jerry grows, emerges, goes into training, and asks questions, while Marcia, the siren, Jim Robinson, and Una enter the plot. A fight, two embassies, a path in the woods, and a revolt follow. The mystery deepens through dryad and satyr to revelations. Gibbs satirizes a planned upbringing: a boy raised apart from the world, then set loose in it, with love and pride as the real tests.
15658-topsy-turvy-land-arabia-pictured-f:
Samuel M. Zwemer and Amy E. Zwemer pictured Arabia for children in this book, published by Fleming H. Revell in New York, Chicago, and Toronto, copyrighted in July 1902. It is dedicated to the boys and girls who are helping to turn the world upside down, and signed from Bahrein, Arabia. Illustrations include Arab boys, and the contents promise a child's view of a far land.

Twenty chapters ask why Arabia is topsy-turvy land, then teach geography, a square house with a black overcoat, and greetings at the corner grocery. Blind Fatimah, dates and sugar-cane, desert children, and Noorah's prayer follow. Boat-builders, proverbs, gold, frankincense and myrrh, slaves and slave traders, and little missionaries fill later pages. The book ends by turning the world downside up: a missionary primer, warm and plain, for young readers.
15727-gritli-s-children:
Johanna Spyri, author of Heidi and Cornelli, wrote this two-volume story of Gritli's children, translated by Louise Brooks, from Grosset and Dunlap in New York. Volume one opens at a country house on the Rhine, where golden June sunshine floods roses round a handsome stone villa. Perfumes mount like incense to open windows, a fountain shaft rises into blue sky, and butterflies sip honey-laden flowers under white marble statues.

Volume one follows the doctor's house at Buchberg, the village and school, Oak-Ridge, and Aunty in demand again, through what Oscar founded and Emma planned to a last journey and a first. Volume two gives the new home, a journey, the beautiful Rhine, and a fisherman's hut, through great preparations and anxiety at Rosemount to an unexpected termination and a happy end. Spyri writes a gentle Swiss family tale of children, aunts, and homes by the Rhine.
15779-joanna-godden:
A 1921 novel by Sheila Kaye-Smith, set on the flat marshes of Sussex and Kent. Joanna Godden farms Romney Marsh country, where the Royal Military Canal runs from Hythe to Rye. Kaye-Smith, a writer of Sussex life, builds her tale on land, work, and will. The novel runs in four parts, from shepherd's hey to last love.

Joanna fights to run her farm well in a world that expects women to marry and yield. First love, a little sister, and last love each test her pride and her judgement. Marsh, sheep, and weather shape every choice she makes. The book endures as a portrait of a strong woman holding her ground, told with close knowledge of marsh farms and their people.
15824-notable-events-of-the-nineteenth-c:
A popular history of the nineteenth century, compiled and edited by John Clark Ridpath and issued by the Christian Herald in New York in 1896. Ridpath calls it great deeds of men and nations and the progress of the world, in short studies. The volume belongs to the Christian Herald Library series for 1896 to 1897. Its preface promises no heavy reading.

Short studies treat wars, inventions, reforms, and famous lives, each complete in itself. Readers meet heroes, explorers, and statesmen without wading through a long narrative. The tone stays earnest and uplifting. The book shows how Victorian families learned history: in bright, brief chapters, meant to stir pride and wonder.
15834-the-book-of-joyous-children:
A book of poems for children by James Whitcomb Riley, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1902. J. W. Vawter supplied the pictures. Riley, the Hoosier poet, dedicates the book to Joel Chandler Harris, praising a life that kept glad youth in heart. His verse speaks in the voice of kitchen and playground.

Poems tell child sagas of the kitchen, not classic lore: games, pets, seasons, and small wonders. Riley's dialect and plain speech make the verses easy to read aloud. Laughter leads, but tenderness follows close behind. The book still charms as a keepsake of childhood: warm, funny, and rooted in home.
16093-the-eternal-maiden:
T. Everett Harre's 1913 novel, published by Mitchell Kennerley in New York, opens with a mythic prelude over a frozen world. Darkness holds the glacial seas. The water god Kokoyah does not breathe, and the earth spirit Tornahhuchsuah sleeps veiled. Men rise like willows from the frozen earth yet neither speak, hunt, eat, nor die. A Great Spirit then moves over that still world.

The story that follows turns to Arctic life, love, and rivalry, as Papik and Attalaq pay court to Ahningnetty, the smiling maiden, and news spreads that their king dogs will fight. Games, dog fights, and the long night shape a people who have lost the fear of danger. Readers get a romantic, old-style vision of the far North and its folk.
16121-brothers-of-pity-and-other-tales-o:
Juliana Horatia Ewing's animal tales, first printed in Aunt Judy's Magazine for Young People, gather here under the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge imprint. Brothers of Pity leads. Father Hedgehog and his Neighbours, Toots and Boots, and The Hens of Hencastle follow. Flaps, A Week Spent in a Glass Pond, Among the Merrows, and The Owl in the Ivy Bush close the set. Ewing dedicates the book to her sister Horatia.

Toots was a real creature. He was an honorary member of the Royal Engineers' mess at Aldershot and sometimes dined at table. The hens' tale comes freely translated from the German of Victor Bluthgen. Ewing writes with humor, tenderness, and close watching of beast life. Children and animal lovers will find these stories charming and humane.
16137-the-hoyden:
Mrs. Hungerford's novel The Hoyden, issued in Tauchnitz's British Authors series in 1894, centers on a wild, high-spirited young heroine. Early chapters show Margaret pleading for the little hoyden with little success, Lady Rylton saying things better left unsaid, and a scheme laid before Sir Maurice, who refuses any part in it. Maurice's heart grows hot as he puts a question to the test, neither losing nor winning.

The story plays out in country houses and drawing rooms, where manners, money, and marriage shape every choice. Hungerford, author of Molly Bawn, writes with wit and warmth about a girl who will not be tamed to order. Readers of Victorian romance will enjoy its sparky dialogue and its spirited heroine.
1618-in-the-shadow-of-the-glen:
J. M. Synge's one-act play, first performed at Molesworth Hall, Dublin, in 1903, is set in the last cottage at the head of a long glen in County Wicklow. Nora Burke, wife of a farmer she believes dead, keeps house with a young herd, Michael Dara, when a tramp arrives and the supposed corpse sits up.

Through talk of loneliness, marriage, and the road, Nora weighs a life of duty against a life of wandering, and chooses the tramp's company at the close. The play is brief, poetic, and unsparing. It is a landmark of the Irish stage, and a bold portrait of a woman refusing her lot.
1623-the-new-magdalen:
Wilkie Collins's The New Magdalen opens in France in the autumn of 1870, during the war between France and Germany, in a cottage on the frontier. Two women, one a fallen woman and one a lady, exchange identities amid surgeons, captains, and ambulances, and the heroine must live a borrowed life in England.

Through a trial of conscience and a public confession, Collins asks whether a woman can outlive a past and be judged by her present self. The novel is earnest and theatrical. It is a characteristic Collins study of identity, guilt, and a society quick to condemn.
16277-new-discoveries-at-jamestown-site-:
John L. Cotter and J. Paul Hudson's New Discoveries at Jamestown, published in Washington in 1957 by the National Park Service, reports digging at America's first successful English settlement. Sold for fifty cents by the Superintendent of Documents, the booklet divides into exploration and daily life. Part one lists what the ground yielded: churches, mansions, row houses, single brick houses, frame houses, workshops, brick walks, drains, ice pits, kilns, ironworking pits, wells, ditches, and roads.

Part two rebuilds daily life three hundred years ago from recovered objects, from houses and hardware to windows, tiles, and fireplaces. Cotter and Hudson write for visitors as well as scholars, plain and vivid. The booklet remains a clear introduction to Jamestown archaeology.
16418-what-great-men-have-said-about-wom:
This cheap pocket booklet, Ten Cent Pocket Series No. 77, gathers what great men have said about women, opening with Shakespeare. Lines from Love's Labour's Lost, Much Ado About Nothing, The Taming of the Shrew, and Henry VIII praise beauty, kindness, and virtue, and later pages add more voices in the same vein.

The booklet is a scrapbook, not an argument, meant for quick reading and quotation. Its charm lies in the old lines themselves, picked for warmth and wit. Modern readers will find it a curious period piece, showing how an earlier age packaged praise of women for a mass audience.
1652-the-survivors-of-the-chancellor-dia:
Jules Verne's Survivors of the Chancellor is told as the diary of J. R. Kazallon, a passenger who leaves Charleston on September 27, 1869, aboard the Chancellor under Captain Huntly. From the Battery quay, with main and top sails set, the ship runs before a northerly breeze toward disaster.

Fire, wreck, and a long ordeal on a raft follow, as Kazallon records the crew's courage, quarrels, and suffering day by day. Verne's diary form gives the horror a plain, immediate force. The novel is a gripping sea tale of survival, and a classic of Verne's adventure manner.
16690-five-months-on-a-german-raider-bei:
F. G. Trayes wrote this 1919 tale of five months held on the German raider Wolf, issued by Headley Brothers in London. Trayes, once head of the Royal Normal College at Bangkok, was seized at sea as an Englishman and kept aboard the raider. He dedicates the book to Danish naval men, lighthouse keepers, lifeboat crews, and folk of Skagen who helped him home.

Trayes tells of life aboard a raider: cramped quarters, strange shipmates, and the slow wait for release. His tone stays grateful and plain, with praise for those who gave aid at the end. The book gives a rare, first-hand view of sea war from a captive's side, short, vivid, and free of grand claims.
17192-the-raven:
Edgar Allan Poe's The Raven appears here in the 1884 Harper edition, pictured by Gustave Dore with comment by Edmund C. Stedman. A weary student, mourning lost Lenore on a bleak December night, hears a visitor at his chamber door. The raven that enters answers every plea with one word, Nevermore, until grief turns to dread.

Dore's engravings track each stanza, from dying embers to the bird's shadow on the floor. Stedman's comment aids readers new to Poe's music and gloom. This handsome edition suits poetry lovers and Poe fans who want the classic poem with pictures worthy of its midnight mood.
17393-men-and-women:
Robert Browning's Men and Women, in the 1898 Crowell edition with notes by Charlotte Porter and Helen A. Clarke, gathers his great 1855 dramatic monologues. The set runs from Transcendentalism and How It Strikes a Contemporary through Karshish the Arab physician and Johannes Agricola. Pictor Ignotus, Fra Lippo Lippi, and Andrea del Sarto follow, with Bishop Blougram's Apology, Cleon, and One Word More to close.

Each poem lets a speaker plead, boast, or confess in vivid, rugged verse, from Renaissance painters to Arab doctors. Browning's range of voice and mind makes the book a landmark of Victorian poetry. Poetry lovers will find a rich, demanding volume, best read aloud, one monologue at a time.
17396-the-secret-garden:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's 1911 Secret Garden opens with Mary Lennox sent to Misselthwaite Manor after no one is left. Chapters follow Mistress Mary quite contrary, across the moor, Martha, and the cry in the corridor. The key of the garden, the robin who showed the way, Dickon, and the nest of the missel thrush follow, with a bit of earth begged for planting. Colin, the young rajah, joins her in the garden's magic.

Burnett writes in warm, plain prose, with Yorkshire speech and growing things at its heart. The locked garden's return to life mirrors two lonely children learning to live. Young readers and their elders will find a beloved classic of friendship, nature, and healing, still fresh after a century.
17568-the-arctic-queen:
This poem, dedicated to Dr. Elisha Kent Kane, commander of the Grinnell expedition in search of Sir John Franklin, honours Kane's enterprise, courage, and heroic self-devotion, and his success as discoverer of the open polar sea. The poem itself personifies the Arctic as a queen. Oene, of all the chilly Arctics queen, ascends to an everlasting throne built on the steadfast centre of the world.

She waits for the middle hour of night, swiftly coming, to begin her reign of ice and darkness. Readers get a mid-nineteenth-century verse tribute to polar exploration, written when Franklin's fate still stirred the public mind. The poem's grandeur suits readers of exploration literature and of period poetry.
17730-a-study-of-the-textile-art-in-its-:
William H. Holmes wrote this study for the Sixth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, printed at Washington in 1888. Holmes asks how weaving, basket work, and cloth arts shaped the forms and patterns of early American art, and how pattern grew out of the craft itself.

He moves from the shape of pots and trays to color, relief work, and net-like designs, showing how a weaver's loom forced straight lines and set patterns on clay and stone. Drawings of mats, trays, and water jars fill the pages. The study still matters for students of Native art, since it ties beauty to the tools and tasks that made it.
17785-divers-women:
Pansy, with Mrs. C. M. Livingston, wrote this book, Divers Women, published in London by George Routledge and Sons, with offices in Glasgow, Manchester, and New York. The volume stands sixth in the Pansy books, a series that also includes Four Girls at Chautauqua, Little Fishers and Their Nets, Three People, Echoing and Re-echoing, and Christie's Christmas.

Later Pansy titles include Spun from Fact, The Chautauqua Girls at Home, and The Pocket Measure. Readers get a popular Christian girls' book, in the earnest, domestic manner of the Pansy series. The book suits readers of Sunday school fiction and of Pansy's large following.
17797-memoir-of-jane-austen:
A family memoir of Jane Austen appears here in the 1871 Richard Bentley and Son edition, a second edition enlarged with additional matter. Its preface notes that the memoir was received with more favour than its writer had ventured to expect. Notices in the periodical press and letters from strangers showed an unabated interest in every particular that could be told about Austen.

Encouraged by that welcome, the writer offers the memoir again, fuller than before. Readers get the first full family portrait of Austen, the source for much of what followed about her life. The book suits Austen readers and biographers, as the foundation memoir of them all.
17860-stories-from-hans-andersen:
Fairy tales by Hans Andersen, retold here in English with pictures by Edmund Dulac, bring together some of his best-known stories in one small book. The London firm Hodder and Stoughton put it out. The tales come from a Danish writer whose stories were already loved far past his own land.

Among them are The Snow Queen, The Nightingale, The Real Princess, and The Garden of Paradise, each told in plain, vivid prose. A child who reads them meets proud queens, a plain brown bird whose song beats a gilt toy, and a girl who feels one small pea through a stack of soft beds. The tales still work as first tales for young readers, and as a short way into Andersen at his best.
18039-manual-of-the-mother-church-the-fi:
Mary Baker Eddy wrote the Manual of The Mother Church, the First Church of Christ, Scientist, in Boston, in an eighty-ninth edition printed by the trustees under her will. Eddy, founder of Christian Science, gives here the rules and by-laws that govern her church.

The rules, Eddy says, did not spring from solemn conclave or one person's whim, but from need, at many dates, as the work required. They guard the dignity and defense of the cause, in plain, careful terms. The book is the church's governing text, and a key source for students of Christian Science and its founder.
18196-life-and-public-services-of-john-q:
William H. Seward wrote this Life and Public Services of John Quincy Adams, sixth president of the United States, with a eulogy delivered before the New York legislature. The book traces Adams from ancestry and childhood through law, diplomacy, and the White House.

Chapters run from study at the Hague and Berlin, marriage, and treaties with Sweden and Prussia, to the Massachusetts Senate, the United States Senate, and the mission to Russia. Seward writes with a statesman's praise for a fellow public man. It is a full, old-style life of a great American, rich in period detail and political color.
18242-behind-the-arras-a-book-of-the-uns:
Bliss Carman wrote Behind the Arras, a book of the unseen, printed in Boston and New York in 1895 by Lamson, Wolffe, with designs by T. B. Meteyard. Carman, a Canadian poet of vision and music, here gives verse on what lies past the veil.

Poems run from Behind the Arras and Fancy's Fool to the moondial, the face in the stream, the cruise of the galleon, the red wolf, and the lodger. Carman writes with a mystic's eye and a singer's ear. It is a lovely, old book of symbolist verse, best for readers who like poems that hint at more than they say.
18275-the-rectory-children:
Mrs. Molesworth wrote this children's book, published by Macmillan in 1897 with pictures by Walter Crane. Its setting is a rectory home, and its chapters follow a household of children through small events that feel large to them. Titles include The Parlour Behind the Shop, Those Young Ladies, A Trying Child, and Biddy Has Some New Thoughts.

Later chapters bring Celestina, a window in the wall, a trip to the seashore, a secret, and Biddy's escapade. The book moves at a gentle pace, with talk, games, and mild scrapes rather than grand adventure. Young readers get a friendly picture of family life, manners, and the small courage of children sorting things out.
1829-mae-madden:
A dream of Italy opens this novel, in which two souls parted since before the stars were named meet again on heaven's outermost border. Mae herself enters as a girl of bright cheeks and restless quickening, seen by Norman Mann, who notes her eagerness and misses the beating heart inside.

The novel follows Mae through love and disappointment in a world of art and society, with Ben Jonson's lines on fortune's wheel as its motto. Mason writes in the high romantic manner of her day. The book's interest lies in its heroine: a young woman whose spirit outruns the men who try to read her.
18437-troublesome-comforts-a-story-for-c:
Geraldine Robertson Glasgow wrote this children's story for Thomas Nelson and Sons, published in London, Edinburgh, Dublin, and New York. The opening places Mrs. Beauchamp in a crowded third-class carriage at Liverpool Street Station, with children, parcels, a dog, and a bicycle in tow.

The title names the small comforts that turn troublesome on a family journey, and the comedy comes from tickets, luggage, and a nurse keeping count of five halves and two wholes. It is a light travel tale of a family on the move, told with patience for children and their grown-ups alike.
18558-the-good-shepherd-a-life-of-christ:
Published by Fleming H. Revell at New York, Chicago, and Toronto, this children's life of Christ tells the Gospel story in simple words with many pictures. Chapters run from why Jesus came to the world and his birth at Bethlehem through his boyhood, John the Baptist, and his works and words. Later chapters cover the man born blind, Lazarus, the prodigal son, and the last days in Jerusalem.

The book closes with the crucifixion and resurrection, plus a section of songs, psalms, and prayers. Maps of Palestine and views of Bethlehem, Nazareth, and the Sea of Galilee aid young readers. It serves as a gentle first Gospel book for children.
18652-the-tale-of-henrietta-hen:
Arthur Scott Bailey wrote this Slumber-Town Tale in 1921, with pictures by Harry L. Smith. Its heroine, Henrietta Hen, thinks herself a speckled beauty with the reddest comb in the world, though she has never left the farm. She clucks from dawn to dusk, boasts over worms she finds, and scolds her neighbors with great pride.

Chapters follow her fine family, wet feet, a swimmer she fears will drown, tricks, a garden visit, and a trip to the fair, where she wins first prize. Aunt Polly Woodchuck lends advice when trouble comes. Bailey keeps the humor warm and the chapters short, making it a fine bedtime tale.
1869-the-man-in-lower-ten:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's Man in Lower Ten, a railway mystery, opens with a narrator going to Pittsburgh, a torn telegram, and a woman in the next car. Numbers seven and nine, a girl in blue, and a fine gold chain all figure in a plot that moves from sleeping cars to a country house.

Rinehart, who would become famous for The Circular Staircase, writes here with the same gift for suspense and for a heroine who keeps her head. The novel's charm is its setting: the Pullman car as a small world, where strangers share berths and secrets. There, a torn scrap of paper can change a life.
1874-the-railway-children:
Bobbie, Peter, and Phyllis lose their father to a sudden arrest and move with their mother to a cottage near a railway line, which becomes their whole world. The children make the line their world: waving to trains, exploring cuttings, and befriending the old gentleman who rides past.

Peter's coal-mine, the engine-burglar, and prisoners and captives give the chapters their adventures, and the story builds toward the father's return. Nesbit writes childhood with rare honesty, and the book's fame rests on its mix of play and real worry, and on a family that holds together by kindness.
18810-alec-forbes-of-howglen:
George MacDonald's novel Alec Forbes of Howglen, in a new edition of about 1900, opens in a Scottish farmyard at summer noontide, desolately dreary in full sun. Not a creature stirs among cow-houses and stables, while inside the ben-end, the best room, silent men in black sit waiting.

A carpenter in shirt-sleeves appears at the door and offers any who wish to see the corpse their time, then climbs back to the upper room where it lies. A stonemason, a religious man more respected than liked for his rebukes, warns him not to jest in the face of death. The scene, told partly in Broad Scots with a glossary supplied, sets a stern farming world before Alec's own story begins.
18821-personal-recollections-of-birmingh:
E. Edwards gathered these sketches from the Birmingham Daily Mail, where they first appeared under the signature S. D. R., and issued them in revised book form in Birmingham in 1877. The earliest pieces were written entirely from memory. Later ones draw on facts and dates supplied by others, a shift Edwards notes frankly in his preface.

The sketches cover first impressions of the city, the Bull Ring riots of 1839, gossip about royalty, old and new banks, and portraits of local men of note. Together they give a street-level view of Victorian Birmingham, its trade, its crowds, and its leading figures. Readers interested in local history get anecdote and detail that a formal town history would leave out.
19126-raemaekers-cartoons-with-accompany:
Louis Raemaekers' cartoons, with notes by well-known English writers, were collected in this 1916 volume, with an appreciation from Prime Minister H. H. Asquith. Francis Stopford introduces the Dutch cartoonist whose wartime drawings gave form to the menace the Allies faced. The book is a work of Allied propaganda in art.

Asquith writes that Raemaekers shows enemies as a neutral sees them, strengthening resolve to accept no half peace, while German papers grant his power yet fault his wit. Readers get a powerful picture history of the First World War, where art served as a weapon for liberty and civilisation.
19157-a-mother-s-list-of-books-for-child:
Gertrude Weld Arnold compiled this 1909 list of books for children, aimed at mothers choosing reading for the home. She quotes over a library door that knowing good books is no small part of learning. Entries give author, title, publisher, price, and a short note on merit and age fit.

Caldecott's picture books earn praise for line, colour, and wit, from A Frog He Would a-Wooing Go to The House that Jack Built. Notes stress pictures that match each word with care. Parents get a thoughtful, old-style guide to children's books, still useful as a map of classic titles.
19199-the-friendships-of-women:
William Rounseville Alger wrote this 1868 book on the friendships of women, inscribed to Anna Cabot Lodge. While gathering matter for a history of friendship, he found women's bonds rich enough for a book of their own. He treats friendship as a gentle and becoming action of good women, in Shakespeare's phrase.

Pairs range from Beatrice Portinari and Giovanna to Hannah More and Mrs. Garrick, the Ladies of Llangollen, and Madame de Stael and Madame Recamier. Later chapters weigh marriage, public life, education, and the rights of women. Readers get a Victorian study of female friendship and woman's place, earnest and wide ranging.
1923-the-poisoned-pen:
Arthur B. Reeve, creator of the scientific detective Craig Kennedy, writes a thriller around a poisoned pen, where letters carry malice and murder. Kennedy and his friend Walter Jameson follow clues of chemistry and motive. Reeve's Craig Kennedy used science, from fingerprints to chemistry, to solve crimes.

Reeve mixes forensic detail with fast plotting, in the style that made his stories popular in magazines. The novel suits readers of early scientific detection, where lab work solves what eyes alone cannot. The poisoned pen plot, with letters as weapons, suits Kennedy's laboratory methods.
19259-his-heart-s-queen:
Georgie Sheldon wrote this 1890 popular romance, His Heart's Queen, published by Street and Smith and later by A. L. Burt. Chapters promise a frightful accident, a wilful Violet who has her own way, a prisoner, a broken will, and a wedding that fails on the day. The plot is pure melodrama, in Sheldon's well-known style.

A young carpenter and a girl are borne to Hughes Street after an accident, laid side by side as supposed siblings, while Mrs. Richardson returns to find her only son hurt and a strange, lovely girl beside him. Readers get a sentimental Victorian romance of love, will, and family claims.
19365-everlasting-pearl-one-of-china-s-w:
Anna Magdalena Johannsen, a missionary in China for sixteen years, wrote this life of a Chinese Christian woman known as Everlasting Pearl. Chapters follow her from birth and infancy through footbinding, childhood, engagement, and marriage to Mr. Lu, with a preface by Walter B. Sloan.

The heart of the book is Pearl's own account of faith: a troubled dream, a vow to repent, and a waking sense that her chains were gone. It offers a close, personal view of a Chinese woman's life and conversion at a time when few such stories reached western readers in her own voice.
19368-the-mide-wiwin-or-grand-medicine-s:
W. J. Hoffman wrote this study of the Midewiwin, or Grand Medicine Society, of the Ojibwa, with songs, music, and rites. It records lodge teachings, scrolls, and healing practices among Ojibwa people, with notes on spelling, music in lilypond and MIDI forms, and variant readings. The work belongs to early American ethnology.

A jongleur, or quack healer cured of a dangerous distemper, fancies himself immortal and able to cure all ills by speaking to spirits, dancing, howling like an owl, and rubbing the patient. Feasts of stag and trout follow. Readers get a detailed record of Ojibwa medicine lore, valuable yet framed by its era.
19408-the-amateur-garden:
George W. Cable wrote this 1914 book, The Amateur Garden, with pictures. Charles Scribner's Sons published it. Contents run from my own acre and the American garden to where to plant what. They run to cottage gardens of Northampton and the private garden's public value. They end with midwinter gardens of New Orleans. Barrie's elm and Felix Adler's hemlock grace his study picture.

Cable lays contour paths with rod, spirit level, hatchet, and stakes ten feet apart. He cuts and fills to disguise small rises. He brings sand, clay, and leaf mould up by barrow as each new path eases the next. A fire of his own acre's dead wood warms his writing. Readers get a charming, practical garden book on small ground well loved.
19541-marigold-garden:
Kate Greenaway wrote and pictured this book of rhymes for children, published in London and New York. Addressed to a little girl and a little boy with wondering eyes, it offers pictures and verses of mills, schools, and nursery life.

One rhyme has a boy begging to be taken to the mill to hear the wheel rush and see pretty water go round and round. Another counts five little girls on a form who fear they will not know their lessons when asked. Greenaway's art made the book a nursery classic.
19598-how-to-live-rules-for-healthful-li:
Irving Fisher and Eugene Lyman Fisk wrote this guide to healthful living, issued by the Life Extension Institute of New York. Its directors included William H. Taft and General W. C. Gorgas, and its aim was plain: prevent life waste and build national vitality through hygiene.

Tables of foods and their values sit beside rules for diet, air, and daily habits, from rice pudding to roast beef with tomato sauce. The book is a landmark of early public health advice, earnest, practical, and very much of the age that first preached prevention.
1960-sight-unseen:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's Sight Unseen is a ghost story told as a mystery, in which a medium's visions and a murder investigation cross. Rinehart, already famous for her detective novels, uses the supernatural as a clue rather than as a solution. The novel's tension lies in deciding what the visions mean.

The story follows a circle of friends, a house with a past, and a woman who sees what others cannot, with Rinehart's usual brisk plotting. Readers who like their ghosts with a detective's logic will enjoy the book, and its ending, which explains without explaining away, is one of Rinehart's cleverest.
1961-books-and-bookmen:
Andrew Lang's Books and Bookmen, published in 1887 and dedicated to Viscountess Wolseley, gathers essays on books, collectors, and reading. Lang opens with a verse address to his patroness, noting that it is no modish thing to love books. He then moves through parish registers, old bindings, and the habits of bookmen.

A register of St. Nicholas, Durham, from 1568, with its keeper entering events out of the common, shows Lang's method: small facts, lovingly noted, building into a picture of reading in past ages. The book is a delight for bibliophiles, and it shows Lang the essayist at his most companionable, gossiping about books as other men gossip about people.
19706-brood-of-the-witch-queen:
Sax Rohmer wrote this occult thriller, published in London in the late nineteen teens. Antony Ferrara, a sinister figure, haunts chapters on phantom hands, the ring of Thoth, beetles, bats, and the lair of spiders, while Dr. Cairn and his son Robert fight a malignant power.

Robert wakes to find his room lit by lurid light and his stern father standing over him with a knife, shaken by an emotion deeper than fear. Rohmer's tale of Egyptian magic in modern London is a classic of pulp horror, lush, strange, and fast.
19889-naughty-miss-bunny-a-story-for-lit:
Naughty Miss Bunny is a story for little children by Clara Mulholland. Miss Bunny longs to be jolly, her papa's word for happy. Grown voices keep telling her to sit still. They warn her not to dirty her pretty white frock. Big people, she thinks, can do what they like. Children must do everything they are told. Her dainty sash will not survive her plans.

Mulholland wrote many tales for Catholic children. A bunny in a frock lets her preach by laughter. The comedy turns on the gap between orders and urges. Every small reader knows that gap well. Illustrations carry much of the fun in such books. The story is a period nursery piece, gentle and sly.
20009-ixion-in-heaven:
Ixion in Heaven is Disraeli's satirical tale of a mortal guest on Olympus. Ixion, a wanderer, calls Jove his only friend at its opening. But for the porch of Jove's temple, this night would finish him, he says. His loving wife and dutiful subjects have ruined him below. Olympus receives him with divine politeness and godly gossip. The mythic Ixion loved Hera; Disraeli's loves society.

The tale first appeared inside The Young Duke in 1831. Its heaven is a London salon with thunderbolts. Gods intrigue, flirt, and talk politics like Regency beaux. Disraeli's classical satire is light but pointed. Earthly ambition looks sillier from Olympus, which is the joke. The piece shows his earliest manner at its most playful.
20052-we-ten:
Barbara Yechton published We Ten, also called The Story of the Roses, in 1896. Ten young people form the close group at the heart of the tale. When Felix cannot go to college, the rest feel his loss keenly. Six of them hold a council in the schoolroom that same day.

Felix bars the four youngest from that council, calling them mere kids. That small slight shows the group's ranks and bonds at once. The story follows friends who share joys, plans, and setbacks. Readers get a warm tale of youth, loyalty, and growing up together.
2012-the-children:
This 1911 volume of essays looks at childhood with a close, poetic eye, treating children not as small adults but as beings with their own logic. Pieces on midwinter, the fields, illness, letters, and the barren shore follow one theme. The essays appeared in 1911, when writers were turning fresh attention to child study and to nursery life.

The writer watches how a child speaks, plays, and sees the world, and finds in those moments a freshness adults lose. The prose is lyrical and reflective, suited to readers who enjoy essays that observe rather than instruct. Their poetic style asks readers to slow down and watch, rather than to sort children into types or lessons.
2015-a-miscellany-of-men:
G. K. Chesterton gathers short essays on types of people he met in Edwardian public life, from the suffragist and the voter to the poet, the miser, and the journalist. Each sketch uses one figure to argue a wider point about politics, faith, or habit. The essays first appeared as newspaper and magazine pieces, written for readers who followed politics and faith closely.

Chesterton writes with wit and paradox, turning a small scene into a defense of common sense or a jab at fashion. Readers who enjoy argument in essay form will find the pieces sharp, funny, and often contrary to the views of his day. Chesterton's targets include snobbery, party cant, and the habit of judging people by fashion instead of character.
20362-girls-and-women:
Girls and Women, from 1890, is a novel of a woman's narrowed life after school. A sensitive woman finds much that is mortifying in her position. All her Greek and Italian books lie packed away from use. She knows no more of science than when she left school.

At odd minutes she reads good novels, and that is all. Literature, for her, ends there, in scraps of stolen time. Novels of this era protest the waste of women's trained minds. Readers get a quiet, pointed tale of talent stifled by custom and home.
20469-ballads-of-romance-and-chivalry-po:
Ballads of Romance and Chivalry gathers popular ballads of the olden time: knights, ladies, quests, and brave deeds in verse. It belongs to a series that reprinted the old singing poetry of Britain. The editor chose pieces for story and swing, not for rarity alone.

In the preface, the editor jokes that there is no end of making selections of ballads. As a subject, they seem only less popular than Shakespeare, and every year brings a fresh output. He also warns against the new habit of confusing old ballads with modern imitations. The book keeps the true old strain apart.
2057-the-last-of-the-plainsmen:
Zane Grey tells the story of Buffalo Jones, the plainsman who gave up killing buffalo and spent ten years capturing them alive to save the species from extinction. Grey joined Jones on a 1907 hunt across the Arizona desert and the Grand Canyon country. Grey met Buffalo Jones in Arizona and travelled with him, so the book rests on firsthand talk.

Chapters follow the desert, the range, the last herd, and hunts for mustangs, cougars, and musk-ox, with Jones at the centre of each. Grey writes with awe for a vanishing West, and for a man who chose capture over the rifle. Jones's vow to save the buffalo, after years of hunting them, gives the narrative its moral turn.
20644-the-book-of-hallowe-en:
Ruth Edna Kelley's The Book of Hallowe'en traces the festival from pagan fires to American parties. It follows the night through Celts, Romans, and the church calendar. Charms, games, and ghost lore from many countries fill its chapters.

Ask a pagan of the old world for his greatest gods, the book begins, and the sun god would surely stand among them. A Greek would call him Apollo, an Egyptian Horus or Osiris, a Norseman Sol, and a Peruvian by another name. From such sun worship, Kelley builds the case for Halloween's deep roots.
20746-the-home-or-life-in-sweden:
June sun fills a large, cheerful room as The Home, or Life in Sweden, begins. A white damask cloth covers a long table set with a fine coffee service. A judge comes to breakfast with a troubled face that soon clears.

Domestic scenes carry this tale of Swedish home life in translation. Family talk, meals, and manners show a world both like and unlike the reader's own. Fredrika Bremer made home life a serious subject. Her work shaped the domestic novel across Europe and America. The book is a novel of home life in Sweden.
20753-the-wonder-island-boys-the-tribesm:
Two tribes clash in The Wonder Island Boys: The Tribesmen, a boys' adventure tale. A wagon serves as a fort as one side falls back to a stream shore. The beaten party takes cover behind it while the winners press the attack.

Castaway boys watch, learn, and step into island dangers as the tale moves. Invention, hunting, and native wars fill the Wonder Island set of books. Such tales fed boys' hunger for wild places and bold deeds. The plain, fast style keeps scenes short and clear, with a new scrape or wonder waiting in nearly every chapter.
20877-mother-west-wind-s-children:
Danny Meadow Mouse watches Mother West Wind's children, the Merry Little Breezes, at play. Thornton W. Burgess opens his 1911 tale by the Smiling Pool and Green Meadows. Sammy Jay, on a fence post, feigns a sun bath while plotting fresh mischief.

Burgess built a beloved world of talking beasts for young readers. Each tale slips in lore of real habits, haunts, and seasons. Peter Rabbit and his kin star across the long set of books. Mother West Wind's Children stands near the start of that world, warm, sly, and perfectly made for bedtime reading aloud.
21041-seen-and-unseen:
A father's last illness held no special mark for E. Katharine Bates, she writes in Seen and Unseen. Servants were banned from hinting that he lay in true danger. Nurse, brother, and godmother kept that grave watch in a hushed house.

Bates, a poet and traveller, turns from memoir to the unseen world of spirits. Ghosts, presentiments, and survival after death fill her grave inquiry here. She writes as a witness, not a scoffer, weighing tales with care. The book shows the keen interwar hunger for proof that love and mind outlast the body's brief, frail house.
21230-susan-a-story-for-children:
Amy Walton wrote this story for younger children, around eleven or twelve years old. Susan lives in London, but her ten-year-old brother is bedridden with a lasting illness. Doctors advise a warmer climate for the winter, so their mother takes him to Algiers.

Susan goes instead to her great-aunt at Ramsgate, a small seaside town in Kent. Other girls are staying there too, including Sophia Jane, Susan's age, whose behaviour seems difficult at first. The two girls learn to see each other better, and Susan learns she is not faultless herself. A French brother and sister add a second thread to the Ramsgate holiday.
21231-penelope-and-the-others-story-of-f:
Penelope Hawthorne sits in the schoolroom window at Easney Vicarage, planning gravely for her brothers and sisters, in Amy Walton's story of five country children. The book continues The Hawthorns, following the same household. Penelope, called Pennie, is famous for her plans, part from her own head and part from books.

New faces join the village world: eccentric Miss Barnicroft and poor Kettles from the cathedral city of Nearminster. Learned Dr Budge also joins, teaching one boy Latin and keeping a pet jackdaw.
