Fletcher and published by White and Allen in New York and London in 1889, comes in a limited edition of five hundred copies, this one numbered 485. Frank M. Gregory supplied the illustrations. Their captions hint at the tale's spirits: It Was the Devil as frontispiece, The Cellar of Bacchus, The Gentlemen of the Rhine, and To the Dance, to the Dance. 

A preface opens by recalling Carlyle's effort to bring Jean Paul Richter before English readers. It notes the differences of taste between English and German readers of that day. The tale itself belongs to Hauff's world of wine cellars, Rhine gentlemen, and dancing ghosts in Bremen. Readers get a short, atmospheric German fantasy in a handsome limited edition.
32137-the-men-of-the-moss-hags-being-a-h:
S. R. Crockett's romance, published by Macmillan in New York and London in 1895, presents itself as a history of adventure. It is taken from the papers of William Gordon of Earlston in Galloway, told over again by Crockett. He dedicated it to Andrew Lang, poet, romancer, and scholar. Crockett calls himself born of the hill-folk. His dedication honours men who fought bravely under the blue banner.

A prefatory note thanks his researchers. James Nicholson of Kirkcudbright examined local records on the period and persons. The Reverend John Anderson of Edinburgh University Library brought to light materials from the Earlstoun Papers and records of the United Societies, long thought lost. Letters from those papers appear in the book. Readers get a Scottish adventure romance with a documentary frame, where moss-hags, hill-folk, and old papers ground a tale of bravery.
32139-an-appeal-to-honour-and-justice-th:
Daniel Defoe's Appeal to Honour and Justice, Though It Be of His Worst Enemies, printed in London by J. Baker in 1715, is a true account of his conduct in public affairs. The British Library notes a first publication in 1715 and a reprint by D. A. Talboys at Oxford in 1841. Defoe fronts the pamphlet with Jeremiah's words: come and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words.

Defoe hopes that at last a calm middle voice may get a hearing. Hitherto, he writes, noise has been so great, and prejudices and passions so strong, that offering any argument or reason for his actions would have been in vain. Readers get a self-defence by one of England's first journalists, pleading moderation against enemies who would not listen.
3227-defenders-of-democracy-contribution:
The Gift Book Committee of the Militia of Mercy edited this wartime gift book. Its title names its cause: defenders of democracy, with contributions from representative men of the day. The volume belongs to the First World War years, when such books raised money and morale by gathering essays, addresses, and poems from public figures.

Readers get a chorus rather than a single voice: statesmen, soldiers, clergy, and writers speaking for the democratic cause in their own styles. The book now serves two purposes. It preserves wartime argument at its most earnest, and it shows how a nation at war asked its famous men to explain, in print, what the fighting was for.
32318-greek-women:
Mitchell Carroll's study, copyrighted in 1907 and 1908, examines the character and standing of women among the ancient Greeks. Carroll, professor of classical philology at George Washington University, argues that women's influence worked quietly yet shaped the character and fate of a people. Historians, he notes, often overlook that force even when it runs through literature, art, and religion.

Rather than stopping at dress, ornaments, and home surroundings, the book asks what Greek women were like and what place they held in society. It treats them as part of a wider civilisation famed for philosophy, poetry, oratory, and art. Readers get a survey that links daily life to the larger Greek achievement in thought and beauty.
32356-roman-women:
Alfred Brittain's study, volume two of Woman in All Ages and in All Countries, examines Roman women from legend through the empire. Published in Philadelphia in 1907, it opens with legendary Rome. One vivid example is Tullia, daughter of Servius, shown as a bad queen in contrast to a good one. An illustration after Hildebrand shows Tullia driving her chariot, by tradition, over her dead father's body after Lucius seizes the throne.

Brittain treats queens, wives, and common women side by side, asking how law, family, and public life shaped their roles. The book links household power to political power, showing women as instigators, supporters, and victims of Rome's great changes. It offers readers a broad survey of Roman social history told through women's lives.
32388-the-new-warden:
Mrs. David G. Ritchie's novel, first published in November 1918 and reprinted in March 1919, is set in Oxford at a moment of change. Its opening chapter, The Warden's Lodgings, looks back to the founders and benefactors who built the grey, sacred city. Then it turns to a new threat: an endless spread of red brick building pressing against Oxford's walls.

Fire and siege belonged to older dangers; the new age brings quiet, steady encroachment. Against that backdrop the story follows college life under a new warden, with tradition, learning, and town growth pulling in different directions. Ritchie writes with affection for Oxford's past and a sharp eye for its present pressures. The novel suits readers who enjoy academic settings, English social comedy, and portraits of institutions trying to hold their character.
32390-black-man-s-burden:
Mack Reynolds's novel, serialised in Analog in December 1961 and January 1962, opens in the Sahara, where a two-vehicle caravan reaches a small camp of Taitoq Tuareg in seven goat-leather tents. Moussa-ag-Amastan, headman of the clan, watches the strange dust pillars raised by air rotors with fear, half expecting spirits from the desert wastes. The visitors bring news of a wider Africa in turmoil.

Reynolds argues through his story that peace will not come while Africans see themselves mainly as warring tribesmen rather than as one people. The caravan's journey becomes a test of that idea, as clan loyalty, outside power, and hopes for unity collide. The book takes its title from Kipling's poem and turns that poem's burden back on its readers with a deliberately provocative question.
32418-oriental-women:
Edward B. Pollard's study, volume four of Woman in All Ages and in All Countries, examines oriental women, with marriage customs at its centre. An opening illustration after Cabanel shows Rebekah and Isaac's agent Eliezer, and Pollard calls their courtship one of the most romantic in ancient or modern story. Rebekah at the well and in her household, he writes, presents a unique picture of womanly grace and beauty.

Her courage in mounting a stranger's camel to travel to a far country for marriage stands out, even beside her gentleness. Pollard uses such scenes to show how courtship, wedding, and household life marked oriental societies. The volume offers readers a broad, illustrated survey of women's lives across the East, from biblical times through later eastern cultures.
32452-british-sports-for-the-amusement-o:
W. Belch's British Sports for the Amusement of Children, a sixpenny coloured children's book printed and sold in London at Newington Butts, presents country sports in short verses and pictures. Pheasant shooting opens the sequence, with the fowler taking aim in September, when birds are in full prime. Rabbit shooting follows, showing rabbits prancing without fear before a gunner's aim cuts their enjoyment short.

Badger baiting, horse racing, and other sports follow in the same pattern, each with a coloured illustration and a few rhymed lines. Belch sold the book alongside entertaining views, scenes from nature, birds, beasts, and an alphabet of nations, all at sixpence coloured. The little book offers a period picture of children's print, country life, and sports that modern readers will rightly view as cruel.
3256-books-and-bookmen:
Ian Maclaren opens this 1912 volume by defining his tribe. Books and bookmen cannot be separated, he says, any more than sheep and a shepherd. Yet he will speak of the bookman rather than his books, and he begins by clearing a confusion. A man is not a bookman merely because he owns many books, for he may be a bookseller or a collector of a different kind.

The essays that follow praise the reader who lives with books: the minister, the teacher, the friend who lends and talks. Maclaren, himself a beloved Scottish preacher-writer, writes with warmth about reading as a way of life. Books kept for company, not for show: Maclaren knows the difference at a glance, and teaches it by example.
32725-work-for-women:
George J. Manson answers practical questions for women seeking paid work, in this Putnam volume of 1883. His chapters grew from articles in the Christian Union in the winter of 1882-3, rewritten from new investigations. For each occupation he asks the same questions: can work be found, how long does training take, how many are in the trade, and what do they earn.

Chapters cover industrial designing, shorthand, telegraphy, feather curling, photography, professional nursing, proof-reading and bookbinding, the drama, book-agents, dress-making, millinery, and teaching. Manson notes one common obstacle: employers fear a trained woman will leave the trade to marry.
3303-prince-hagen:
Upton Sinclair mixes Norse myth with American money in this play. Gerald Isman, a poet, meets Mimi, a Nibelung, and Alberich, king of the Nibelungs, with Prince Hagen, his grandson, close behind. Mrs Isman and Hicks, a butler, hold the domestic side, while Mrs Bagley-Willis rules society. John Isman, a railroad magnate, Estelle, his daughter, and Plimpton, the coal baron, bring capital to the stage.

Rutherford, lord of steel, De Wiggleston Riggs, cotillon leader, and Lord Alderdyce complete the order. Myth and monopoly bargain together, and Hagen's ancient curse meets modern finance. Sinclair's fantasy argues, in comic form, that gold still rules men, whether it comes from the Rhine or from a railroad. The play is odd, ambitious, and unmistakably his.
33066-the-garden-of-eden:
Max Brand's Garden of Eden, copyrighted in 1922, opens with Ben Connor, a westerner in disguise. His broad shoulders are tailored to look fashionably slender and his deep chest is hidden by a stoop learned on Broadway between sunset and dawn. He wears spats, a glowing Scotch tweed, and a Panama hat, a city costume that fools no one for long.

Brand, a master of the western, uses Connor's disguise to set up a story of identity, romance, and frontier justice, where clothes, manners, and a quick hand all matter. The novel's title points to a place of innocence and temptation at once, and Brand keeps the action moving between town and open country. It remains a lively, well-plotted western for readers who enjoy a hero playing a part he cannot quite sustain.
33086-the-duchess-of-wrexe-her-decline-a:
Hugh Walpole's Duchess of Wrexe: Her Decline and Death, a romantic commentary published in New York in 1914, opens the Rising City sequence while standing complete and independent in itself. Walpole warns nervous readers that the book is grouped with two stories to follow under the heading of The Rising City. Connected in place, idea, and time with some shared characters, it is not a fragment waiting for a sequel. The duchess's story ends here.

The novel follows a powerful woman's decline and death in a rising city, where new wealth, new buildings, and old families collide. Walpole, author of Fortitude, writes with a keen eye for social climbing and for the pride that outlives power. It is a period novel of ambition and decay, and the first panel of a larger picture that Walpole promised to complete in the books that followed.
33265-woman-s-club-work-and-programs-or-:
Caroline French Benton's guide, copyrighted in 1913, offers first aid to club women, with work and programs for women's clubs. Benton, author of A Little Cook Book and Easy Entertaining, writes for women who ran clubs, planned meetings, and sought order in their busy civic lives. The book draws in part on articles that had appeared in the Woman's Home Companion.

Its chapters give practical help: how to plan a program, run a meeting, and keep a club lively through the year. The tone is clear and friendly, suited to club officers and members alike. For readers of women's history, the guide is a vivid record of the club movement at its height, when women built learning and friendship into organized civic life.
33273-lives-of-celebrated-women:
This volume of Lives of Celebrated Women, by the author of Peter Parley's Tales, gathers short lives of famous women for young readers. Published in Boston in 1844 and entered by S. G. Goodrich, it opens with Ferdinand and Isabella, the Spanish monarchs whose reign shaped a new age. Its preface promises lives that teach by example, in the plain, instructive style of the Peter Parley books.

The book suits readers who want history in brief, moral portraits, each life told as a lesson in courage, wisdom, or virtue. Its tone is earnest and old-fashioned, and its choice of subjects reflects the tastes of its time. For students of children's literature and women's history, it is a revealing window on how the 1840s taught girls about great women.
33423-a-man-in-the-open:
Roger Pocock's Man in the Open, copyrighted in 1912, follows a hero through Labrador, a happy ship, youth, an ordeal by torture, and a burning bush. Its second part moves to two ships at anchor, the Trevor accident, love, and a landlord, with further turns that test the man in the open air. Pocock, illustrated by M. Leone Bracker, writes of adventure in wild places.

The novel's appeal lies in its outdoor vigor, as its hero faces nature, foes, and his own heart in the far north and beyond. Its pace is brisk, its scenes vivid, and its tone hearty. For readers who enjoy adventure tales of the old school, A Man in the Open offers a lively story of a man proved by the open world.
33510-stories-for-helen:
Miss Eliza Leslie selected and revised four moral tales for young readers in this 1845 collection, drawn from her earlier Atlantic Tales. The advertisement states her hope plainly: that juvenile readers may find a little instruction blended with a little amusement. The stories are written for girls and set in homes, schools, and neighborhoods where small faults carry real consequences.

The opening tale follows Rosamond Evering, a girl who repeats everything she hears and exaggerates it, to her parents' distress. Further stories cover a boarding-school feast, a week of idleness, and Madeline Malcolm. Leslie's clear, direct prose makes the book a pleasant window onto nineteenth-century children's literature and its lessons in honesty, industry, and kindness.
33612-the-land-of-strong-men:
A. M. Chisholm writes a western novel of ranching, love, and conspiracy in this 1919 book, illustrated by Frank Tenney Johnson. Forty-seven chapters follow Angus from a deathbed and a lost-and-found beginning through assertions of himself, love and war, gains and losses, a hold-up, a race, a fight with a grizzly. Judge Riley, drunk and sober, the Frenches, old Sam Paul, Dorgan, and Faith Winton people the story.

Later chapters bring an auction, an unmasking, duplicate deeds, sudden death, outlaws, a trail, a red avenger, and a great show-down before peace. Chisholm balances ranch work, romance, and mystery, with cattle rounded up before heavy snows and driven to the ranch. Readers of classic westerns will enjoy its large cast, its action, and its strong, plain-spoken heroes.
33722-donalblane-of-darien:
J. Macdonald Oxley writes a boys' adventure of Scotland's Darien scheme in this 1902 Toronto book, illustrated by W. Rainey. The hero's unusual name promises a tale, and Oxley begins with a glance back to the close of the seventeenth century, when the remarkable Scotsman William Paterson rose to prominence in England. Twelve chapters follow Donalblane carrying his point, off to Darien, a rescue and retreat, across the Atlantic, a brush with buccaneers, and the founding of the city of Darien.

Later chapters add a successful embassy, perilous plight, the chase of the manatee, a midnight attack, and New York and home. Illustrations show a child placed on a chest, a liking for the sea, ravening swine, appalling eyes, and a harpoon raised in a bow. Oxley turns a tragic colonial venture into sturdy adventure for young readers.
33762-the-adventures-of-elizabeth-in-ru-:
The author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden recounts a walking tour of Rügen in this 1904 book, with a map of the island. Rügen, the biggest island Germany possesses, lies in the Baltic off Pomerania, and Elizabeth wished to walk around it that summer, though no one would walk with her. Walking, she argues, is the perfect way of moving if you want to see into the life of things, and the one way of freedom.

Eleven days of contents carry her from Miltzow to Lauterbach, Vilm, Göhren, Thiessow, Sellin, Binz, the Jagdschloss, the Granitz woods, Stubbenkammer, Glowe, Wiek, and Hiddensee, before she returns home. Driving binds a traveler to horses' legs, bicycling and motoring hurry past delicate wayside joys. The book is a witty, observant travel diary for walkers and lovers of the Baltic coast.
33787-rockhaven:
Charles Clark Munn writes a Maine coast romance in this 1902 Boston novel, illustrated by Frank T. Merrill. It is dedicated to all who despise hypocrisy, admire manly courage and womanly devotion, and respect simple faith. Forty-five chapters open on Rockhaven itself, introduce Winn Hardy, the Rockhaven Granite Company, Jess Hutton, and Mona Hutton. Forty-five chapters move through Sunday on Rockhaven, the hand of fate, a friendly hand, the Devil's Oven, and the parting of the ways.

Later chapters follow a matter of business, the growth of a bubble, a path of moonlight, fog, a cloud over Rockhaven, two rascals, the starting and progress of a corner, a climax. Munn balances coastal life, granite quarrying, speculation, and romance. Readers of regional fiction will enjoy its sea air and its moral steadiness.
33792-poems-of-emile-verhaeren:
Alma Strettell chose and turned into English these poems of Emile Verhaeren, published in London and New York in 1915. Verhaeren was born at Saint Amand, near Antwerp, in 1855, and grew up beside the Scheldt among flat Flemish fields, dykes, and marshes. His youth in that misty country left a lasting mark on his verse.

The poems range from village scenes, rain, snow, and bell-ringers to bright hours of love and joy. Strettell's notes present him as a leading voice of young Belgium, praised in France for lyric power. The book gives English readers a broad first path into a poet of landscape, feeling, and color.
33918-mr-punch-with-the-children:
J. A. Hammerton edited this volume of the Punch Library of Humour, gathering Mr. Punch with children in 175 pictures. Drawings by Phil May, George du Maurier, Charles Keene, John Leech, Gordon Browne, and other humorists show children at home, at play, and in mischief. Punch had run since 1841, and each library volume stands complete in itself.

The pictures favor the comic side of nursery life: tears, tantrums, and small triumphs, drawn with affection. Hammerton's set aimed to give the cream of national humor in handy form. The book still delights readers who love Victorian cartoon art.
33927-not-quite-eighteen:
Susan Coolidge, author of What Katy Did, published this set of short tales in Boston in 1894. The stories follow girls and young women who are not quite grown: a lucky bunny, a wilful girl, wolves at Saint Gervas, three little candles, and a pony that kept a store. Each tale turns on a small choice or a kind act.

Coolidge writes with warmth for young readers, praising courage, patience, and good humor without preaching at length. A blessing in disguise and a granted wish close the set. The book remains a gentle sample of the girls' stories that filled American shelves in the 1890s.
3398-my-first-visit-to-new-england-and-o:
William Dean Howells gathers New England memories in this volume from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. Its contents name a biographical sketch, my first visit to New England, and first impressions of literary New York. Long before he began the papers that make up the volume, Howells writes, he had meant to write of literary history in New England.

He meant to write it as he had known it in the lives of its great exemplars, during the twenty-five years he lived near them. The papers that follow keep that promise in part: visits, first meetings, and impressions, rather than a formal history. Readers get New England's literary age as one man lived it, neighbor to its makers and junior to most of them.
34025-ancient-rome-the-lives-of-great-me:
Mary Agnes Hamilton told the lives of great men of ancient Rome in this volume, published at Oxford in 1922 by the Clarendon Press. Lives run from Brutus and Tarquin, Lucretia, Mucius, and Cloelia through Regulus, Coriolanus, Pyrrhus, and Fabricius to Hamilcar, Hannibal, the Scipios, the Gracchi, Cato, Marius, Sulla, Pompeius, Crassus, Cicero, and Caesar.

Sections open with the people and city of Rome, then treat early heroes, great enemies, the Scipios, and the Gracchi. Hamilton writes for young readers in clear, lively prose. The book offers a classic introduction to Rome through its leading lives.
34107-the-curry-cook-s-assistant-or-curr:
Daniel Santiagoe's Curry Cook's Assistant, in its third London edition of 1889, teaches English cooks to make curries in their original style, as cooked in Ceylon and Madras. Santiagoe, son of a butler and fiddler of Colombo, had served at exhibitions at Liverpool and Glasgow.

The book opens with home-made curry powder, then gives plain receipts for beef, chicken, game, egg, and vegetable curries, with notes on heat, spice, and method. Its charm lies in its plain voice and its care for true flavour over show, a guide for cooks who want the dish as its makers knew it.
34135-a-book-lover-s-holidays-in-the-ope:
Theodore Roosevelt wrote this book of open-air holidays, published in New York in March 1916 by Charles Scribner's Sons, with pictures. A frontispiece from a painting by Theodore B. Pitman shows Roosevelt on the brink of the Grand Canyon. Roosevelt, author of Through the Brazilian Wilderness, African Game Trails, and The Rough Riders, turns here to reading and rambling outdoors.

The book joins a love of books with a love of the open, in the former president's vigorous voice. It serves readers who like nature writing with a literary bent. The volume offers Roosevelt at leisure, book in hand, under open sky.
34199-peeps-into-china-or-the-missionary:
Phillips's Peeps into China, or The Missionary's Children, was published by Cassell in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne. Phillips had written the Tropical Reading-Books and The Orphans. Leonard Graham, ten, and his sister Sybil, thirteen, learn in their rectory garden that the family is going to China. Their father is to be a missionary there, and the start is set three months off, in August. Leonard dreams of pigtails, splendid kites, sedan chairs, and tea growing.

Twelve chapters mix the children's voyage with instruction. The religions of China and Chinese childhood get full chapters of their own. Little Chu and Woo-Urh appear as Chinese playmates; Leonard has an exploit in Formosa. The boat population, Canton, a bride and bridegroom, and processions fill the later peeps. The story was written to teach English children about China through a family's move.
34403-the-clock-strikes-thirteen:
Mildred Wirt wrote The Clock Strikes Thirteen, a Penny Parker mystery copyrighted in 1942. Penny is the daughter of Anthony Parker, editor of the Riverview Star. The book stands in a long list of Penny Parker tales.

Penny walks through the dark newsroom after the last edition has gone to press. She plays a hold up joke on her father in his office. Chapters promise night riders, a black hood, a melon patch, and a disappearance. Penny's clue, false records, and a trap set drive the plot. The title's extra stroke of the clock marks the heart of the mystery.
35138-literature-for-children:
Orton Lowe, an assistant superintendent of schools in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, wrote this guide, published by Macmillan in 1922. Copyright dates from 1914, when the book was first set up and printed. Part one opens with the value of good books as its first chapter.

Books and literature in elementary schools and the learning of lyric poetry by heart follow there. Part two gives selections for memorizing, graded from the first year to the eighth in the contents. Part three turns to sources of standard prose for children, making a teacher's handbook for stocking young minds with verse and story worth keeping.
35154-a-hero-of-the-pen:
E Werner wrote this novel, turned into English by Frances A Shaw and issued by R Worthington in New York in 1880. Werner was known in English for Good Luck and Broken Chains. Chapter names such as Love and Death, The Heiress at Bay, The Dawn of War, and The Pen and the Sword show the mix of love and strife ahead. A strange cavalier and a strange presentiment set the plot in motion.

The scene is a town on the Mississippi, midway from Lake Itasca to the Gulf, on a clear January day in 1871. Twenty years before, the place held a dozen rough wooden houses; now it is a busy, thriving centre. Against that fast growth, rival lovers and a fateful hour work out the tale.
35186-a-round-dozen:
Susan Coolidge, author of What Katy Did, gathered twelve stories for children in this volume. Roberts Brothers published it at Boston, with copyright in 1883, and this printing is dated 1892. The first story, The Little White Door, opens in Switzerland. Coolidge asks her school readers what they know of the pink patch on the map, then paints the green valleys, blue lakes, and chalets under the snows.

The other tales run from Little Karen and Her Baby to Helen's Thanksgiving and At Fiesole. Queen Blossom, The Secret Door, and The Two Wishes bring in the fairy side of the collection. Toinette and the Elves has its heroine kneeling to see a tiny figure at her side. The book closes with Jean's Money, and What It Bought, and How the Storks Came and Went.
35224-sketches-in-canada-and-rambles-amo:
Anna Jameson published her Winter Studies and Summer Rambles in Canada in 1838, in three volumes. This 1852 Longman edition reprints the most amusing and interesting chapters as Sketches in Canada, and Rambles Among the Red Men.

Her preface jokes that nobody reads prefaces on a railway journey. The leaves are turned for something to arrest attention or fleet the time. Jameson had crossed the Atlantic to join a husband she barely knew, in a Toronto she came to dislike. The marriage failed; the book succeeded. Her summer rambles took her among the Ojibwe of Manitoulin Island, whose lives she recorded with unusual sympathy. The sketches remain a founding text of Canadian letters, written by a woman who looked at the colony with clear, disappointed, observant eyes.
35331-stories-of-great-men:
Stories of Great Men is a set of short lives by Faye Huntington. Lothrop of Boston held the rights in the year 1887 for the book. Huntington had writ Stories of Remarkable Women and Those Boys before. Twenty-six chapters run in letter order from Alexander to Xenophon. A front picture shows Alexander the Great at the head of the set.

Addison, Agassiz, Bacon, and Caesar fill the early alphabet of lives. Disraeli, Everett, Farragut, and Gordon stand in the next rank here. Hannibal, Irving, Judson, and Knox carry the middle of the book. Lincoln, Morse, Newton, Penn, and Rush take their turns in order. Savonarola, Tennyson, Webster, and Xenophon close the alphabet of great men. Alexander was son of King Philip of Macedonia, born at Pella. At thirteen he had one of the world's great men as teacher.
35387-e-mile-verhaeren:
Stefan Zweig wrote Emile Verhaeren, a life and study, for Constable at London in 1914. A photograph of the poet by Charles Bernier, never before printed, fronts it. Contents fall in three parts, opening with the new age and the new Belgium. Youth in Flanders, the first books, the monks, and a breakdown follow. A flight into the world closes the first part of the study.

Part two treats the tentacular towns, the multitude, and the rhythm of life. Verhaeren's poetic method and his drama get their chapters there. Part three turns to cosmic poetry and the lyric universe. The ethics of fervour, love, and the art of his life follow. Zweig closes with the European importance of the Belgian poet's work. The study gives a poet of steam, cities, and crowds in full stature.
35411-myra-s-well-a-tale-of-all-hallow-e:
George Francis Dawson's Myra's Well, a tale of All-Hallow-E'en in verse, was printed by Gibson Brothers at Washington in 1883. The poem opens on the night of all nights of the year, when ghosts and warlocks haunt the earth and spirits bring messages to those who would behold the future. Frosty moonlight bands a farm-house room hung with hams and bacon-flitches, its hearth cold and black, the only sound the tick-tack of the clock.

On the hill above, a lordly marble pile seems to vanish and return as clouds cross the moon. Inside sits young Sir Bertram Morven, alone, reading the Persian tale of the lover who knocked at the beloved's door. Dawson writes in rhymed couplets of a deliberate gothic cast, all rafters, moonlight, and eerie tones. The tale is a Halloween ghost poem of the gift-annual kind, built on atmosphere rather than incident.
35502-the-basket-woman-a-book-of-indian-:
Basket Woman is a book of Indian tales for children by Mary Austin, in a school edition. The book was copyrighted in nineteen oh four and again in nineteen ten. A photo of the Basket Woman serves as frontispiece. Fifteen tales fill the contents, and a pronouncing vocabulary closes the book.

Two tales bear the Basket Woman's own name at the head of the list. Others tell of a stream that ran away and a coyote spirit with a weaving woman. A cheerful glacier, a fire bringer, and a crooked fir take their turns. The first story opens at a homesteader's cabin in a moon shaped hollow. Land before it stretches away golden and dusky between hills and a high mesa.
35579-the-nation-s-peril-twelve-years-ex:
An exposé of the Ku Klux Klan, published at New York in 1872. Friends of the compiler issued the volume. E A Ireland entered the copyright that year. Its subtitle promises a complete exposition of the order. Purpose, plans, operations, and political significance all fall within the claim. A Boston lecture at Tremont Temple underlies the book.

A gentleman's diary supplies the core testimony. He had lived twelve years in the South. Official records add corroborating matter. The March 1872 lecture excited national correspondence. Readers demanded the facts in convenient form. Stories of outrage and crime fill the pages, claimed as authenticated. Exodus supplies the motto: redemption from bondage with a stretched-out arm. The book belongs to Reconstruction's paper war.
35631-a-letter-on-shakspere-s-authorship:
A Letter on Shakspere's Authorship of The Two Noble Kinsmen, by William Spalding, came out in a new edition at London in 1876. John Hill Burton added a life of Spalding to this edition. The New Shakspere Society published the work. Spalding had taught rhetoric at Edinburgh and logic at St Andrews. A foreword calls the letter one of the ablest pieces of Shakspere criticism ever read.

The letter asks what part Shakspere had in the play named. It also treats the marks of his style and the secret of his supremacy. Burton says even readers who reject the claim gain from the close reasoning. Drama as an art is weighed throughout. The essay shows Victorian scholars at work on a hard question of authorship.
35796-i-walked-in-arden:
Jack Crawford published the novel I Walked in Arden in New York in 1922. Edward Jevons, called Ted, tells his own story, and he warns at the start that no one can fix where a life truly begins. Born in New York City, he was taken to England at six and raised in London until he was eighteen, never seeing America in those years.

The contents trace his path back across the ocean. He sets out along a new trail, camps in the desert, and meets a man named Prospero. He enters Deep Harbor society, rides a horse called Satan, and plays a part in a melodrama. Later chapters bring a first Christmas shared, consent sought and won, an ordeal, and a sailing for home. An epilogue dated Christmas 1918 closes the book. Readers get a first-person tale of a young man split between two countries and one love.
36132-the-parent-s-assistant-or-stories-:
Maria Edgeworth wrote these tales for children, long a famed home school book. A new drawn form came out in London in 1903. Anne Ritchie adds a front note on the author and her work. Chris Hammond drew the plates for this printing.

Tales bear names like The Orphans, Lazy Lawrence, and Simple Susan. Each tale turns on a fault, a test, or a kind act. Plots teach care with keys, gifts, pets, and hard earned coin. The prose stays plain and warm, made for young readers at home. Parents were the first buyers, as the title itself makes clear.
3622-the-duke-s-children:
Anthony Trollope returns to the Palliser family in this novel, first serialized in 1879 and 1880 and published in book form in 1880. The book opens when the Duchess is dead, leaving the Duke of Omnium a widower with grown children. Lady Mary Palliser loves Francis Oliphant Tregear, a gentleman without fortune, while her brother Lord Gerald falls into further trouble.

The Duke must learn to be a father as well as a statesman, and his children must choose between duty, love, and money. Chapters follow meetings at Matching, a tavern called the Bobtailed Fox, and a major deposed from his place. The novel suits readers who have followed the Pallisers and want Trollope's late, tender view of family pride.
36267-when-were-our-gospels-written:
Charles Bradlaugh published 'When Were Our Gospels Written?' in 1867, and the Freethought Publishing Company issued the fourth edition at London in 1881, printed by Annie Besant and Bradlaugh. A prefatory note points readers to larger storehouses: the three volumes of 'Supernatural Religion' and the second part of the Freethinkers' Text-Book by Besant cover the same ground with exact references.

The pamphlet answers a work of the same title by Constantine Tischendorf, translated and commended by the Religious Tract Society. The society's own preface concedes the stakes: on the credibility of the four Gospels the whole of Christianity rests, as a building on its foundations. Bradlaugh proposes to examine the character of Tischendorf's advocacy, then the genuineness of the four Gospels as the society affirms it. He notes the pamphlet's proud record of printings in German, French, Dutch, Russian, and Italian before beginning.
36279-wood-and-garden:
Gertrude Jekyll wrote Wood and Garden as notes and thoughts, practical and critical, from a working amateur. A second edition came out in 1899, with seventy-one illustrations from photographs by the author. After a short opening chapter, the book moves month by month through the garden year.

January treats the beauty of woodland in winter, the nut-walk, thinning of overgrowth, and a nut nursery. February turns to ivy berries, colored leaves, pruning shrubs, and lilacs. March brings flowering bulbs, the rock garden, heaths, and the pruning of roses. April follows with daffodils in the copse, grape hyacinths, flowering shrubs, and the sweet scents of the month. Jekyll writes as someone who works her own ground and watches it closely.
36321-misrepresentative-men:
Harry Graham's Misrepresentative Men, published by Fox, Duffield at New York in 1905, gives comic lives in verse. Graham wrote under the name Colonel Streamer, had earlier made Ruthless Rhymes for Heartless Homes, and Strothmann drew the illustrations. The foreword boasts that great biographers succeed by imagination and a total disregard for fact. Graham claims he can tell what great men did not do. His subjects run from Theodore Roosevelt through Bacon, Adam, and Joan of Arc.

Paderewski, William Tell, Diogenes, Thomas Lipton, Marat, Ananias, and Nero complete the gallery, and an aftword and a postlude close the book. The dedication verses lay the rhymes at an unnamed lady's feet and beg kind treatment from the critics. The frontispiece shows Diogenes in what is called the altogether. Each life is a short burst of rhymed nonsense biography, and the poems treat presidents and emperors with the same cheerful disrespect.
36330-a-word-to-women:
Word to Women is a book of essays by Mrs Humphry, Madge of Truth. James Bowden of London issued the volume in eighteen ninety eight. Mrs Humphry also wrote Manners for Women and Manners for Men books. Those sister volumes sold by the tens of thousands at one shilling.

Essays treat mother and daughter, our school girls, and what about sewing. Mothers and sons, clever children, and ultra tidiness follow in the list. Good manners at home, candour, golden silence, and our debts come next. The domestic girl, the girl bachelor, and growing old close the set. Her first essay praises the golden mean between narrowness and latitude.
36333-little-erik-of-sweden:
Madeline Brandeis wrote Little Erik of Sweden, a story book for children printed in New York in 1938. Grosset and Dunlap issued it with photographs in place of drawings. The front pages name the children who posed for the pictures, with Carsten Grande as Erik, a boy who plays the piano and sings like the hero of the tale.

Erik's friend Nils and his sister Greta appear in the cast list too. Swedish words run through the text, set apart so young readers can spot them. A view of Stockholm opens the book. Children in America get a friendly look at how a boy lives in Sweden, told as a story and shown in real photos of the places and the people.
36431-the-palace-in-the-garden:
Mrs Molesworth wrote this children's novel, published in London in 1887. Three children, Gussie, Tib, and Gerald, are summoned down to grandpapa's study one morning while they watch for the first primrose man of the year.

The narrator is Gussie, who argues with her siblings about how to begin and settles on telling it her own way. The contents promise a scored-out name, a door in the garden wall, what Gerald found, and a fairy of their own. Later chapters bring three starlings and the story of the old house. Molesworth, author of Carrots, writes in a warm household voice, with mystery kept gentle for young readers.
36458-mentally-defective-children:
Alfred Binet and Th Simon wrote a study of children who learn with great trouble. W B Drummond turned the work into English for Edward Arnold in London. An opening note in the book is dated July 1914. An added part holds the Binet-Simon tests of mind by Margaret Drummond. The old terms in the title reflect the time, not current use.

Chapters set out how to spot such children in school and how to test them. Teachers, school heads, and doctors each get a clear role. Tests cover reading, sums, spelling, and thought. The book shaped early views on special schooling, though its terms and views are now dated.
36497-the-happy-hypocrite-a-fairy-tale-f:
Max Beerbohm wrote The Happy Hypocrite, a fairy tale for tired men, first issued in April 1897. Lord George Hell, who revelled with the Regent, is called half again as wicked as any of that set. He is greedy and disobedient, sits up late at Carlton House, and eats and drinks too much. At thirty-five he is a great grief to his parents.

Worst of all, he hides none of it, and seems proud of being horrid. Beerbohm argues that candour is good only when it shows good acts. Lord George at last atones for his faults in a strange, hidden way. His sudden exit from society is explained in secret. Readers are asked to judge him anew once the full tale is told.
36519-the-childhood-of-distinguished-wom:
The Childhood of Distinguished Women, by Selina Bower, author of From Advent to Advent, was published in London by Jarrold and Sons. Bower writes from Ringland Vicarage, Norwich, and her plates show Windsor Castle, the Tower of London, Greenwich Hospital, and Norwich Cathedral. The book opens with the Princess Alice, second daughter and third child of Queen Victoria and the Prince Consort.

Alice, born on April 25, 1843, had lately died, and Bower writes in fresh sorrow at her loss. The sketch gives her christening on June 2, with the King of Hanover among the sponsors, and quotes the Queen's letters on her names, Alice, Maud, and Mary. The child is shown quick at lessons, sweet in temper, and a companion to her father in mind beyond her years. Bower's plan is to show great women first as children.
3655-the-parent-s-assistant-or-stories-f:
Maria Edgeworth writes stories for children in this collection, first framed by a preface addressed to parents. Edgeworth quotes Pope, that education forms the common mind just as the twig is bent, the tree's inclined. She argues that the grand difficulty in education is to ascertain facts about how children actually learn. Her stories test that idea in practice.

The tales follow children through small moral trials: truth telling, generosity, industry, and obedience, with consequences shown rather than preached. Edgeworth, a leading Irish educator, wrote for the nursery and the schoolroom alike. The book suits parents and teachers who want early children's fiction with a clear, humane purpose.
36582-advice-to-sunday-school-children:
Advice to Sunday School Children is a religious tract issued by the New-York Religious Tract Society. It was sold at the society's depository at 142 Broadway, New York, as number fifteen of its second series. Fanshaw printed the little pamphlet.

The advice opens with a direct address: my dear children. When the Saviour was on earth, it reminds them, little children were brought to him, and he took them in his arms and blessed them. The tract then presses the lesson home in the manner of its time. The children have been taught, it says, that they are all sinners, and that God will punish the wicked after death in a dreadful place. Jesus Christ, nailed to the cross, died to save little children who come to him. He will bless them while they live and take their souls to heaven when they die.
36674-in-god-s-garden-stories-of-the-sai:
In God's Garden tells stories of the saints for little children. Amy Steedman wrote it, with sixteen pictures from Italian masterpieces. Jack of London published it for young readers and their parents. Steedman dedicates the book to her mother on its front pages. A preface called About This Book sets the garden figure at work.

God has planted a garden for Himself, fairer than any earthly garden. Its flowers are the white souls of His saints in that sweet figure. Some saints stand tall and stately like lilies in white and gold. Some hide like violets, known by the fragrance of kind deeds alone. Tales that follow give those hidden and famed lives to children.
36772-the-hearts-of-men:
Fielding published The Hearts of Men with Macmillan at New York in 1901. His earlier book The Soul of a People heads the title page in full. A dedication thanks Foster, whose urging brought the latter part into being. Thirty-two chapters in two parts weigh religion from every side in turn.

Opening pages stack rival definitions of religion from scholars and poets alike. Spencer, Kant, Arnold, and others give their lines before Fielding adds his own. Chapters then ask what use religion is, whence faiths come, and what God, law, and heaven mean. Creed and instinct, prayer, miracle, art, and life after death fill part two. A Burma seasoned mind tests faith against fact with calm persistence.
36833-the-camp-fire-girls-at-onoway-hous:
Hildegard Frey wrote a tale of Camp Fire Girls at a house called Onoway. The book came out in New York in 1916. Frey wrote of the girls in Maine woods and at school. Gladys drives a car at full speed after a bull in a plate. Migwan and Hinpoha stand at a pane in the first page.

A calm, glad summer is their hope as they view the yard. Rows of young green things fill that yard in neat lines. The magic garden of the sub-title waits in that green ground. Car trips, camp work, and friend tests fill the girls' days. Each girl learns by tasks done in the open air. Young readers get Frey's warm set once more.
36872-making-a-rose-garden:
Making a Rose Garden is one of the House and Garden Making Books, a set of small handbooks for home makers and amateur gardeners. Companion books treat lawns, tennis courts, fireplaces, roads and paths, poultry houses, rock gardens, and water gardens. A photo shows an English rose garden with grass paths.

The set aims to make clear, in text, pictures, and diagrams, how to have the chief features of a modern country or suburban home. The rose book notes that most botanists count more than a hundred species of the rose kind. A French botanist lists and describes 4,266 kinds from Europe and western Asia alone. From that mass the book guides the choice of plants, beds, and care. Home gardeners get a short, clear path to a rose plot of their own.
37068-successward-a-young-man-s-book-for:
Edward Bok published Successward in 1895 as a book of advice for young men starting out in life. Bok wrote it while he was still young himself. As he says in his preface, the fight for success was not a memory for him but a daily fact. He aimed the book at young men who wrongly thought success was a gift held by the rich and the lucky few.

Nine chapters take up self-knowledge, the true meaning of success, business, social life, dress, religious life, women, and marriage. The first chapter argues that a young man must study his own nature and powers before he tries anything, since no two men are made alike. Readers get plain, direct counsel from a writer close to their own stage of life.
37165-games-without-music-for-children:
Lois Bates, a kindergarten writer known for a Kindergarten Guide and books of recitations and guessing games, published this set of games without music in eighteen ninety seven. Longmans, Green issued it in London and New York. The games need no piano and no singing. Each one turns a small piece of daily life into acted play for a schoolroom of infants.

The first part holds thirty seven schoolroom games. Children lay the breakfast table, weigh, measure, shop, tie a bow, take father's tea, and visit grandmamma. A second part moves outdoors with ball games, Puss in the Corner, and Wolf and Sheep. The book ends with guessing rhymes grouped by subject: household objects, animals, flowers, the seasons, and favorite nursery tales. Bates wrote for teachers who needed orderly, cheerful occupation for very young classes.
37180-penelope-brandling-a-tale-of-the-w:
Vernon Lee wrote Penelope Brandling, a tale of the Welsh coast in the eighteenth century, published at London in 1903. She dedicates the story of northern wreckers to Augustine Bulteau, in return for a piece of Parian marble picked up in Mediterranean surf. The tale is framed as a memoir dated May 15, 1822.

Sophia Penelope Brandling, widow of Sir Eustace Brandling of St Salvat's Castle in Glamorgan, writes at her sons' wish. Knowing how soon oral tradition blurs, she sets down the circumstances that cast her family's lot in foreign parts and remote colonies instead of its ancestral home. Readers get a wrecking-coast romance told as an old woman's testimony.
37310-the-blue-grass-seminary-girls-on-t:
Carolyn Judson Burnett sends her schoolgirls to sea in The Blue Grass Seminary Girls on the Water, from A L Burt of New York, copyrighted in 1916. The subtitle promises exciting adventures on a summer cruise through the Panama Canal. Burnett had already written the girls' vacation adventures, mountain trip, and Christmas holidays.

The tale opens on the Willing farmhouse porch in Kentucky, where Shirley Willing begs her father for a trip. Her chum Mabel Ashton joins in, but neither girl can say where they want to go. Both fathers then surprise them: this time the dads are coming along.
37927-the-boy-volunteers-with-the-french:
The Boy Volunteers with the French Airmen is a war adventure for boys by Kenneth Ward, copyrighted in 1917. Its heroes, Ralph and Alfred, have already marched through Belgium with the retreating army. The story opens at Antwerp, where rumour of attack fills the streets and a Zeppelin hangs in the west.

The sight of the airship plants one wish in both boys: a trip in a flying machine. Stranded without Ralph's father, who is held in Germany, they live on army kindness while they aim at a flying corps. The chapters ahead take them into an aviation camp and on to the trenches with the British. Lessons about the aeroplane sit beside a thrilling flight in a storm. A fight and landing in Belgium, a bomb raid to the Rhine, and a terrible fight in the clouds close the list.
38003-color-key-to-north-american-birds-:
Frank Chapman, curator of ornithology in the American Museum of Natural History, wrote the 'Color Key to North American Birds' as a working guide for naming birds by their colours. The front pages list Chapman's earlier bird books, among them a handbook of birds of eastern North America and 'Bird-Life,' a guide to common birds with coloured plates by Ernest Thompson Seton. A bibliographical appendix backs the key, as the full title promises.

Chapman's other listed works show his range: bird studies with a camera, the warblers of North America, and camps and cruises from eight years of travel. He covered over 60,000 miles gathering material for museum groups of American birds. The color key itself serves the same aim in pocket form, letting a watcher match a bird's colours to its name.
38100-ancient-faiths-and-modern-a-disser:
Ancient Faiths and Modern is a study of old worship by Thomas Inman, a Liverpool doctor, printed in 1876. Its full title calls it a talk on worships, legends, and gods in Central and Western Asia, Europe, and elsewhere before the Christian era. Inman had earlier written Ancient Faiths Embodied in Ancient Names.

Inman says the study grew from years of thought that began in his medical work. He links old rites and signs to customs of faith still alive in his own day. The book is given to readers who thirst after knowledge and are not held back by fear of fancied dangers.
38128-memoirs-of-leonora-christina-daugh:
Leonora Christina, a king's girl of Denmark, left her own stark memoirs. Her sire was Christian the Fourth of that north crown. The book's own spell forms stand as first writ in this text. Many notes, set at page feet and at the back, aid the tale. Plates from the first press run aid this form as well.

Her life ran through court pride, a fall, and long jail years. A king's girl held in a tower is the grim core men know. Her own hand tells what she bore and how she held her soul. Such a voice from a cell has few mates in all past books. North past fans get a rare, first hand tale. Each page bears weight.
38189-a-treatise-on-sheep-the-best-means:
Ambrose Blacklock wrote A Treatise on Sheep, here in a twelfth edition printed in London in 1853. The full title promises the best means for their improvement, their general management, and the treatment of their diseases. A Swedish proverb on the title page says sheep have golden feet and turn the soil to gold where they tread.

A chapter on wool and the history of the wool trade widens the book beyond the farm. Another section treats the management of sheep in Australia, where flocks were remaking a colony. Blacklock dedicates the work to a Dumfries-shire landlord praised for zeal in improving the soil. Plates show the breeds and their points. The book served shepherds, farmers, and landlords who saw wool as wealth. Twelve editions say the advice was used.
38353-elsie-s-widowhood-a-sequel-to-elsi:
Martha Finley wrote this sequel to Elsie's Children, published by Dodd, Mead and Company at New York under an 1880 copyright. A motto from Holmes heads it: alone she wanders where with him she trod, no arm to stay her, but she leans on God. Twenty-five chapters carry Elsie Travilla through her bereavement.

Finley's preface confesses it was not in her heart to give her favorite child the sorrows of widowhood. But the public made the title and demanded the book, and the public is autocratic. She aims to show how the love of Christ can make life happy even under sore bereavement. Chapter one finds Violet, called Vi, stepping into her mother's dressing-room to find her sister Elsie seated on a cushion at their mamma's feet, face half hidden in her lap. Tears tremble in her soft brown eyes while mamma's hand caresses her hair.
38730-the-moral-instruction-of-children: The Moral Instruction of Children belongs to the International Education Series, a set of volumes meant to give teachers an orderly course of reading and training. The series was edited by William Harris, the United States Commissioner of Education, who added introductions and commentary. Neighbouring volumes cover Froebel and the mind of the child. This volume takes up how children should be taught right and wrong.
38992-black-tales-for-white-children:
Black Tales for White Children is a set of Swahili stories, translated and arranged by Captain Stigand and his wife. Houghton Mifflin published the book at Boston and New York in 1914, with pictures by John Hargrave. The preface explains who the Swahili are, a coast people born of Arab and Persian settlers mixing with the peoples of the interior.

The tales were never written down before. Storytellers in the coast towns told them, and mothers told them to children at night, passing them mouth to mouth for hundreds of years. The Stigands heard them in towns, on the march, and round camp fires, and wrote them as nearly as told. The book preserves an oral tradition for young English readers.
39012-famous-american-statesmen:
Famous American Statesmen is a book of short lives by Sarah Bolton, published by Crowell in New York in 1888. Bolton also wrote Poor Boys Who Became Famous and Girls Who Became Famous. A saying of John Bigelow fronts the book: a nation has no possessions so valuable as its great men, living or dead.

The lives run through the founders and the great senators and secretaries of the republic. Bolton wrote for young readers, telling each man's rise in plain and admiring terms. Such collective lives taught history as character. Her famous-men books were school and Sunday prizes across America for a generation.
39060-wild-oats-or-the-strolling-gentlem:
John O'Keeffe wrote Wild Oats, a comedy in five acts, played at the Theatre Royal in Covent Garden. Longman printed the play in London from the prompt book, by leave of the managers. A plate shows Lady Amaranth in a sharp scene. Inchbald adds remarks at the front.

Inchbald opens with respect for the author's gifts and his sad lot. O'Keeffe wrote blind, she says, and never saw the marks his pen made. His days passed with no sight of sun or any thing he could see. Yet his mind stayed strong, lit by fancy, and his new kind of mirth made the town laugh. She calls this play his one try at a drama above opera and farce.
39207-tales-for-fifteen:
James Fenimore Cooper wrote these two tales in 1823, under the name Jane Morgan. The book here is a 1959 facsimile reprint, made from a copy at Yale, with a new opening essay by James Franklin Beard of Clark University. Cooper was not yet the famed author of the Leatherstocking tales.

The first edition came from Charles Wiley of New York in June 1823. Its preface says the author hoped the short tales might do some moral good. The set, Tales for Fifteen, takes its name from the price or the short span of each tale. Scholars prize it as rare early work by a major American writer, caught before fame.
39210-the-ice-queen:
The Ice Queen is an adventure tale by Ernest Ingersoll for young readers. Harper and Brothers entered the rights in the year 1884 at Washington. Ingersoll had writ Friends Worth Knowing and Knocking Round the Rockies. Twenty-seven chapters run from children thrown on their own to a rescue. A front picture shows Jim landing at least one good blow.

Aleck, a brass foundry hand of eighteen, leads his sister Kate out skating. Their young brother, called the Youngster, joins the long lake trip. Fitting out the Red Erik and a log cabin camp fill the start. Norse tales, skating by compass, and an ugly ferriage come next. Snowed under, saved from starvation, and Arctic visitors crowd the middle. Adrift on an ice raft and a night in an open boat follow. Wild dogs attack more than once in the late chapters of peril.
39339-superwomen:
Albert Payson Terhune wrote Superwomen, printed at Cleveland in 1916. Moffat, Yard held the rights, in a line of international fiction. Terhune writes from Sunnybank, Pompton Lakes, New Jersey, that year. Twelve lives make the contents, each a famed woman of history. Lola Montez, the dancer who kicked over a throne, opens the set.

Ninon de l'Enclos, Peg Woffington, and Helen of Troy follow her. Madame Jumel, Adrienne Lecouvreur, and Cleopatra fill the middle. George Sand, Madame du Barry, and Lady Blessington come next. Madame Recamier and Lady Hamilton close the dozen lives. The Montez life opens at a London theatre in 1843, jammed from pit to roof. Manager Lumley had whispered that he had a find, Terhune writes. That whisper pierced clubs, boudoirs, and counting-rooms across the town. Terhune gives bold women in brisk, fond sketches.
39401-the-frontiersmen:
Gustave Aimard's Frontiersmen is a novel of western New York in 1783. The Lupton Publishing Company issued it in New York. Tryon County was then an almost unbroken wilderness. A few pioneers had cut log huts from the forest. Others roved alone with no companion but a rifle. The county was inhabited by roving bands of the Six Nations, mostly Oneidas in the tract the story uses.

Aimard's introduction recalls how the confederacy split during the Revolution. The Oneidas, and part of the Tuscaroras and Mohawks, adhered to the Colonies. The other nations were leagued with England under Colonel Butler and Johnson. A traveller in that wilderness might stumble on a settler's clearing and trade news for welcome. The narrative promises acquaintance with that portion of Tryon County in due course.
39605-hand-book-for-horsewomen:
De Bussigny's Hand-Book for Horsewomen was published by Appleton at New York in 1884. The author was formerly a lieutenant of cavalry and instructor of riding in the French army. His preface sets the two styles against each other: the English method, born of field sports, and the continental school system, nursery of cavalry. Each side sneers at the other, as pedants or as barbarians, and both seem unreasonable to the unprejudiced.

English riders leave their horses much alone if they can gallop and jump, keeping an even pressure on the bit. The school masters the hind legs, the propelling power and seat of resistance, balancing leg and spur against hand and bit until the horse stands in equilibrium. So horses are made to passage, piaffer, or even trot backward. The handbook teaches ladies the school system in full.
39634-sketches-of-successful-new-hampshi:
Sketches of Successful New Hampshire Men gathers steel portraits and short lives, published by John B Clarke at Manchester in 1882. The publisher's preface counts eighty-eight men whose success in their callings made them stand out in the professional, business, and political world. Clarke hopes the book is the first of a series covering the state's prominent men.

He argues that a state's glory centers in its great men and noble women, whose lives should be known to all who care for her fame. The sketches stand in the order they were furnished. State pride fills the volume.
39659-ethnology-of-the-ungava-district-h:
Lucius Turner spent years at Fort Chimo collecting the life of the Ungava Inuit for the Smithsonian. This ethnology report, the eleventh of its annual set, is his monument. Ungava then lay in the Northwest Territories, at Hudson Bay's far shore.

Turner lived among the people he describes, through winters that broke other men. Tools, houses, dress, tales, and tongues fill his record. Word lists stand at its back, for scholars of the language. The plain text form of the book carries notes on its own making: marks for long and short vowels, and signs unpacked for plain readers. A founding record of the eastern Arctic, written from inside its cold.
39681-the-corner-of-harley-street-being-:
Corner of Harley Street presents the familiar correspondence of Peter Harding, a doctor. The book was issued at Boston and New York in nineteen thirteen. Its contents list letters by their writers' names, addresses, and dates. The doctor writes from his London street to kin and friends across the country and beyond.

One letter goes to a surgeon in Devon, dated in March. Others reach a brother at Cambridge, a colonel in India, and a friend at Mentone. A sister at an orphanage in Dorset and a son at Rugby both receive letters. The first letter in the text answers one that rose to the top of the pile on his breakfast table. He read it only later, before his dressing room fire, he says, and writes back in a warm, easy tone.
39851-victorian-literature-sixty-years-o:
Victorian Literature, sixty years of books and bookmen, is a survey by Clement Shorter, issued at London in 1897. A Whitman verse stands at the front, on births bringing richness and variety to each age. Shorter opens by telling how the book came to be. A kindly publisher asked him to add one more volume to those marking the sixtieth year of the Queen's reign.

He was pleased at the chance, he says, to gather up a few impressions of pleasant reading hours. A line from Emerson guides the survey: every age must write its own books, and the books of an older period will not fit a new one. Shorter then walks through the writing of the Victorian years as a reader who lived among its books and their makers.
40040-flowers-shown-to-the-children:
Flowers Shown to the Children is a nature book for young readers, with pictures by Janet Harvey Kelman and descriptions by Smith. Jack of London and Edinburgh published it in the Shown to the Children series. Forty-eight coloured plates show 150 flowers.

The opening letter speaks straight to children. Old flower books, it says, often left their pictures uncoloured, so the flowers were hard to know again outdoors. This book gives coloured pictures where the flowers look like real flowers. The first plate groups the lesser celandine, two buttercups, and the marsh marigold. Companion volumes in the series cover beasts and birds on the same plan. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
40137-the-red-white-and-green:
Herbert Hayens wrote a boys' war tale of a flag of three hues. The book came out in 1901 with Nelson of London. Hayens wrote A Captain of Irregulars and A Vanished Nation. Plates show white coats as they pour a volley in at page 190. A sword shakes at a foe in flight at page 364.

Will the corps march leads the list of parts in this tale. A lad of the right sort and a land in full rise come next. Vienna burns, a jail takes the lad, and Pesth sees hard work. A fight in the hills and more war steps fill the mid arc. Young past fans get a bold, fast school tale. Guns and grit rule it.
40156-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
One stretch of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs here from Ichthyology to Independence, through the long I range of the alphabet. The Britannica eleventh edition came out in 1910 and 1911 and set the high mark for general reference in English. Its articles were written by named experts and run deep.

Ichthyology opens the slice, drawn from Greek words for fish and for a treatise, as the branch of zoology that treats the build and life of fishes. Idealism, Illinois, and Imam stand among the heads the transcriber notes name. The notes record small print fixes, as longitudinal set right and United set right in the Illinois article. Keying rules explain marks for roots, Greek letters, and raised figures. Reference fans get a deep cut through one letter of a landmark set.
40264-regiment-of-women:
Clemence Dane wrote a novel set in a girls' school, first issued in 1917 and reprinted in 1922. The title plays on John Knox's old blast against the rule of women. Its first scene shows a school secretary, Henrietta Vigers, hunting for a pupil whose mother has rung up.

Miss Hartill, the mistress in charge, waits at her raised desk with hands folded and a patient, sharp air. The room holds a fish bowl, trays of silkworms, and rows of inky desks. Dane builds her tale from such school staff and their hold on the girls in their charge. The book drew wide notice for its close look at that closed world.
40455-master-of-men:
Master of Men is a novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, published in New York by P F Collier and Son with copyright in 1908. Oppenheim had already written The Mischief-Maker, Havoc, and The Malefactor. The volume is headed The Yellow House, and this issue forms volume one of a set.

The story opens on a hill road winding upward in long bends. A workman pushes his bicycle toward the summit, changing hands on the machine. He wipes the sweat from a grimy forehead under streaming sunshine. His open throated clothes show magnificent shoulders and great physical strength. The climb troubles him little, and he steps forward blithely. Oppenheim builds the tale on such a figure of strength entering a world of wealth and intrigue. It is early work from a master of the popular thriller.
40481-concerning-children:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman, writing as Charlotte Perkins Stetson, published Concerning Children in London and Boston in 1903. Putnam's Sons and Small, Maynard and Company shared the edition. She had already written Women and Economics and The Yellow Wall Paper, both named on the title page. She dedicated the book to her daughter Katharine, who had taught her much of what stands in it.

Fifteen essays make up the contents. The first, The Precious Ten, opens the argument, and later pieces treat the effect of minding on the mind, teachable ethics, and unconscious schooling. Others argue for a place for children, and for the respect due to youth. Six mothers and the nurse-maid get chapters of their own. The book ends on social parentage, her claim that children belong to society as well as to the home. Parents of 1903 got a bold new doctrine of childhood.
4065-side-lights-on-astronomy-and-kindre:
A popular astronomy book explains telescopes and kindred fields for general readers. A chapter on the Huyghenian eyepiece notes that a small telescope, used by hand as a spyglass, needs little support, but regular use demands a proper mounting.

Later chapters turn from instruments to stars, planets, and the wonders they reveal, in clear, patient prose. The book belongs to the age when amateur stargazing grew with cheap optics and public lectures. Readers curious about the night sky will find a friendly guide to how telescopes work and what they show.
40946-emancipation-and-emigration-a-plan:
Emancipation and Emigration, the ninth of the Principia Club Papers, was printed at Boston in 1878. Its full plan is to move the freedmen of the South onto the government lands of the West. An open letter to those freedmen, dated from Cambridgeport in August 1878, stands at the front.

The writer says he gave much of the last forty years, and much money, to the fight against the slave power. He warns that the freedmen's rights are now traded away by corrupt men, and urges a move west as the safe path. Pages set out the plan of work, answer doubts raised against it, and name a National Farmers' Association as part of the scheme.
41027-the-revolt-of-the-star-men:
The Revolt of the Star Men, by Raymond Gallun, ran in Wonder Stories Quarterly in the winter of 1932. An editor's note fronts the tale. Insects, it argues, prove that life with an outside skeleton can weather any catastrophe. Their shells have lasted forty million years, the note says. Space men built on that plan are no wild dream. A picture shows a bulk tearing a machine gun from its mountings. The story opens in the reading room of the space liner Ekova. Jan greets a man she thought far away: Hekki.

A week before, he had left for the Taraal desert on Mars, hunting ancient art. Now he smiles with a secret and talks of business. His stateroom has hidden him for most of the voyage. Gallun builds his adventure on two worlds, Earth and Mars.
41270-the-australian-explorers-their-lab:
George Grimm wrote The Australian Explorers, their labours, perils, and achievements. George Robertson and Company issued it in 1888. Melbourne and Sydney share that issue in print. Grimm ministered at Saint Paul's, Balmain West, Sydney. He tutored theology for the Presbyterian Church too. Discovery runs from Cook's landing to the centennial year.

The book goes to John Dunmore Lang's memory. Pleasant intercourse with Lang moves the gift, he says. The tale of Australian exploration must not die, he opens. Men laid their bones in the desert for it. A new generation grows uninformed, he warns. Explorers' journals have grown scarce with time. Private hands treasure the few that remain. Gratitude owes those men a kept record, he holds. A centennial clergyman's roll of explorers kept Burke, Wills, and Stuart before the school children of a new nation.
41338-the-memoirs-of-an-american-citizen:
Robert Herrick wrote The Memoirs of an American Citizen, a novel in the form of a life story, published by Macmillan in New York in 1905. Herrick dedicated it to Will Payne, and an old exchange about eye-witness and hearsay stands at the front.

The chapter list draws a Chicago career. It opens on the lake front and in the Harrison Street police court, then moves to Jasonville, Indiana. Headings mark the climb: First Blood, The Bomb, The Trial of the Anarchists, and Another Boost. Love, marriage, and the will of a woman enter the tale, then a strike, treachery, and a squeeze. War and happiness close the list. Readers get a business life in the raw city, told by the man who lived it, with the Haymarket shadow over the early chapters.
41350-stories-from-the-faerie-queen-told:
Jeanie Lang told Stories from the Faerie Queen to the children. Jack at London and Dutton at New York shared the book. Le Quesne pictured each story in it. Chisholm edited the children's series. Three hundred years ago a poet lived in England.

Spenser was brave, true, and gentle, it tells. He loved all that was beautiful and good. His eyes saw Fairyland more clearly than men's. Eight stories are chosen from his poem. Una and the Lion opens the list. Saint George and Britomart follow there. A sea-nymph's son stands later in it. Florimell and the witch close the contents as named there. I should like the crystal ball to shew me my husband, one says. Lang gives Spenser a nursery door into Fairyland.
41402-the-yellow-house-master-of-men:
Oppenheim's The Yellow House, issued in New York by Collier, is a novel of English county society, copyrighted in 1908. The narrator is the daughter of a small country vicar, newly settled in Northshire with her father and sister.

Practically the whole county has called at the vicarage: the Countess from Sysington Hall, the Holgates, and Lady Naselton, who takes the narrator up as her sponsor in society. Callers first checked the spelling of the family name, Ffolliot, and relaxed on learning these were the right Ffolliots, cousins to the Warwickshire line. Only two households hold back: Bruce Deville of Deville Court, and the woman who lives in the Yellow House. The held-back calls set the mystery moving.
41595-the-funny-side-of-physic-or-the-my:
Doctor Crabtre's Funny Side of Physic, or The Mysteries of Medicine, was published at Hartford by Burr and Hyde in 1872. Its title page promises the humorous and serious sides of medical practice. It also bills itself as an expose of medical humbugs, quacks and charlatans in all ages and all countries.

The preface says the author spared no pains of research and fixed his facts in the mind with apt anecdotes. Crabtre praises the true physician as the best of men and pours indignation on the quack. He argues that the public little understand how much ignorance has been hidden behind the title of Doctor, or how patients are trifled with in every city and village.
41634-martin-van-buren:
Edward M Shepard wrote this life of Martin Van Buren for the American Statesmen series, edited by John T Morse, junior. Houghton, Mifflin of Boston and New York printed the standard library edition in 1899, with copyrights of 1888 and 1899. This is volume eighteen of thirty-two, grouped under domestic politics, the tariff, and slavery. Plates show Van Buren and his home, Lindenwald, near Kinderhook.

Chapters open with American politics when his career began, under Jefferson's shadow. Early law practice, the state senate, and the attorney-general's chair follow. The United States Senate, party leadership, and the Democratic victory of 1828 lead to the governorship. Secretary of state, minister to England, vice-president, and president close the rise, with the crisis of 1837 ahead.
41641-just-sixteen:
Just Sixteen gathers short tales for girls by Susan Coolidge. Roberts Brothers of Boston put the book out in 1890. Coolidge had won young readers with her What Katy Did set. Sixteen tales fill the contents, each with its own young hero or heroine. A Little Knight of Labor leads the set in a snow storm tale.

Sandyport by the Sea takes its first great winter storm in it. Snowy Peter, the Do Something Society, and a shipwrecked scent bottle follow. Two girls at two parties and a pink sweetmeat fill the mid list. Fir cones, a balsam pillow, and Colonel Wheeler round the set out. A child of the sea folk closes the book of girl tales.
41810-a-spanish-anthology-a-collection-o:
Spanish lyrics from the thirteenth century down to the present day fill this anthology, issued in the Silver Series of Modern Language Text-Books. The editor adds an introduction and notes to aid study. Marks in the text show page and line numbers, so the notes at the back can be traced with ease. Signs for joined vowels are also explained for the reader.

The poems and fragments form the main body of the book. Notes at the end list changes made to the first printing and clear up doubtful points. As a school text, the book gives English-speaking students a wide span of Spanish verse in one volume. The notes help them read old and new poems with care.
41827-dick-merriwell-abroad-or-the-ban-o:
Dick Merriwell Abroad, or The Ban of the Terrible Ten, by Burt Standish, was copyrighted in 1904 and 1905 and published in New York. Standish was author of the celebrated Merriwell stories, called the favourite reading of over half a million American boys. Chapter one is the story of Queen Mary.

Well, here we are, boys, in Scotland, one says: the land of feuds, clans, Wallace, and Bruce. A meeting at a castle, an inn, and Budthorne struggle follow. Bunol plot and demand, a fight in the castle, and the haunts of Robin Hood fill the early chapters. A haunted mill, sunset on the Grand Canal, and a ring of iron come later. Steel meets steel, Teresa swears an oath, and the party stands before the Parthenon. Readers get a Merriwell tour of Europe at full adventure pace.
42136-rebel-women:
Evelyn Sharp's Rebel Women, published at New York in 1910, collects short sketches of the militant suffrage campaign in England. Chapters such as Women at the Gate, To Prison while the Sun Shines, Filling the War Chest and Votes for Women--Forward draw on scenes Sharp witnessed as a participant and journalist. Several pieces first appeared in the Manchester Guardian, the Daily Chronicle and Votes for Women.

The opening sketch follows a woman on an omnibus watching a crowd surge toward the gate of St Stephen's at Whitehall. Policemen hold the way while battered women press forward, and the narrator measures her own timidity against their resolve.
42229-riding-and-driving-for-women:
Belle Beach wrote Riding and Driving for Women, issued by Charles Scribners Sons in New York in nineteen twelve, with many plates. The book is in two parts. Part one treats riding in eleven chapters. Part two treats driving in eight chapters. An index closes the volume. Beach gave the book to a friend whose help, she says, made it possible.

Riding chapters treat form, hands, and mounting in a side saddle. Later chapters treat riding astride, hunting, and the show ring. Dress, saddles, bridles, and the choice of a saddle horse get full care. Driving chapters treat form, four in hand and tandem work, and show ring appointments. Bits, bearing reins, and harness close the guide. Plates show right and wrong stances side by side. Women riders of the age got a full, strict coach in print.
42393-sarchedon-a-legend-of-the-great-qu:
Sarchedon: A Legend of the Great Queen, by Whyte-Melville, was issued in London by Ward, Lock and Company, and dated June 1871. The pictures are by Waller. The romance is dedicated to Austin Layard, the excavator of Nineveh, as a tribute to the man who dug a nation's records out of the desert sands.

The tale is set in the ancient east of Semiramis, the great queen of its title. Chapters named The Seven Stars, Merodach, The Temple of his God, and A Banquet of Wine open the Assyrian part. The story then crosses to Egypt: Pharaoh on the Throne, The Captive in the Dungeon, and Deliverance. A ride for life and a city of refuge close the middle book. The novel joins Bible lands and Layard's new-found Assyria in one romance of queens and captives.
42407-misrepresentative-women:
Harry Graham wrote Misrepresentative Women, illustrated by Dan Sayre Groesbeck and published at New York in 1906. Graham had already done Misrepresentative Men and More Misrepresentative Men. A frontispiece shows Truth viewed with horror for being nude. Contents open with a publishers' preface, then Eve.

Lady Godiva, Miss Marie Corelli, and Mrs Mary Baker Eddy follow in verse portraits. Mrs Grundy, Mrs Christopher Columbus, and Dame Rumor complete the gallery of types. The Cry of the Children, An Epithalamium, and pieces on the decline of gentility among the young fill out the volume. Readers get light society verse that pretends to slander famous women while actually rhyming about everyone.
42591-in-the-open:
In the Open is a book of nature essays by Stanton Davis Kirkham. Paul Elder published it at San Francisco and New York in 1908. Its subtitle calls the pieces intimate studies and appreciations of nature. Kirkham also wrote Where Dwells the Soul Serene. Real friendship for birds, bees, and flowers is urged there. The contents begin with The Point of View and Signs of Spring. Bird Life and Songs of the Woods follow in order.

The Ways of the Ant gets a chapter of close observation. Autumn Studies and The Winter Woods mark the turning year. Laughing Waters, The Mountains, The Forest, and The Sea close the book. A frontispiece passage praises a flock of wild geese on the wing. The essays prize friendship with nature over bare science.
42796-the-box-car-children:
Gertrude Chandler Warner wrote a children's story copyrighted in 1924, with pictures by Dorothy Lake Gregory.
