It opens on a hot summer evening in the village of Middlesex, where a strange family moves into a tumble-down house. The father is very drunk, helped up the steps by his thirteen-year-old son.

By the next day the father is dead, and the four children, whose mother is already gone, face the hard baker and his kinder wife alone. The youngest, Benny, lets slip that they have a grandfather in Greenfield, and his sister hushes him anxiously. Chapters of flight, shelter, and housekeeping follow, toward a new grandfather and a united family. Orphaned children fending for themselves carry the tale.
42938-horsemanship-for-women:
Theodore H Mead wrote Horsemanship for Women for Harper and Brothers at New York in 1887, with pictures by Gray Parker. Part one treats amateur horse-training in seventeen lessons. Early lessons bring a horse to the whip and teach it to hold the bit lightly, with curb and snaffle in turn.

Later lessons cover bending the neck, moving the croup, the walk, trot, and gallop, and the pirouette. Part two turns to etiquette in the saddle: dress, mounting, the seat, and road manners. Part three treats leaping. Part four guides buyers of a saddle-horse, with the points of the horse set out in letter order and a list of diseases. Plain steps serve new riders.
43027-getting-gold-a-gold-mining-handboo:
Getting Gold is a gold-mining handbook for practical men, issued among Griffin's standard mining publications. The publisher's list around it shows its company: a metallurgy of gold by Kirke Rose of the Royal Mint, and a practical treatise on cyaniding gold and silver ores. The handbook speaks to the man on the ground, not the lecturer.

Its neighbours in the list promise hints for intending explorers, prospectors, and settlers, from a mine manager's pen. Getting Gold belongs to that shelf of the gold-rush decades: short, plain manuals that taught a newcomer how gold is found, won, and judged. The Griffin list itself, with prices in shillings and praise from the Times and the Mining Journal, shows how large a trade served the mines. The book is a tool of the industry's great age of expansion.
4313-the-odd-women:
George Gissing gave this novel a title from the census term for women left unmarried by a shortage of men. Its contents open with the fold and the shepherd, a woman adrift, and an independent woman, then follow Monica's majority, a casual acquaintance, and a camp of the reserve. Weddings, discord, and the clank of chains follow.

The odd women here seek work, training, and a life beyond marriage, and Gissing treats their hopes with respect and doubt. Later chapters bring confession and counsel, retreat with honour, and a new beginning. The novel is a landmark of Victorian fiction about women's work, and it still speaks to readers today.
43131-mary-a-nursery-story-for-very-litt: Mrs Molesworth wrote Mary as a nursery story for very little children, with pictures by Leslie Brooke. Macmillan issued it at London and New York in 1893. Mary wakes early one May morning and wonders if today is her birthday. She is not yet four, and Thursdays confuse her, since two have passed without the day arriving. She hopes her mother has not made a mistake, since May is a nice short word, only one letter more than Mary.
43133-imogen-or-only-eighteen:
Imogen, or Only Eighteen, was written by Mrs Molesworth. Chambers published the novel in London and Edinburgh. Bone drew the illustrations. Chapter one is called The Spirits of the Fells. Grey Fells Hall, called the Fells for short, is the house. Old deeds in the squire's safe give its true name. The Helmont family fills it most of the year. Only the three months of the London season leave it empty. The squire is very rich and very liberal, Molesworth says. He likes to see people happy about him. The boys run from Captain Helmont of a cavalry regiment to Cecil at Eton.

Two daughters are married; three remain at home. Papa and Mamma have their cronies too, though fewer than the children. Imogen enters a house where a family party is almost unknown, and not desired.
43365-the-buke-of-the-order-of-knyghthoo:
The Buke of the Order of Knyghthood, translated from the French by Sir Gilbert Hay, was printed at Edinburgh in 1847 for the Abbotsford Club. The text comes from the manuscript in the library at Abbotsford, Sir Walter Scott's house. Beriah Botfield dedicates the specimen of early Scottish literature to the club's president and members, dating his letter January 1, 1847, from Norton Hall.

The preface argues that fifteenth-century Scottish literature deserves more attention, especially as England's contemporary writing is comparatively dull. Hay, chamberlain to Charles the Sixth of France, was named among the makars by Dunbar and Lyndsay, then forgotten until Mackenzie's lives of Scots writers in 1722. In the text, the letter yogh is printed as gh, as the transcriber notes. Hay's translation adapts the French order-of-chivalry treatise for a Scottish court.
43454-peeps-at-many-lands-sweden:
William Liddle and his wife wrote Sweden for the Peeps at Many Lands series, printed at London in 1911. Twelve full page plates in colour, by Anders Zorn, Carl Larsson, and others, show dress, coasts, and town life. The series gave young readers short, bright tours of lands near and far, each in one small book.

Chapters move from Swedish past to Gothenburg, a summer break at Marstrand, and a trip across Sweden by water. Stockholm gets two chapters, then work and play, schools, Dalecarlia, and customs follow. Gothland and Visby, fairy tales, Christmas, and midsummer close the tour, with famed Swedes at the end. Clear heads, maps of custom, and strong art make the land feel close and lived in.
4360-vendetta-a-story-of-one-forgotten:
Marie Corelli wrote this novel of revenge and return under the subtitle A Story of One Forgotten. Its preface warns readers not to judge the tale before its end, and its thirty-seven chapters carry a hero through injury, exile, and a long-plotted reckoning. Corelli, already known for Ardath, Thelma, and A Romance of Two Worlds, writes in her high romantic manner.

The vendetta of the title is both a plot and a passion, pursued across years and countries. Corelli mixes Italian color, fierce feeling, and moral argument, as her heroes often do. Readers of Victorian sensation fiction will find the book's pleasures familiar: secrets, disguises, and a final settling of accounts.
43600-wonderful-stories-for-children:
Hans Christian Andersen wrote the tales in Wonderful Stories for Children in Danish, and Mary Howitt turned them into English for Wiley and Putnam at New York in 1846. Andersen had already won fame with The Improvisatore. Ten tales fill the volume, opening with Olé Luckoiè, the story-teller at night.

Olé comes in stocking feet, flirts sweet milk into children's eyes, and blows on their necks until their heads grow heavy. In bed, the children hear his tales. The Daisy, Tommelise, and The Rose-Elf follow. The Constant Tin Soldier and The Storks are here too, along with Little Ida's Flowers and The Garden of Paradise. Howitt's version brought Andersen to English children early.
43617-the-memoirs-of-harriette-wilson-vo:
Harriette Wilson wrote her own memoirs, and Nash of London reprinted the first two volumes in 1909. A note at the front fixes her birth in London on February 22, 1786. Her father, John Dubochet, kept a small shop in Mayfair. By 1805 she was close to the sixth Duke of Argyle.

The memoirs first came out in 1825, in paper parts from Stockdale's shop. So great was the crush to buy that a barrier had to be set up to rule the crowd. Thirty editions are said to have sold in one year. The Duke of Wellington, Beau Brummell, and lords by the score came to her house. The editor praises her sharp ear for talk. She caught the very tone of the great men of her salon.
43835-lumen:
Camille Flammarion wrote this book of starry talks, Lumen, in an authorised rendering from the French printed at New York in 1897. A note at the front records a compliment: a minor planet found at the Paris Observatory in 1875 was named Lumen in honour of the author. Fifty-two thousand copies of the French original, the title page adds, had been sold.

Contents arrange the book as five conversations. The first treats death, the soul, and the speed of light, ending with Lumen seeing his own life again from the heavens. The second journeys on a ray of light and climbs back up the ages. Others take up time and space, former lives under a star of Virgo, and the endless variety of life on other worlds, down to a telescope of time.
43880-the-mediaeval-mind-volume-1-of-2-a:
Mediaeval Mind, volume one of two, is a history of medieval thought by Henry Osborn Taylor. Macmillan issued the two volumes at London and New York in 1911. Its subtitle promises the development of thought and emotion in the Middle Ages. Book one, the groundwork, opens with the genesis of the mediaeval genius.

The Latinizing of the West and Greek philosophy as antecedent follow in the contents. Intellectual interests of the Latin fathers and the Latin transmitters fill two chapters. The barbaric disruption of the empire and the Celtic strain in Gaul and Ireland close the opening movement. Taylor humane scholarship made the era mind intelligible to modern readers.
43881-the-mediaeval-mind-volume-2-of-2-a:
The Mediaeval Mind, volume two, continues Henry Osborn Taylor's history of thought. Macmillan brought the two volumes out in London in the year 1911. The work traces the development of thought and emotion in the Middle Ages. This second volume opens with Book Four on the ideal and the actual. The heart of Heloise and Walther von der Vogelweide fill its chapters.

Book Five treats symbolism: scriptural allegories and Hugo of Saint Victor. Cathedral and mass, hymn and imaginative poem, stand in that part. Book Six turns to Latinity and law in the mediaeval world. The spell of the classics and the growth of Latin prose follow. Mediaeval appropriation of the Roman law gets a full chapter there. Book Seven closes with scholasticism, its spirit, scope, and method weighed. Classification of topics and stages of evolution end the contents list.
44485-roy-blakeley-lost-strayed-or-stole:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote Roy Blakeley, Lost, Strayed or Stolen, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York with a copyright of nineteen twenty one. Howard L Hastings drew the pictures. The book has the backing of the Boy Scouts of America. Roy tells the tale in his own bright voice. Pee wee Harris is his friend and fellow scout.

Roy starts with the scout laws and says the eighth law is his best one. That law bids a scout to be cheerful and to smile a lot. Chapters then chase a lost or strayed thing through town, camp, and woods. Titles promise scout strategy, footprints, a shack, and two endings. Young readers get jokes, hikes, and good turns in fast mix.
44624-sweden:
Victor Nilsson wrote a history of Sweden for a series of popular world histories, printed at New York and London in 1899 with a front picture of Gustavus Adolphus. The contents run from early times and old finds through the Viking age and the coming of Ansgar. They pass to the Folkung kings and the wars between union men and their foes.

Later chapters follow Gustavus Vasa and the change of faith. Then comes the age of power under Gustavus Adolphus, Queen Christine and Charles the Twelfth, and the age of freedom that came after. The book closes with the Bernadotte kings, reform of the diet, and the reign of Oscar the Second up to the writer's own day.
44679-siam-land-of-free-men:
H G Deignan wrote Siam, Land of Free Men, for the Smithsonian in war years. The work stands eighth in the War Background Studies of that house. It came out at Washington on February fifth, nineteen hundred forty three. Deignan kept the bird rooms of the National Museum then.

Land, folk, and old days fill the first pages of his survey. Sukhothai and Ayuthia, dead kingdoms, mark Siam’s proud past. Tonburi and the new Siam, called Thailand, close the tale. The great neck of land between India and China frames it all. Wave on wave of peoples broke on that shore from the north. Faith crews from Ceylon, horse tribes, and sea raiders all struck it. Three shares now split Further India: French, English, and Siamese. Rice fields, teak rafts, and shrines fill the book’s eight plates.
44920-the-normans-told-chiefly-in-relati:
Sarah Orne Jewett wrote this history of the Normans for the Story of the Nations series, published by Putnam in 1898 and dedicated to her grandfather. The frontispiece shows Falaise, birthplace of William the Conqueror.

The contents open with the men of the dragon ships: Northmen hall-life, sea-kings, and viking voyages. Then come Rolf the Ganger winning Normandy from Charles the Simple, William Longsword, and Richard the Fearless escaping from Laon as a boy. Later chapters follow Richard the Good toward the conquest that the title promises. Jewett, the Maine novelist of country life, brings a storyteller's hand to the dukes of Normandy. School and home readers get the Conquest's long prelude.
4529-biographies-of-working-men:
Grant Allen published these seven short lives in 1884, choosing men who rose by work rather than by birth. His subjects are Thomas Telford, stonemason; George Stephenson, engine-man; John Gibson, sculptor; William Herschel, bandsman; Jean Francois Millet, painter; James Garfield, canal boy; and Thomas Edward, shoemaker. Allen drew his facts from standard lives of engineers, Stephensons, Gibson, Herschel, Millet, and Garfield.

Each life shows a craft learned by hand, long patience, and a chance seized at the right hour, from Telford's heather hills between England and Scotland to Garfield's canal work in America. The book is plain, encouraging biography, written for readers who like real examples of effort rewarded. It suits young readers and anyone who wants short, true stories of how skill and grit can carry a working man or woman far.
45320-ladies-and-gentlemen:
Irvin Cobb wrote tales of folk in high rooms and small towns alike. His book first came out in 1927. He gave it to his friend Lillie in its front pages. A Lady and a Gentleman leads the set of tales. The Order of the Bath and Two of Everything come next.

We of the Old South and Killed with Kindness fill the mid set. Peace on Earth and Three Wise Men of the East Side stand there. A cowboy, a lady, and her pa make one tale's odd three. Cobb's first tale starts in a whir of hotel crowds. Rail crowds pour like streams through each door, he says. Warm wit rules all.
45523-famous-authors-men:
Harkins profiles Famous Authors (Men) for Page at Boston, with copyright in 1901 and a fourth impression in 1906. He had written a companion volume on famous women authors, and portraits face most chapters. Twenty sketches run from William Dean Howells to Winston Churchill.

Contents include Bret Harte, Mark Twain, Lew Wallace, George Cable, Henry James, Stockton, Joel Chandler Harris, and Weir Mitchell between the leaders. The Howells sketch opens by saying he has reached an age to look back but will instead keep looking forward until he shuffles off this mortal coil. Howells was born at Martin's Ferry, Ohio, on March 1, 1837, and at nine worked rising at four in the morning to sell his father's Dayton paper about town.
45586-auld-lang-syne-selections-from-the:
Auld Lang Syne gathers selections from the papers of the Pen and Pencil Club, printed for private circulation by the Chiswick Press in 1877. A Burns motto heads the volume: should auld acquaintance be forgot? Short pieces from February 1864 onward fill the contents, each tied to a club date.

Mentia Taylor writes on cradle and witchcraft, Marian James on bells and chivalry. Lewis Morris offers mirror, shadows, and lights and shadows in verse. Frances Power Cobbe treats organ boys, and Professor Seeley writes on stumbling blocks and expediency. Annie Keary, Arthur Munby, Austin Dobson, and Edwin Arnold all appear. Joseph Mazzini writes on rest. The set preserves a literary club's parlour work.
45591-beadle-s-dime-book-of-practical-et:
Beadle's Dime Book of Practical Etiquette is a manners manual published by Irwin Beadle in 1859. It promises a guide to true gentility and good breeding, covering the ballroom, the evening party, the dinner party, the card table, business and the home circle.

The introduction opens with the words that open every heart: that man is a gentleman, that woman is a lady. Politeness, the committee argues, is not effeminate affectation but a learnable usage, and its great underlying law is simply the Golden Rule. The manual addresses itself to those who err from ignorance rather than willfulness, and flatters itself that an attentive reader may learn to move with credit in any circle. It is gentility democratized at ten cents, the etiquette book as dime novel.
45599-a-woman-s-hardy-garden:
A Woman's Hardy Garden is a practical gardening book by Helena Rutherfurd Ely. Macmillan first published it in 1903. Ely wrote from her own farm, called Meadowburn. Photographs of her garden illustrate the text. The dedication thanks the friend who helped make the garden.

Sixteen chapters run the gardener's year. Soil preparation comes first. Laying out borders around a house follows. A chapter shows how to plant a small plot. Seed-beds and planting methods earn their own chapters. Annuals, perennials, and biennials divide the flowers. Roses and lilies get chapters of their own. Spring bulbs, shrubs, and garden furniture follow. Insecticides and the tool-room close the practical course.
45716-the-life-of-our-lord-in-simple-lan:
Warne of London and New York tells the life of Christ in simple words for small children, with many plates through the text. A plate of Jerusalem and one of King David stand near the front of the book. The tale starts with God who made earth, sea, hills, fish, birds, and beasts in ages past.

Adam and Eve come last in that making and live in Eden till Satan tempts them to eat banned fruit. Sin and death enter the world, yet God's Son will come to die and save their souls, the book tells its young readers. Abraham and David mark the line from which that Son will spring in God's own time. Gabriel then comes to Mary at Nazareth with news of a child to be named Jesus.
45762-games-and-songs-of-american-childr:
William Wells Newell's Games and Songs of American Children, collected and compared, was published by Harper in New York in 1884. The editor's note states the find: a children's tradition exists in America, kept up apart from print, and scarcely noticed before. In this branch of folk-lore, the American vein is richer and purer than the British one so far worked.

Newell is careful about his ground. The lore of the nursery divides into the tradition of children and the tradition of nurses; this book takes only the children's own. These are the formulas of play handed down from child to child, often without older minds knowing of them. The games show how old English lore of the kind relates to the continent's, and American custom often lights up the games of other tongues. The learned references are pushed to an appendix, to keep the text's bright air unclouded.
45856-the-smugglers-picturesque-chapters:
The Smugglers: Picturesque Chapters in the Story of an Ancient Craft is a history by Charles G Harper, printed at London in 1909. Paul Hardy and old prints illustrate it. Doctor Johnson's dictionary gives the tone. A smuggler, it says, is a wretch who imports or exports goods without payment of the customs.

The contents open with the owlers of Romney Marsh, who ran the ancient export smuggling of wool. Tea and tobacco smuggling grew in the eighteenth century, and repressive laws failed against it. The Hawkhurst gang terrorised whole districts and made an organised attack on Goudhurst. Chapters treat murders by smugglers in Hampshire, and the trial and execution of the murderers. Church towers served as smugglers' cellars. Cornwall, the Dorset and Devon coasts, and smugglers' epitaphs close the survey. Harper tells the craft's story parish by parish.
45963-mildred-at-home-with-something-abo:
Martha Finley wrote a shelf of tales of Elsie Dinsmore and of Mildred Keith. This book, Mildred at Home, came out in 1884. Its front list names the Elsie books in their long row. Mildred's own books stand in a row of their own as well. The sub-title adds news of her kin and friends.

Mildred's home life is the core of this part of her tale. Past books told of her youth, her wed life, and Roselands. Here the home hearth and its folk fill the stage. Faith, duty, and love rule each small trial she meets. Finley's fans read these books by the score at home. Mildred stands as a calm guide for the young.
46170-fathers-of-men:
E W Hornung turns from Raffles to a school story in a novel issued by Charles Scribner's Sons at New York in 1912. His list on the front pages prices Fathers of Men at one dollar thirty.

The contents open behind the scenes, then change and chance. Very raw material settles in, earns nicknames, and learns boy-to-boy manners. A haunted house and Spraydon's masterpiece season the terms. One new boy in Heriot's house talks too much at the master's table. The other shuts a stubborn mouth tighter than before. Bound volumes of Punch entertained them in the study. Dark horses, fame and fortune, and the old boys' match build toward close of play. The extreme penalty waits near the end. Hornung knew school from inside, as father and pupil.
46372-ocean-s-story-or-triumphs-of-thirt:
Frank Goodrich and Edward Howland tell the ocean's story in this big subscription book. Triumphs of thirty centuries is the bold subtitle, from the ark to the iron steamships. More than two hundred spirited illustrations fill the graphic description, the title page promises to buyers.

A gigantic cuttle fish, pictured at page 649, leads the front illustrations here. Maritime adventures, achievements, explorations, discoveries and inventions crowd the long title's list. Shipbuilding's rise, diving, dredging, deep sea sounding and submarine exploration close the wonders, in a parlor book sold door to door across America in its day.
4644-the-adventures-of-mr-verdant-green:
Cuthbert Bede, a pen name, tells the adventures of Mr. Verdant Green in three parts, revised here to match the first editions of 1853, 1854, and 1857. The book follows a fresh, green young man to Oxford, where college jokes, tutors, and fellow students cure his dumps, in Swift's phrase from the frontispiece. Minor spelling changes between editions, such as shew for show, are noted in the editorial matter.

Verdant Green blunders through examinations, friendships, sports, and scrapes, learning town and gown manners as he goes. Bede writes with affectionate humour, and the book became a classic Oxford tale. Readers get a light, old-fashioned university comedy, full of period slang and student life, and a useful picture of Oxford in the middle of the nineteenth century.
46714-synthesis-of-2-methyl-4-selenoquin:
Yu-Gwan Chen wrote a doctoral dissertation on the synthesis of 2-methyl-4-selenoquinazolone, 2-phenylbenzoselenazole, and its derivatives. He submitted it at Columbia University in 1922 for the degree of doctor of philosophy in pure science. The work was undertaken at the suggestion of Professor Marston Taylor Bogert. Chen's contents divide into a review and an experimental part. A pharmacological review and a tinctorial review open the study.

The abstract states the aim plainly. Organic selenium compounds of the ring-forming series were to be studied for properties leading to drug and dye uses. The methods were a critical review of the compounds and the making of new ones. Four methods of preparing the first compound are given. The second compound's nitro, amino, acetyl, and benzylidene derivatives follow. An azo dye from it, and dyeing trials with azo dyes, close the experimental work.
46861-the-runaway-donkey-and-other-rhyme:
The Runaway Donkey and Other Rhymes for Children is a verse book by Emilie Poulsson, the author of Finger Plays for Nursery and Kindergarten. The Project Gutenberg text follows the Boston issue of 1905, from Lothrop, Lee and Shepard. Pictures by Bridgman run through the book.

The title rhyme tells of Barney the donkey. He sees the stable door ajar and bolts. Two girls chase him as fast as they can go. A long set of Pony Rollo rhymes follows. They tell of the pony's coming, his tricks, his name, and his play with a small dog. Other rhymes take up a kindly deer, farm voices, pigeons, clothes, and a pond. One asks who gives us our Thanksgiving dinner. Some pieces had first appeared in St Nicholas and other children's magazines.
46934-flower-children-the-little-cousins:
Flower Children, the little cousins of the field and garden, is a verse book by Elizabeth Gordon. Volland and Company published the book at Chicago, copyrighted in 1910 by the firm. Ross drew the pictures of the flower children for its pages. Gordon dedicates the book to every child flower that blooms in the garden called home.

Each flower speaks in a short rhyme of its own in the book in turn. Said Crocus: my, this wind is cold, most wish I had not been so bold, in the first verse. Trailing Arbutus loves to grow beneath the snow in the second of the poems. The conceit is simple and was beloved: every common flower is a child with a temper, a season, and a lesson, drawn in colour for the nursery shelf.
4713-the-veiled-lady-and-other-men-and-w:
F. Hopkinson Smith gathers stories in The Veiled Lady and Other Men and Women, opening with a note to readers on the title. The collection is labelled The Veiled Lady as the easiest way out of a dilemma, he says. Yet the title may mislead. Beyond doubt these covers hold a charming Houri, to whom nightingales sing lullabies, and a beautiful Venetian whose love affairs upset a quarter.

Other figures include a common-sense, motherly nurse whose heart warmed toward a companion in an adjoining berth. They add a plucky New England girl with courage of her convictions, and a prim spinster whose only consolation was the boarder opposite. Rough sea-dogs with friendly feelings fill the book. Contents list Loretta of the shipyards, a coat of red lead, Miss Murdock special, and Captain Joe and the Susie Ann. Readers get warm, varied American stories, told with humour and heart.
47135-the-american-jew-as-patriot-soldie:
The American Jew as Patriot, Soldier and Citizen, by Simon Wolf, edited by Louis Edward Levy, was published in Philadelphia in 1895. A statue of religious liberty in Fairmount Park fronts the book. A text from John heads the title page: ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. Wolf dedicates the work to all who love and seek the truth.

The editor's preface argues that prejudice and ignorance are twins, each able to breed the other, and that the willful sort is the most stubborn of all. Wolf's aim is to force a fair verdict on the Jewish share in building the state, above all in its wars. Names, units, and records make the case that Jews served as patriots from the Revolution onward.
47186-model-women:
Model Women is a book of lives by William Anderson, author of Self-Made Men. Hodder and Stoughton published the work at London in 1870. A motto from Seneca stands at the front: noble examples stir us to noble deeds. Anderson addresses the volume to young women in a dedicatory letter.

Anderson says the aim of lives is to teach by example. He claims perfection for none of his models, yet holds each worthy of a place in young hearts. He would not have women trade home for market or nursery for arena. Still, he argues, a woman is more than a housekeeper or nurse. She should be trained as a thinking being. He urges her to face the wrongs that bind her freedom and narrow her use. The lives that follow show women of mind and action from many fields.
47218-the-daughter-of-heaven:
The Daughter of Heaven, by Pierre Loti and Judith Gautier, was translated by Ruth Helen Davis and published in London in 1913. The head opens mid play, at the second tableau: the grand throne room in the palace at Pekin. A cast list follows, in two courts.

At Pekin rules the Emperor of Peking, a Tartar of the Tsing dynasty, aged thirty. His councillor is Fount in the Forest, and Tartar dignitaries attend. At Nanking rules a little Chinese Emperor, the Son of Springtime, aged seven or eight. The Daughter of Heaven herself is Chinese Empress of the Ming dynasty, aged twenty four or twenty five. Gardeners, spies, executioners, and soldiers fill the cast. Act one is the garden of the Nanking palace. Readers get a French verse drama of rival Chinese courts.
47256-days-in-the-open:
Days in the Open is a book of outdoor sketches by Lathan Crandall, published by the Revell company in 1914. Louis Rhead drew the pictures. The book opens with verse by Kipling about rods, reels, and a smoky camp, and with a comic song of monks who fish on a Thursday because Friday is a fast day.

Crandall writes of brooks, trout, and grayling, and of boys learning the water. The pieces mix story, memory, and plain love of fishing. One sketch looks back fifty years to a freckled boy in a battered straw hat. The book belongs to a time when a day outside was still the common wealth of American boys.
47293-bird-children-the-little-playmates:
Bird Children is a book of verses about birds for children by Elizabeth Gordon, with drawings by Ross. Volland published it at Chicago in 1912, and this copy is the sixth edition. Its subtitle calls the birds the little playmates of the flower children. Gordon dedicates it to all children who love birds and flowers.

Each bird gets a short rhymed portrait with a picture. Sir Rooster is a noisy chap who crows at eleven, one, and two. The hen is a kind old dame who talks all day about her joys. The guinea hen wants only simple food for her huffy brood. The verses teach the farmyard and garden birds by name and habit.
473-stories-to-tell-to-children:
Sara Cone Bryant gathers fifty-three tales for telling aloud in this companion to her guide on storytelling. The Little Red Hen, the Gingerbread Man, the Boy Who Cried Wolf, the Elves and the Shoemaker, and David and Goliath sit beside lesser-known tales from many lands. Notes for the teller open the book.

Bryant shapes each tale for voice, not print, with short sentences and clear action. Stories suit school, home, and library hours. The volume remains a handy store for tellers who want tried tales that hold small listeners from first line to last.
47356-studies-on-homer-and-the-homeric-a:
Studies on Homer and the Homeric Age, volume one, is a work by Gladstone. Oxford University Press printed the three volumes in the year 1858. Gladstone sat as member of Parliament for the University of Oxford then. This first volume holds the Prolegomena and a study called Achaeis. Achaeis treats the ethnology of the Greek races in the poems.

The first section weighs the state of the Homeric question of his day. Results of the long controversy stand summed before his own argument starts. Homer's place in classical education fills the second long section here. Gladstone holds Homer should not be read as a poet only in schools. The third section argues the poems bear true historic aims within them. Signs of those aims stand listed, even where beauty paid the cost. The poet's date and his standing as a first witness close it.
47382-the-sounds-of-spoken-english-a-man: A language manual fills this item, The Sounds of Spoken English, a manual of ear training for English sounds. The hosted opening is taken up by the publisher's series in which the book stands, a modern language series under a general editor named Rippmann. Page after page lists the set's French courses, with prices, editions, and press praise.
47583-the-curlytops-at-silver-lake-or-on:
Howard Garis wrote this Curlytops tale, published by Cupples and Leon in New York in 1920. Julia Greene illustrated the children's holiday at Silver Lake for the publisher. A plate shows a motor boat chugging alongside a sailboat on the water in the story.

Ted and Janet, the curly-headed brother and sister, visit Uncle Ben at the lake. Trouble, their baby brother, and a lively pet or two fill the days in Garis's manner. Garis had written the Uncle Wiggily books before the Curlytops, and boats, swims and rescues crowd a summer written for the youngest chapter-book readers.
47609-nursery-comedies-twelve-tiny-plays:
Nursery Comedies: Twelve Tiny Plays for Children is a play book by Lady Bell, issued by Longmans, Green in a new impression of 1911. Bell dedicates it to Hugo, Elsa, and Molly. Four of the plays are adapted from her Petit Théâtre des Enfants: Cat and Dog, The Wigwam, Rather a Prig, and Foolish Jack, the last from Grimm. Three are versions of well-known stories.

Cinderella, The Golden Goose, and What Happened to Henny Penny are those story plays. Little Petsy, The Monster in the Garden, Miss Dobson, Quite by Ourselves, and The Best Children in the World complete the twelve. The Henny Penny play opens with the hen in a fright, crying for help. Cockie Lockie asks what is happening. A passage preserved in the copy gives her muddled answer.
47677-ars-amatoria-or-the-art-of-love-li:
Ovid's Art of Love stands here in plain English prose, made by Henry Riley with full notes in 1885. The poem runs in three books. Its first line bids the reader who knows not the art of loving to read and learn. By art, ships speed with sails and oars.

By art, light chariots fly, and by art must Love be guided, Ovid holds. Venus has made him the pilot and driver of Love, he boasts. Cupid is unruly but a child, and tender years are easy to rule. A bull bears the plough in time, and a proud horse takes the bit. Riley's word for word prose lets English readers meet the Roman's sly counsel whole.
47693-a-glimpse-at-guatemala-and-some-no:
A Glimpse at Guatemala is a travel and archaeology book by Anne Cary Maudslay and Alfred Percival Maudslay, published by John Murray of London in 1899. Maps, plans, and photographs fill the volume. The archaeological results behind it were appearing in the Biologia Centrali-Americana.

Alfred Maudslay made seven expeditions to Central America. Some 200 plates from them had already been issued, in a costly work few could own. His wife joined the 1894 expedition and kept the record he could not. Her journal made this cheaper volume possible. The route runs from Guatemala City to Antigua and the volcanoes. Lake Atitlan, the Quichés and Cachiquels, and Coban follow. Ruins at Rabinal lead to Copan, described as it stood in 1885. Quirigua, Ixkun, and Chichén Itzá come next. Palenque, Tikál, and Menché close the travel.
4782-when-we-dead-awaken:
Henrik Ibsen's When We Dead Awaken, translated by William Archer, is Ibsen's late dramatic epilogue. Archer notes that from Pillars of Society to John Gabriel Borkman, Ibsen's plays followed at regular two-year intervals. Indignation over abuse heaped on Ghosts cut the gap to An Enemy of the People to a single year. Borkman appeared in 1896, and a successor was expected in 1898, but Christmas brought no rumour of a new play.

In a man over seventy, that breach seemed ominous. The new National Theatre in Christiania opened in September of the following year. Archer, meeting Ibsen for the last time, heard he was at work on a play he thought of calling a Dramatic Epilogue. Ibsen wrote it with such labour and passionate agitation that those around him were almost alarmed. Readers get Ibsen's final play, about an artist, a model, and lives that wake too late.
47954-the-old-world-in-the-new-the-signi:
The Old World in the New is a study of immigration by Edward Ross. The Century Company issued it in New York in 1914. Ross taught sociology at the University of Wisconsin. Photographs illustrate the book throughout. Chapter one treats the first make-up of the people. Puritan stock and Virginia's settlers stand there. Indentured servants and convicts are not passed over. Free land sifted the stock, Ross argues.

Later chapters take each new people in turn. The Celtic Irish come first, then the Germans. Drink, crime, work, and thrift are weighed for each. Ross asks what the newcomers do to America. His book was a leading voice in its debate. Later readers find some judgements harsh. It remains a key text of its era.
48057-ten-tudor-statesmen:
Ten Tudor Statesmen, by Arthur Innes, was printed by Eveleigh Nash in London in 1906. Innes also wrote England Under the Tudors. A painting of Henry the Seventh from the National Portrait Gallery serves as frontispiece.

In his preface, Innes says the studies are in no way a history of the Tudor period. His aim is a clear picture of character: each event is weighed only as it bears on the man under study. He notes two curious points. Eight of the ten were ministers, and not one of the eight was of noble birth, which shows how the Tudor dynasty shifted political weight. Four of them perished on the scaffold and one at the stake.
48290-old-wonder-eyes-and-other-stories-:
Mr and Mrs Lippincott, the wife writing as Grace Greenwood, made this book of tales for children. Gaut and Volkmar and Cowperthwait brought it out in Philadelphia in 1858, with plates from designs by White. The Lippincotts gave the book to a child named Maggie at Christmas 1857.

Old Wonder-Eyes heads a list of thirteen short pieces. Young readers meet Old Horace and a pet pig named Humpy, a rooster-mother, and a curious dog. Other tales tell of Willie Watson, a kite, a stolen birds' nest, and Grace Darling. Snowdrop, Philip Annesley's Return, and a first day in trousers add more scenes of child life, and a hymn ends the book.
48305-the-fleets-behind-the-fleet-the-wo:
The Fleets Behind the Fleet is W Macneile Dixon's account of the work of merchant seamen and fishermen in the war, copyrighted in 1917 by George H Doran. Dixon was a professor at the University of Glasgow. A sailor's garland edited by John Masefield stands at the head of the book.

The first chapter, A Maritime Nation, tells readers to stop picturing British sea power as battleships and cruisers. Think instead of trade routes, dockyards, busy ports, and a coast of 7,000 miles, of liners and tramps and east coast trawlers. Britain, he argues, is built by nature to be the home of a sea people, captives and masters of the sea at once. Later chapters call the merchant service the key-stone of the arch and take up sea warfare in the new style. The mine-fishers and the sea traffickers get chapters of their own.
48318-in-pastures-green:
Peter McArthur, a Canadian farmer-poet, wrote these farm papers, published in 1916 and dedicated to all city men talking of going back to the land. If each one who does not go buys a copy, he says, he will be entirely satisfied.

The book runs by the calendar. Its January opens with the opening of an apple-pit in winter: the farmer shovels off the snow, chops the frozen earth, and lifts out Spies, Baldwins, Russets, and Pippins. McArthur contrasts the humdrum Canadian way with the songs the Greeks would have sung. A sound Spy, he notes, traded at school for two empty cartridges, a pencil stub, and a rivet. Readers get farm life written from inside.
48341-gunshot-roentgenograms-a-collectio:
Major Clyde Ford of the Medical Corps made the Gunshot Roentgenograms, issued as Bulletin Nine of the Surgeon General's office in October 1915. The plates are X-ray pictures taken at Constantinople during the Turko-Balkan War of 1912 and 1913. They show gunshot wounds in the Turkish army.

The table of plates sorts wounds by body part. Head and jaw fractures come first, then the spine. The upper extremity takes the most plates: humerus, elbow, radius and ulna, wrist, and fingers. Chest, pelvis, and the lower extremity follow. Each plate names the bone struck and whether the missile lodged.
48504-the-double-garden:
The Double Garden is a book of essays by Maurice Maeterlinck, the Belgian writer, translated by Teixeira de Mattos. Dodd, Mead published it at New York in 1904. Maeterlinck's earlier books, The Life of the Bee and The Treasure of the Humble, are listed at its front. Sixteen essays make the volume, printed first in journals in London and America.

One essay mourns a little bulldog who died at six months old. His intelligent eyes opened to look out upon the world, to love mankind, Maeterlinck writes, then closed again on the cruel secrets of death. Other essays turn to flowers, time, and the inner life in his usual dreamy manner. The title joins the garden we tend with the garden of the mind. Maeterlinck wrote as a poet among prose, and these pieces show his gentle, mystical way of finding great meanings in small living things.
48695-the-stag-cook-book-written-for-men:
The Stag Cook Book, written for men by men, was collected and edited by Sheridan. George Doran issued it in New York in 1922. Robert Davis wrote the introduction. The book is given to bachelors and married men alike who have tried to cook something. A verse at the front mocks the old saw that civilized man can not live without cooks. With a saucepan, a spoon, and a kettle, it claims, a man can shine.

Davis argues that cooking is a gift, not an art, while eating is an art. He retells the tale of Charles Lamb and roast pig. A wave of burnt pork swept England from that essay, he jokes. Recipes from named men follow, for camp, grill, and tiny kitchenette alike.
48788-on-a-chinese-screen:
On a Chinese Screen is W Somerset Maugham's book of sketches from his travels in China, published by William Heinemann of London in 1922. Maugham dedicated it to Syrie, and its title promises pictures hung side by side rather than one long story. His earlier books, from Liza of Lambeth to The Moon and Sixpence, are listed at the front.

The contents run to more than fifty short pieces. The Mongol Chief, The Cabinet Minister, The Altar of Heaven, The Opium Den, and Her Britannic Majesty's Representative stand among them. Named portraits such as Henderson and The Fannings appear as well. One opening shows a row of hovels by a city gate and a string of laden camels stepping past. Maugham drew the treaty-port world in brief, cool scenes.
49038-the-underground-railroad-from-slav:
Wilbur Siebert wrote this full history of the Underground Railroad, first printed in 1898 and reprinted here by Dover in 2006 without cuts. Albert Bushnell Hart wrote the introduction. The front picture shows Levi Coffin receiving a company of fugitives on the edge of Cincinnati, from a painting by Webber.

Hart opens by calling slavery the most grave, far-reaching, and long-fought question in American life since the founding of the Union. Other great questions, he notes, turned on money and goods, but the fight over slavery turned on moral grounds and human rights. Siebert's history traces the secret network that helped enslaved people escape to freedom, route by route and helper by helper. A fold-out map of the routes, now printed on three pages, anchors the book. It remains a standard source on its subject.
49163-journal-of-a-soldier-of-the-sevent:
The Journal of a Soldier of the Seventy-First, or Glasgow Regiment, Highland Light Infantry, covers the years 1806 to 1815. Edinburgh publishers issued it in 1819. Their advertisement vouches for the writer.

The publishers say they took pains to check his statements. He relates nothing, they conclude, but what passed under his own observation. His education explains his writing better than expected from a private soldier. The contents start with his parentage and schooling. He attempts the stage and fails, joins a recruiting party, and sails for the Isle of Wight. Rank-and-file memoirs of the Napoleonic wars are rare, and a literate private's is rarest of all.
49364-inmates-of-my-house-and-garden:
Inmates of My House and Garden is a nature book by Mrs. Brightwen, published in London by Fisher Unwin in 1895, with illustrations by Theo Carreras. Brightwen had written Wild Nature Won by Kindness. She dedicates this book to Eleanor Ormerod, the entomologist. A view of the grove at the south front of her house forms the frontispiece.

The title names her subject exactly. The inmates are the wild creatures that shared her house and garden: birds at the window, insects in the rooms, and small beasts about the grounds, all won by patience and feeding. Her earlier book was praised as a charming companion for young people in their holiday haunts. Books like hers taught Victorian families to watch the life at their own doors, and to keep pets of creatures most people shooed away.
49396-germany-turkey-and-armenia-a-selec:
Germany, Turkey and Armenia is a selection of documentary evidence relating to Armenian atrocities, printed in London in 1917. Contents draw letters from German missionaries in northwest Persia, a German eyewitness at Moush, and Danish Red Cross nurses formerly with the German military mission at Erzeroum. Zeitoun exiles, a Baghdad Railway official, and Swiss residents add testimony.

An Aleppo section prints a German school teacher's appeal to representatives of the German people in February 1916. Places of exile such as Der-el-Zor appear in letters from a German lady missionary on the Euphrates. Reports by Muslim officers close the appendix of the grim file. Historians get allied-era primary evidence from inside the Ottoman Empire.
49734-the-boy-aviators-in-nicaragua-or-i:
The Boy Aviators in Nicaragua; or, In League with the Insurgents is a boys' adventure novel by Captain Wilbur Lawton. Hurst and Company published it in New York, copyrighted 1910. It opens the Boy Aviators series. Companion volumes take the boys to Africa, on secret service, and on a polar dash. The books sold cloth-bound at 50 cents each. Twenty-nine chapters fill this first adventure.

The boys start for the tropics as storm-clouds gather. Billy Barnes of the Planet joins the cast early. Rogero is checkmated, and Frank flies to the rescue. The boys dynamite their way to freedom. Wireless saves them; leagued with insurgents at last, they face death. The opening scene is New York in December. The steamer Aztec waits at her East River pier below Brooklyn Bridge, among drifting ice.
49766-some-famous-women:
Louise Creighton wrote Some Famous Women, published by Longmans, Green and Company in London in 1909. Creighton also wrote first histories of England and France and a life of Edward the Black Prince. Her book gives short lives of twelve women, from early saints to Victorian travellers, each with illustrations.

The subjects begin with Saint Hilda and Joan, the Fair Maid of Kent. Jeanne d'Arc and Margaret Beaufort follow. Later chapters treat Rachel, Lady Russell, and the prison reformer Elizabeth Fry. The scientist Mary Somerville and the traveller Isabella Bird appear near the end, with Florence Nightingale between them. Creighton wrote for general readers and schools, offering women from church, court, and public life whose stories show very different kinds of work and fame across a thousand years of history.
4984-the-hidden-children:
Three riders draw bridle in the middle of the Bedford Road in this Revolutionary War novel, facing a tavern shot to splinters. The sign dangles by one hinge. Buckshot mars the freshly painted house. Blue paper fills broken windows. A wanton fire has been set at the northeast corner. The misused house seems to watch them out of patched eyes.

The hidden children of the title move through this war-torn country, where loyalty, danger, and family secrets cross. The work arrives without a named author here. Readers get a romance of the American Revolution, atmospheric in its ruined taverns and roads, and centered on young people caught in a war larger than themselves.
4996-number-seventeen:
Number Seventeen opens outside a London theater in drizzle, where a red-faced commissionaire pockets sixpences summoning cabs for playgoers leaving Daly's latest musical comedy. All London, as the phrase goes, flocks to the show. Most of the crowd owns no motor cars and cannot afford taxicabs. So they hurry on foot toward tubes and omnibuses.

Into that ordinary crowd steps a mystery, centered on the title's number seventeen. The record carries no author byline. Readers get an Edwardian London thriller that begins with theater crowds and rain. Then it draws its hero into a puzzle where a number, a cab, and a stranger matter more than they first seem.
50057-the-early-cave-men:
Katharine Elizabeth Dopp wrote The Early Cave-Men, Book II in an industrial and social history series, issued in 1904. Dopp taught at the University of Chicago. The book, subtitled The Age of Combat, was made for the primary grades. It holds a map and many drawings by Howard V Brown.

Stories follow the Fire Clan as they win a cave and spend their first night in it. They get rid of Sabre-tooth, hold a feast, and make the cave ready for winter. Later tales show them boring holes in trophies, making new weapons, and dressing skins for clothes. A flood, a council, and a journey to the Fire Country follow. Strongarm makes a great discovery near the end.
5007-the-poisoned-pen:
A reporter narrator hurries uptown from the Star office to find his friend packing in haste for Danbridge, and this mystery opens with a suitcase lying open on a bed. Clean laundry goes in without its wrapping paper, and five minutes is all the time allowed before the six o'clock train, because Danbridge is on everybody's lips.

The quiet Connecticut town is the scene of a notorious case, and the two men travel to investigate it. The author goes unnamed in the catalog record. Readers get a detective story in the newspaper tradition, where a journalist's nose for news drives the inquiry and a small town hides a large crime.
50077-maternity-letters-from-working-wom:
Maternity is a book of letters from working women about pregnancy and childbirth, published in London by Bell. The head of the text carries adverts for kindred books of social study. One is Round About a Pound a Week, by Pember Reeves, praised as the best piece of social study published in England for many years. Another treats the feeding of school children.

The illustration shows an annual congress of the Women's Co-operative Guild. It was through such bodies that working women's testimony was gathered and printed. The letters tell, in the women's own words, what it meant to bear children on a working-class wage. They speak of food forgone and work kept up to the last day. They speak of fears and of costs. Books of this kind changed social policy by evidence.
50242-ludwig-van-beethoven:
Pitts Sanborn wrote a booklet on Ludwig van Beethoven, first held under rights in 1939 by a New York concert society. An editors note says Sanborn first called it Beethoven and his Nine Symphonies and made no claim to fresh finds. The editor kept those pages near whole and added matter on other major works.

Concert works, overtures, piano and song works, and chamber music join the nine great works for full band in the added parts. Beethoven was born on December 16, 1770, at Bonn on the lower Rhine, the booklet states. His grand father, a Flemish singer, came to Bonn young and rose as a court music maker there.
50371-when-gretel-was-fifteen:
Nina Rhoades wrote a girls' novel published in August 1921, drawn by Elizabeth Withington. Rhoades had written Marion's Vacation, Dorothy Brown, and the Brick House books for younger readers. Contents open with the girls at Miss Minton's school. Easter in war time and breaking up day follow.

At Miss Minton's long supper table, twelve pupils and five teachers sit in silence. The head's hand trembles slightly as she lays down the evening paper. Every face grows grave at once, for they all know what the news means. The wartime opening sets the tone. Gretel at fifteen faces school, friendship, and the shadow of war in the chapters ahead.
50520-early-french-prisons-le-grand-and-:
Major Arthur Griffiths, a former prison inspector in Great Britain, wrote Early French Prisons as part of a history of crime from early times to the present day. The volume treats the Grand and Petit Chatelets, Vincennes, the Bastille, Loches, the galleys, and the prisons of the French Revolution.

Griffiths starts with the feudal age and the first Paris prisons, then traces fights with kings, the rise of Richelieu, and the power of the Bastille. Later chapters cover the man in the iron mask, poison scares, life on the galleys, and the last days of the Bastille. Lists of noted prisoners and clear chapter guides make the old system easy to follow.
50764-colour-in-the-flower-garden:
Gertrude Jekyll's Colour in the Flower Garden (Country Life Library, 1908) teaches planting as painting, the garden composed in colour month by month and border by border. A March study and a border of early bulbs open the course. Then come the wood, the spring garden, and the weeks between spring and summer, each with plans and photographs.

The June garden and the main hardy flower border stand at the center, followed by the borders in July, August, and September. Special chapters treat gardens of one colouring, climbing plants, plants in pots, wood and shrubbery edges, and a beautiful fruit garden. Planting for winter colour and a closing word on form in planting end the lessons. Jekyll writes for owners who will work their own ground, and her plans show exactly where every plant is to go.
50783-the-alien:
Raymond F Jones writes a book-length novel in The Alien, an original unabridged publication of World Editions, copyrighted in 1951 at New York. The publisher's blurb imagines archaeology among the stars: relics of a race extinct for half a million years, a race that held the secret of restoring life. One member of that race can be brought back after 500,000 years of death.

Chapter one puts the laboratory ship Lavoisier beyond the orbit of Mars, riding with the Smithson Asteroidal Expedition. Doctor Delmar Underwood radios Doctor Illia Morov at Terrestrial Medical Central, inviting her out to the fragments for a month.
50872-not-fit-for-children:
Not Fit for Children is a science fiction story by Evelyn Smith. The Project Gutenberg text was taken from Galaxy Science Fiction for May 1953. Its tag line asks which side, in trade between worlds, counts as the natives.

The tale is told among a family of stranded beings who speak mind to mind. Two youngsters, Qan and Ppon, hide their sharper thoughts from their mother. Their grandfather works on a slow change of form that should let the family go home. The children are warned that grave matters are not fit for them. The joke of the title is that the young ones know far more than the grown ones think.
51185-all-jackson-s-children:
Daniel F Galouye wrote All Jackson's Children, a tale from Galaxy Science Fiction in January 1957, with art by Finlay. A front line says the folk's chances hung on a prayer they had to answer themselves. Angus McIntosh rubs grime from the name plate of a wrecked cargo carrier. Bruce Drummond stands with him in a vine filled gorge.

The plate reads RT 3070 VG Two, a Vegan robot trader. Drummond grins at the salvage worth of its robots. Angus urges a swift exit at once. The hold is empty though the ship came down full, he notes. Robot crews must serve a built in drive, he warns. No one knows what drive this crew holds. The tale turns on that risk.
51293-the-law-and-medical-men:
Vashon Rogers wrote The Law and Medical Men, a small handbook printed at Toronto and Edinburgh in eighteen eighty-four. Rogers was a barrister of Osgoode Hall, and he signs his preface from Kingston in November of that year. He hopes the book fills a small gap on the shelves of both doctors and lawyers. It is meant, he says, as a primer, not a full survey.

Short parts treat early practice and laws, fees, and who should pay the doctor. Later parts take up who may practise, neglect and malpractice, and crime in practice. Witness work, experts, and experts in insanity cases each get a part. Defamation, ties with patients, dissection, dentists, and druggists round out the book. Rogers acts as a compiler, giving the words of judges in most cases.
514-little-women:
Louisa May Alcott follows the four March sisters through Civil War years and beyond in this beloved novel. Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy live in modest Concord with their mother while their father serves as chaplain. Christmas without gifts, plays, picnics, and neighbor Laurie fill part one; weddings, work, and loss fill part two.

Alcott writes with warmth, humor, and plain moral sense, letting Jo's pen and Beth's music carry the heart. The book grew from Alcott's own family life, yet it speaks to any home. It endures as a classic of girlhood, where love, work, and pluck shape four very different lives.
51552-war-stories-for-my-grandchildren:
Veteran officer John Foster printed his Civil War memoir in Washington in 1918 for private circulation. He wrote for his grandchildren, and the contents trace his service in clear order. Chapters cover the Missouri campaign, Fort Donelson, Shiloh, Corinth and Memphis, guerrilla warfare in Kentucky, East Tennessee, and service with the Hundred Days Men, plus an appendix.

The narrative starts with the Twenty-fifth Indiana Infantry at Evansville and its move to St Louis in Missouri. Foster quotes his own early letter home at length, urging his wife to bear parting with courage. That mix of campaign fact and family letter gives the memoir its shape. Readers get battles and marches told by a veteran who kept the home front in view.
51589-the-rag-and-bone-men:
Algis Budrys wrote The Rag and Bone Men, a science fiction story printed in Galaxy Magazine in February 1962. The narrator, who calls himself Maurer, walks up a hill with a man named Charpantier. Both carry bags for the Foundation, gathering Earthly parts for a man they call the Veld. Maurer remarks that he no longer thinks the Veld sane. Charpantier asks how one would determine that.

The blurb states the situation plainly. An unfortunate castaway is marooned far from home, with nothing to share his loneliness but humans. The gathered parts are absurdly specific: six radio tubes, three pieces of Lucite a quarter inch thick, a roll of wire, a heat lamp. The Veld wants to build something unEarthly out of Earthly parts. Budrys turns a junk-collecting errand into an uneasy story about who is mad, the builder or the men who humour him.
51653-wenonah-s-stories-for-children:
Wenonah's Stories for Children is a children's book by Clara Louise Burnham and Warren Proctor. It was printed at Boston by the Harmony Shop, with copyright in 1918. The book is inscribed to Edith Bullen.

Lois Robbins is ten years old and her brother Harold is eight. The book opens with their sharp disappointment: they are not going to the seashore this summer. Their father tries to cheer them. He warns them not to make up their minds against a good time. That, he says, is like turning a bowl upside down, so that nothing can run into it. The trip takes the children into the country where the Indians roamed. There they meet Wenonah, whose stories give the book its name and its heart.
5172-aladdin-o-brien:
Gouverneur Morris's novel follows Aladdin O'Brien, a boy who grows into a young man of charm, mischief, and restless ambition. The book opens with a Sunday-school walk that turns into a forbidden river outing with Margaret, and its three books trace Aladdin from childhood pranks toward love, work, and the wider world.

Morris writes with humour and sentiment, giving Aladdin a storyteller's gift and a habit of exaggerating his own exploits. The novel offers a light, nostalgic portrait of American boyhood and young manhood, in the manner of the popular romances of the early twentieth century.
51777-other-fools-and-their-doings-or-li:
Other Fools and Their Doings shows life among the freedmen. One Who Has Seen It signs the title page. J S Ogilvie and Company issued it at New York in 1880. Thirteen chapters carry the tale. The Bean Island People open the action. The scene is South Carolina in April 1876.

Deacon Atwood and Captain Black ride a sandy road there. Heat slows their horses on that ride. Chapters run through Distrust and a Glorious Fourth. Legal Redress and a thickening cloud build the plot. Portentous Darkness fills chapter eight. An attack and a massacre raise the stakes high. The Scallawag closes the chapter list. A front plate shows a tense meeting at page 190. Fiction of the postwar South, the book shows its era's hard views in the plain speech of its own time.
51779-our-sentimental-garden:
Our Sentimental Garden is a garden chronicle by Agnes and Egerton Castle. Lippincott issued it in Philadelphia, and Heinemann in London, in 1914. Charles Robinson drew the illustrations for the garden tale. The Castles inscribe it to kind neighbours at Rogate, the Wyndhams by name. Those friends saw grace in the wildest tangle from the very start.

A poem to Villino Loki opens the chronicle in verse and song. Over the hills and far away, a place of flowers crowns a rise. There the year runs from May to May in a breath of paradise. Small furry things at play meet the eye with perfect trust there. Month by month the garden's making and moods fill the prose.
5179-a-siren:
Thomas Adolphus Trollope's novel A Siren opens on Ash Wednesday morning in Ravenna, after the last night of carnival. It then turns back four months to show how its story began. Its books follow singers, a marchese, an impresario, and a young woman whose voice. Charm draws men into rivalry, as carnival glitter gives way to quieter consequences.

Trollope, brother of the more famous Anthony, sets the tale in the Papal States, among theatres, churches, and provincial society. The novel mixes romance with Italian local colour, and it will appeal to readers who enjoy nineteenth-century stories of art, ambition, and love in an old Italian city.
52124-the-joyful-wisdom-la-gaya-scienza-:
Friedrich Nietzsche's Joyful Wisdom, or La Gaya Scienza, forms volume ten of his complete works in the authorised English translation edited by Oscar Levy, published at Edinburgh in 1910. Thomas Common translated the prose. Paul V Cohn and Maude D Petre rendered the poetry. A verse motto has the poet staying confined to his own house, mocking every master mind that never mocked itself.

An appendix prints the songs of Prince Free as a Bird, dated from Ruta near Genoa in autumn 1886. Translator's notes explain wordplay, like doubling a number unfairly. The Gay Science is Nietzsche's sunniest book, mixing aphorism and song. Levy's edition first gave English readers the whole Nietzsche.
52190-ecce-homo-complete-works-volume-se:
Ecce Homo is the self tale of Friedrich Nietzsche, in English dress by Ludovici, with its verse turns made by a team of hands. It stands as the seventeenth part of the first full set of his works in English, shaped by a named editor. The set came out at Edinburgh and London in the early nineteen hundreds.

A hymn to life, set to music by the author in his youth, stands at the head of the part. Lines from his great work on the prophet of the desert fall like figs from a tree in its first pages. Good and sweet, they burst their red skins as they drop, the quote says. A north wind for ripe figs is their voice to his friends.
52302-those-brewster-children:
Florence Morse Kingsley's Those Brewster Children was published by Dodd, Mead at New York in 1910, with illustrations by Emily Hall Chamberlain. The story opens at dusk on a winter afternoon: Elizabeth Brewster sits at her sewing-room window watching her three children pile damp snowballs on the lawn. Carroll is tall and sturdy for eight years, Doris slim with reddish blond hair, and Baby Richard, three, toils to keep up with the others.

Mrs Brewster calls them in from the cold, then finds the Norwegian maid Celia has let the range overheat and the saucepans boil furiously. The frontispiece caption promises that the occasion was not wholly barren of material for a trained psychologist. Kingsley also wrote The Singular Miss Smith and And So They Were Married. The novel is domestic comedy of a young family's household, told from the mother's tired, amused viewpoint.
52314-nooks-and-corners-being-the-compan:
Nooks and Corners is a home craft guide by J Panton. The book is the mate to a past guide that ran from kitchen to garret. Prints show hall plans, buffets, and stair glass in the new home taste. The book came out in London in the year eighteen eighty nine.

Parts treat the move, the hall, snug nooks, and the room for billiards. A plea asks if the child room should be done away with in plan. Girls rooms, christening feasts, and the sick room earn parts in turn. Tips on boys, home bills, and trips for a change close the guide. The work served wives who ran the great homes of the age.
52339-ancient-scottish-lake-dwellings-or:
Ancient Scottish Lake-Dwellings or Crannogs, with a supplementary chapter on remains of lake-dwellings in England, is an archaeological work by Robert Munro published by David Douglas of Edinburgh in 1882. A plate of Lochspouts, looking northwards, fronts the volume.

Munro explains in his preface that his first object was a record, for general readers, of remarkable discoveries lately made in the south-west of Scotland. The branch of archaeology was until then little known. Reports of the work had appeared in the collections of the Ayrshire and Wigtownshire Archaeological Association, at the urging of Cochran-Patrick, who proposed this handier volume. Munro widened the plan, adding a survey of earlier writers and explorers, so that the book stands as a compendium of all then known about ancient British lake-dwellings.
52420-the-new-departure-or-thoughts-for-:
E Hoare, vicar of Trinity, Tunbridge Wells and honorary canon of Canterbury, wrote a penny pamphlet of thoughts for loyal churchmen, reprinted from The Churchman and sold by Elliot Stock at London. It is one of the difficulties of perfect fairness in controversy, Hoare begins, that we often cannot ascertain the real opinions of considerable bodies of men. This is especially so, he says, when people are not united as a corporate body.

Without a corporate statement, he argues, there is no dogmatic or authoritative account of their views. The new departure of the title is a church party's turn he resists. Penny pamphlets were the Victorian church's pamphlet war ammunition. Hoare was a leading evangelical spokesman.
52452-it-might-have-happened-to-you-a-co:
It Might Have Happened to You is a portrait of Central and Eastern Europe by Coningsby Dawson. John Lane published it in New York and London in 1921. Its subtitle calls the book contemporary, written in the war's raw aftermath. The title is an argument aimed straight at the comfortable reader.

The first chapter presses that argument without mercy. Your safety, Dawson tells the reader, was an accident of birth. No merit of your own kept the disaster from your door. The chapters then tour the broken lands the title warns about. Christmas Eve in Vienna and a hospital in Buda appear early. The soul of Poland, an imperial bread-line, and Poland's common man follow. The book closes on a Europe suspended between peace and war.
52664-prehistoric-men:
Prehistoric Men by Robert J Braidwood, a Chicago Natural History Museum popular volume first issued in 1948, explains how science reads the time before writing. Braidwood notes that more than 99 per cent of man's story is prehistory: humans are at least half a million years old, but writing began only about 5,000 years ago. The record left behind is things, not books, and several kinds of scientists study it together.

Ten chapters move from how we learn, through the changing world and cultural beginnings, to early moderns, the first revolution of farming, and the end of prehistory. Braidwood was a research associate at the University of Chicago's Oriental Institute; drawings are by Susan T Richert.
5269-driven-back-to-eden:
E. P. Roe's Driven Back to Eden, first serialised in St Nicholas magazine, tells a simple story written expressly for young people. Roe, doubting whether he could beguile honest little critics with words that did not tell an interesting story. Roe aimed to present an experience that might be verified in real life, avoiding all that was merely fanciful.

The tale follows a family driven back to a simpler, country life, finding in Eden a place of work, faith, and renewal. Readers get a gentle, moral story for the young, in the manner of nineteenth-century family fiction, where hardship teaches contentment and home becomes a garden again.
52827-for-the-sake-of-the-soldier-volunt:
For the Sake of the Soldier is a book on the free work of the wives of a north town in the great war, by Rita Macleod. Three poems in it are past leave of a day sheet of that town, on the men in the ditches, on a great fight town, and on the come back. Its front words praise the work of wives past all the lands of the realm.

Brave heart, calm, self bar, and self gift, with tire less work and zeal, make a host of gifts, that front says. Those gifts go past way to pay for the dread loss and shock wives have borne. In this land too the wives rose to the hour as fast as their kin in any part of the world. No count can do full right to the work they have done and still do, it holds.
52924-the-colleen-bawn-or-the-brides-of-:
Dion Boucicault wrote The Colleen Bawn, or the Brides of Garryowen, a home drama in three acts. The play was printed but not published, with its first cast named in full. It opened at Laura Keene's Theater in New York on March 27, 1860. Boucicault took the part of Myles na Coppaleen himself. Laura Keene played Anne Chute, and Agnes Robertson played Eily O'Connor, the colleen bawn of the title.

Hardress Cregan, Danny Mann, Kyrle Daly, and Father Tom fill out the cast. Dress notes set the time in the last years of the 1700s, with broad-skirted coats and top boots. Father Tom wears a broad-brimmed hat, worn black suit, and white cravat. The printed play lets readers stage, in the mind, a famed Irish drama of love and class.
52946-three-sides-of-paradise-green:
Augusta Huiell Seaman wrote this girls' novel, printed at New York in 1918. Two school friends at Bridgeton High School start journals at the wish of a loved teacher. The book takes its shape from those journal pages and from life at a place called Paradise Green.

A strange man known only as Monsieur brings a mystery into their days. Chapters turn on two mishaps, a search of his room, a portrait, and finds made by a sharp young friend known as the Imp. The tale runs to August 1914, when war news breaks in. School life, friendship, and a slow-solved puzzle carry the story to its close.
53007-observations-on-the-diseases-of-se:
Observations on the Diseases of Seamen, by Gilbert Blane, is here in a second edition, printed in London in 1789, with fixes and additions. Blane was a doctor to the Prince of Wales, to the Duke of Clarence, and to St Thomas Hospital. The book is split into parts and books, by time.

The first book gives the medical history of the fleet from March 1780 to July 1781. Chapters take the fleet health in blocks of months. The second book runs from August 1781 to the end of the war in April 1783. Readers get a naval doctor own record of sickness at sea, kept fleet by fleet and month by month in wartime.
53098-the-mary-frances-garden-book-or-ad:
The Mary Frances Garden Book, or Adventures Among the Garden People, is by Jane Eayre Fryer. William F Zwirner illustrated it for the John C Winston Company at Philadelphia, copyright 1916. Fryer dedicates it to all boys and girls who love to help things grow.

A plate shows the garden which Mary Frances and Billy planted. Companion volumes teach cooking among the kitchen people and sewing among the thimble people, in the same story form. A caution page warns that the stringent new copyright law protects text and illustrations alike against any reproduction.
53099-willow-pollen:
Jeannette Marks wrote poems issued at Boston in 1921 by the Four Seas Company. She gave the book to the memory of her mother, Jeannette Holmes Colwell Marks. A long proem in free lines praises a woman who bore the griefs of others in silence and wind and sky.

The title poem is dated June 3, 1920, at Fleur de Lys on Lake Champlain, where rain falls like apple blooms and bees move in willow pollen. Scores of short poems follow, on stars, bread, work, sea gulls, and a railroad station. Place poems name Ravello, Chester on the Dee, and the river Seiont, and lost love threads the last pages.
53144-correspondence-of-the-family-of-ha:
Edward Maunde Thompson edited this set of family letters for the Camden Society, printed in 1881. The Haddocks of Leigh, in Essex at the mouth of the Thames, took to the sea early, and the letters run from 1657 to 1719. Thompson traces the line to Captain Richard Haddock, who served in the Parliamentary Navy under the Commonwealth.

Richard held command of the ship Victory in 1642 and got a reward of £40 for good service in 1652. For more than a hundred years, Haddock sons followed fathers into the Navy, many of them also named Richard.
53262-manners-for-men:
Manners for Men, by Mrs Humphry, was published at London in 1897. Bowden issued it from Henrietta Street, Covent Garden, in that year. A first edition in February was followed by a second in March, the page boasts. Woman ideal man opens the contents at page one of the guide.

In the street, in a carriage, and in a hansom follow as early chapters. Smoking, the omnibus, and horseback fill the next heads of the contents. Dinner parties, public dinners, and restaurants get long treatment in the list. Five o clock tea, the play, and the ball come after in the roll. Dress, country life, and visiting cards close the heads shown in the book. Madge of Truth tells Victorian men how to behave in every room.
53366-the-book-of-fair-women:
The Book of Fair Women was published in New York in 1922 by Alfred Knopf, with thirty-two plates from photographs by Hoppe and an introductory essay by Richard King. The portraits are arranged by country and named one by one. America leads with Lady Lavery, Mrs Lydig Hoyt, and Miss Marion Davies among its five.

Princess White Deer stands for the Red Indian portraits, Lady Diana Duff-Cooper and Miss Gladys Cooper for England, Tortola Valencia for Spain, and Mrs Wellington Koo for China. A preparer's note, added to this copy, warns that the introduction is a product of its time in its ideas about race. It credits the book, though, for including portraits of non-white women at all. King opens by staging a battle of words between Beauty and Ugliness over old maxims.
53423-better-than-men:
Better Than Men is a book of animal sketches by Rush Hawkins, published by Bouton at New York in 1896. Hawkins dedicates it to his beloved wife, whose goodness passes all understanding. The contents name the players: Tim the dissipated, Carlo the soldier, Jeff the inquisitive, and Toby the wise. Two dogs and two innocents abroad follow, with a piece on Columbus by an old showman.

In his opening Hawkins explains his serious proposition. The sketches present traits of the lower animals worthy of the human animal's attention. To write so that readers infer that certain animals are better than men in some elemental virtues is, he owns, rather imprudent. To the optimist it may even appear irreverent. He holds that men are born morally corrupt, as the fall of Adam is said to have left them.
53650-mothers-to-men:
Zona Gale, author of Friendship Village, published a novel at New York in 1911. It opens in dark and driving rain on a highway, where a small boy plucks at the coat of the man tramping ahead of him. The child complains that the hole near his biggest toe chokes his toe awful.

The man squats in the mud and offers his back, but the boy runs on, resolved to see if he could walk all the way. As they go, the child asks what velvet is. The word came into his head among nice things, yet it sounds like a coffin too. Behind that lies the black velvet coffin of his mother, which the father had no money to buy.
53762-the-somme-volume-2-the-second-batt:
Michelin published a guide to the battlefields of the Somme, and volume two covers the second battle of 1918 around Amiens, Montdidier, and Compiègne. The guide was made for visitors touring the ground by motor car soon after the war. It mixes travel help with a careful account of the fighting.

Lists of hotels in Amiens and Compiègne, with phone numbers and map notes, serve the tourist first. The narrative then sets out the plains of Picardy between the Ancre, Avre, and Oise rivers. It places the German drive that opened on March 21, 1918, and the fighting that followed. Readers get routes, maps, and history in one volume built to be used on the ground where the battles were fought.
54050-little-wideawake-a-story-book-for-:
Sale Barker wrote this story book for little children, published in London and New York in 1877 with four hundred pictures. Its title is Little Wide-Awake, and the first story in the hosted copy is headed Some of My Little Friends. It begins by introducing Rosie, a bright girl with blue eyes and fair hair.

Rosie is ten, strong, merry, and a bit of a romp. At Christmas at Cranley Grange, her home in the country, her older brother Charlie is coming home from school for the holidays. The narrator drives to the station with Rosie and her younger brother Frank, and the children jump about so much that the whole ride is one long fright.
54054-historical-record-of-the-twelfth-o:
Richard Cannon compiled the Historical Record of the Twelfth, or the East Suffolk, Regiment of Foot, issued in London in 1848. The book gives the regiment's formation in 1685 and its subsequent services to 1847, with plates. Cannon worked at the Adjutant-General's Office, Horse Guards.

A general order of January 1, 1836, printed in front, explains the series: the king commanded that the services of every regiment be published, with its stations, battles, sieges, and trophies. The names of officers and men killed, wounded, or honored were to be recorded too. Badges and devices borne by the corps, and the causes for which they were granted, were to be set down as well. Official memory is the aim.
54055-letters-to-children:
Bridgman, a missionary in China, wrote Letters to Children about the country he served. The Massachusetts Sabbath School Society of Boston published them, and a second edition appeared in 1838. Eighteen letters, each a short lesson, carry the whole survey.

The index shows the plan. The first letter sorts the Chinese religions: the followers of Confucius, of the Tao, and of Buddha. Temples, priests, and idols follow, then pagodas. Soldiers, merchants, mechanics, farmers, scholars, and sailors each get a letter. The condition of women, the marriage ceremony, and the great crimes of lying, gambling, and bribery fill the middle letters. Two letters praise the translators: Morrison, who put the Bible into Chinese, and Milne. American children learned China from a missionary's pen.
54106-neighbours-on-the-green:
Oliphant gathered nine tales of village life in Neighbours on the Green, printed by Macmillan in 1889. She called them old wives' tales and gave the book to old friends of the place. The tales all spring from Dinglefield Green, a broad triangle of soft grass with pretty houses round it. None of the folk there, the teller says, were very rich.
