The first tale treats her neighbour Nelly and her sister Martha. Others bear the names Lady Denzil, Lady Isabella, and a stockbroker at Dinglewood. A tale of science, a tale of an elderly romance, and one of a widow's fortune fill out the set. The last is called My Faithful Johnny. Oliphant writes with a warm, sly eye for rank, money, and love in a small place where all know all.
54135-whist-or-bumblepuppy-thirteen-lect:
Pembridge published 'Whist or Bumblepuppy?' in London in 1895, in a revised and enlarged edition of thirteen lectures addressed, with a wink, to children. Reviewers quoted at the front call it the best attempt yet seen to shame very bad players into trying to improve. The Field praises its sensible maxims dressed up in amusing and palatable form, and the Sunday Times calls it one of the soundest books on whist ever written.

Lectures begin with an introduction and the lead, then take up the play of the second, third, and fourth hand. Discarding and its difficulties follow, with more lectures on the points most needed for a complete knowledge of the game. Pembridge writes as a counsellor: even a mediocre player, the notices claim, can scarcely find a better one.
54473-vanderdecken:
Vanderdecken is a sea tale by H De Vere Stacpoole. The author had fame from a blue lagoon tale of isle love. Its name is that of the ghost sea chief of the Flying Dutchman lore. The book came out in New York in the year nineteen twenty two.

Parts move from a plan and a scheme to whale bays and isle camps. Signs of banned trade goods and a night raid raise the stakes at sea. A sea fight, a below decks turn, and a new chum fill the mid run. Strange men on a beach and a lost lad named Tommie mark the close. Old myth and new crime mix in the brisk salt tale.
54561-the-old-east-indiamen:
The Old East Indiamen is a maritime history by Keble Chatterton, a lieutenant in the naval volunteer reserve. The head of the text carries a list of travel books from the same publisher, on Nigeria, China, New Zealand, and Siam. A plate shows the East Indiaman Thomas Coutts as she appeared in the year 1826.

The East Indiamen were the great ships of the East India Company, carrying tea, silk, and spices between London and the East for two centuries. They were merchantmen built like warships, sailing in convoy under company discipline, and their captains ranked as a sea aristocracy. Chatterton wrote sea history for general readers in the last years of sail's memory. His book gathers the ships, the voyages, the fights with French cruisers and pirates, and the slow end of the trade when steam and free commerce broke the company's world.
54606-the-flower-garden:
Ida D Bennett wrote a handbook on the flower garden for country homes. McClure, Phillips and Company issued the book in New York, rights from 1903. It stands in The Country Home Library of practical guides. Early chapters treat the garden's place and plan, soils, and fertilizers.

Hotbeds, cold frames, seed buying, and starting seeds in flats follow in order. Window boxes, vines, bulbs, and foliage plants fill the later parts. A plate praises sweet alyssum and golden saxatile for rockwork use. Home gardeners gain a full, plain course from seed to bloom.
54685-half-a-dozen-housekeepers-a-story-:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote a story for girls in six chapters, printed at Philadelphia in 1903 with pictures by Mills Thompson. March came in like a lion that year in Maine, and pussy willows shivered in their brown skins. Girls at the Wareham Female Seminary still skated and slid in the afternoons and read Virgil by a window seat.

Bell Winship, a born leader among the girls, sends five small notes one morning to five friends. Each note asks for the honour of a meeting at ten sharp in room twenty seven on the second floor. Her test, named in the first chapter head, is about to begin for the six.
54703-things-to-be-remembered-in-daily-l:
Things to Be Remembered in Daily Life is a small book of moral thoughts. John Timbs wrote it, known for a past book of odd facts. It came out in London in the year 1863 in a neat form. Time and man's life are the great themes of its short pages.

Timbs owns the themes are vast for so small a book in the hand. He likens it to the old dream of the world in a nut shell. Books breed fast, and the age calls for the pith of things, he says. He draws great truths from the quick and the dead in short cuts. Sketches of men of his own day give the book a fresh hook. Tales from the past are not left out of the mix he made. A pair of lines on fame and shame states the aim of the whole.
54761-children-of-men:
Bruno Lessing wrote Children of Men, a book of short stories published in New York by McClure, Phillips and Company in 1903. A line from Lamentations gives the title: He doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men. A picture of sheep coming over a hill stands at the front.

Twenty-three stories fill the contents, and their titles map the Jewish New York of the garment trade. The Sader Guest, The Poisoned Chai, and Urim and Thummim draw on ritual and law. A Yiddish Idyll and Hannukah Lights turn to home and feast. The Americanisation of Shadrach Cohen faces the new country head on. The first tale opens in a shop where 30 sewing machines whir like devils. Readers get the immigrant East Side told from inside.
54830-the-graves-of-the-fallen:
The Graves of the Fallen is a short account of the work of the Imperial War Graves Commission, written by Rudyard Kipling at the Commission's request. The pictures, by Douglas Macpherson, show the cemeteries and memorials as they will look when finished.

The book first names the Commission itself. Its members include the war, colonies, and India secretaries, with members named by Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and Newfoundland. Kipling himself sat among the members named by royal warrant. The account then tells how the Commission began in the first days of the war. It sets out how the graves of the fallen were found, marked, and gathered into lasting cemeteries.
54965-miss-beecher-s-domestic-receipt-bo:
Miss Beecher wrote the Domestic Receipt Book in 1846. Harper and Brothers issued it at New York. The book supplements her Treatise on Domestic Economy. Five aims shape its preface. First, a fresh set of receipts fills it. Plain, well-cooked dishes for daily comfort lead.

Second, each receipt passed the test of fine housekeepers. None was copied from other books, she states. Best practical cooks gave their own trials here. Third, each receipt stands short, simple, and clear. Any domestic who can read may use it, she says. Fourth, small dinner parties get full coaching. Young housekeepers gain ease from that help. Fifth, rich dishes for company stand beside healthful ones. Catharine Beecher's kitchen manual brought system and conscience to the American cookstove.
54982-a-text-book-of-diseases-of-women:
Charles Penrose, formerly professor of gynecology in the University of Pennsylvania, published his 'Text-Book of Diseases of Women' in a sixth edition, revised, with Saunders in 1908. The book carries 225 illustrations and a long reprint history back to 1897. In his preface to the sixth edition Penrose says he has made the changes and additions that growth of knowledge in his field required.

Penrose writes for the medical student and tries to give the best teaching of modern practice without old theories. For most diseases he recommends only one plan of treatment, hoping to avoid confusing the student or the doctor who consults the book. Contents begin with the general causes of disease in women and methods of examination, then move to diseases of the external genitals, the vagina, and the perineum.
54990-the-brown-brethren:
Patrick MacGill, author of The Great Push, published a war novel with a New York house in 1917. It opens at the Café Belle Vue near Cassel, crowded at nightfall with soldiers in khaki. A whole division, back from the firing-line, is resting before its return to the trenches.

Even in rest the men see the red agony of war painting the horizon and hear the big guns rumbling far off. A service song heads the chapter, strict on parade and off to the café with his mates. Chapters follow the brown brethren through Christmas Eve and Christmas Day at the front, trench fever, a sniper, and the Somme. MacGill writes from inside the ranks.
55001-in-a-toy-shop-a-christmas-play-for:
Effa Preston wrote In a Toy Shop, a short Christmas play made for small children to perform. The Paine Publishing Company of Dayton, Ohio, issued it, with a 1922 copyright, at a price of 25 cents. The same firm sold song sheets for school programs, and its list of welcome and closing songs faces the play.

The scene is the inside of a toy shop at night. The counter stands at the back of the stage, with stools in front of it. No toys are in sight, since the shop is closed, and the owner stands ready to leave in his hat and coat. Teachers and parents get a simple holiday piece built for young actors, with a single easy set.
55065-american-thumb-prints-mettle-of-ou:
Kate Stephens wrote American Thumb-Prints, essays on the stamp of the nation’s men and women. J B Lippincott issued the book in Philadelphia and London in nineteen hundred five. Stephens gave the book to the memory of her father. He had helped found a law school in eighteen hundred seventy eight.

The first essay, Puritans of the West, takes up Kansas folk. Outsiders called them wild for new causes and crowd fervor. Stephens finds them plain in mind and firm in their own views. Later essays treat a western school town and two Saint Louis neighbors. The New England Woman gets a full study. Ben Franklin and his borrowed jokes close the book on a lighter note.
55137-the-mystery-queen:
The Mystery Queen, by Fergus Hume, was copyright 1912 and published in New York, with illustrations by Howard Somerville. Hume was the author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, The Yellow Holly, and The Opal Serpent. A frontispiece shows a woman crying piteously: take me away, take me away.

Contents list twenty one chapters. A strange visitor opens, then a complete mystery. Duty before pleasure, an amateur detective, and muddy water follow. The inventor, the hermit ladies, and aviation come next. Mahomet coffin, another mystery, and on the trail fill the middle. An amazing adventure, a bold determination, and a busy afternoon follow. Absolute proof, Dan diplomacy, and at bay come later. Queen Beelzebub end and sunshine close the list. Chapter one is headed a penny for your thoughts. Readers get a Hume detective novel of 1912, sensation in every chapter title.
55323-garryowen:
H De Vere Stacpoole wrote a novel printed at New York in 1909, and gave it to his small dog Whisky, called a true sportsman and a loyal friend. Stacpoole had earlier written The Blue Lagoon. Chapter one sets the tale at Drumgool, a great old house as plain as a barn.

Drumgool stands in the roar of the sea, with a moss dressed sea god blowing a shell by the front door. From its top windows the Atlantic shows blue in summer and grey in winter. Round it stretch bogs, gorse, heather, and thirty miles of hills where the golden eagle still haunts the high ground.
55764-dave-porter-s-great-search-or-the-:
Edward Stratemeyer wrote Dave Porter's Great Search, a boys' tale issued in Boston in 1917 with art by Walter Rogers. A front note walks new readers through the whole Dave Porter run, from Oak Hall school days through South Seas trips, gold field hunts, and Bear Camp fun. Dave has now left school and taken up civil engineering as his trade.

The sub title calls the book the perils of a young civil engineer. A long horse ride that whets the boys' hunger fronts the art. Dave's old trait, a keen search for what is lost or hid, drives the plot once more. Stratemeyer keeps the same wide awake American boy, grown now to work, risk, and charge of men.
55775-historical-and-descriptive-narrati:
Stevenson wrote the tale of twenty years spent in South America, and Hurst, Robinson of London published the first volume in 1825. He had been private secretary to the president of Quito, and secretary to Lord Cochrane with the Chilean fleet. A view of Callao, with Lima far off, stands at the front.

The preface argues that the new states, freed in the late revolution, are still near unknown in Europe. A man with first hand matter, Stevenson says, has a duty to print it. He gives the colonies as they stood before the change: their rule, their church, their classes and customs, and their produce. His own travels run through Arauco, Chile, Peru, and Colombia. The revolution itself fills the frame of the work.
55777-historical-and-descriptive-narrati:
Historical and Descriptive Narrative of Twenty Years' Residence in South America, volume two, is a work by Stevenson, printed at London in 1825. Stevenson had served as private secretary to the President of Quito, as governor of Esmeraldas, and as secretary to Lord Cochrane, the vice admiral of Chile. The set runs to three volumes and covers Arauco, Chile, Peru, and Colombia.

The contents of this volume move across Peru in close detail: farms, first wheat, fences, fruit, and beasts. Visits to Caxatambo and Huaras bring mines, ore work, frauds in silver, and the ways of the people. The book also tells of the revolution, its rise, course, and results, from an eyewitness post.
55778-historical-and-descriptive-narrati:
Volume three of Stevenson's Historical and Descriptive Narrative of Twenty Years' Residence in South America came from Hurst, Robinson and Company at London in 1825. Stevenson had been private secretary to the President and Captain General of Quito and later secretary to Lord Cochrane, vice admiral of Chile. The three volumes cover Arauco, Chile, Peru and Colombia, with the revolution's rise, progress and results.

This volume opens with the first revolutionary symptoms at Quito, where Morales, Quiroga and Salinas are seized and a junta forms under the Marquis of Selva Alegre. A second revolution brings the massacre of the prisoners, the coming of Montufar, and Quito taken by Sucre. Lima in 1811, the proclaimed constitution, the Cusco rising and the battle of Chacabuco carry the narrative on.
55818-the-complete-testimony-of-the-fath:
Andrews wrote this Seventh-Day Adventist study, printed at Battle Creek, Michigan, in a second edition of 1876. A publisher's catalogue of Adventist books fills the front pages first. The work itself gathers what the church fathers of the first three centuries said about the Sabbath and the first day.

In his preface Andrews argues that scripture gives thin support for first-day sacredness. Advocates, he says, filled the gap with quotes from early writers, and zeal for a changed Sabbath bent their honesty. No writer, he claims, called the first day the Lord's day until nearly a hundred years after John on Patmos.
55821-from-the-angle-of-seventeen:
From the Angle of Seventeen, by Eden Phillpotts, is a schoolboy novel of 1912. Little, Brown issued the Boston printing in 1914 with rights from 1912. Corkey, head boy of Merivale, narrates his last days at school in it. The Doctor calls him in, and it is not about fireworks at all.

His aunt Augusta, his trustee, has found him a London clerk post instead. The Apollo Fire Office will take him on its staff in a fortnight. Exams in mathematics and grammar stand between him and the job there. Four years short of his majority, he must leave school for business. Youth views work, family, and pride from the angle of seventeen.
5591-the-nuts-a-christmas-story-for-my-c:
Georg Ebers wrote The Nuts as a Christmas story for his children and grandchildren, told by a wounded colonel nursed back to health in the family's house. The colonel may not walk long, and after pottering about, he rests in the comfortable old easy chair known as grandfather's chair. At twilight he lights the last of three pipes the doctor allows him daily, then signs to the children, who gladly obey, loving his stories.

The convalescent must not talk for more than half an hour, so his tales come in measured, cozy installments. Ebers frames the Christmas story as family listening. Readers get a warm holiday tale, told in a chair at twilight, for children gathered close.
55941-beethoven:
Romain Rolland wrote this study of Beethoven, translated by Constance Hull. Henry Holt published it at New York in 1917, with an introduction by Edward Carpenter and a brief analysis of the sonatas, symphonies, and quartets by Eaglefield Hull. Twenty-four musical illustrations and four plates accompany it, with Beethoven at forty-eight, from a painting by Kloeber, as frontispiece.

Carpenter's introduction argues that Beethoven was not only a great musician but a great leader and teacher, who freed the human spirit from petty bonds and recorded the profoundest experiences of life. Rolland, he says, traces the tragedy of Beethoven's life to a liberation of the spirit. He joins it to the composer's democracy and sympathy with the suffering masses, and finds the sense of joy that suffuses the later work. Rolland builds the life from small touches drawn from many writers and biographers.
56287-simplex-munditiis-gentlemen:
A New York guide of 1891, printed at the De Vinne Press, teaches gentlemen how to dress and behave. Part One treats dress by the hour: morning wear, afternoon dress, and evening dress, then the overcoat, and attire for riding, driving, traveling, yachting, and lounging. Further heads cover house wear, linen, underclothing, the art of dressing the collar, and the walking stick and umbrella.

The introduction holds that dress is the embodiment of taste and refinement, and that a man need not be rich to dress well. Simple elegance is the rule: when a thing becomes vulgarly popular, the gentleman casts it aside. The day has three divisions, the morning wear belonging before six, the afternoon dress not worn before two, and the evening dress not before six.
56362-a-troublesome-flock-a-mother-goose:
A Troublesome Flock, printed at Boston in 1916, is Elizabeth Guptill's Mother Goose play for children. Walter Baker sold it at twenty-five cents in his edition of plays. The cast calls for twenty-five children: ten boys and fifteen girls. A note explains that fewer can manage it by cutting or doubling parts.

Old Mother Goose heads the list, with the Old Woman that Lived in a Shoe. Mother Hubbard, Contrary Mary and the Bachelor's Wife follow. Bo Peep, Miss Muffett and Baby Bunting stand among the girls. Jack, Georgie Porgie, Humpty Dumpty, Jack Horner, Simple Simon and Willie Winkie fill the boys' side. The publisher's pages at the front advertise Pinero's plays at fifty cents each.
56404-a-book-of-gems-or-choice-selection:
A Book of Gems arranges choice selections from the writings of Benjamin Franklin, the preacher, not the statesman. Headington and Joseph Franklin arranged the pieces, and John Burns published the book at Saint Louis in 1879. An index to subjects runs for pages, sorted by letter from Campbell's successors onward.

The subjects are church matters through and through: baptism of believers only, communion, church organization, and church membership. Headings treat adhering to the Bible, an apology for creeds, the design of miracles, and bodies resurrected rather than spirits. Short pieces on zeal, controversy, and courtesy in fellowship fill out a handbook of one preacher's teaching, priced for cloth, library, and morocco bindings.
56688-handbook-of-railroad-construction-:
Handbook of Railroad Construction is a work guide by George Vose, a build man of roads of iron. It came out at Boston in eighteen fifty-seven, with past one hundred and fifty plates. Its aim is to give, in the most plain way, all rules, charts, and sums for the place, build, gear, and run of rail roads. A quote from a great war chief heads the book.

Vose notes that build men of the United States are oft not schooled for their work. Past the base sums of count and form, the book shows how to size spans of wood, stone, and iron, walls, piers, track, and steam horse craft. It is meant as a desk mate, not a school book, and gives the plain count each task needs. Great hands of France and England feed its rules.
56692-editha-s-burglar-a-story-for-child:
Editha's Burglar is a story for children by Frances Hodgson Burnett. It was printed at Boston by Jordan, Marsh and Company, with copyright in 1888. The pictures are by Henry Sandham. She gives her leave for her picture to be used in the book.

The list of pictures tells the shape of the tale. Editha spends most of her time in the library reading her father's big books. Burglars break into the house next door, at number eighteen. Her father must go away to Glasgow. A burglar comes to her own house, and the small girl faces him without fear. The man is so taken with her that he laughs until he doubles up. The story became one of Burnett's best loved short tales for the young.
56824-good-form-for-all-occasions-a-manu:
Florence Howe Hall wrote a manual of manners, dress, and entertainment for both men and women, printed at New York and London in 1914. Hall had written Social Usage at Washington. The book stands in a Harper household list beside The Young Mother's Handbook at one dollar and Principles of Correct Dress. Good form at one dollar net was the cheap mark of the shelf.

Calls, cards, weddings, dinners, dress for each hour, and the right word at the right time are the stock of such a guide. Hosts and guests learn what to do and what never to do. Young clerks and brides of the age bought certainty in print. Manners books show a world where one wrong fork could cost a place in good society.
56884-trip-to-the-sunny-south-in-march-1:
Trip to the Sunny South is a travel narrative printed at Birkenhead by Griffith and Son for private circulation. The author signs with initials only, and dates the preface from Bebington in April 1885. The trip was made in March of that year, on a doctor's advice. Doctor Banks prescribed a sea trip, saying it would do more good than any medicine. A companion in the same humour joined, and the pair made for the Mediterranean overland.

Then Genoa, Turin, Leghorn, Pisa, Naples and Rome, down to Reggio. Sicily follows, with Messina, Catania and Syracuse. Malta and Gibraltar close the journey home. The preface reckons six weeks and five thousand miles. It is a Victorian holiday journal, printed for the circle that asked about it.
57125-the-bitter-cry-of-the-children:
The Bitter Cry of the Children is a study of child poverty and child labour by John Spargo, published by Macmillan of New York in 1906. Robert Hunter, author of Poverty, wrote the introduction. A photograph shows a day nursery matron examining a child's throat, flanked by the little mothers who minded babies.

The first chapter is called The Blighting of the Babies. Spargo, a socialist writer, marshals the facts of infant death, sweatshop work, and stunted schooling. The title borrows the cry of an earlier London pamphlet on the poor. His argument is that a rich nation was spending its children. The book became a standard text of the child labour reform movement. It stands with Hunter's Poverty as documentary evidence in the progressive case against industrial neglect.
57297-veiled-women:
Marmaduke Pickthall wrote a novel of veiled women in the near east. The book came out in London in 1913. Pickthall wrote Said the Fisherman in his past works. Nine and twenty parts fill the book's long list in full. Its tale runs more than two score times ten pages in print.

Wives, kin, and town talk drive its home and street scenes. The veil stands as sign and screen in each fresh turn. Pickthall knew those lands from long stays in his own life. His prose keeps a kind eye on all sides of the clash. Talk, faith, and pride mix in the lives he draws. Each part adds a new thread.
57313-the-feeding-of-school-children:
Mildred Emily Bulkley wrote a study of feeding school children, printed at London in 1914 with a first word by Tawney. It came from a London foundation set up to study want. The Ratan Tata Foundation backs research into wages, the cost of living, and ways to bar and ease poverty.

Tawney led the foundation then, and Bulkley served as its secretary. Such studies were printed as books or short papers on the problems of poverty. The foundation also answered letters from any who asked on these themes. A school meal question sat square in its field, since food, health and the pay of workers all met in the child's dinner.
57398-education-of-women:
Carey Thomas, president of Bryn Mawr College, wrote this study of women's education in the United States as number seven in a series of monographs on American education. Nicholas Murray Butler edited the series for the United States Commission to the Paris Exposition of 1900, and the State of New York contributed this volume to the educational exhibit.

Thomas argues that the higher education of women is taking place on a vast scale and in many forms at once. Every phase of the great experiment can therefore be studied side by side. She divides the subject into liberal college education, meant first to train the mind, and professional education aimed at money-making work. Colleges, she notes, fall into three classes: coeducational schools, independent women's colleges, and women's colleges tied to colleges for men.
57482-the-picture-gallery-explored-or-an:
The Picture Gallery Explored is a book of instruction for children, issued in London in 1825. Harvey and Darton published it for young readers. Its subtitle promises an account of ancient customs and manners. Tales and lives of eminent persons are mixed through it. Only the talk between the tales is new, the preface says. The compiler drew the rest from writers of merit.

She tells how she loved true stories as a girl. She sought more facts on the persons she admired. Names off the beaten track are chosen on purpose. A visit to a cousin frames the lessons. Two girls, Ann and Susan, set out on that visit. Dialogue carries the facts from piece to piece. Such books taught history as parlour talk. They aimed to make the past a family pleasure.
57600-the-chinese-kitten:
Edna Brown wrote The Chinese Kitten, copyrighted at Boston in 1922, with pictures by Antoinette Inglis. Brown gives the book to Muff, the dearest kitten. A front picture shows a small box in bright red paper, tied with a white ribbon, wrapped so its finder could not fail to see it. Contents open with the surprise, then at the beach. About Arcturus and friends from home follow.

When school begins, Dora's birthday, and about Boston fill the next heads. Sunday afternoon and the kitten's story come in turn. The victory park, Hallowe'en, a busy Saturday, Thanksgiving, and Christmas close the tale. The first chapter opens in a kitchen. Lucy Merrill whispers to her sister Dora that she thinks Uncle Dan has a surprise for them. Dora is setting the table for supper, and Lucy, in her mother's big apron, is peeling peaches at the dresser.
57614-the-spanish-galleon-being-an-accou:
The Spanish Galleon, an account of a search for sunken treasure in the Caribbean Sea by Charles Sumner Seeley, was published by A C McClurg and Company of Chicago in 1891. The narrator is William Morgan, a lineal descendant of a brother of Henry Morgan, the Welsh buccaneer. He tells the kinship in no spirit of pride, he says, but as a clue to his own bent.

On August 18, 1886, Morgan floated in the Caribbean on a waterlogged chest, west of Martinique. His sloop had capsized in a squall the morning before, drowning her captain and crew. He was bound for a small uninhabited island called Key Seven. Chapters of island life follow: house building, pig hunting, boat building, and bread making. The galleon is found, castaways appear, and treasure trove closes the tale.
57666-famous-leaders-among-men:
Sarah Knowles Bolton wrote life tales of famed men who led their age. Bolton wrote shelf on shelf of such books for the young. Poor boys, girls, authors, and men of science fill her lists. A front plate shows Napoleon in his prime. A quote at the start names grit as the true gap twixt great and small.

Each life shows how drive and firm will lift a man. Weak men fail where strong men push through, she holds. Tales from life, not dry dates, carry her point home. Young readers were her chief aim in all these books. Short lives in clear prose make hard work feel grand. The set suits school and home shelves alike.
57689-the-punishment-of-children:
Felix Adler wrote The Punishment of Children, a short book on right discipline. The Abingdon Press issued it in New York in April nineteen hundred twenty. Adler places it in the American Home Series for parents. Kind cure, not blind rage, is the law of his whole plea.

Man must play doctor to his foes and cure their wrong, Adler holds. How much more, then, to the loved child whose traits mar his days. First rule of all: never punish a child in anger, he says. Socrates told his rude servant he would beat him were he not so mad. Rage grows with our hurt nerves, not with the size of the fault. A small fault can spark a vast storm in a tired parent. Slight faults earn slight pains, grave faults grave ones, by his scale.
57700-toronto-by-gaslight-the-night-hawk:
Toronto by Gaslight is a set of night side sketches by News sheet men. Sheppard brought out this third print in eighteen eighty five at twenty cents. Its next name calls it the night hawks of a great city seen close. The sketches ran in the Toronto Daily News in May and June of that year. Night toil, all night food dens, and cab man tales open its scheme.

Pool boys, gamblers, and sucker fleecers fill the next ranks of vice. Night police sights, cell nights, and court days stand in the scheme. Dance halls, slum homes, and freed jail men crowd mid part names. Grace Marks the girl slayer and child farms give grim turns there. Rail scenes and a corpse on the night fast train close the list.
57799-the-house-of-arden-a-story-for-chi:
The House of Arden: A Story for Children, is by E Nesbit, author of The Story of the Amulet and The Treasure Seekers. T Fisher Unwin published it at London in 1908, illustrated by H R Millar. Nesbit dates the dedication, to John Bland, from Dymchurch in 1908.

Fourteen chapters follow the Arden children through the Mouldiworp, Boney's times, and the landing of the French. A highwayman, a secret panel, Guy Fawkes, and the prisoners in the Tower fill the middle. Elfrida catches the Mouldiworp in one plate, and the finding of the treasure closes the story.
5792-the-stories-mother-nature-told-her-:
The Stories Mother Nature Told Her Children gathers nature tales for young listeners, opening with a starfish on a summer journey. The little starfish has five fingers and five eyes, one at the end of each finger, and more tiny feet than can be counted, though without legs he cannot walk very fast. Later chapters visit Coraltown on Roncador Bank and a child called Little Sunshine.

Each story turns a creature or a season into a gentle lesson about growth, kindness, and the living world. Children meet sea, shore, and sky through personified guides who speak in friendly, clear prose. The book suits read-aloud families and early readers who enjoy Victorian nature stories, where wonder and moral teaching walk hand in hand.
58064-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Grant Allen was put in order by David Widger as a guide to the author's books in that free store. Its first work is the list itself: The British Barbarians, The Woman Who Did, Hilda Wade, and An African Millionaire. Then come the full contents of each book in turn, so a reader can see at a glance what a tale holds before he opens it.

The British Barbarians shows its thirteen heads bare. Biographies of Working Men names its seven lives, from Telford the mason to Edward the shoemaker. The Colonel Clay tales of the Millionaire run in their twelve tricks, from the Mexican Seer to the Old Bailey. Hilda Wade and Recalled to Life stand in full. Book fans get a map of one man's whole shelf in one short roll.
58115-like-another-helen:
Like Another Helen is a novel by George Horton, published in Indianapolis by Bowen-Merrill, with copyrights of 1900 and 1901. Relyea illustrated it. The title line is its motto: and, like another Helen, fired another Troy. Horton dedicates the book, by permission, to Prince George of Greece, high commissioner in Crete.

The frontispiece shows a girl turning a sword hilt toward her father, her head thrown back and her eyes closed. The contents open with youthful enthusiasm and friendly shores, in a comic opera town. A first of May, a demand and a coward, and smoke by day and fire by night lead to war in earnest. An amateur surgeon, a man in a barrel, a deserted town, and an ambush fill the middle chapters. Horton knew Greece and Crete from consular service, and his romance of a new Helen is set in the island's struggle of those years.
58133-twentieth-century-culture-and-depo:
Maud Cooke wrote Twentieth Century Culture and Deportment, or the lady and gentleman at home and abroad, printed at Philadelphia in 1899 with phototype engravings. Rules of etiquette cover calls, invitations, parties, weddings, receptions, dinners, teas, street and public place manners. Dressing well, conversation, courtship, children, letter-writing, and home decoration follow.

Manners make the man, the preface quotes, and all persons should know how to appear to advantage in polite society. The volume promises a complete guide to self-culture for the new century's aspirants. A bride and bridesmaids in wedding dress illustrate the heavily pictured chapter heads throughout the book. Social historians get a full etiquette system.
58333-the-fall-of-man-or-the-loves-of-th:
The Fall of Man, or The Loves of the Gorillas, calls itself a scientific lecture on the Darwinian theory of development by sexual selection. It is credited to a learned gorilla and edited by the author of The New Gospel of Peace. G W Carleton and Company issued the book at New York in 1871, and it was stereotyped at the Women's Printing House. The dedication lays the work at the feet of Charles Darwin.

The editor jokes that no placing could be fitter for the work of Darwin's kinsman, hind-thumbless though his feet be. He adds that a Shakespeare may be but an oyster raised to the one-thousandth power, or a Darwin the cube root of a ring-tailed monkey. The book is a comic squib on the evolution debates of its day, told in the voice of an ape.
5834-bimbi-stories-for-children:
Louise de la Ramee gathers children's stories in Bimbi, opening with The Nurnberg Stove, where August lives in a little town called Hall. Hall, the narrator notes, is a favorite name for towns in Austria and Germany, but this Hall holds August's particular story. Further contents include The Ambitious Rose Tree, Lampblack, The Child of Urbino, and Findelkind, each a fable of art, pride, or kindness.

Readers meet children, artists, and humble folk whose wishes meet magic, loss, and grace in turn. De la Ramee writes with sentiment and moral warmth, favoring beautiful objects and brave hearts over clever twists. The book suits families reading classic children's tales aloud, and readers who enjoy Victorian stories where feeling matters more than realism.
5835-the-story-hour-a-book-for-the-home-:
Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora Smith offer The Story Hour as a book for the home and kindergarten, opening with a Froebel epigraph. Ear and heart, Froebel says, open to the genuine storyteller as flowers open to spring sun and May rain, and the volume that follows puts that belief into practice. An introduction by Wiggin guides parents and teachers in telling stories well.

Here is a classic manual of storytelling, with tales chosen for young children and advice on voice, pacing, and attention. The book treats stories as education through delight, not as lessons in disguise. It suits teachers, parents, and students of early childhood education, and it preserves a Victorian approach to the kindergarten that still charms.
58379-montessori-children:
Montessori Children is a book about the Montessori method by Carolyn Sherwin Bailey. Holt published it in New York in 1915. Posed photographs illustrate the children's work and play. The contents open with a portrait of the doctor herself. With Margherita in the Children's House follows that sketch. That chapter shows the true Montessori environment at work. Valia's chapter treats the physical education of the system. The Freeing of Otello, the Terrible comes next in the list.

That chapter shows conscience awakened through directed will. The Christ in Bruno treats a new spiritual sense. Mario's Finger Eyes shows the sense training of the method. Raffaelo's Hunger presents the teaching of colour and its value. The Going Away of Antonio treats directing the child will. Andrea's Lily gives the nature training of the method. Bailey tells the system through single children and their changes.
58512-when-polly-was-eighteen:
Emma Dowd's novel of a girl at eighteen was published by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1921, and dedicated to Julia Darling Peck. The chapters ahead promise a birthday fête, a letter, and work in a place called Paradise Ward.

The book opens on Chimney Hill in June, where Polly leans against a great oak and studies David's unreadable face. David had been merry at the start of their walk, then shut his lips and fell grave for no plain cause. Polly knows his jealous moods from before college, rarer now but more bitter when they come. Baffled, she asks him outright why he does not laugh.
58581-the-story-of-the-siren:
E M Forster spins a small strange tale in The Story of the Siren, printed by Leonard and Virginia Woolf at the Hogarth Press in 1920. The narrator watches his notebook on the Deist Controversy sink through the Mediterranean, opening like a slate book with pale green leaves. It was meant for his fellowship dissertation, and his aunt sighs that he should have finished it in the hotel.

A boatman strips to dive for it while the party, aunt, chaplain, and colonel among them, sails on to the next grotto. The narrator stays behind on a sunlit rock. Sea light and myth drift together.
58638-rogues-haven:
Rogues’ Haven, a novel by Roy Bridges, was issued at London by Hodder and Stoughton. Bridges had written The Bubble Moon and The Vats of Tyre before it. The book is dedicated to a friend of the author. Its first chapter brings on a man named Bradbury, and the second moves to a hall.

A Mrs Mary Howe and a journey planned fill the early chapters. The journey begun leads through darkness to a band of riders. A green curtained room and a Mr Charles Craike deepen the plot. The scruples of Roger Galt get a chapter of their own. Events at a stone house, and a Captain Ezra Blunt, raise the stakes. The tale has the cut of a romance of rogues, roads, and hidden houses.
58659-resurrection-seven:
Stephen Marlowe wrote this tale of a long space flight and timed awakenings. The tale ran in Worlds of If in May 1952. Ten wonders were planned for the age long flight, the blurb says. Eric wakes in the seventh tub after near two hundred years.

Fluid boils off as his heart speeds to warm his cold body. He lay in deep sleep at one beat each two minutes. Six tubs stand empty, each for a man who lived and died. Each span was twenty five years with a new ship generation.
5890-games-for-hallow-e-en:
Mary Blain gathers party games in Games for Hallow-E'en, published in New York in 1912. Hallow-e'en is the last night of October, she explains. It is the eve or vigil of All-Hallow's or All Saints' Day. No holiday in all the year is so informal or so marked by fun for grown-ups and children alike. The games that follow suit that informal spirit, favoring laughter over ceremony.

You get a practical party book of old-fashioned Halloween amusements, from fortune games to active play. Blain writes plainly for hosts and hostesses planning an evening's fun. The book suits families, teachers, and Halloween enthusiasts curious about how the holiday was celebrated a century ago, and it offers games still playable today with little preparation.
59356-the-almost-men:
The Almost-Men is a science fiction story by Irving Cox the younger. It appeared in Worlds of If in October 1955. A motto opens the tale. All learning, it says, must begin with a need. A people whose old ideas fail must find a new way of thinking.

The story opens before dawn in a prison compound. Lanny wakes in his earth burrow beside his brother Gill. Their foster father Juan orders them to flee. Enemy police spheres hunt eight hunters from the night before. A surrender treaty bars men from using metal. The young, born since the invasion, resist the Almost-men more fiercely than their elders. Lanny cannot recall what he did the night before.
59424-the-railway-man-and-his-children:
Mrs Oliphant wrote The Railway Man and His Children for Heinemann and Balestier at Leipzig in 1892, as volume one of two. Oliphant also wrote Kirsteen and Within the Precincts. The tale opens with startling station news: Miss Ferrars is to marry Mr Rowland the engineer.

Word runs through the station like wildfire, with tones of wonder on every side. Ladies cry poor Miss Ferrars, since a lady of good family weds a man they say is no gentleman. Gentlemen answer that Rowland is a very good fellow. Mrs Stanhope, with whom Miss Ferrars lives, is torn between joy at her friend's settlement and doubt about her sphere. Class and love drive the opening.
5954-religious-reality-a-book-for-men:
A. E. J. Rawlinson writes for thoughtful men who want faith stated plainly, without jargon or convention. The Bishop of Lichfield, in his preface, says such readers do not fear theology, which he calls a reasoned account of religion. They want the Christian faith shown as reasonable, and the problem of evil faced honestly.

Rawlinson draws on wide contact with undergraduates, soldiers, and ordinary civil life. He links belief to real problems of living and to demands that are large, not easy. The book aims to give men a faith they can think with and act on, day by day.
59672-a-day-with-ludwig-beethoven:
A Day with Ludwig Beethoven is a small book on the great tune man by May Byron. It stands in a set of such day books. Its mates in that set treat two more great men of tune. The front plate is a paint work by a named hand. A line from the great song of joy of the man stands past that plate. Joy, thou spark of God head from the skies, that line says.

At day break, on a warm morn in the year eighteen fifteen, the book starts. A short, thick set, strong built man came to his sit room. At once he set to work to make his tunes. Not that he broke the sleep of the rest of the house by sounds on the great key board, the book says.
59724-the-baritone-s-parish-or-all-thing:
The Baritone's Parish, or All Things to All Men, is a novel by James Ludlow. Revell published it in New York, Chicago, and Toronto in 1896. A frontispiece shows two singers with heads touching in a grand finale. Ludlow also wrote The Captain of the Janizaries. That tale treats Scanderbey and the fall of Constantinople. A King of Tyre and That Angelic Woman are also his. The opening pages meditate on pulpit and choir gallery. The two are closely related in city churches, it says.

Yet ministers and choirs usually know little of one another, it laments. That is to the loss of both parties, the narrator holds. To musicians the minister often seems a recluse. The clergyman looks on his choir as itinerant minstrels. The pastor of Saint Philemon's breaks that pattern in the tale. The novel joins church work, music, and city life.
59726-the-fairy-green:
Rose Fyleman wrote verses of fairies and small girls in The Fairy Green. Methuen and Company issued the book in London, first in October 1919. The hosted form is the seventh, from October 1922. The book is given to all teachers of little children.

Parts sort the poems under Fairies, Bird-Lore, and A Little Girl. A child sees the fairy queen on a dragon-fly, stars in her hair. Pleas to tread soft where fairies creep show Fyleman's gentle touch. Young readers gain light, loved verses that made her name in schools.
59730-behind-the-screen:
Behind the Screen is a book on the film trade by Samuel Goldwyn, published in New York in nineteen twenty three. Goldwyn dedicates it to the motion picture industry that brought him success and friends. A photograph of Mr and Mrs Douglas Fairbanks fronts the volume. The book first ran in a picture magazine, as its copyright pages show.

Goldwyn writes from inside the new Hollywood studio world he helped build. Stars, studios, and the making and selling of films are his subject matter. The view is that of a producer, not a critic or a fan. For readers of film history, it preserves how a leading maker explained his own trade in its early years.
59831-the-lay-of-the-nibelung-men:
Arthur Way turned the great German epic of the Nibelungs into English verse. Cambridge printed The Lay of the Nibelung Men at the University Press in 1911. Way had Englished Homer and the Greek tragedies before he took up this sterner song.

Of Kriemhild, and of her dream, the tale opens. The fostering and knighting of Siegfried follow, then his ride to Worms. He wars on the Saxons and first sees Kriemhild. The love-quest to Isen-land wins the warrior-maid Brunhild for Gunther. The strange bridal, the queens' bitter words, and the net of betrayal woven for Siegfried darken the roll. How Siegfried was murdered, and how mourned and buried, stand at the heart of the lay.
59840-island-trail-at-walnut-canyon-waln:
Island Trail at Walnut Canyon is a National Park Service guide booklet for Walnut Canyon National Monument, eleven miles east of Flagstaff, Arizona. Visitors could borrow it free or take it home for ten cents. Numbered stakes along the trail key to its paragraphs.

The trail drops 185 feet by ramp and stairway to the Saddle, then circles the Island at the level of the ruins. Walkers see more than 100 of the canyon's 400 small cliff dwellings. The walk runs five-eighths of a mile and takes about forty minutes. Walnut Creek, the booklet notes, was dammed in 1904 to form Lake Mary, which supplies Flagstaff.
59872-our-den:
Waterworth wrote this boys holiday tale of a den and expected savages. Partridge printed Our Den in London for young readers. A front plate shows three figures dripping from head to foot. Chapter one heads The Savages are Expected in the holiday home.

Father calls it stuff and nonsense to host young savages there. Mother laughs merrily, as she generally did when others would cry. The boy narrator reads and looks up at the word savages. Contents promise a fortified den, a bell buoy, and punishment. A mysterious visitor, an oak chest, and a lost will fill the later chapter heads.
59876-rago-and-goni-the-tree-dweller-chi:
Rago and Goni, the Tree Dweller Children, is a tale for school readers by Belle Wiley. The author taught method in English at a training school in Rochester. Past books by her hand told of cliff and lake folk of old times. This book bears a rights line of the year nineteen sixteen.

Brother and sister Rago and Goni live in trees in a land long past. Parts treat their food, the beasts, the hunt, the clan, and fire in turn. A raid and a home run close the ten part tale for young minds. Plain words and short lines suit the book to class room read aloud time. The tale gives first folk life as a soft first step to old world lore.
59935-pegeen:
Pegeen is a novel by Eleanor Hoyt Brainerd, printed at New York with copyright in 1915. Brainerd also wrote Misdemeanors of Nancy. She dedicates the book to her mother, who, like Pegeen, has the neighboring heart. The tale opens as a very small person walks into a painter's studio.

Please, sir, I have come to see to you, she announces. John Archibald turns from his easel in amazement, faintly tinged with alarm. She is Pegeen O'Neill, and she will begin in the kitchen, which they say is a sight. She has brought her own cleaning rags, since men never have such things around. Brainerd tells how a waif takes charge of a bachelor's home.
60001-john-rawn-prominent-citizen:
Emerson Hough wrote John Rawn, Prominent Citizen, published by the Bobbs-Merrill Company at Indianapolis in 1912. M Leone Bracker drew the illustrations. Hough dedicated the novel to Woodrow Wilson, as one of the leaders in the third war of American independence. Four books divide the tale. The first opens with certain notable details in genesis. Purely Incidental and In Victory Generous follow.

John Rawn announces his arrival midway through the first book. Kelly Row, its woodshed, and a test fill the early chapters. The second book gives the new Mr Rawn and Graystone Hall. John Rawn, Prominent Citizen stands as a chapter title at the center. The extreme monogamy of Mr Rawn opens the third book. The royal progress of Mr and Mrs Rawn opens the fourth. The novel tracks a self-made man's rise with an ironic hand.
60019-book-of-nations-for-children:
Book of Nations for Children is a small picture geography printed at Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in 1848. Werden published it for young readers. Each page pairs a woodcut with a few plain lines about a people. The Spaniards live in Spain, it begins: they are tall and thin, with dark complexions, and their gentlemen bow low and kiss ladies' hands.

The Indians are described as the people who held this country before the white people came, copper coloured, in small huts. Italy is one of the most beautiful countries in the world, full of vineyards and grapes. South America holds various races, and Russia is cold, its ground snow covered most of the year. The Russians are strong, hardy, and industrious, the book says. Such primers taught children the world as their elders pictured it in 1848. Its simple certainties now read as a record of that picture itself.
60169-the-house-of-helen:
The House of Helen is a novel by Corra Harris. George Doran published it in New York in 1923. Parts had appeared in a Curtis magazine. Harris had earlier written A Circuit Rider's Wife. The tale is set in a small Georgia town.

The town of Shannon opens the book. It lies in a green valley below the Blue Ridge. Thrifty people built it after the Civil War. Its houses are small and painted to fancy. White church spires rise like forefingers of faith. Business moves at leisure on credit in the square. A red-brick courthouse wears a shining tin dome. The town clock keeps such true time that half the men carry no watches.
60548-specimen:
Specimen is a tale of the far worlds by Charles de Vet, first put out in a sheet of such tales in the eighth month of nineteen fifty eight. Its hook lines stand at the head in brief. The Zades had their one test man of Earth. What would come in the end to the whole of his kind hung on what came to that one. It was as plain as that, says the hook.

The tale is told by the clerk of the work, who was in the room of the chief when they brought the strange one in. The man of Earth was as tall as a mean Zade and of much the same hue. He could have passed for one of them, save that he had no dwarf wings.
60901-the-vanished-pomps-of-yesterday-be:
The Vanished Pomps of Yesterday is a book of reminiscences by Lord Frederic Hamilton. Doran published this new and revised edition in New York in 1921. Its subtitle calls it random reminiscences of a British diplomat. Hamilton also wrote The Days Before Yesterday. He dedicates the book to Emily, Lady Ampthill, his first chiefess. A note to the second edition explains a changed story. The boating accident account at Potsdam differs from the first edition. The lady concerned asked for the alterations of detail, he says.

His recollections of her story were at fault, he admits. A few verbal alterations also mark this present edition. The contents open with a special mission to Rome. Berlin in process of transformation follows in the chapter heads. Evenings with Wagner and opinions of Liszt appear there. Bismarck stands among the chapter's named figures. Hamilton recalls a Europe of courts that had vanished.
6092-the-fair-haven:
Samuel Butler presents The Fair Haven as a work in defence of the miraculous element in Christ's ministry on earth. It is written by the late John Pickard Owen, with a memoir by William Bickersteth Owen and an introduction by R. A. Streatfeild. It argues against rationalistic impugners and certain orthodox defenders alike.

Chapters treat Strauss and the hallucination theory, the character and conversion of St. Paul, Paul's testimony, ill-judged methods of defence, and the Christ-ideal. Butler's defense, cast as another man's book, tests how miracles can be argued honestly. The volume closes with a conclusion and appendix.
61006-young-man-from-elsewhen:
Sylvia Jacobs springs a surprise in Young Man From Elsewhen, from the March 1961 issue of Worlds of If. The head tag says the old man was sure of one thing: there were far fewer things in heaven and earth than were dreamt of in his philosophy, till today.

The tale opens in a great Los Angeles station. A redcap pushes a wheelchair under a lofty ceiling, while hundreds mill about the early trains. The old man in the chair has a blanket over his knees, in spite of July heat. His daughter walks beside him in a stream of warnings. Take the medicine at lunch, keep the chair out of the aisle. No club car drink, for the arthritis. Three cigars a day at most. Hell's fire, he protests; he was taking trains before she was born.
61007-in-the-garden:
In the Garden is a science fiction story by Lafferty, printed in Worlds of If in March 1961. A banner at its head describes the world of the tale. It was a dull, routine little world, that banner reads. It did not even have a city; everything it had was in the garden.

A survey ship's instruments open the story above a small moon. The life recorder chirps like a bird over strong traces below. Higher tests find backboned life across most of the surface. The cognition scanner then hunts for thought on the body. For hours it finds nothing as the ship hovers in its station. At last a signal comes, clear and definite, from one small place. It reads as thought limited within a pale, Steiner observes.
61062-the-great-revival-of-the-eighteent:
Edwin Paxton Hood wrote The Great Revival of the Eighteenth Century, a history of the religious awakening that swept Britain in the 1700s. Hood first published his chapters as papers in the magazine Sunday at Home, and he asks readers to take them as vignettes rather than a strict history. An American edition adds a closing chapter on the revival in America.

Hood's pictures center on London and the great mining towns of England, where preachers such as Whitefield and the Wesleys won their largest crowds. The editor's note is candid that the book gives only a partial history, weighted toward the Methodist movement. The added American chapter sketches the work of Edwards, Whitefield, and the Tennents in the colonies. An index was also added for this edition. Readers get a warm, scene-based account of the awakening and the zeal that drove its leaders.
61079-snythergen:
Hal Garrott wrote Snythergen, a tale for children published in New York in 1923 by Robert McBride and Company. Dugald Walker drew the pictures, some in color. Garrott dedicated the book to Hal and Jean, and the chapter list runs to 16 episodes across 155 pages.

The headings promise a strange, playful world. A ticklish tree, a pig that learns to talk, and a house at the end of a rope all wait inside. A bear goes out on ice and later meets a grasshopper pig. One picture shows Santa Claus telling a bear not to talk with its mouth full. Chapters like The Pie Room and Toy Foods keep food at the center of the fun. Young readers get a string of tall, merry episodes.
61199-a-bad-town-for-spacemen:
A Bad Town for Spacemen is a science fiction story by Robert Scott, from Worlds of If of July nineteen sixty two. A returned spaceman tells it in the first person from New York. New York had always been counted safe ground for men of his service. This time, half an hour after touchdown, he feels the change in the air.

Health, baggage, and security checks now seem set only to foul the crews up. A crowd on the street makes plain it will not part for him. He steps into a bar, against all sense, for old memories of better days. The room falls silent as he enters in his uniform alone. Drink prices have risen, and the girls' hair and dress have changed too. Drunks mutter with glances at him while he drinks at his table.
61241-the-pentateuch-in-its-progressive-:
Reverend Henry Cowles's The Pentateuch, in Its Progressive Revelations of God to Men was published by Appleton at New York in 1874, designed for both pastors and people. Its motto is the Ethiopian's question in Acts: understandest thou what thou readest? Cowles's preface explains his topical plan: the line of thought in the five books needs no help, but their great themes want due presentation. He discusses them critically where objections arise, and practically for their moral bearings as revelations of God.

The modern objections to Genesis, more or less related to true science, get special examination, being much in public attention. Cowles promises that all real truth is welcome. The transcriber notes the period's unstandardised spellings are left as printed. Cowles was a Congregational theologian of Oberlin, writing against the first wave of Darwin-era criticism of Genesis.
61325-the-shakespeare-garden:
The Shakespeare Garden is a book by Esther Singleton, printed at New York in 1922 with many illustrations from photographs and old wood cuts. Singleton notes that Shakespeare knew two kinds of gardens. One was the stately garden that graced the castles and manor houses of the nobility and gentry. The other was the small and simple garden such as he had himself at Stratford-on-Avon.

The first part traces the garden of delight from the medieval pleasance through the Italian Renaissance garden to Tudor gardens. It treats the curious knotted garden, the flower lovers and herbalists, and the old garden authors. The second part walks through the flowers of Shakespeare by season. Spring brings primroses, cowslips, and daffodils that come before the swallow dares. Summer brings roses newly washed with dew and lilies of all kinds. The book joins the plays to the plots and borders of their age.
61405-down-to-the-worlds-of-men:
Alexei Panshin wrote a tale of trial by survival called Down to the Worlds of Men, first run in Worlds of If in July 1963. The tale is told by Mia Havero, a girl of fourteen who lives aboard a great Ship. She and twenty eight other young folk are loaded into a scout ship with horses and packs, to be dropped on a planet.

The old rule, the head note says, is sink or swim: live on a world with no space flight, or be wiped out. Mia is short, dark, and sharp witted, and she scorns a red headed boy who asks to pair with her. The drop is made as a lark by a hot pilot, and the test of the young castaways starts at once.
61451-a-friend-in-the-kitchen:
A Friend in the Kitchen, by Mrs Anna Colcord, is a cook book of some 400 choice recipes. Its full title promises what to cook and how to cook it in plain terms. Directions on healthful cookery go with the tested recipes in the book. How to can fruit and a week menu form part of its household counsel.

Proper food combinations and rules for dyspeptics fill further sections of the guide. Food for infants and simple dishes for the sick get chapters of their own. Wholesome drinks and tables on the food values of common foods follow in it. Time required to digest foods is set out in a table for the careful eater. A portrait of the author stands at the front of the kitchen friend.
61519-trench-warfare-a-manual-for-office:
A field manual of trench warfare by J S Smith. E P Dutton published it at New York in 1917. Smith served as a second lieutenant with the British Expeditionary Force. He was an American from Philadelphia, an editor's note explains. He enlisted in a Vancouver battalion in 1914. Belgian front service led to a British commission in 1916. He dedicates the book to Americans serving under alien flags.

The contents cover the whole trench system. Readers learn trench location, dugouts, latrines, and revetments. Sandbags, corrugated iron, traverses, and listening posts all get sections. Later parts treat wire, bombing squads, explosives, and gas masks. Platoon duties and reliefs close the course. Few manuals show the Western Front's daily machinery so completely.
6167-business-hints-for-men-and-women:
A. R. Calhoun offers Business Hints for Men and Women, opening with common sense farming: wealth, land and labor, money, sources of wealth, and the farmer as producer and seller, with business methods essential. Documents to understand follow, with deeds, abstracts of title, and parties to a deed.

Forms of deeds and mortgages, wills, letter writing, and bills, receipts, and accounts complete the manual. Calhoun explains how to make a will, handle administrators and debts, write business letters, and discount bills. The book gives plain, practical guidance for men and women handling money and property.
61837-tarzan-and-the-ant-men:
Tarzan and the Ant Men, by Edgar Rice Burroughs, sends the ape man into a land of tiny warriors, in an edition of the war years. The book was produced under wartime rules for saving paper. It is still complete and unabridged, the notice on the title page states. Burroughs built a long line of Tarzan tales on such finds.

A lost race of small men gives this adventure its hook. Tarzan, shrunk or set among the ant men, must fight at their scale. Burroughs mixes jungle craft with a fable of size and power. The ant men keep slaves, make war, and ride small beasts. Their world mirrors the great one in miniature, with its own kings and battles. Readers of the series got a fresh lost land in this volume.
61857-bashful-fifteen:
Meade wrote a school story printed at New York in 1892. Meade had written Out of the Fashion, A Sweet Girl Graduate, The Medicine Lady, and A World of Girls. Curiosity opens the contents, then the new girl and ribbons and roses. The queen of the school and breaking in a wild colt follow.

A fashionable watering place called Eastcliff stood about a mile from Mulberry Court, the old fashioned house with old world gardens where the schoolgirls lived. There were about fifty of them in all, the tale says. Captivity, who is to provide the needful, and the Janet May stall fill the middle. Taking sides, checkmate, a wild Irish princess, and Lady Kathleen lead on. Bridget O'Hara's stall, Persian cats, an Irish welcome, and Bruin my dog crowd the close. The holy well, wild hawk, under a spell, and Norah to the rescue end a schoolgirl romp.
62005-an-account-of-the-ladies-of-llango:
An Account of the Ladies of Llangollen is a short pamphlet by a late Welsh clergyman, printed at Llangollen and sold for two pence. Its title page shows the two ladies of its tale. Lady Eleanor Butler and Sarah Ponsonby were Irish ladies of rank and beauty, the first page says. They loved each other so truly that neither could bear the parting that marriage would bring.

They resolved on lives without marriage, refused many fine offers, and fled from home. Caught and brought back, they were pressed again toward weddings, in vain for the one most hunted. In a short time the ladies fled again, each with a small sum in hand. Their cottage at Llangollen, and their lifelong life together there, became a sight of Wales that visitors crossed the country to see.
62315-domestic-animals-a-story-book-for-:
Domestic Animals is a story book for children, printed at Pittsfield, Massachusetts, by Werden in 1848. It is number two in its little line, and it works through the farmyard beasts one by one, each with a picture. The lessons are plain and short, made for very young readers.

The horse comes first, called one of the noblest and most useful of beasts, gentle when well managed. The dog follows, man's companion in all civilised lands, from lap dog to mastiff. The cat gets a full page of wonders, from worship in Egypt to beds of down in China. The pig and the camel round out the start of a simple natural history for the nursery.
62355-a-voyage-round-the-world-being-an-:
A Voyage Round the World is Captain William Betagh's account of a privateering cruise begun in 1719. The London edition here is dated 1728. Betagh served as captain of marines in the venture. Its aim, stated on the title page, was to cruise against the Spaniards in the great South Ocean.

Betagh calls his book the true history of the whole affair. He says the facts are vouched for by many who took part and by papers from the owners. The dedication goes to the lords of the Admiralty, headed by Lord Torrington. In his own address Betagh notes that he had been a navy purser for some years before this cruise. He sailed under Captain Shelvocke, a command he came to regret. The book is a participant's brief in a famous, quarrelsome expedition.
62385-clorinda-walks-in-heaven:
Coppard wrote these tales, Clorinda Walks in Heaven the title piece. Golden Cockerel Press printed the book in Berkshire in 1922. Some tales first ran in Cornhill, English Review, and The Dial. Contents open with The Hurly-Burly on a thriving small farm.

The Weetmans, mother, son, and daughter, keep a turbulent house there. Phemy the servant gets orders from dawn to dark without rest. Clorinda, The Cherry Tree, and The Elixir of Youth follow next. Felix Tincler, Craven Arms, and Pomona Babe close the tale list. A broadside ballad and a tale called Cotton stand in the later contents list.
62742-ludwig-van-beethoven:
Ludwig van Beethoven is a life of the composer for young people, translated from the German of Franz Hoffmann by George Upton. McClurg published it at Chicago; this copy is the third printing, of 1910. It belongs to the Life Stories for Young People series. A picture shows a child shrinking from Beethoven and hiding in his mother's dress.

Chapters tell of the childhood at Bonn, a walk, and new friends. A merciful punishment and the move to Vienna follow, and the end closes the tale. An appendix adds facts for older readers. The picture of Ries consoling Beethoven for his lost hearing ends the illustrations. Hoffmann's tale made the deaf composer a hero for schoolchildren.
62748-a-story-garden-for-little-children:
Maud Lindsay wrote A Story Garden for Little Children, a set of tales. Front pages list her books, among them The Story-Teller for Little Children and Bobby and the Big Road. Little Missy stands in the same list of pictured books for the young. A note in praise of Lindsay says a new collection from her needs no heralding. Those who know her stories, it holds, know her gift already.

Lindsay had proved herself a teller made for small ears and small hearts. Her tales suit the nursery, the kindergarten, and the home hour. A story garden, by its title, grows short tales like beds of flowers. Each tale is made to be read aloud in a brief sitting. The book gives gentle stories for little children, in the plain warm style that made Lindsay a household name in her field.
62866-the-young-game-warden:
Harry Castlemon wrote The Young Game-Warden, copyrighted in 1896 and published in Philadelphia. Castlemon also wrote the Gunboat series, the Rocky Mountain series, and The House-Boat Boys. The story starts with Silas Morgan and two brothers, then a mysterious letter that sets the plot moving.

Twenty-three chapters bring in Hobson's house, a plot that succeeds, a haunting, and Joe's first official act as a game warden. Other chapters ask who fired the four shots and send the boys on a run for home with a treacherous guide. Readers get a boys' adventure about poaching, law in the woods, and a young warden earning his badge.
63217-discovery-at-aspen:
Discovery at Aspen, by Sophie Ruskay, was printed at New York by A S Barnes in 1960, in the Wonderful World Books, with art by Janet D'Amato. It opens five days before a trip: Judy Lurie sorts her last summer's clothes for the trunk. Her parents, Minna and John, will take her to Aspen for the long break, and friends crowd in to wish them well. John slips off to his studio and his viola while the women talk.

The heads trace the stay: Aspen's path from silver dust to music, a first sight of the town, Smuggler's Café, and the ghost town of Ashcroft. Dogs, a climb, and a near scrape with rescue fill the back half. A dream takes shape by the close. Young readers get a bright summer tale of peaks, songs, and a girl finding her feet.
63499-dick-and-larry-freshmen:
Dick and Larry, Freshmen, by Francis Lynde, was published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1922 and also ran in Boys' Life. George Avison drew the pictures, including a frontispiece of a back carrying the ball eight straight times toward Rockford's goal. The heroes meet on a train rolling east from a summer of railroad work in Colorado.

Dick Maxwell, a railroad manager's son, and big, shy Larry Donovan are nothing alike but sunburn, yet college soon names them a pair. Bridge scraps, a drop out, a red wagon scholarship, and flood water fill their first year. Lynde writes college sport and loyalty in the open air style boys then loved.
63613-the-space-between:
Robert Ernest Gilbert wrote this science fiction tale for Planet Stories, where it ran in the spring of 1955. Jak, a spaceman with a string of numbers after his name, flies a battered ship he calls the Box. A sleek spacecopter from Enceladus pulls alongside, matching his speed, and the collision whistles scream.

His wife Drusilla, in a flowing red robe, has a headache and a fixed demand: no hospital but the Wollongong Obstetric Hospital on Earth will do for her baby. Jak coaxes, apologises, and magnetises her shoes to keep her off the ceiling. The cover note casts him as a man with but one life to give for his planet. Gilbert mixes domestic comedy with deep space danger.
63688-he-was-buried-a-sermon-for-easter-:
Thomas Macgill preached this sermon, He Was Buried, for Easter Even, printed at Clapham in 1849. Macgill was curate of Clapham and evening preacher at the Magdalen Hospital. A note adds that any profit from the sale would go to the funds for building a temporary church in Clapham. His text is three words from Paul's first letter to the Corinthians: he was buried.

Macgill opens at every funeral his hearers have known. Who has not watched a beloved friend carried to the grave, he asks, or felt the majesty of death even at a stranger's passing? Then he turns the congregation to one funeral in particular: that of the Prince of Life, who lay among the dead to destroy death itself, borne by few mourners.
63817-fog-of-the-forgotten:
Basil Wells wrote a science fiction tale that first ran in Planet Stories in the winter of 1946. On a world wrapped in fog, the hero Ho Dyak climbs a net of vines up the cliffs above the lowlands. He wears layer on layer of padded clothes against the cold heights. In a pouch he guards five banned metal scrolls.

The scrolls came from a shut room of the Upper Shrine of Lalal, the one god of Arba. The fighting priests of that shrine hunt him down the slopes. Ho Dyak wants to see what lies above the fog sea and to reach the high lands his people once ruled. The tale sets faith that bans old science against one man's wish for light and truth.
63948-common-sense-about-women:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson wrote Common Sense About Women, a set of short essays on women’s lives. Lee and Shepard issued the book in Boston in eighteen hundred eighty two. Higginson marked his daughter Margaret’s name on the gift page. The essays first ran as lone pieces in print.

Four groups sort the essays by theme here. Body and mind themes lead, with Darwin, Huxley, and Buckle in view. The home group weighs work, cash sense, and the word obey. Society essays touch dress, manners, schools, and law. Girls as students and as cooks both earn chapters. Women as wage earners get plain talk, not pity. Higginson writes for a young land still torn on the point, he says.
63959-the-harim-and-the-purdah-studies-o:
Elizabeth Cooper goes behind closed doors in The Harim and the Purdah, studies of Oriental women, printed in New York by the Century Company. Cooper had writ My Lady of the Chinese Courtyard. A dancing girl of Jeypore fronts the book.

Eighteen chapters range from Egypt to China. Egyptian women of the past and the modern Egyptian woman lead. Marriage, divorce, and polygamy get a chapter, and the woman of the desert follows. Indian social life and Indian home life fill a broad span. Marriage as the goal of woman, Indian motherhood, and woman's sorrow stand in the run. Hyderabad and the Mohammedan woman come next. Burmah and China close the tour, with a last head on changing China.
64189-a-selection-from-the-norse-tales-f:
A Selection from the Norse Tales for the Use of Children is a story book by Dasent. Edmonston and Douglas published the volume at Edinburgh in 1862. Dasent chose the tales from his larger gathering of Norse folk stories. A notice at the front explains why some tales were left out.

Dasent writes that some good people found parts of the full tales too outspoken for children. Tales such as Why the Sea is Salt and The Master Thief were cut from the volume. He jokes that the stories left behind may grow proud at their new rank as moral tales. He also owns that he still sees no harm in the omitted stories. The tales kept include True and Untrue and The Old Dame and Her Hen. Fine pictures and a bright binding dressed the book for young readers.
64404-con-fen:
Con Fen, a science fiction tale by James Adams, ran in Planet Stories in May 1953. A blurb at the head gives its comic set up in brief lines. The Shisti and the assistant Shisti of Mars chose Chicago for their vacation spot. No worries for them, since they were invisible on their holiday.

Plenty of rich food waited, for the joint was loaded, the blurb goes on. A whole year of frolicking lay in store for the pair of Martians. Only one thing they overlooked in their planning for the trip. A curious convention was going on in the city at the same time. The landing on the green planet was one of utmost perfection, Koosh tells himself. Martian craft all but fly themselves, he reflects with pilot pride.
64606-a-china-cup-and-other-stories-for-:
A China Cup and Other Stories for Children, by Felix Volkhovsky, was published in London in 1892. Fisher Unwin issued this second edition in the Children's Library. Malischeff drew the pictures. Eight tales make the book. The first follows a lump of china clay. A workman digs it from the pit with his spade. The lump groans at being torn from mother earth. It is thrown into a waggon and jolted down a steep hillside. At the factory it is plunged into a tub of water.

Later tales tell of Scarlet-Comb the cock defending the right. A tiny screw, a dream, and a dog named Browny follow. An old sword makes a mistake. A closing tale explains how all these tales came to light. Volkhovsky writes fable-like stories with a Russian flavour.
6467-letters-to-his-children:
Theodore Roosevelt's Letters to His Children, first published in 1919 and edited by Joseph Bucklin Bishop, gathers letters written over more than twenty years. A few went to friends or relatives about the children, but most went to the children themselves, from early childhood to maturity. Whenever Roosevelt was separated from them, in the Spanish War, on a hunting trip, or while they were at school, he sent messages of constant thought and love.

Long before they could read, he sent picture letters, crude drawings of his own fitted to childish imagination. A mid letter from the White House, November 15, 1903, tells Kermit about dogs Hector, Brier, and Sailor Boy. They lie around Seaman's house in excellent health, Sailor Boy and Brier affectionate, Hector kindly but uninterested. Roosevelt writes fatherhood in brief, warm notes, full of animals, games, and cheer.
6492-biographies-of-working-men:
Grant Allen tells the lives of seven men who rose from plain work to wide fame, from a stonemason to a canal boy who became a president. Telford, Stephenson, Gibson, Herschel, Millet, Garfield, and Thomas Edward each get a short, clear life story, drawn from longer books Allen names with care. The focus stays on work done well, day after day.

No life here turns on luck alone; each man learns a trade, keeps at it, and finds a way past want or doubt. Allen writes for readers who like plain facts and steady effort more than praise. Together, these lives form a kind of lesson in how skill, patience, and grit can lift a worker into history.
65098-daughters-of-men:
Hannah Lynch wrote a novel of new Greek life and its gay flaws. The book's rights date to 1892 in this copy. Lynch wrote Troubled Waters in her past works as well. She gave the book to Demetrios Bikelas with a warm note. Of his kind take on her mirth she had no doubt, she writes.

We love none the less those we laugh at, that note holds. Our own weak spots show in theirs, she goes on to say. Her chief care is that her sight and call ring true in it. Daughters of men in Greek homes bear the tale's bright weight. Town wit and home plots mix in her keen prose. Each scene tests her pledge.
65206-shen-of-the-sea-a-book-for-childre:
Arthur Bowie Chrisman wrote Shen of the Sea, a book of tales for children. E P Dutton issued it in New York with a nineteen hundred twenty five copyright. The book won the John Newbery Medal for that year. Else Hasselriis drew more than fifty black silhouette pictures for it.

Sixteen tales fill the contents list. Their heroes have names such as Ah Mee, Ah Fun, and Hai Low. One tale tells how chopsticks came to be. Others tell of a rain king’s daughter and a moon maiden. The title tale names the Shen as demons of the sea. Young readers get short, strange tales told in a Chinese story style.
65207-women:
Women is a book by Booth Tarkington, put out at Garden City, New York, in the mid nineteen twenties. A list at the front runs his past works in a long roll, from tales of a small town boy to great novels of a mid west city and its rich. The new book stands last on that roll.

Its form opens with a first word, or preamble, that sets the frame for what comes next. Tarkington was famed for tales of American home and town life that mix wit with a keen eye for manners. In this book he turns that eye on women of his day: their talk, their aims, and the games of love and rank they play in his world.
65258-god-hath-spoken:
God Hath Spoken is a book of doctrine by Harris Dark, published at Murfreesboro, Tennessee, in 1947. The Dehoff Publishing Company issued the book for its author in that year. Contents list sixteen chapters on the teaching of his church in the volume. God Hath Spoken, generic and specific commands, and intolerance open the list of chapters.

Where Did So Many Denominations Come From stands fourth in the contents of the book. Which Church Is Right and Why Not Be Just a Christian follow in order of the chapters. Seventh Day Adventism Reviewed, leadership, and congregational objectives and activities come after in turn. How Much Is Liberal and What Must I Do to Keep Saved close the shown contents. Dark writes in the plea of the Churches of Christ: one church, the Bible only, and no creed but the word, argued chapter by chapter for the plain reader.
