65260-the-physical-training-of-children:
The Physical Training of Children is a health manual by Chavasse, a surgeon of Birmingham, England. An American edition of eighteen seventy one adds a long opening essay by Getchell. Getchell taught diseases of women and children at Jefferson Medical College. The book treats the child in three stages, infancy, childhood, and youth.

Each stage repeats the same heads of care in its own fuller form. Washing, clothing, diet, sleep, and exercise come first for the infant part. Teething, vaccination, and the common ailments of babies follow in order. For childhood the nursery, amusements, and schooling join the list of topics. Youth brings air, household work for girls, and the choice of a trade. The opening laments that mothers reach motherhood knowing nothing of child care.
65337-the-age-of-justinian-and-theodora-:
William Gordon Holmes wrote a history of the sixth century, and volume one came out in a second edition in London in 1912. Holmes says he revised and slightly grew the work after notes from critics of the first edition. Some critics, he adds, found him too loose in his notes, and not all of them agreed with each other.

Holmes states his aim plainly in reply, to show not just one age but the sweep of all time in short form. Chapter one tours Constantinople in that century, its past, its ground plan, and its folk. Later chapters treat the empire under Anastasius and the rise of Justin and of Theodora.
65446-six-frightened-men:
Six Frightened Men is a science fiction tale by Randall Garrett. It ran in Imagination Stories in June of the year 1957. A blurb warns of an unexplored planet where anything could happen fast. None of the crew expected a creature impossible to fight or kill. The narrator tells how he joined the Exploratory Wing of the Space Corps.

Recruiters warned him that planetfall puts a man's life in his hands. Alien worlds may hold hostile life that no man has ever met. He jokes that he would not join a tea party of old ladies. The scene cuts to Pollux Five, a yellow wind blasted desert world. He crouches behind a spiral rock with the fierce wind sweeping past.
65496-pioneer-work-in-opening-the-medica:
Elizabeth Blackwell wrote Pioneer Work in Opening the Medical Profession to Women. Longmans put out her autobiographical sketches at London and New York in 1895. She had written on the moral education of the young before it. Chapter one, Early Years, is dated from 1821. Family life in England and walks around Bristol open the tale.

Missionary meetings, the Bristol riots, and early religious impressions follow. The family emigrates to the United States, and schooldays in New York begin. Anti-slavery talk, a removal to Ohio, and a boarding-school venture come next. Chapter two turns to earning money for study, from 1845. The medical idea takes shape, against her own disinclination to the study. The moral aspect of the work conquers that dislike, she writes. Teaching at Asheville and Charleston earns the fees for her training.
65579-gray-hairs-made-happy-an-interesti:
Brown of Providence printed this short tale for children in 1831. Its full title is Gray Hairs Made Happy, and its theme is set in a line at the head: youth has its joys, and age has its cares. The heroine is a girl named Mary.

Mary sits by a grass plot near her home, knitting stockings for her mother. A poor old man with white hair and a bent back comes slowly past, leaning on a stick. Boys trail him, laughing at his worn coat, rusty hat, and thin cheeks. When he trips on a stone, they laugh the more. Mary's kind heart feels his pain, and the tale turns on how a child should treat the old and poor.
65717-the-age-of-justinian-and-theodora-:
The Age of Justinian and Theodora is a history of the sixth century by Holmes, in two parts. The part at hand is the second, in its second form, put out at London in the early nineteen hundreds. A note at the front tells how print faults were fixed and Greek words set in plain marks.

Its parts in this half run from the Persians and the first war of the emperor with them, to the schools of thought at Athens and their fate. The book tells the reign of the great emperor and his queen as a tale of wars, law, faith, and court craft. Lists of fixes at the back reach to both parts of the work.
65722-rhymes-of-a-child-s-world-a-book-o:
Rhymes of a Child's World is a book of verse for children by Miriam Clark Potter, illustrated by Ruth Fuller Stevens and published in Boston in 1920. Potter dedicates it to her mother and father, who always had time to waive grown-up matters and read a small rhyme. Some poems had appeared in the Youth's Companion, Saint Nicholas, and Little Folks.

The contents begin in the house. My Dearest Is a Lady, Bubbles, and the Grown-Up World open the book. Tea time, umbrellas, the March wind, and tiptoes follow. Princess Fire, the dolls, bread and butter, and the company man fill the nursery round. Rain on the roof, a lighthouse lamp, muffins, and a Thanksgiving kitchen song stand among them. Potter writes from inside the child's small world, where a fat little cloud and a looking glass are events enough for verse.
65748-tales-from-westminster-abbey-told-:
Tales from Westminster Abbey Told to Children is a book by Mrs Frewen Lord, printed at London in 1894. It is dedicated to the memory of Dean Stanley. As a child the writer had enjoyed his walks and talks with children in the Abbey, and the book keeps them in grateful recollection.

The first chapter recalls being taken over the Abbey by Dean Stanley with other children many years before. Stanley, she explains, was the Arthur of Tom Brown's School Days, who grew up to be a clergyman and dean. He liked nothing better than taking people over the Abbey. Anyone who went with him, she says, would always remember some of the stories he told. The book carries a portrait of the dean, a plan of the Abbey, and a view of its west front. Its tales open the great church to young readers through the stones and tombs.
6595-advice-to-a-mother-on-the-managemen:
Pye Henry Chavasse, a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons, writes plain medical advice for mothers on rearing children and on sudden illness and accidents. His preface notes that the book had reached a twelfth edition, with twenty thousand copies sold in under three years, and had been turned into French, German, Polish, and Tamil. It was widely known wherever English was spoken.

Chavasse speaks as a doctor and a friend, with clear rules for food, care, and first aid at the moment of need. His tone is firm but kind, and his advice aims at the home, not the clinic. Advice to a Mother remains a vivid record of how Victorian doctors taught mothers to keep children safe.
66049-pictorial-beauty-on-the-screen:
Victor Oscar Freeburg's Pictorial Beauty on the Screen was published by the Macmillan Company at New York in 1923. Its argument is that a motion picture must be judged as pictures, not as a cheap copy of a play or novel. Rex Ingram supplies a prefatory note agreeing: to rank among the arts, the cinema must be more than clear photographs in motion. A film needs form, composition, and a right spread of light and shade.

Freeburg dedicates the book to James Cruze, whose Covered Wagon he takes as the model of pictorial beauty blended with epic story. Freeburg's preface says he enjoys the movies as pictures and in no other way, and that the pictorial side is where they most need to grow. The book is a plea, from inside the young industry, for film as a visual art.
66092-a-gallery-of-children:
A Gallery of Children is a book of tales for the young by Milne, published by David McKay at Philadelphia. Pictures by Saida, whose full name was Le Mair, fill the book with colored plates. The first tale tells of a Princess who loved the flowers and trees in her father's garden. Silvio the gardener loved them too, and loved the Princess, until the King grew angry at his low place.

Twelve tales make the gallery. They include Sparrow Tree Square, The Twins, and Miss Waterlow in Bed. Sand Babies, Poor Anne, and A Voyage to India follow. Barbara's Birthday, The Baby Show, The Magic Hill, and Castles by the Sea close the set.
66293-peril-of-the-starmen:
Peril of the Starmen is a science fiction story by Kris Neville, taken from Imagination for January 1954. Its tag line has the starmen's ships landing near Washington to meet Earthmen with friendly smiles: a great day, and quite possibly our last.

Herb, one of three chosen men, is called in by the Oligarch he hates. People live on the planet they need, unfortunately. The starmen's universe is unstable, its binding force fading; unless new energy is freed within a month, disintegration begins. The only cure is to blow up the Earth on schedule. Herb's party must learn the Earthmen's language under sleep tapes, land, lull suspicion, and ask permission for the deed. Herb believes, and the belief is the terror: he cannot fail, and he cannot want to succeed.
66471-like-another-helen:
Like Another Helen is a tale of old India by Sydney Grier, the hand of past tales named on the title leaf. It is the next in a set of tales of the past of that land. It was put out at Boston in the year nineteen hundred and two. The book is sworn to a chief of horse who gave the hand long help. A line from a bard stands past the sworn leaf. And, like a next Helen, fired a next Troy, that line says.

The list of parts tells the frame of the tale. The whole book is in notes from one maid to a next. The thoughts of a young maid on her go out to the world head the run. In which is set forth the false heart of man comes next.
66572-the-voyage-of-vanishing-men:
Stanley Mullen wrote this science fiction story, printed in Imagination in April 1955. Earthmen had never ventured beyond the galaxy, but a survey was ordered and a ship sent out. Three earlier expeditions had gone into the far dark and vanished completely.

The fourth ship, Venture IV, went out countless light-years, and something happened that nobody could explain. Only one man came back: Braun. The tale is framed by a bartender at a way station to the stars, who reckons bar work teaches more about people than a degree in psychology. Readers get a space mystery built on a survivor who may not be telling all he knows.
66631-after-the-manner-of-men:
Francis Lynde wrote a tale printed at New York in 1916, with drawings by Arthur Becher. A list of his other books stands at the front. It names The Real Man, Scientific Sprague, and The Taming of Red Butte Western among them. The book is given to Joseph Frater, a loyal friend of many years.

Lynde owes Frater much of the stuff of the tale and all of its air, he says. Contents open with a town man and a sow's ear, then a golden youth. Carfax joins up, rock proves stubborn, and blind alleys follow. Later heads name rue, dull steel, a burnt child, and the logic of fact. The front picture shows a man asked if he truly thought someone was shooting at him.
66655-a-new-story-book-for-children:
Fanny Fern wrote A New Story Book for Children, published in New York in 1864 and dedicated to Little Effie. Fern, whose real name was Sara Willis Parton, was among the best-paid American writers of her day. Her book opens with a story about herself. Nobody, she writes, could be more astonished than she to find herself famous. She had sat in a small room at the top of a lodging house, scribbling pen names on coarse paper to choose one for a first article.

Some thirty pieces follow. Grandpapa's bald head, the ploughboy poet, and Old Hickory stand among sketches of John Brown and the boy Walter Scott. Stories of a faithful dog, a deaf and dumb French boy, and three gifted sisters fill the middle. The book mixes biography for children with moral tales, in the brisk, funny voice that made Fern's newspaper columns famous.
66668-butterflies-and-moths-shown-to-the:
Butterflies and Moths, shown to the children, is a book of the two insect tribes. Kelman drew the forty-eight coloured plates, and Theodore Wood wrote the text to them. Jack issued the book in London, with Platt and Peck in New York.

The volume stands eighth in a series edited by Louey Chisholm. Its shelf-mates treat beasts, flowers, birds, the sea-shore, the farm, trees, nests and eggs, and stars. Many of the insects were drawn from one private cabinet. The artist thanks its owner in a front note. The plates open with two fritillaries, silver-washed and pearl-bordered. Tortoise-shells follow, then the peacock with its caterpillar and the red admiral. A painted lady, a marbled white, the speckled wood, and the wall come next. Meadow brown, ringlet, heaths, and the green hair streak round the set.
66669-the-sea-shore-shown-to-the-childre:
Janet Harvey Kelman drew the forty-eight coloured pictures for The Sea-Shore Shown to the Children, and Theodore Wood wrote the text. The book sits in the Shown to the Children series edited by Louey Chisholm. A list of sea-shore wonders sorts the plates into chapters. Fishes open the set, with gobies, a smooth blenny, a dragonet, and a pipe-fish.

Later chapters work through the shell-bearing kinds in order. One chapter treats soft-bodied sorts such as the cuttle, whelk, and limpet. The next takes two-shelled kinds, from the oyster and cockle to the shipworm and razor shell. Crabs form the fourth chapter, with notes on how crabs grow, see, hear, and smell.
66670-trees-shown-to-the-children:
Janet Harvey Kelman painted the thirty-two coloured plates and Smith wrote the text for 'Trees,' the sixth volume in the 'Shown to the Children' series edited by Louey Chisholm. Smith addresses young readers directly, promising accounts of trees likely to grow wild in this country, with drawings of leaves, flowers, and fruit to help children name each one.

Before the tree-by-tree plates begin, Smith answers the question children are sure to ask: how do trees grow? Roots suck up water from the soil, the text explains, and it rises through tiny cells to the leaves. Green leaves also take carbonic acid gas from the air and split it into oxygen and carbon. The oak, shown first, gets a plate with leaf spray, catkins, and fruit.
66687-fairy-tales-for-workers-children:
Herminia Zur Mühlen wrote these fairy tales for workers' children, turned from the German by Ida Dailes and printed in Chicago by the Daily Worker Publishing Company. The book holds four tales: The Rose-bush, The Sparrow, The Little Grey Dog, and Why. Lydia Gibson drew the cover and the colour plates.

The first tale shows the plan of the whole book. A rose-bush in a fine garden thanks the gardener who tends her and offers him her best blooms for his sick wife. He refuses: she belongs to the lady of the white house, who bought her. The bush learns that the lady's wealth comes from a factory where workers drudge, and that among men the fruit of work often goes to those who did no work. The tales use fable form to teach class lessons.
66755-animal-life-in-field-and-garden:
Jean-Henri Fabre wrote this nature book for the young, turned into English by Florence Constable Bicknell and printed by the Century Company of New York. Fabre had written The Story-Book of Science and Our Humble Helpers. Uncle Paul does the talking, as in Fabre's other books for children. Teeth open the talks, in all their shapes.

Bats get three chapters: their wings, their smell, and their hearing. The hedgehog, the mole, owls, rats, the raven, and the cuckoo follow in a long parade. Snakes, toads, and the grain-weevil come near the end, with a chapter on instinct. Fabre teaches by close watch of small lives in field and garden, and by tales that make facts stick.
66877-mr-wu-based-on-the-play-mr-wu-by-h:
Mr Wu, a novel by Louise Jordon Miln, is based on the play by Vernon and Harold Owen. Stokes copyrighted it in 1918, and Burt published it. Forty four chapters carry the story from Wu Ching Yu and Wu Li Chang to English wedding bells.

Chapter one sets grandfather against grandson. Old Wu, eighty and a mandarin rich beyond the dreams of avarice, sits in a chair of carved teak. His grandson, aged ten, stands before him still and silent, a glint of terror crossing his eyes. The old man likes the fear fiercely, knowing it holds nothing craven: only love of him and of home, and reluctance to leave both. The boy wears padded yellow silk, while the mandarin's clothes are coolie plain. Contents promise a marriage journey, a girl named Nang Ping, a lotus garden, the signal of a gong, and the story of a sword.
66884-joseph-and-his-brethren:
Joseph and His Brethren, by W K Tweedie, was published in London in eighteen seventy-two by T Nelson and Sons. Tweedie also wrote Seed-Time and Harvest and Parables of Our Lord. His subject is the biblical story of Joseph, sold by his brothers and raised in Egypt.

The preface argues the story is simple enough to rivet childhood and deep enough for sages. Tweedie sets out to trace the wisdom and watchfulness of Providence through it. Man's wickedness is restrained and turned to good, he argues, even in prison and exile. The verse motto shows Joseph drooping in Pharaoh's dungeon, with God beside the throne. Victorian families used such volumes to turn Sunday reading into moral instruction at home.
66909-the-ladies-of-the-white-house-or-i:
The Ladies of the White House is a history by Laura C Holloway. Forshee and McMakin published it in Cincinnati in 1881. Its subtitle promises the social and domestic lives of the presidents from Washington to the present time.

Holloway studies the women who ran the presidential household. She notes that earlier histories barely mentioned them. The preface argues their influence shaped each administration. Steel and wood engravings illustrate the book. It covers a full century, from 1789 to 1881. Books like this one opened a new field in American history. They treated the home life of power as a subject worth recording.
66925-lady-rum-di-doodle-dum-s-children:
S B Dinkelspiel tells fairy tales in Lady Rum-Di-Doodle-Dum's Children, published in New York in 1914. The dedication names Lady Rum-Di-Doodle-Dum as mother of all the bald-headed, pug-nosed little baby creatures in the world. The preface jokes that Bernard Shaw writes more preface than book, and promises to be briefer.

The contents open with Flip, who was supposed to be a secret, then Peter spilling the dew out of his pocket. Mr Smith, the King of Fairies, ends that trouble. John and Mary watch hundreds of lovely colors in a glass. Whimsy rules the nursery here.
66970-bees-shown-to-the-children:
Ellison Hawks wrote this book on bees for young readers, part of the Shown to the Children series edited by Louey Chisholm. Hawks belonged to the British Bee Keepers' Association and had written a book on stars in the same series. The book is given to two young friends, Annie and Katie. Colour and black-and-white pictures run through the text.

Hawks opens with a letter to the girls about a hive as a city. In that city live soldiers, food gatherers, bread-makers, and a queen who rules them all. Each day crowds of workers pass in and out of the gates by the hundred. The image sets up a close look at how bees live and work.
67132-society-for-superseding-the-necess:
The twenty-first report of the Society for Superseding the Necessity of Climbing Boys, printed in London in 1837, records a campaign to end the use of small boys to sweep chimneys. The society was founded on February 4, 1803, and backed a new machine method of sweeping instead.

The front pages name the King as patron, the Bishop of Winchester as president, and a committee of lords and members of Parliament. The report calls the past year the most successful yet, even though the number of subscribers had fallen. It opens with a short account of the society's origin and aims for readers meeting the cause for the first time. The cause was one of the noted child-labour reforms of the age.
67433-dixie-kitten:
Eva March Tappan wrote this story of a cat for young readers, printed in Boston in 1910. A bold note before the tale promises that it is a true story about a real cat, and that it ends happily. Dixie Kitten is a slender cat with soft black fur shot through with gleams of tawny yellow, three black paws and one yellow one, and yellow eyes that miss little.

The chapters follow Dixie from her home nest of soft hay, where her mother feeds and guards her, through leaving home and finding a friend. She meets troubles, becomes a little mother cat herself, is deserted, and at last settles in a new house. Tappan writes the cat's small life with close attention to what a kitten sees and feels.
67454-rich-men-s-children:
Rich Men's Children is a novel by Geraldine Bonner. The Bobbs-Merrill Company published it at Indianapolis in 1906. Relyea illustrated the volume for its readers. A frontispiece shows a man pleading to see Rose for a moment. The contents list twenty seven chapters of mining wealth. The Bonanza King opens the tale at page one. A Young Man Married and The Daughter of Heth follow. Out of Night and Storm and Nurse and Patient come next.

Snow-Bound and The Unknown Eros fill the middle chapters. The Sons of Their Fathers states the book's theme outright. Dominick Comes Home and The Gods in the Machine follow. The Root of All Evil and The God Descends give blunt titles. Rose's Point of View stands late in the contents. The Last Interview and a moving storm center close the list. Bonner writes of western fortunes and their heirs.
6755-canada-for-gentlemen:
James Seton Cockburn's letters from Canada, printed by his father to save the worn manuscript from many hands, form Canada for Gentlemen. The hope was that the letters might aid young emigrants, telling of troubles agencies seldom mention, with lessons often worth more than tales of uniform success. Names of friends are changed to fictions.

Cockburn writes home in a plain, personal voice, on land, work, and the hard first years. His letters feel private, not polished for print. Canada for Gentlemen is a frank, useful emigrant's record, valuable to readers of Canadian settlement history.
67641-idealia-a-utopian-dream-or-resthav:
Idealia, a utopian dream or Resthaven, is a tale by Alfarata Chapman, copyrighted in 1923 at Albany, New York. The writer, a cataloguer at the New York State Library, married John Thompson in September 1921 and died the next June, in 1922, with the tale a few lines from its end. Her husband brought it out at the urging of her friends.

The front pages give her life in brief: a brilliant young woman, schooled with honours at Albany, and a gifted, graceful writer. The tale itself dreams of Resthaven, a place of rest, and paints its people with, her husband says, characteristic sweetness and grace. The book stands as both a utopia and a memorial.
67679-the-council-of-seven:
The Council of Seven is a novel by JC Snaith, published in 1921. Snaith had written The Undefeated, The Sailor, and other tales. The catalog title is clipped, but the title page gives the full name.

The story opens in London on a September evening. Helen Sholto, leaving her office for her club, sees a newsbill shouting of an amazing speech by John Endor, a member of Parliament. His words warn that ties between Britain and America will bring growing anxiety, with hidden forces at work on both sides of the Atlantic. The paragraph shocks her like icy water. A rough workman buying the same paper swears savagely beside her, and the scene sets up a tale of secret power and public danger.
67695-buds-and-blossoms-or-stories-for-r:
Buds and Blossoms, or Stories of Real Children, was written by a lady and printed by Hatchard in London in 1832. Her introduction explains the title. Her own children, listening to stories, always ask whether a tale is all true, about a real little boy and girl, and their faces fall when she must answer no.

So she writes of real children, her own: Emily, Edwin, and Charles, alive as the reader reads, and offered as playfellows on the page. The first story, The Wish, has Emily, nearly six, asking how her mother first taught her about God. The answer goes back to when Emily was little more than two, asking who could reach up and draw the pretty pictures of the sun and moon she saw in the sky.
677-the-heroes-or-greek-fairy-tales-for-:
Charles Kingsley retold three Greek myths for young readers: the tales of Perseus, Jason and the Golden Fleece, and Theseus. He keeps the gods, monsters, and sea voyages of the old stories, but tells them in a plain, warm voice meant for children at home. Each hero faces a hard task and must show courage, patience, and care for others.

Perseus sets out against the Gorgon, Jason sails with the Argonauts in search of the fleece, and Theseus meets the Minotaur in the maze. Kingsley frames the myths as lessons in how to act well, not just as wonders. The book has lasted as a first door into Greek myth, because it keeps the adventure while making the old tales easy to follow.
67967-peter-parley-s-annual-1855-a-chris:
Peter Parley greets his young friends once more, glad at their holiday faces. His Annual for 1855, a Christmas and New Year present printed in New York, packs prose and verse for the fireside. Tales of brigands, desert treks, and a fearful shark crowd the prose list.

History comes in tales: Cardinal Wolsey, the youthful Nelson, Gustavus Vasa, and Glastonbury Abbey with King Arthur. Plain facts get their turn too, in pieces on rope making, lighthouses, the Chinese, and the American sea serpent. Four poems close the set. Parley, the pen name of Samuel Goodrich, taught a generation of American children through such gift books. Holiday faces, Parley says, make him feel young again.
68097-report-on-the-new-york-botanical-g:
Olmsted Brothers, the landscape firm, wrote this report on the New York Botanical Garden, dated August 1924 and printed in New York that year. The board of managers had asked the firm to study the grounds as a base for full plans to improve them. The report revises a first draft made in December 1923 after further study and talk.

The writers confirm the board's worry: the grounds are far less beautiful than the leading garden of the metropolis should be. Parts treat upkeep of the grounds, then betterment of what exists, naming the shrub collection, herb grounds, borders, and cherry garden. New departures follow: a rhododendron glade, model gardens, an iris garden, and a landscape garden. Later parts wrestle with motor traffic through the grounds and the area near the museum. The board's resolution and an index close the volume.
681-creatures-that-once-were-men:
Maxim Gorky gathered stories of men who had fallen out of settled life in late Tsarist Russia: tramps, thieves, and drifters living on the edge of towns and ports. They were once workers, soldiers, or clerks, but drink, debt, or bad luck cut them loose. Gorky knew this world at first hand and wrote it without softening its dirt or its hunger.

The tales turn on small choices: a job refused, a coin stolen, a kindness given or withheld. Beneath the rough talk, the men still argue about God, freedom, and what a human life is worth. The book made Gorky's name as the voice of Russia's outcasts, and it still hits hard as a portrait of pride and ruin among people the world had passed by.
68196-alien:
George O Smith writes a tale of a strange visitor in Astounding Science-Fiction for October 1946. Police lieutenant Timothy McDowell takes a call at his desk as the tale opens in plain style. A riot at McCarthy's on Boylston Street stands reported by O'Leary on the phone.

Riots at McCarthy's rank as nothing new, McDowell growls, yet this one stands apart from the run. Witnesses say a huge man with feathers in place of hair started the fuss in the bar. He would not take off his hat, and when he did, the crowd's laugh turned his temper in a flash. The bartender went through the plate glass, and fifteen hundred dollars of fine Irish whiskey lay wrecked.
68217-friendly-counsels-for-freedmen:
Friendly Counsels for Freedmen is a small tract by the Reverend Waterbury, issued at New York by a tract society. It speaks directly to men and women who have come out of bondage. The opening pages welcome them to the privileges of freemen. Providence, the writer says, has loosed their fetters, and the war was the means used to bring the change.

Readers are urged to give thanks for freedom when they pray. Their state now is in some ways better and in some ways worse, the tract admits. A kind master once took care of them, but now they must take care of themselves. In slavery they had little care beyond their task. As their own men they must think and work both, and seek a living by labour they can do.
68226-concerning-women:
Suzanne La Follette published Concerning Women with Albert and Charles Boni at New York in 1926. A saying of Mary Wollstonecraft heads the first chapter as its motto. Seven chapters move from the beginnings of emancipation through woman's status past and present. Marriage, its money side, and women's paid work fill the middle of the book.

La Follette argues that women count as free only when books about them turn antiquarian. A settled order, she says, teaches the ruling sex to see itself as mankind itself. The other sex then looks like a lower class made for its comfort. What is to be done and signs of promise close her case in turn. Cool reason drives a bold feminist brief.
68302-history-for-ready-reference-volume:
J N Larned edited History for Ready Reference, Volume Three, Greece to Nibelungen, held in 1894. Entries run in letter order and are built for swift search. Main titles stand at the left margin in capitals. Subtitles are indented and text follows after a blank line, a note on form explains.

References to other articles in the work stand indented in capitals. Citations of outside works are indented and set in italics. Page numbers are placed between paragraphs in braces in this digital text. Blocks of stray text are moved to a near break between subjects, the note says. Em dashes and space saving marks are replaced with spaces. The volume lets a reader find a fact on Greece or on the Nibelungen tale in moments, with sources named for more depth.
68359-poetry-for-children:
Poetry for Children, by Charles and Mary Lamb, was published by J M Dent and Company, illustrated by Winifred Green, with a prefatory note by Israel Gollancz. The prefatory essay, addressed to the gentle reader, lingers on the Blue-coat boys of Christ's Hospital.

The writer gazes lovingly at the quaint figure in long blue gaberdine, red leathern belt, and yellow stockings, still seen in crowded London streets. He mourns that London is no longer to be the school's home, and fancies he sees a pale Grecian walking with a younger lad of crisply curling black hair.
68376-nick-carter-stories-no-120-decembe:
Nick Carter Stories, number 120, dated December 26, 1914, is a weekly detective paper from Street and Smith of New York, priced at five cents. The tale in this number is An Uncanny Revenge, or Nick Carter and the Mind Murderer. Chapter one is headed A Tragedy of the Stage.

The famous detective's household meets at breakfast, a rare full table. Chick Carter, the leading assistant, sits with Patsy Garvan and his wife Adelina, and with Ida Jones, Nick's woman assistant. Ida came home after three in the morning, bright-eyed, and tells the table that they missed a sensation the night before, the strangest and most pitiable thing she ever saw.
68390-down-among-men:
Will Levington Comfort wrote Down Among Men, published by George H Doran at New York in 1913. A foreword frames the tale as one told through several nights. It is dedicated to the men of the upper room. The story told is of a man who came up through the dark and the fighting.

He was punished by men, broken by self, and healed by a woman. She paid the price; she was the man-maker. The first chapter is named Kao Liang, the millet of China. Inland seas of it grow in Manchuria, brushing the caps of Russian soldiers one fall. Comfort opens his tale of the road at Liaoyang's fields.
68557-you-no-longer-count-tu-n-es-plus-r:
René Boylesve wrote a French novel, rendered into English by Louise Seymour Houghton and issued by Scribner in 1918. Its title in French is Tu n'es plus rien. The book runs to thirty six chapters. It opens as a woman comes out of a swoon caused by a sudden, sharp shock.

She hears whispering in the next room and feels a hand test her pulse. Her thoughts slip back to a summer month in a suburban home outside Paris. Men were leaving for training camps as families made holiday plans. The novel builds its mood from memory, illness, and a sense of loss.
68759-the-economic-position-of-women:
The Economic Position of Women is a volume of papers from the Academy of Political Science at Columbia University, published in New York in 1910. Scholars and reformers of the day contribute its studies. The contents divide into history, problems of women in industry, and social action.

Helen L Sumner opens with the historical development of women's work in the United States. Mary Van Kleeck reports changes in women's work in binderies. Alice P Barrows treats the training of millinery workers, and Elizabeth B Butler training for salesmanship. Emily Greene Balch writes on the education and efficiency of women. Florence Kelley examines the industrial work of married women. John Martin argues the economics of equal pay for equal work in New York City schools. The volume is a founding document of American labour feminism's research wing.
68891-the-alley-cat-s-kitten:
Caroline Fuller published The Alley Cat's Kitten at Boston in 1904, illustrated from her own photographs. Fuller also wrote Across the Campus, a story for girls. She dedicates the book to a friend who helped build rabbit houses and befriended alley cats.

Sixteen chapters follow the alley cat, her kitten, rabbits black and white, a calico cat, and a family living in a piano box. Later chapters move to a lake and a farm, meet Clytie, the cat with mittens, and end on Christmas Eve. Readers get a warm animal household story where cats and rabbits share the stage and the photographs prove the pets were real.
68899-sparrow-the-tramp-a-fable-for-chil:
Lily Wesselhoeft wrote a fable for children, with pictures by Jessie McDermott, first printed in 1888 and again at Boston in 1902. A publishers' note tells a touching fact. The lamented author of Little Women in her last days read the manuscript with great delight, and its publication owes much to her interest in it.

Posy steals a lump of sugar at breakfast and swears it is only for Dicky. It went all to pieces in my mouth, she owns, when taxed with eating it. Mrs Polly, a parrot, guards her red tail feathers from Posy's tweaking fingers. Sparrow the tramp, a bird hero, learns and teaches lessons of kindness in a tale Louisa May Alcott herself blessed.
68984-helps-and-hints-for-hallowe-en:
Laura Rountree Smith wrote a handbook of games and stage pieces for the last night of October. March Brothers of Lebanon, Ohio, copyrighted it in 1920. The book opens with party plans for Nut Crack Night, the old English name for the feast. It tells how to word the invites and deck the rooms with black cats, owls, bats, and witches.

Later parts give stunts, drills, and short plays. A shadow play and a pumpkin climbing game stand among the stunts. The plays include The Hallowe'en Ghosts, The Witch's Dream, and The Play of Pomona. Old fortune tricks fill more pages. Guests crack nuts, float walnut shells, and throw apple skin to learn the name of a future mate. It is a full kit for a school or home party of that era.
69111-a-gallop-among-american-scenery-or:
Augustus Silliman wrote A Gallop Among American Scenery, for Appleton in 1843. The New York and Philadelphia house entered the book that year. Sketches in it had appeared in the columns of the New-York American. Silliman gives the little volume to his brother Benjamin, with affection. Contents open with the banks of the Potomac and a country pastor.

Mount Vernon, a medical student, and the resurrectionists follow in the list. Old Kennedy fills four sketches in the middle of the contents. Lee's partisan legion and the Hudson river take their turns. A night attack on Fort Erie and the battle of Lundy's Lane bring war. Lake George, Ticonderoga, Montreal, and the cataracts of Niagara follow. White Mountains, bass fishing off Newport, and Green-Wood cemetery close the ride. Silliman gallops through scenes and military tales of the young republic.
69125-the-higher-education-of-women:
Emily Davies wrote The Higher Education of Women, printed at London in eighteen sixty-six. Her opening argues that any inquiry meant to lead to action must start with a clear end in view. In education, she says, the received ends are quietly set aside when women are in question. Maurice's end of forming a nation of living, orderly men is taken to mean men only.

Milton's account of learning, too, turns out on close reading to be built for boys from twelve to twenty-one. Davies asks what the teachers of girls should aim to make of them. Parts then treat ideals, things as they are, and things as they might be. Professional and domestic life are weighed, and a part of specific suggestions closes the case.
69136-the-lure-of-piper-s-glen:
The Lure of Piper's Glen, by Theodore Goodridge Roberts, was copyrighted in 1922 and reissued at Garden City in 1925. Fifteen chapters follow logging men, road crews, and river drivers in the woods of Racket River country. A front plate shows Homer Steeves, Flora, and Jim on a sled with dogs.

The opening describes spring breakup, when crews leave the headwater camps and snowmelt lifts the ice. Stream drivers wear greased boots spiked with fifty steel caulks per boot to bite a foothold on rolling logs. Chapters promise games fair and foul, a queer old woman, a widow's gift, and a man-hunter. Roberts writes the timber trade with close knowledge and rough affection.
69452-shells-and-pebbles-a-story-for-chi:
A story book for children, issued in London by a group that spread Christian knowledge, follows a boy on his first real trip to the sea. Henry Miller is eight years old and has lived all his life in a county far inland. He was taken to the shore as a baby but can recall nothing of it.

Henry spends two or three days with his father in a town on the south coast of England. On the beach he learns for himself that the sea is salt and picks up shells and other shore finds. The tale aims to teach young readers to use their eyes and ask those who know more than they do.
69593-the-history-of-the-jews-from-the-w:
The Rev H C Adams wrote a history of the Jews from the war with Rome to his own time. The Religious Tract Society issued it in London in 1887. Adams was vicar of Old Shoreham and wrote Wykehamica and Schoolboy Honour. A contents list maps the long tale by reigns and years.

Early chapters treat the revolt of Judas and the siege of Jerusalem by Titus. Later parts run through Trajan, Adrian, and the revolt of Barchochebas. Constantine, Julian, Justinian, and Mahomet mark the road east and west. General readers of the time got a compact survey of a people's trials across many lands.
69612-the-sea-scouts-of-the-kestrel-the-:
Percy Westerman wrote The Sea Scouts of the Kestrel, the story of a cruise of adventure in a small yacht on the English Channel. Seeley, Service and Company published the book in London, with coloured illustrations. Westerman wrote many sea stories for boys, among them Clipped Wings and Sea Scouts Abroad.

The frontispiece shows Brandon fighting his way forward in a gale to cast off the rope that holds the Kestrel to the Merlin. Chapters bring fog, a derelict, a rescued man, and a plot by a villain named Blueskin. A stowaway, a convict, and the peril of the Race, a dreaded tide-rip, raise the stakes. The cruise ends in a race for a cup, a dead heat, and a rescue from the deep. Pluck and seamanship carry the young crew through.
69667-the-giftie-gien:
The Giftie Gien is a short story by Malcolm Jameson, first printed in the magazine Unknown Worlds in April 1943. Illustrations by Kramer accompany the tale. The title plays on the old wish for the gift of seeing ourselves as others see us.

The story opens at five o'clock in the office of a household appliance firm. The sales manager sits watching his salesmen come in, folded hands resting on his stomach, sure he is the best manager the company has ever had. His secretary waits beside him with her notebook, expecting no weighty words. The scene sets up a complacent man for whatever gift the title promises. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
69683-men-without-women:
Men Without Women, by Ernest Hemingway, came out at New York in 1927, from Charles Scribner's Sons. Its list of past books names The Sun Also Rises and In Our Time. Fourteen tales make up the set. Most first ran in famed journals in America and France.

The first tale, The Undefeated, opens in Madrid. Manuel Garcia climbs to the office of Don Miguel Retana with his suitcase, and begs for work. Retana thought him dead. Manuel has had one bull fight this year, and read of it in the papers. A stuffed bull head hangs over the desk. That bull, Mariposa, killed his brother Antonio, the hopeful one, nine years back. More tales treat wounds, love, and loss in terse prose. Readers get stark tales of men alone with pride and pain.
69693-life-of-beethoven:
Louis Nohl wrote a life of Beethoven, turned from German by John J Lalor. Jansen, McClurg and Company issued it at Chicago in 1881. The book stands in a set of lives of musicians. A portrait of Ludwig van Beethoven fronts the work.

Nohl opens with praise for music as the most loved of the arts. He notes how slowly Beethoven's works won a hearing from the crowd. Tales of the crabbed composer strolling Vienna with a notebook fill the first pages. Readers gain a warm, dated life of a master whose name stirred awe in all who met him.
69705-gardening-for-women:
Gardening for Women, by the Hon. Frances Wolseley, came out in 1908 with thirty-two pictures. Wolseley ran the Glynde School for Lady Gardeners in Sussex, and the book speaks from that post. Part one asks if work in gardens can serve as a true trade for women who must earn a wage.

Chapters treat the training required, landscape work, jobbing work, and flower dressing for rooms. Others give hints on dress, food, and cottages, and on taking a post as head gardener. One part looks at the health side of the work, and one at posts in South Africa. Part two lists schools for lady gardeners in Britain, on the mainland, and in America, Canada, and Australia.
69772-a-christmas-snowflake-a-rhyme-for-:
Anna Granniss wrote this Christmas rhyme for children, printed at Hartford under copyright in 1903 and illustrated with photographs. She dedicated it to the memory of a baby sister and a little brother who went away one Christmas many years before. A second thousand was soon called for.

A little white snowflake looks down from the sky with a tear in its eye. The ground is bare and brown, and the children at the windows cry because no snow has come and Santa cannot travel without it. Two lovely large flakes dance by, and the little flake begs them to fall with it before night. Pictures show Santa scanning the skies and the reindeer at home. The rhyme is a tender snow prayer in verse.
69775-pen-portraits-of-literary-women:
Helen Gray Cone and Jeannette L Gilder edited this first volume of pen portraits of literary women, printed by Cassell in New York with an 1887 copyright. Cone wrote the brief lives that frame the pieces. The book answers a set on British authors that had left women out, save for one. Its plan adds place and scene to the traits of each writer.

The volume treats Hannah More, Frances Burney, Mary Wollstonecraft, Mary Shelley, Mary Lamb, Maria Edgeworth, Jane Austen, Joanna Baillie, Lady Blessington, and Mary Russell Mitford. Behind Charlotte and Emily Bronte the wild moors stand in view. Each portrait mixes the woman's own words with the words of those who knew her work.
69790-the-three-just-men:
The Three Just Men is a thriller by Edgar Wallace, published by Hodder and Stoughton at London, continuing the adventures of the just men of his earlier novels. Its first chapter is headed The Firm of Oberzohn, and the second introduces the three men of Curzon Street.

The chapter list promises a vendetta, a snake that strikes, a golden woman, lights going out, a message written in braille, the story of Mont d'Or, and a death tube. The story opens with a newspaper advertisement offering a high salary for a lady laboratory secretary, no experience required but a recognised examination in physics and elementary chemistry. Preference, the advertisement adds, goes to an applicant whose family has some record in the world of science.
69862-days-and-hours-in-a-garden:
The author who signs with the initials EVB published 'Days and Hours in a Garden' in a ninth edition with Elliot Stock in 1896. Its motto comes from Bacon: God Almighty first planted a garden. The records were inscribed in 1884 to Richard Cavendish Boyle, whose love for nature and art years had not chilled. A preface to the seventh edition admits nothing new has been added, yet hopes for new readers.

The garden itself supplies the change: shrubs grow taller, laurels are felled to let in the south sunshine, and the axe and pruning knife stay busy all winter. A Sequoia already rises fifty feet and measures over nine feet round, while the Douglas fir and the cedar of Lebanon grow into one another. The book keeps a gardener's calendar of gains and losses across the seasons.
7006-bonnie-prince-charlie-a-tale-of-fon:
G A Henty sets Bonnie Prince Charlie at Fontenoy and Culloden, opening on a dull September evening in 1728. Apprentices have barred the shutters, supper stands in the long room over the shop, and Bailie Anderson, his wife, foreman John Gillespie, and two apprentices wait through a long grace. A knock sounds below, twice repeated, before the bailie finishes, and old Elspeth is sent to look through the grille.

These are not times, the bailie warns, to open to the first stranger who knocks. The knock proves the return of a prodigal, and the tale that follows carries a Scots lad from shop to battlefield, through the Jacobite rising to its end at Culloden. Henty writes for boys, with loyalty, daring, and defeat in full color.
70200-pen-portraits-of-literary-women:
Pen Portraits of Literary Women, by themselves and others, here volume two of two, was edited by Helen Gray Cone and Jeannette L Gilder. Cassell and Company in New York issued the volume with copyright in eighteen eighty seven. Biographical sketches by Cone aid the portraits. Six women fill the volume. Harriet Martineau opens the set.

Martineau was born at Norwich on June twelfth, eighteen oh two, of Huguenot refugee stock. Her father Thomas Martineau was a Norwich manufacturer, and her mother Elizabeth Rankin was a true Northumbrian woman. Harriet was the sixth child in a family of eight. Her childhood was sickly, repressed, and unhappy, and she wrote later that her life had no spring. At eleven she went to the school of Mr Perry, who laid a solid foundation for her education. Portraits of George Sand, Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Margaret Fuller, the Brontës, and George Eliot follow.
70310-the-starmen:
The Starmen is a science fiction novel by Leigh Brackett, printed at New York by Gnome Press in 1952. It is the first edition, copyright that year. A shorter version had appeared in 1951. The hero is Michael Trehearne.

The opening scene is set behind Saint-Malo in Brittany, at the Midsummer Fires. Tourists crowd the stony turf to watch the old Breton festival of the sacred bonfire. Trehearne stands alone, as he always stands, finding the ritual too quaint to endure. Trehearne turns and sees a face so like his own that he is startled. The stranger asks how long he has been here, expecting another answer than the one he gets. From that meeting the novel lifts its Earth-bound hero toward the stars.
70352-sir-christopher-wren:
Lawrence Weaver wrote Sir Christopher Wren, published in London and New York in 1923. The Country Life offices and George Newnes issued the London edition. Scribner handled the American one. The subtitle names Wren a scientist, scholar, and architect.

Weaver names his chief source at the start. The Parentalia, compiled by Wren's son Christopher, mines notes, letters, and discourses. The son's book is badly built yet full of charm. It also covers Wren's father, a dean of Windsor, and his uncle, a bishop of Ely. Stephen Wren published the family papers in 1750. Later lives by Elmes, Phillimore, and Milman all dug in the same mine. A plate of Wren's chief works opens this study of England's great church builder.
7039-the-angel-adjutant-of-twice-born-me:
Minnie Carpenter tells of Staff Captain Kate Lee, the angel adjutant of Twice Born Men, with an introduction by General Bramwell Booth and a foreword by Commander Evangeline Booth. Booth calls the book an intimate and living picture of a woman whose fine character and ceaseless labor held singular charm and amazing fruitfulness. The Salvation Army, he notes, has been happy in its women officers.

Long denied public testimony and the chance to proclaim the Saviour's mission, women in the movement proved their worth. They stood as effective, acceptable, and successful as their brethren, as teachers and rulers in Christ's kingdom on earth. The book follows Kate Lee among the twice born, those remade by faith. It is a portrait of service, courage, and a life spent for others.
7045-marching-men:
Sherwood Anderson's Marching Men, dedicated to American workingmen, opens in Coal Creek, Pennsylvania, at Nance McGregor's bake shop. Uncle Charlie Wheeler stamps on the steps, laughs and whistles softly, and taps the showcase before the Reverend Minot Weeks. A boy fumbles wrapping his loaf, and Uncle Charlie waves at the pretty name Norman McGregor, vowing to change it to a name that will stick.

Norman, he says, is too soft and delicate for the boy. The novel that follows carries Norman McGregor from a coal town boyhood toward a vision of workingmen marching together, disciplined and purposeful. Anderson writes of labor, manhood, and the hunger for order in industrial America, in his plain and searching style.
70494-second-stage-lensmen:
Edward Elmer Smith wrote Second Stage Lensmen, a science fiction novel serialized in Astounding Science Fiction from November 1941 to February 1942. The book continues the Lensman saga of the Galactic Patrol. An opening history explains that crime outran the police once Bergenholm's inertialess drive opened the galaxy to commerce.

The Patrol's elite wear the Lens, a living telepathic jewel that kills anyone but its matched owner. Kimball Kinnison, first in his class, commands the new ship Brittania against the pirates of Boskone. Their strange new power source threatens Civilization itself. Kinnison captures a Boskonian warship to learn its secret. Smith builds space opera on a huge scale: whole fleets, hidden empires, and a war behind the war.
70536-the-land-of-hidden-men:
The Land of Hidden Men is a wild tale by Edgar Rice Burroughs. It first ran in a tale sheet in nineteen thirty-one and came out as a book past the name Jungle Girl the next year. A front quote tells of deep wild things no man may look on and live. The ghosts of an old race that built great towns in that wood are chief past them, it says.

Gordon King, a young man of the new age, will not be scared off by such talk. He hires a guide of that land to lead him to the wild. At the edge of a gorge, past which the trail ends, the guide halts and will go no more. He vowed to bring his lord to the wild, he says, not to step in it. King lights a smoke and bids him talk it past.
70657-prayer-and-praying-men:
Prayer and Praying Men is a devotional work by Edward Bounds, issued in London by Hodder and Stoughton. George Doran Company took the copyright in 1921 in the United States. Bounds is named as author of Preacher and Prayer and Purpose in Prayer. Hodge wrote the introduction to this volume for its readers.

Contents march through the praying men of the Bible as the book examples of its art. Praying saints of the Old Testament fill the first two chapters of the list. Abraham the man of prayer, Moses the mighty intercessor, and Elijah the praying prophet follow in order. Hezekiah the praying king, Ezra the reformer, Nehemiah the builder, Samuel, and Daniel the captive complete the shown contents. His method here is biography: each life is read as a school of prayer for the praying men and women of his own day.
70779-the-highland-glen:
The Highland Glen, by Matilda Wrench, was published in 1847. Wertheim issued the tale in London that year. Its profits went to the suffering Highlanders, the title page states. Plenty and Famine is its second title. The tale opens with an invitation to the reader. Western Argyleshire is the scene, with its glens and lakes. A traveller is rowed up a loch against the tide. The Serpent's Fall lies at its head. Craggy mountains tower over the deep blue water. One guide is a student of St Andrew's home for the vacation. He rows visitors to earn money for his college books. His father is a small tenant on the Lochiel estates.

Legends fill the rowing talk. A shepherd of old was changed into a mountain for straying.
70797-personal-hygiene-and-physical-trai:
Personal Hygiene and Physical Training for Women is a health manual by Anna Galbraith, a physician. This text is the second edition, thoroughly revised, published in Philadelphia in 1916. The first edition came out in 1911. Galbraith also wrote The Four Epochs of Woman's Life and held posts at the Woman's Medical College in New York.

The book runs to 393 pages with pictures. It teaches women the care of the body and the training of it by exercise. Galbraith writes from years of practice and teaching in women's medicine. Her manual belongs to the wave of health books that brought medical advice to women readers at home in the early twentieth century.
70812-the-dramatic-instinct-in-children:
Child Life Institute staff prepared this study of the dramatic instinct. Abingdon Press issued the fourth edition in New York in 1914. A Stevenson verse on leaden soldiers fronts the small study. Part one treats the nature of the instinct in three ages.

Early, middle, and later childhood each show the instinct at work. It rests on imitation, construction, and motor activity in the child. Part two weighs its moral and inspirational value for schools. A summary and references close the American Home Series pamphlet. A note ties the pamphlet matter to a larger Manual of Play by Forbush in print.
70826-young-peggy-mcqueen:
Gordon Stables wrote Young Peggy McQueen, issued by Collins with original illustrations. A plate shows Peggy standing on a rock in the sunlight. Two books divide her adventures, from a forest play to a cannibal isle.

Peggy is twelve, and lives in a little caravan, her home upon wheels. On the first of May she rises at half-past four to dip her face in the dew, a custom said to keep a girl sweet and beautiful all year. Her bloodhound Ralph votes for bed instead. Later chapters bring minstrels, a bloodhound on the trail, then storm and wreck. On the island she fights a bloodless battle before white wings appear upon the waves.
71414-british-freewomen:
Charlotte Stopes wrote this study of British freewomen and their old privilege. Sonnenschein printed it in London in 1894 with full contents. Stopes took her degree at Edinburgh University before this work. Chapter one treats ancient history and British women at first.

Modern bases of privilege and royal women fill the next chapters. Queens consort, regnant, and regent each get their own section. Noblewomen paid and received homage and held courts baron, it shows. They could be knights, sheriffs, earl marshal, and castle governors. County women as freeholders and femes soles fill the fifth chapter of the study.
71427-two-young-lumbermen:
Edward Stratemeyer wrote Two Young Lumbermen, or From Maine to Oregon for Fortune, printed at Boston in 1903. It belongs to the Great American Industries Series. Pictures by Shute show log jams, bears, and forest fires.

Dale Bradford works at the Enterprise Lumber Mill in Maine, where a lack of logs may shut the mill down. With his friend Owen he heads west to seek his fortune in the lumber trade. The chapter list promises log rolling, a log jam on the Penobscot, a storm on the lakes, and work in an Oregon forest. Dale comes into his own at the close.
71476-grandfer-s-wonderful-garden:
Eleanora Stooke wrote Grandfer's Wonderful Garden, issued at London by the Religious Tract Society. Stooke had written Little Maid Marigold and Whilst Father was Fighting. A plate shows Harold and Billy busily making a bonfire.

Billy Brown, aged ten, rides the fast train from Paddington to Exeter, frightened that it is running away. A young soldier, Tom Turpin of the Devons, home on leave from France, calms him. Billy's father is dead, and his mother was killed in a Zeppelin raid the month before. Chapters promise a fright, a Sunday, gardening, and Grandfer's secret. A bird picture book and a surprise from Granny come before spring.
71527-14000-miles-a-carriage-and-two-wom:
Frances S Howe wrote Fourteen Thousand Miles, a Carriage and Two Women, privately printed in nineteen oh six. The copyright is held by Howe. Many reports first ran in the Boston Evening Transcript, and later letters ran in the Leominster Daily Enterprise. Two women drove more than fourteen thousand miles in a carriage over years of summer and autumn trips. A plate shows them ready for a seven hundred miles drive.

A foreword says a first trip of two hundred miles along the Connecticut River kept its charm through all later drives. Chapters treat Old Orchard, Boston, the White Mountains, and Franconia Notch. Later drives reach the Catskills, Lake George, Canada, and Bar Harbor. The women drove a large, roomy buggy with one horse, to townsfolk protest that such trips were not proper for ladies. Their book is a bright record of grit, roads, and rest.
71557-the-secret-history-of-the-court-of:
Rachel Challice uncovers intrigue in The Secret History of the Court of Spain During the Last Century, from D Appleton of New York in 1909, with thirty illustrations. Her note insists the material comes solely from Spanish sources, some of them books unknown in England, read in the library of the Royal Palace at Madrid. English readers may find views they do not expect.

The chapters open with Ferdinand, Prince of Asturias, plotting against his parents and Godoy, then Napoleon's checkmating of the royal family. Ferdinand the Seventh's home life, Isabella's girlhood, and the regency of Maria Cristina follow.
71694-even-stephen:
Even Stephen is a science fiction story by Charles A Stearns, first printed in Infinity in July 1957. Its heading gives the theme: it only takes one man to destroy a pacifist utopia, if he has a gun and will use it. A henna-haired young man in a vermilion cape boards Stephen's vehicle on the thirty-third air level.

He grapples the two craft together with his right arm and climbs into the seat beside Stephen. His own skimmercar whisks off at a thousand miles an hour, left to its traffic-dodging mechanism. The visitor is barbarically splendid, with steel dentures like most of his generation, born toothless after the last Blow-down. More to the point, he has a gun: a moisture rifle that can steam the flesh off a man's bones at three hundred paces, quite illegal. He orders Stephen to turn toward the sea.
71941-children-of-men:
Children of Men is a tale by Eden Phillpotts, the hand of past tales named on the title leaf. It was first put out in nineteen twenty three at London. Its parts fall in a fore tale and three books. The list of parts is long, and most of its heads are short and plain. The tale is set in the moor lands of the west of England.

A pledge of love heads the fore tale. On a high moor post and a save stand past it. The first book names its chief man at its head. At a red house, a farm past a note of loss, and on a bridge of a small stream come next. The young, a hunt war ren, the rest day, a feast, and a gift fill the first run.
71942-plants-and-their-children:
Plants and Their Children, by Mrs William Starr Dana, author of How to Know the Wild Flowers, was published by the American Book Company in 1896, illustrated by Alice Josephine Smith. The book is arranged to begin with the opening of the school year and follow it to its close.

Dana's directions to teachers ask that specimens of the objects described stand on show in the schoolroom. Children should collect and handle the specimens themselves whenever possible. While pupils train in reading, she writes, their powers of observation and reasoning grow, and a lifelong interest in nature takes root.
72070-floor-of-heaven:
Floor of Heaven, a story by Hamm with pictures by Adkins, ran in Amazing Stories in January 1961. The three crew members of the Ad Astra grin at one another at the opening. Their motors have kicked off, and silence whispers in the ship. Behind them lies the satellite launching station of Earth.

Ahead of them, a faint red dot, is Mars, the goal of the flight. This was the crowning point of a half century of preparation, the tale says. Bryan, nominal head of the expedition, touches the shutter studs of the windows. Bryan and Hughes look back at the majesty of the retreating Earth. Hamm writes the first Mars voyage in the sober style of the age.
7208-kathleen:
Christopher Morley's Kathleen opens at Merton College, Oxford, where Kenneth Forbes must finish the first chapter of a serial story before the Scorpions meet at eight. The literary society counts eight members, each to write a chapter in turn. Named on a grotesque undergraduate whim, it made Forbes, first operator for his fertile wit, spend the whole Christmas vacation on his opening.

On the first Sunday of term, while the rest of college dines in hall, Forbes sits at his desk driving his pen in desperation. Morley dedicates the book to the real Kathleen, with apologies, and the joke of a story written by committee gives the novel its light, teasing start. Oxford talk, youth, and invention set the tone.
72157-salome-s-burden:
Salomes Burden, or The Shadow on the Homes is a tale by Eleanora Stooke, with four plates. Stooke was known past a shelf of tales for the young. Past fifteen heads fill it, from its heros pain to days of more joy. It opens in the warm half past a hot day, as the sun sinks like a ball of fire past the wide sea.

A cool wind springs up and the folk of a fish town come to their doors to chat in the fresh dusk air. That town owns but two houses of mark, the church house and a grey stone house past a low rise past the sea. The best kept plot of the town is that of Salome Petherick, a lame girl of past ten years and four. She has been lame from birth and walks past the aid of two sticks.
72307-the-quare-women:
Lucy Furman wrote this story of the Kentucky mountains, The Quare Women. Atlantic Monthly Press printed it Boston, copyright 1923, four impressions by 1924. A note ties its air to Hindman Settlement School in Knott County. Contents open with the quare women arrival in the hills.

Taking the night, the Fourth of July, and the singing gal follow. A widow man, devil ditties, a funeral, and moonshine fill middle. Aunt Ailsie hears a passel of quare women camped above the courthouse. Folks pour up the hill till court can hardly sit that week.
72325-uncle-ben:
Uncle Ben is a tale for small folk by Oliver Optic, put out at Boston in eighteen sixty five. It stands in a set of small tale books for the young named for a river town. Its rights were put on the rolls in eighteen sixty two in the name of the man past his pen name. His past sets for boys are named on the title leaf. A plate of a rest past a tree stands at the front.

The tale opens on a warm day of the high year. Frank and Flora Lee, with Charley Green and his two small kin girls, have gone out to spend the day in the field. It is the month of ripe field fruit, and the small band bear tin pails to fill with wild red fruit.
72445-parents-and-children: Parents and Children shares its maker with Home Education, a course of lectures to ladies by Charlotte Mason, as the list of works by the same author shows. That pairing frames the book: thought on how parents raise and teach their children, from a voice known for home training. The head of this copy gives trade lists alone, with no chapter text, so its scope is stated here at that level.
72498-war-in-heaven:
War in Heaven, by Fletcher Pratt, is an article on space warfare from Fantastic Universe of mid 1953. Pratt was better known as a historian of war on land and sea than as a writer of tales. The editors promise well-thought answers that will surprise would-be spacemen.

Pratt opens by mocking the stock scene: a mighty ship looses a sheet of energy at a foe. Oh yeah, he asks, and how would you make such a sheet, or keep a beam tight across thousands of miles? Death-rays, force screens, and tractor beams will not work by any science we know, he argues. The one ray that might harm crews is ultra-violet, which the sun pours out for free. Solid shot and space mines, the title argues, win wars more cheaply.
72506-listen-children-listen:
Wallace West wrote this tale of dread, listen, children, listen, taken from a magazine of late 1953. A headnote gives its germ: the old man was long dead, but his widow still awaited his return, and one night she heard. A passage before the tale counts the shapes of horror, from a coyote's howl to moonlight in a huge old mirror.

The teller's grandmother was fey, the neighbours said. She foretold weather by a pain in her heel, knew by a sixth sense when kin were coming down from Indianapolis, and heard angels singing at funerals. To the teller and his sister she seemed as old as the gullies in their clay fields. She sang bloody old hymns and ballads in the wreck of a fine alto voice. The teller still has nightmares of those years, and of a recent murder at a farmhouse nearby.
72541-preliminary-report-on-a-visit-to-t:
Jesse Walter Fewkes made a first report on the Navaho National Monument. The report is Bulletin 50 of the Bureau of American Ethnology. It came out in Washington in 1911 from the state press. His chief sent it in with a note dated March 16, 1910. A plate of Kitsiel, a cliff town, fronts the book.

Roads from Flagstaff to Marsh Pass are mapped in words first. Fewkes then tells what the old cliff homes show at first view. Stone rooms, towers, and pots speak of folk long gone. He marks the work as a first look, not the last word. Past and land fans get a prime source in brief.
72544-midwifery-and-the-diseases-of-wome:
Joel Shew published his descriptive and practical work on midwifery with Fowlers and Wells at New York in 1856. The title page claims the superiority of water treatment in full. Disorders of menstruation, chlorosis, leucorrhea, hysteria, and spinal weakness head the long list. Pregnancy, abortion, hemorrhage, childbirth, and nursing follow, with many cases of treatment.

The introduction answers four plain questions friends of the Water-Cure often asked. Shew began hydropathic midwifery in 1843 and had printed smaller works since then. He cites women who bore children under old methods and under water care, and found the second far easier. Diet, air, exercise, and bathing form his regimen. Reform medicine speaks here in earnest, hopeful tones.
72625-fifty-christmas-poems-for-children:
Florence Hyett selected Fifty Christmas Poems for Children for Appleton, and the anthology appeared in 1923, with a woodcut cover by Nightingale. A question from Eugene Field serves as motto: why do the bells of Christmas ring, why do little children sing?

The index of authors begins with the anonymous, who supply the oldest pieces. An old carol, a shepherd's song, the cherry-tree carol, the holly and the ivy, and I saw three ships all appear. The compiler thanks authors and publishers for the poems borrowed. Appleton sold the book as a gift annual in permanent form. Such anthologies standardized the child's Christmas: carols first, then the moderns, all in one cloth volume. It was meant to be read aloud in the week when the schoolroom emptied and the tree went up.
72713-blind-tim-and-other-christmas-stor:
C O Solberg wrote Blind Tim and Other Christmas Stories Written for Children, issued at Minneapolis by Augsburg Publishing House with copyright in nineteen twenty six. Three editions ran within a year. A poem translated from the Norwegian, In Childhood I Saw Him, stands first. Blind Tim follows in four chapters. Six more stories fill the book. A note says most plots rest on actual occurrence.

Stories include Rags, A Queer Christmas Tree, and Bigbeard and Little Sander. No Christmas, Buddy Christmas Tree, and Three Pines close the set. The last two stories had not appeared in print before, the note adds. Poems in the text could serve as declamations, it notes. The opening poem tells of seeing Christ in childhood, youth, and manhood. Lutheran children get warm Christmas tales from a Norwegian American press.
72779-what-to-eat-and-when:
What to Eat and When is a book on food and health by Susanna Cocroft. She was the author of Let's Be Healthy and The Woman Worth While. The book came out in a fourth edition from G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1916, with fresh matter and changes to date. A portrait of the author stands at its front.

The contents show a plan that starts from first grounds. The first chapter treats the ends of food: the making of heat and force, the make-up of the body, and the building and repair of cells. It treats the need of exercise as well. The second chapter sorts the stuffs of food into classes and sets them out in tables. The work is a guide to diet for the home reader of its day.
73404-enfranchisement-of-women:
Enfranchisement of Women is a piece by the wife of John Stuart Mill. It first ran in a great sheet of the realm in the year eighteen fifty one. The host print was made at New York in eighteen sixty eight. That print came from the desk of a sheet of the revolt of women. A note to the reader stands at its head. That note says this form gives the whole of the piece.

Most of our readers, the piece starts, will learn from these pages a new thing. A set stir has rose in the United States, it says, and in the most high and bright part of them. That stir is on a new doubt. The doubt is not new to men of thought, it owns.
73489-anne-s-terrible-good-nature-and-ot:
E V Lucas wrote these stories for children, first published in 1908 and often reprinted, with illustrations by A H Buckland. The frontispiece shows a girl giving an old woman one hundred and four of her threepenny bits, to the woman's intense astonishment.

The title story opens on Anne Wilbraham Bayes, whose good nature is perfectly appalling. It came from neither parent: her father insists on silence at breakfast, and her mother thinks first of the top left-hand drawer. The contents add the thousand threepenny bits, Roderick's pros, the monkey's revenge, and the anti-burglars. A day in the life of a shilling is narrated by the coin itself. Children get Lucas's gentle satire on goodness carried too far.
73556-especially-dance-hall-women:
Alma and Paul Ellerbe wrote this tale of a dance hall, opening with the line that a gold strike is likely to change a man's viewpoint. Long Jim Briggs wanders into Al's Dance Hall one night to find Captain Mac drunk and throwing things. She has deep red hair and skin as white as blanched almonds, and Jim admires her greatly. He has given up prospecting at times to earn carpenter's pay to spend on her.

Captain Mac has broken a big mirror, and the other girls say Al will make her pay a month's costs for the place. A saucer she throws cuts Jim over the eye, and all laugh. Then Rosie Ellen McCarthy, a decent Irish girl, looks out of her eyes and begs Jim to take her out of the hall.
73868-box-garden:
Box Garden, a tale by Allen Lang, ran in Science Fiction Adventures in April 1958. The hero at the bar had big ears and hated television commercials. He talked of bansai, spelled with an s, the blurb teases. The narrator sat to his left, trying to see the set.

The ears of the man blocked the view of the television. The commercial was on, and the narrator did not want to miss it. Leaning forward, he bumped the man’s shoulder by accident. The big eared man took the nudge as an invitation to talk. He was tired, he said, of being treated like an adult dwarf. Lang builds the tale on that bar room opening and its grumble.
74142-raw-men:
Frank Richardson Pierce wrote an Arctic tale that tests what men owe each other. A front note says Pierce knows the far north at first hand. He holds that self-keeping is not the first law of nature. His tale is meant to prove that claim in action. Ice, fur wealth, and a frail ship set the stage.

A Swede at the wheel talks with an Eskimo scout in brief speech. The pack ice grinds toward shore and wipes out the blue lead. Bergs pile high where the pack has ground to a halt. The ship's holds bear a fortune in furs. Each man weighs risk with a calm, hard eye.
74224-social-devices-for-impelling-women:
Social Devices for Impelling Women to Bear and Rear Children is a paper by Leta Hollingworth of Bellevue Hospital, New York City. A quote from Ross on social control heads the study. Ross notes that public opinion and religion once joined to crush women's hopes of a life of their own. That pressure served the breeding work of the family. The gain, Ross holds, would not be worth the price.

Hollingworth calls this a prime case of social control: rule over the one group that can bear the young and so keep society alive. She asks readers to drop soft views of motherhood and face facts, citing Sumner on the burdens children add to parents. Child-bearing, she argues, is like soldiering: needful, risky, and a sacrifice. The paper is a cool, bold study of custom and pressure.
74293-chats-with-children:
Chats with Children, or Pearls for Young People Strung from the Word of Truth, is a devotional book by Amy Le Feuvre. Pickering and Inglis published it at London and Glasgow, with coloured and plain pictures. A bishop's praise stands at the front: Le Feuvre's books need no introduction, they are always inspiring.

The first chat opens with a memory of a very ugly looking house the author loved as a little girl. It faced the street with straight rows of bare, square windows, and no creeper or flower to be seen. But inside it was delicious and comfortable, with a lovely old garden hidden behind high walls. From such memories Le Feuvre draws her lessons for children. Her chats join story, scripture, and counsel in the gentle voice that made her a household name in Christian homes.
74521-the-prospector-and-the-silver-quee:
The Prospector is Cy Warman's story of the life of Nicholas C Creede, published at Denver by the Great Divide Publishing Company in 1894. Portraits of Creede, D H Moffat, Captain L E Campbell, S T Smith, and Walter S Cheesman illustrate the volume. Warman's preface states its purpose: to tell the simple story of an unpretentious man, and to show what the prospector has endured and accomplished for the West.

His introduction begins with the making of the land itself. An ocean displaced, a hemisphere risen, winds leveling the plains, and at one last throe the mountains of silver and gold rising up. Cliff dwellers ruled the land, then the Red Man, then the prospector, who brushed away the mysteries. Creede, discoverer of the great silver camp that bore his name, stands as the type of that hero.
74556-one-thousand-books-for-children:
One Thousand Books for Children is a reading guide compiled by Penrhyn W Coussens. Coussens also edited a book of poems children love. The Chicago edition is dated nineteen eleven. Lists are split by age and by sex in the contents. Girls eight to ten come first, then older girls in bands. Boys follow in the same bands, up to eighteen. Lists for boys and girls together cover the youngest readers.

Subject lists follow the age lists. Myths, fairy tales, legends, and folk lore hold one section. Nature study and science with handicraft hold others. Bible stories and poetry take their own sections. Supplementary reading and indexes of titles and authors close the volume. An introduction praises the supplementary reader in schools. It has done much to improve the literary taste of the pupil, it argues.
74674-portraits-of-women:
Gamaliel Bradford wrote Portraits of Women, a book of short lives put out at Boston and New York in 1916. Plates from paint works of the past fill the book. Bradford gives it to his daughter, with a jest line from Twelfth Night. Most parts first ran in the press from 1912 to 1915.

Lady Mary Wortley Montagu leads the set, with her dates set out in a roll. She was born in London on May 26, 1689, and wed in the year 1712. She lived in the great Turk town from 1716 to 1718, by that roll. Lady Holland and Miss Austen come next in the set. Madame d Arblay, Mrs Pepys, and the great letter smiths of France fill the rest. Sevigne, Du Deffand, and Choiseul stand for the French art of the pen. A last life tells of Eugenie de Guerin, a maid of deep faith.
7488-celtic-tales-told-to-the-children:
Louey Chisholm retells Celtic tales for children, with pictures by Katharine Cameron. She worked from several variants and retellings: Joyce's Old Celtic Romances, Cameron's Reliquae Celticae, O'Grady's pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne, Hyde's Three Sorrows of Story-telling, and Fiona Macleod's Laughter of Peterkin. The book is dedicated to Christopher, and its note explains its sources with unusual care.

The tales open in Erin, where none was greater than the great Concobar, whose fair realm poets sang and whose palace inspired the sweetest songs of Ireland. Heroes, kings, sorrows, and wonders follow, told in simple language for young listeners. Chisholm's collection remains a gentle doorway into Irish and Scottish legend, where the old stories keep their strangeness and their beauty.
74912-the-indian-queen:
The Indian Queen, by Ann Stephens, author of Ahmo's Plot and The Indian Princess, was published by George Routledge and Sons in London. Chapter one, The Stroke for a Throne, opens on the banks of Seneca lake, where an Indian council fire is lighted.

The chiefs of the Six Nations sit in a grave circle round the fire, after weeks of feasting. In their midst stands a young woman in crimson robes. This is Mahaska, the white queen, who loves to call herself Mahaska the Avenger. She was Katharine, daughter of Frontenac, the French Governor General of Canada, by an Indian woman, a daughter of the Seneca chief Nemono. A dying prophet's will brought the half white girl to rule the nations. Most chiefs accepted her with blind fidelity. A few, from ambition or contempt for women, oppose her will and raise a party against her.
75350-the-education-and-employment-of-wo:
The Education and Employment of Women, by Josephine Butler, came out in 1868. Macmillan published the essay in London; Brakell printed it at Liverpool. Butler opens on a conspiracy of silence.
