Most people fancy nearly all women marry and are kept by husbands, she says. Those who know better rarely speak. The governess is held up as the one outlet for a woman above a housemaid. One advert offered a home, with no salary, for a nursery governess. Three hundred women answered it. Surprise at that, Butler writes, holds something of despair.

Facts, she argues, have outrun custom: brains now do the business of the world. The census of 1861 counted nearly six million adult English women. Wives numbered 3,488,952; spinsters over twenty, 1,537,314. Marriage, as a living, is shown to be a precarious thing.
75456-books-and-men:
Agnes Repplier wrote Books and Men, first held in 1888 and shown here in an 1899 Boston and New York printing. Seven essays fill the book. Heads treat children past and present, the gains of old beliefs, and what children read. Decay of feeling and quirks of reviews get essays too.

One essay weighs gloom as a stance and one treats the Cavalier. Repplier opens with the turn from broad past tales to lives and memoirs. Such small lights show how daily life shifts bit by bit, she says. She cites hard tales, such as a wife held close for twenty years. The style is brisk, wry, and full of book talk.
75516-a-book-of-dear-dead-women:
Edna Worthley Underwood took her title from Browning for this 1911 collection of tales, A Book of Dear Dead Women, printed first in 1909. One story, The Painter of Dead Women, came back from The Smart Set with thanks.

The contents move through history and romance: one of Napoleon's loves, told from the diary of a Polish countess in 1806. Then come the mirror of La Granja, the concerto pathétique of Liszt, Sister Seraphine, and the sacred relics of Saint Euthymius. The opal isles, the house of gauze, and the king close the volume. Underwood wrote lush, fatal stories about women whom beauty and history had already claimed. The dead of her title are muses, not corpses; each tale polishes one face out of the past.
75619-satan-s-garden:
Satan's Garden is a weird tale by Hoffmann Price, printed in the magazine Weird Tales in April and May 1934. A bill heads the story: a terrific adventure in Bayonne, two beautiful girls, occult evil, and sudden death in the lair of the hashish-eaters. An editor's note praises Price as one of the masters of quality fiction in the magazine's pages.

The note sketches the author as a West Point graduate, expert swordsman, orientalist, and former soldier of fortune. His life, it says, is itself a thrilling tale. The story opens late at night in Bayonne, long past the hour of tinkling glasses and songs to the guitar at crowded tables. The first chapter is titled Invisible Scourge. Price's gifts for narrative and his warm imagination are promised in full for the strange tale that follows.
75629-economics-for-helen:
Hilaire Belloc wrote this plain guide to the science of wealth for a reader he calls Helen. Arrowsmith printed it in London in March 1924, in a first run of numbered copies on hand-made paper. A crown octavo run came the same month for the crowd.

The Elements fill part one. What is wealth asks the first chapter, then the three things wealth's making needs: land, labour, and capital. How wealth is made, and how it splits by nature into rent, interest, and keep, follow. Exchange, free trade and its shield, and money close the part. Plain heads and short steps mark Belloc's way of teaching a hard field to a keen young mind.
75734-a-thoughtless-seven:
Amy Le Feuvre, who wrote Probable Sons and Teddy's Button, told this tale of seven careless children. The Religious Tract Society printed A Thoughtless Seven in London, with twenty-seven plates. The boys and she were at daggers drawn: the front plate shows the war.

Thoughtless is chapter one; Thinking is chapter two, and the whole book lives between those two words. Le Feuvre wrote shelf on shelf of such tales: The Mender, Dwell Deep, Bunny's Friends, and Jill's Red Bag stand in her long list at the front. Her seven must learn what their haste and noise cost others. The lessons come by small harms and kind rebukes, in her known gentle hand, for the Sunday shelf.
75781-east-of-eden:
East of Eden is a novel by Isa Glenn, published at Garden City by Doubleday, Doran in 1932. The hosted text is the first edition, with the publisher's sketch of the heroine at the front. Glenn had written A Short History of Julia and Transport before it.

The heroine is Eva Litchfield, a novelist of genius. The sketch calls her lovely and untouchable, like a crystal that one blow may leave whole and the next may shatter. Her marriage to Nicholas Van Suydam, of the old Dutch family of Manhattan, is doomed to sorrow. The tale plays against the world of books in New York. That world is drawn with wit and a light touch of satire. The title is taken from the words that open the book, on man's exile from Eden.
75783-mothers-of-men:
William Henry Warner and De Witte Kaplan wrote Mothers of Men, a novel printed at New York in 1919, with a frontispiece by Blumenschein. Marie Helmar sits opposite a thin, hard-featured solicitor whose great bone spectacles magnify his eyes like a gigantic insect's. Her father indulged hobbies that carried him into every country on the globe, the man regrets.

Marie followed her wandering father weeping to the cemetery only yesterday, after a convent childhood of colourless days. Weekly letters from far countries, pictured only by geography maps, broke her monotony among the nuns. At last her father came home to Vienna and took a house on the Blumen Strasse for her. War-era family drama follows the inheritance news.
76138-odd-made-even:
Odd Made Even is a girls tale by Amy Le Feuvre in its third print. A Religious Tract group of London brought it out with Copping cuts. Le Feuvre wrote Heather Mistress, Odd, and Teddy Button in past years. Betty, a child of moods, heads part one in a fire side spat. She pokes the fire fierce and swears she hates all folk at that hour.

Town life sickens her, and life it self sickens her, in that wild speech. Molly, her fair calm mate, sighs that Betty is so un ev in mood. Part names run through an old friend, a strange meet, and rose songs. Red manor, changed wealth, old women, and new lords fill mid parts. A bolt from blue, a dam lost, and for small Betty sake close ranks.
76222-the-valley-of-eyes-unseen:
Gilbert Collins, author of Flower of Asia, wrote this novel, first published in London by Duckworth and Company in 1923. He dedicated it to broader understanding, deeper sympathy, and unthreatened peace between the peoples of East and West. That aim hangs over the whole tale.

A prologue sets the frame. The narrator sits in his rooms in Peking on a bitter January morning, years before. A fire blazes in the grate, two oil stoves stand out in the room, and the cold of a North China winter presses at the walls. His house boy brings the morning paper, a poor local sheet with hazy print and wild errors set by Chinese compositors. From this small scene the tale of the valley opens. Readers get a Western man's story laid in China, told in memory.
76394-the-love-of-an-uncrowned-queen:
Wilkins wrote The Love of an Uncrowned Queen, a new and revised edition with pictures, printed in London in 1903. Its subject is Sophie Dorothea, consort of George the First. With her story go her letters to and from Philip Christopher Count Königsmarck, first published from the originals. A portrait of Sophie Dorothea, from a painting once at Ahlden, fronts the book. Wilkins had written on Caroline, queen consort of George the Second.

A preface to the revised edition tells how the book grew. First published in April 1900, it drew more notice than Wilkins looked for. He followed Sophie Dorothea's footsteps through her life. He visited Celle where she was born, Hanover of her unhappy marriage, and Ahlden where she was held for more than thirty years. In 1897, in a Leipzig bookshop, he chanced on the fact that unpublished letters existed.
76417-the-children:
Edith Wharton wrote a novel printed at New York and London in 1928, first printed in September of that year. Wharton gives the book to her patient listeners at Sainte Claire. Four books of numbered chapters make the frame, thirty two chapters in all. As the big liner hung over the tugs swarming about her in the bay of Algiers, Martin Boyne looked down from the promenade deck.

First class passengers struggled up the gangway, their faces all lifted to his inspection without knowing it. Not a soul I shall want to speak to, as usual, he thinks. Some men's luck in travel was past belief, he muses, always meeting old friends or famed folk. Boyne's luck is about to turn in the shape of a troop of children. Wharton writes divorce age childhood with a cool eye.
76476-missing-men:
Vincent Starrett wrote Missing Men for his detective Lavender, and the book announces its puzzle in capitals. An important broker and an eminent actor mysteriously and simultaneously vanished, and the police were worried. Then the beautiful daughter of a retired business man hysterically reported her father gone without a trace. It became a matter for Lavender himself.

The narrator is Lavender's friend and foil, a stout man who climbs four flights to the detective's rooms and perishes of thirst on the landings. Lavender finds the stairs a protection and a blessing. Starrett, a Chicago journalist and Sherlockian of fame, wrote detection in the Holmes manner with an American accent. Three men missing at once is his kind of lock, and Lavender keeps the only key in Chicago.
76576-the-belle-of-bowling-green:
The Belle of Bowling Green, by Amelia Barr, is a novel of old New York. Burt issued the New York printing, rights held in 1904 by Dodd, Mead. Plates by Everett show the lovers at rest on park benches in happiness. A verse prologue toasts the merchant princes of the Bowling Green days.

That green acre holds New York heroic and civic memories, chapter one says. Chapters run from Monday Daughters to the star of peace at close. A chain of causes, the miracle of love, and marriage fill the middle. Renunciation rose and reproof of the sword add moral weight in turn. Old Dutch and English families ground the romance in city lore.
76905-sweden:
Sweden, by Dudley Heathcote, was published in London in 1927. Black issued the book, with pictures by Heaton Cooper. Stockholm town hall fronts the volume in colour. Thirteen chapters and an index make it up. Some chapters had first run in journals such as The Spectator and Country Life. The land and people open the tour. Gothenburg, the coast of Bohuslan, and the Gota Canal follow. Stockholm and its skerries take two chapters.

Gothland, Dalecarlia, and Lapland carry the reader north. A night in a Lapp hut and the midnight sun give local colour. A Swedish Christmas and winter sports close the book. Thirty two pictures, most in colour, show castles, falls, and timber ports. Heathcote writes a holiday guide for travellers who would go beyond France and Italy.
76963-the-silver-glen:
The Silver Glen is a historical novel by Bessie Dill, published in London in 1909. Its subtitle calls it a story of the rebellion of 1715. The tale is told by Barbara, Lady Fleming, in the year 1755, at the request of her kinsman Sir Henry Erskine. A portrait of John Erskine of Alva faces the title page.

The introduction tells of old letters and the origin of the book. The chapters then follow Barbara Stewart. She leaves school, comes home to Rosyth for the last time, and finds a new guardian. At Alva she joins a charming household and first hears of the Silver Glen. She learns some Scottish history at Dysart. Soon she is aware that something important is afoot. The rising of 1715, when the Jacobites rose for the old Stuart line, is retold through a girl's eyes in a country house.
77036-a-millionaire-at-sixteen:
A Millionaire at Sixteen, or The Cruise of the Guardian-Mother, is a boys' adventure novel by Oliver Optic. Lee and Shepard of Boston published it, with copyright of 1892. It stands in the first series of the All-Over-the-World Library, beside A Missing Million and A Young Knight-Errant. The frontispiece shows a moment of alarm, with someone calling Mr Belgrave back for heaven's sake.

The hero is Louis Belgrave, whose adventures began in A Missing Million. Optic dedicates the volume to his friend and co-labourer Nathan Bangs Williams. The series list in the front matter shows the plan: boys cruising in European waters, the West Indies, the Orient, and up the Nile. A young millionaire with a yacht of his own was a rich fantasy for the book's first readers.
77200-from-a-london-garden:
Adcock's first name is given on the title page only in short form. The poems had appeared before in journals such as the Spectator, the Outlook and Chambers's Journal. The book holds some forty short poems. Their titles include Transfigured, The Earth-Bond, The Pride of Lazarus, Manhood, Wages, Life and Time and The City Asleep.

Death then steps in and makes the god of Love deathless in the heaven of her dreams. The second, The Earth-Bond, holds that earth and heaven are both God's. The speaker owns a love for the known earth, its meadows, sea and sky, above the unknown heaven. Other poems take up parting, dreams, work without honour, a dead friendship and a last tribute. The tone stays lyrical and grave, with the city and its sleep never far away.
77278-the-motives-of-men:
George Coe wrote a study of human motives, published at New York in 1928 and reprinted the next year. It opens with an old hymn's line that man wants but little here below. If that were true, Coe says, we should be in a bad fix, for wants are the lever that pries men loose.

Four parts follow the argument. First, disillusion with modern man creeps in, through war, evolution, psychology, and industry. Second, that disillusion is itself illusory, since childhood and new schooling reveal wider capacities. Third, our capacities are in bondage, even our respectable faults deeply depraved. Last comes release, through cooperative thinking and the realm of free spirits.
77401-holbein-s-ambassadors-the-picture-:
Mary Hervey studies a famed painting in Holbein's Ambassadors: The Picture and the Men, printed in London in 1900. The study holds nineteen plates and two facsimile pages. The painting hangs in the National Gallery in London, as the front plate shows.

Part one traces the picture from 1533 to the present day, with a dated list of its moves. Part two turns to Jean de Dinteville, one of the two men in the paint. Hervey tells his youth, his first posts to England, and his long embassy of 1533. She covers the crowning of Anne Boleyn, his short posts of 1535 to 1537, and his fall and rise at court.
77472-pan-s-garden:
Algernon Blackwood gathered tales of nature and the unseen into a volume Macmillan published in London in 1912. Graham Robertson drew the pictures. The first and longest tale is of a man whom the trees loved, and it opens on a painter of trees named Sanderson.

Sanderson paints trees by a kind of inborn sight of what each one is. No two beeches in the world, he holds, are alike. Hosts ask him down to paint a prized lime or birch, for he catches the self of a tree as some men catch that of a horse. His drawing is often wild and wrong, and he has had no lessons. Yet the tree stands alive under his brush, shining, frowning, or dreaming, friend or foe. The rest of the book holds snow, wind, sand, and fire tales of the same haunted kind.
77948-the-haunts-of-men:
A story collection by Robert W Chambers, published at New York by Frederick A Stokes. The contents carry copyrights from 1895 through 1898. Chambers had just won fame with The King in Yellow. Twelve pieces fill this volume, mixing war tales and society stories. The God of Battles opens the book. Pickets, Smith's Battery, and Yo Espero follow.

A verse envoi and love poems frame the fiction. One opening lyric asks how lovers will seem when they meet immortal. War, though, supplies the strongest thread. Battles in Cuba and older campaigns echo through the tales. An international affair and an ambassador extraordinary add diplomacy. Chambers moved easily between horror, romance, and military adventure. This volume shows the range that made him a bestseller.
77968-the-land-of-forgotten-men:
Edison Marshall wrote this northern tale, printed by Little, Brown, and Company of Boston in 1923. W Herbert Dunton drew the front plate, showing a woman starting a long stalk toward a caribou herd with Pete at her side. Marshall's name was already known for The Voice of the Pack and The Snowshoe Trail.

Big Chris stands on a beach at night, looking through a dark harbor mouth into storm. He thinks his world an outcast land, cursed and left by God, and himself a pariah in it. A drunk Remittance Man sleeps in a shack in the native village. Fishing is the one trade of those far waters, and Larson, a web foreman, knows their grip. Marshall sets the tale in a hard, cold country of forgotten men.
78010-the-unknown-seven:
The Unknown Seven is a detective story by Harry Coverdale, published by Chelsea House in New York in 1923. Detective Kingdon Cole opens the case standing in a dark doorway in fog and drizzle, watching a second-story window across the street through the October night.

Contents promise a woman in a limousine, temptation, a Doctor Latham, and Cole receiving a warning. Later chapters reach the unknown seven themselves, a room numbered 2512, a seventh ingredient, and a final face to face confrontation. Chelsea House sold inexpensive clothbound mysteries to a wide market in the nineteen twenties. The crowded contents page, with duels of wits and traitors unmasked, shows the pace and machinery readers of that market expected.
78108-the-bitter-tea-of-general-yen:
The Bitter Tea of General Yen is a novel of China by Grace Zaring Stone. The Bobbs-Merrill Company published it in Indianapolis in 1930. Barbara Macfarlane drew the illustrations. Stone dedicates the book to Eleanor, who was grown up when necessary. The first chapter places Megan in a European house in Shanghai. Rain has stopped, and the pools reflect a cloudy sky.

From her window Megan watches the road beside the French Concession. Barbed wire bounds the concession wall. Senegalese soldiers examine traffic at the entrance to the Avenue Joffre. Rickshaws, wheelbarrows, and motors pick through the puddles. A large car speeds in from Siccawei. To avoid a small Ford it swerves, skids, and crashes into a telephone pole. Megan hears the crash and the tinkle of glass. The wreck at the gate breaks the dreamy quiet of her first days in the house.
78393-the-cat-who-went-to-heaven:
The Cat Who Went to Heaven is a tale for the young by Elizabeth Coatsworth. Lynd Ward drew the bold wood style prints for the small book. Rights date the work to the year nineteen thirty. Fresh prints of the tale ran fast in its first year of life.

A poor artist paints the great Buddha and the beasts who served him. A small cat who brought luck to his hut waits and hears each tale. The cook sings while the brush lays horse, deer, and tiger in place. The core doubt is if the cat can join that blest march in paint. Soft grief and grace mark the prized tale of the kind heart.
78515-five-and-ten:
Fannie Hurst wrote Five and Ten, a novel with rights from 1929, here in a Broadway edition from Collier. Hurst gives the book to New York, city of cities. Two mottoes face the tale: whited sepulchres fair outside and full of dead men bones within, and Socrates on those who want fewest things as nearest the gods.

John Rarick lies awake in long insomnia, mouthing to himself that he is a rich man, a very rich man. Wheels of industry pour gold into his coffers by their own force now. Jenny, his wife, sleeps by him in a signed bed, her narrow face crossed by cares even in rest. Rarick rose from a farm near Keokuk and boy nights of no sleep after field work. Wealth, want, and a marriage ground a tale of the five and dime king.
78541-the-three-wise-men:
The Three Wise Men is a western story by Ernest Haycox. It opens on a street emptied of folk and filled with sun. They came ambling down it one by one, the first lines say. Each stopped opposite a rickety building that had once housed a dollar bar. Each looked about with careless, uninterested glances, then dodged into a stairway.

Above the old bar lay a barn like room, empty of gear save for a huge sheet iron stove, a card table, and four chairs. Deep sawdust covered the floor. Near the table lay a layer of torn cards, cigar stubs, and other such leavings. On the table sat a lone plug of very black tobacco and four water glasses. The air smelled of stale smoke, with a hint of good whiskey beneath. First the marshal, then the mayor, then the judge took their seats.
78656-duologues-and-scenes-from-the-nove:
Rosina Filippi arranged these duologues and scenes from Jane Austen's novels for drawing-room performance; Dent and Company published them in London in 1895. Filippi's preface makes her case plainly: Austen is a true writer of comedy, dramatic to her fingertips, whose people never sink into caricature. Her scenes are complete in themselves, needing, as Dumas said, only a passion, two persons, and a screen.

Seven picked scenes make the book. They are to be played with no scenery, but in the exact dress of the period, 1792 to 1807. Short monologues are added here and there to make the plots clear to hearers who do not know the novels. A pen-and-ink sketch by Margaret Fletcher goes with every scene. The aim is to give amateur actors good short pieces, of which Filippi found too few.
7868-a-child-s-story-garden:
A Child's Story Garden, compiled by Elizabeth Heber for kindergarten and primary grades in Indianapolis schools, gathers tales chosen to build literary culture and high ideals through story. Contents include Siegfried the king's son, the song of the pine tree, a Christmas story, and myths of Arachne and Pan.

Other pieces bring the birds of Killingworth, the bell of Atri, the anxious leaf, how dimples came, and a proud little apple blossom. Grace Garfield's pictures accompany thanks to many authors and publishers. Mothers and teachers will find short, moral tales fit for reading aloud.
78746-sweden:
Carl Laurin wrote this portrait of Sweden as seen through its artists' eyes, printed at Stockholm in 1911 by Norstedt. Grenville Grove Englished the text, and Henry Buergel Goodwin edited the translation and rendered the verses. Color plates from Swedish paintings carry the argument: the land is to be known by the men who painted it with love, as Dürer and Rembrandt and Whistler painted their mothers.

Laurin writes against two faults of his countrymen, the bombast of false national pride and the habit of running Sweden down. He asks for a patriotism that is ardent yet discreet. The book moves through Swedish nature and Swedish life as the painters of its golden age saw them, a handsome gift-book for Sweden's friends abroad.
78885-an-island-garden:
Celia Thaxter made a garden on Appledore, the largest of the Isles of Shoals, and wrote its story for Houghton Mifflin in 1894. Childe Hassam drew the pictures. Friends and strangers, she says, begged her summer after summer to tell how it was done. The book is her answer, the fruit of sweet and bitter trials.

Her first bed, as a lonely child on a lighthouse island ten miles from the mainland, was not more than a yard square. Marigolds grew there, fire coloured blossoms that were the joy of her heart. She kept even the withered flowers hid between the rocks, so dear were they. From that scrap the great garden among the ledges grew, year after year. The book joins plain counsel on seeds and soil to tender thoughts on the friends who loved the flowers and come no more.
78898-100-professions-for-women:
Betty Van Deventer lists a hundred trades open to women in Little Blue Book number 705. E Haldeman-Julius edited the series at Girard, Kansas. The booklet dates to 1928.

Her opening chapter argues for economic independence. Fifteen years back, few women chose business or professional life. A woman without a husband, father, or brother to feed her counted as unfortunate. Now daughters of rich parents plan careers for the thrill of it. The bachelor girl replaces the simpering old maid. War work sped the change. Women who tasted big accomplishment could not return gladly to humdrum housekeeping. The Little Blue Books sold for a nickel or a dime. They carried self-improvement to farms and small towns across America.
78919-in-camp-and-kitchen:
A handy guide for emigrants and settlers fills this book, In Camp and Kitchen, printed in London in 1912 by the author of The Successful Home Cook. A Kipling verse about the call of the road heads the title page. The first chapter treats cooking in the open and the simplest cooking apparatus a settler needs.

The ideal colonist, the book says, can turn his hand to anything and set a table with almost no utensils. Contents move from the camp kitchen to stores, water, and waste, then to bread and yeasts. The day's food and work, cooking of fish, meat, and vegetables, plain recipes, and hints for the handy man complete the guide.
78952-flower-legends-for-children:
Hilda Murray's Flower Legends for Children was published by Longmans, Green of London, New York, and Bombay, with pictures by Eland. The book is richly illustrated, as this copy's list of plates shows. A girl stands in a lily garden among ruins on the cover. Flower fairies sleep inside roses and irises on the flyleaf, and cherubs pack an old cannon with ropes of flowers at the contents.

A dedication in verse, signed by the illustrator, tells the child reader that the best and sweetest flowers are those whose beauty is but the shrine of purity. Fifteen legends follow, one to a flower: the moss rose, the tulip, the forget-me-not, roses red and white, the rowan, and the fleur-de-lys. The aspen, hawthorn, almond tree, laurel, Christmas rose, poplar, mistletoe, narcissus, and red lily complete the garland.
79003-last-and-first-men:
Olaf Stapledon wrote Last and First Men, a story of the near and far future first published in 1930. The book is framed as a chronicle told by one of the Last Men, reaching back to the First Men of our own age. Its early chapters cover a Balkan Europe, a European war and its wake, and a war between England and France, then the fall of Europe as America and China rise as rivals.

From a first world state the tale runs through dark ages, fresh human species, and wars with Mars. Men remake themselves into great brains and new forms across vast spans of time. Stapledon builds a history of mankind to its end, told at a scale few novels had tried before.
8152-henrik-ibsen:
Edmund Gosse wrote this biography of Henrik Ibsen, tracing his life from childhood and youth through early influences, Bergen from 1852 to 1857. The satires of 1857 to 1867, and the successive periods of his maturity to his last years. Later chapters assess his personal and intellectual characteristics, and the volume includes portraits, a drawing by Gustav Laerum, a facsimile of Ibsen's handwriting, and a bust from about 1865.

Gosse, who knew Ibsen's work intimately, wrote when analyses of the plays were already numerous in many languages, yet no full English life existed. His biography remains a classic introduction, clear and sympathetic, to the playwright of A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler. For theatre readers, it is the place to start on Ibsen the man.
8523-val-d-arno-ten-lectures-on-the-tusc:
John Ruskin gave these ten lectures on Tuscan art in the Val d'Arno, the valley of the Arno, tracing the art directly antecedent to the Florentine Renaissance. Lecture titles run from Nicholas the Pisan and John the Pisan through Shield and Apron, Parted Per Pale, and Pax Vobiscum. Marble Couchant, Marble Rampant, Franchise, The Tyrrhene Sea, and Fleur de Lys follow, with an appendix and plates.

Ruskin, the great Victorian art critic, argues that Tuscan sculpture and painting grew from faith and craft, not from sudden genius. Readers get Ruskin lecturing at his most detailed, on Pisano sculpture and the Arno valley's shores. The volume suits students of Italian art, and of Ruskin's moral criticism.
8531-tales-and-novels-volume-10-helen:
Maria Edgeworth's Helen fills volume 10 of her Tales and Novels in Ten Volumes, with engravings on steel, in the 1857 edition. The volume gives Helen in two parts, chapter by chapter, as Edgeworth's tale of a young woman's reputation, friendship, and truth-telling, in the society of her day.

Edgeworth, the Anglo-Irish novelist who influenced Scott and Austen's generation, wrote Helen late in her career. It shows her mature art: clear prose, social observation, and a heroine whose honesty is tested. Readers of classic Irish and English fiction get a substantial novel in a handsome collected edition. The volume suits those reading Edgeworth in sequence, or meeting Helen first.
8772-the-learned-women:
Moliere's Learned Women, Les Femmes Savantes, appears here in Charles Heron Wall's English prose translation, with short introductions and notes. First acted on March 11, 1692, with Moliere himself playing Chrysale, the comedy sets an honest bourgeois against his wife Philaminte and daughters Armande and Henriette. Ariste, Belise, the suitor Clitandre, the wit Trissotin, the learned Vadius, and servants Martine, Lepine, and Julien complete the cast, with a notary to settle matters.

Philaminte's academy of would-be learned ladies, and Trissotin's pretentious verse, are the satiric targets, while Henriette's plain wish to marry Clitandre drives the plot. Moliere mocks pedantry, especially when it invades the household and ruins good sense. Wall's prose keeps the comedy accessible to readers without French, and the notes explain its jokes. It remains a sharp, funny classic of the comedy of manners.
908-treatise-on-parents-and-children:
George Bernard Shaw wrote this treatise on the relations of parents and children, with essays on trailing clouds of glory, the child as father to the man, and what a child is. He tackles the sin of Nadab and Abihu, the making of monsters, small and large families, and children as nuisances, child fanciers, and childhood as a state of sin.

Shaw argues, with wit and provocation, that children are persons, not property, and that schools and homes often crush what they claim to nurture. His prose is brisk, combative, and full of paradox. The book is a bracing Shaw manifesto, and it still challenges readers who think children should be seen and not heard.
915-library-work-with-children:
Alice I. Hazeltine writes a practical guide to running a children's library, from book choice and storytelling to rooms, hours, and the training of staff. The book grew from real library work, not theory alone. Hazeltine worked at the New York Public Library, a leader in children's rooms.

Hazeltine argues that a children's room should welcome young readers and help them find books they love. Librarians and teachers will find here the methods of an early professional, still useful for anyone who serves young readers. Her guide, published in the early twentieth century, helped train a new profession.
918-sketches-of-young-gentlemen:
Charles Dickens, as Boz, sketched young gentlemen for the young ladies of Great Britain, Ireland, Wales, and the Channel Islands, to whom the volume is humbly dedicated. He parades the dandy, the bashful youth, the military aspirant, and other types, each with his dress, talk, and airs.

Dickens writes with satirical affection, catching the vanities and hopes of young men on the town. His sketches are short, vivid, and theatrical, full of London shops, balls, and lodgings. The volume pairs with his sketches of young couples, and it charms readers who enjoy social comedy in miniature.
926-ten-thousand-dreams-interpreted-or-w:
Gustavus Hindman Miller offers interpretations for ten thousand dreams, arranged so a reader can look up a symbol and find what it was said to mean. The book promises both scientific and practical readings of dreams. Miller's dream book, first published in the early twentieth century, sold widely.

Miller lists animals, places, people, and events, with short, plain meanings for each, in the style of popular dream books of his day. Modern readers will enjoy it as folklore and curiosity, not as a guide to the mind. Its alphabetical list lets a reader find a dream symbol in seconds, which explains its appeal.
9469-the-call-of-the-twentieth-century-a:
David Starr Jordan, head of Stanford University, gave young men this address in 1903, at the dawn of a new century. He speaks straight to boys on the edge of adult life, and to the men they will become in the 1920s and 1930s. His theme is plain: each youth holds his own future self in his hands. What he does now will shape that man's health, mind, and soul.

Jordan urges clean habits, hard study, honest work, and care for the body and the nerves. He warns that lust and waste can spoil a life before it starts. He also trusts that a trained mind can meet the new age with hope. A reader gets a frank, old-style pep talk, full of moral drive and faith in self-rule.
9475-the-lovels-of-arden:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon, famed for Lady Audley's Secret, wrote The Lovels of Arden as a sensation novel of love and rank. The tale follows Clarissa and her kin through Hale Castle, London rooms, and country houses, as love, pride, and plots collide. Chapters bear titles like Dangerous Ground, Smouldering Fires, and Clarissa's Elopement. Braddon, called queen of the circulating libraries, knew how to hold a reader.

Temptation, a fatal turn, and a fresh start shape the later acts, as Clarissa's fate hangs on choices made in haste. The prose moves fast, with sharp scenes and bold feeling. A reader gets a classic Victorian page-turner, rich in romance, scandal, and the social traps of its age.
9586-personal-poems-complete-volume-iv-o:
Volume four of Whittier's complete works gathers all his personal poems, verse to friends, heroes, and the dead. Early poems lament Charles B. Storrs and S. Oliver Torrey, salute Channing, Kossuth, and Wordsworth, and mark Ichabod and The Lost Occasion. The Cross honors a Quaker jailed for aiding runaways, while later pieces praise Sumner, Garibaldi, and Bryant. Each poem ties a name to a moral hour.

The volume spans Whittier's whole public life, from young reformer to honored elder. His voice stays plain and warm, even when the theme is loss. A reader gets a full gallery of a poet's friendships and causes, and a moving record of nineteenth-century America's conscience.
96-the-monster-men:
A scientist on a Borneo island grows men in vats, and one creation turns on him. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Monster Men opens with a man dissolving a body in nitric acid to hide a crime. Professor Maxon seeks to restore his daughter's lost lover by artificial means.

Number 13, the latest creation, gains a soul and a name through love and suffering. Treachery, a bull whip, and buried treasure drive the middle chapters. Virginia Maxon must judge man against monster. The novel blends horror, romance, and early science fiction. Burroughs asks whether a made man can claim a soul, a question later science fiction kept asking.
9660-the-first-blast-of-the-trumpet-agai:
John Knox wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women in 1558, a fiery tract against rule by women. Edited here by Edward Arber in 1878, the book opens by rebuking godly preachers for their silence on what Knox calls an abominable empire. He names a traitress and bastard queen as its head, and summons prophets' examples. The preface sets the blast's hard tone.

Knox answers objections, admonishes readers, and declaims against female rule as contrary to God and nature. His prose burns with Reformation zeal. A reader gets a notorious Tudor polemic, vital for grasping Knox, Mary Tudor, and the age's fierce debate on queens.
a-child-s-story-garden: Elizabeth Heber compiles a child's story garden for mothers, teachers, and young pupils. Its stories include Siegfried the king's son, the myth of Arachne, the myth of Pan, the bell of Atri, and the anxious leaf. Teachers in Indianapolis schools had used these tales in kindergarten and primary grades. Heber chose them to build literary taste and to suggest high ideals through story.
a-christmas-mystery-the-story-of-three-w: William John Locke tells a Christmas mystery built around three wise men. The story opens with a dead man, an uncanny place, and a cry that it is fey. Its characters sense beating wings and a presence they cannot explain. Locke blends suspense, wonder, and the Christmas theme into a short seasonal tale.
a-little-pilgrim-in-the-unseen: Margaret Oliphant writes a little pilgrim in the unseen, a wistful vision of the next world. The pages sprang from thoughts that arise when the door of the unseen opens suddenly close by. They follow a gentle soul who never knew doubt into the new world. Oliphant offers a glimpse of its glory through a pilgrim's eyes.
a-little-pilgrim-stories-of-the-seen-and:
A Little Pilgrim, published in 1888 by Margaret Oliphant, gathers stories of the seen and the unseen. Oliphant frames the collection with a remarkable opening: a woman describes what it felt like to come to the very point of death after a long illness, and to return. There was no pain in it, she says, only a sense of sinking down through everything that should have held her.

From that threshold, the stories follow a little pilgrim into the world beyond death. Oliphant imagines the unseen country gently, as a place of rest, learning, and reunion rather than terror. The collection became one of her best-loved works, offering Victorian readers a tender vision of what might wait after dying.
a-miscellany-of-men:
G. K. Chesterton sorts his essays by types of men, as his contents page shows. Here are the suffragist, the poet and the cheese, and the man who thinks backwards. Here too are the mad official, the free man, the fool, and the miser. Each essay takes one figure and turns him over in Chesterton's hands until he looks new.

Chesterton writes about voters, priests, journalists, and Scotsmen with jokes that carry arguments about democracy, faith, and common sense. His method is paradox: defend the ordinary man against the experts, and find wisdom in old customs. The pieces first appeared as journalism, and they keep a newspaper's pace and sparkle.
a-mother-s-list-of-books-for-children: Gertrude Weld Arnold compiles a guide to children's reading arranged by the child's age rather than school grade, revising an earlier privately printed list for home use. The book groups fairy tales, rhymes, nature myths, legends, saints stories, and verses for boys and girls, with notes meant to help parents match each title to its reader. Published in Chicago in 1909, it favours titles chosen for home reading over classroom sets.
a-siren:
Thomas Adolphus Trollope's A Siren unfolds in six books around Ravenna at Carnival. Book one begins on Ash Wednesday morning, after the last night of Carnival. The diva has vanished, and the city wakes to scandal. Books two to four go back four months to tell how the trouble began.

Paolina Foscarelli, the siren singer, arrives with an impresario's report and a great love to be taught. The Marchese Lamberto di Castelmare, his uncle, a cardinal, and a contessa circle her voice. Book five, Who Did the Deed?, turns the novel into a murder inquiry, with a post-mortem and a prison visit. The friar's testimony and the trial close the case. Thomas Adolphus, Anthony's elder brother, lived in Italy and wrote its modern life. His Ravenna of priests, attorneys, and opera is drawn from residence, not tourism.
a-study-of-the-textile-art-in-its-relati: William Henry Holmes studies the textile art in its relation to the development of form and ornament, in this paper from the Bureau of Ethnology's sixth annual report. The contents move from form and colour in textile art through relations of form to ornament into a geometric system grown within the art. Relief phenomena, reticulated work, superconstructive and adventitious features, and geometry imposed on adopted elements show how weaving shapes decoration.
advice-to-a-mother-on-the-management-of-:
Pye Henry Chavasse, a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons, addresses mothers directly. His preface boasts of a thirteenth edition. The twelfth, of twenty thousand copies, had sold out in under three years. Translations into French, German, Polish, and Tamil followed. The contents divide the child's life into three parts: infancy, childhood, and boyhood and girlhood.

Each part covers washing, clothing, diet, exercise, sleep, and the nursery, then dentition, vaccination, ailments, and the treatment on the moment of pressing illnesses and accidents. Chavasse writes in a question-and-answer, conversational manner meant to calm a young mother at midnight. The manual was the child-care authority of its age, and it now reads as a full record of Victorian nursery practice.
aladdin-o-brien:
Gouverneur Morris opens Aladdin O'Brien with Poe's Annabel Lee and a forbidden river. Aladdin entices Margaret from Sunday-school to a skiff he barely knows how to row. He whistles through his front teeth and blows grapevine smoke through his nose. To be with him, the narrator says, was a delicious lesson in corruption.

The river nearly drowns them both, and Margaret's scarf becomes the book's token. Aladdin grows into a charming, reckless young man of politics and newspapers. Washington draws the grown pair into its intrigues, where his luck and nerve keep rescuing him. Morris writes a picaresque of American charm: a boy with a lamp-like gift for escaping scrapes. Margaret's steady love measures the man against the child. The novel's lightness is deliberate, a fairy tale of the republic's capital.
alec-forbes-of-howglen: George MacDonald tells the story of Alec Forbes of Howglen, a Scottish lad whose growth is shaped by school, friendship, and faith. The novel follows Alec from boyhood into manhood among the folk of a northern parish, with MacDonald's blend of realism and spiritual reflection. It remains one of the author's best-loved Scottish novels, warm in its portrait of community life.
arnim-die-majoratsherren:
Property passed rigidly from heir to heir becomes a curse in Arnim's Die Majoratsherren, given here in German. The Lords of the Entailed Estate turns a dry legal institution, the entail, into the engine of a dark family drama. Inheritance and family pride grind the characters between them like millstones.

Arnim blends realism with the uncanny in his characteristic way, letting old houses and older papers gather menace. Portraits, wills, and decaying rooms carry the family's buried guilt. The novella asks what wealth does to love when law forbids it to move freely. German Romanticism rarely aimed its strangeness at so concrete a target. The result reads like a ghost story with a lawyer in it.
arnim-isabella-von-agypten:
Gypsy wanderers and settled townsfolk collide in Achim von Arnim's novella Isabella von Aegypten, presented in German. Isabella, a young gypsy leader, crosses into a richly imagined past of emperors and camps. Love strains against the boundary between her people and the settled world that fears them.

Arnim helped collect the folk songs of Des Knaben Wunderhorn, and that folk learning saturates his fiction. Antiquarian detail and Romantic invention braid together here into something strange and beautiful. The novella asks who belongs and who must wander, questions its century pressed hard. Its heroine carries both pride and sorrow in equal measure. Few German tales of the period feel so lush and so sad at once.
b09-hutten-obscure-men:
Epistolae Obscurorum Virorum, Letters of Obscure Men, appeared in Latin in 1515 as a joke with teeth. Crotus Rubeanus began the mock letters, and Ulrich von Hutten wrote much of the crushing second part of 1517. The letters pretend to come from dim scholastic monks writing to a master at Cologne.

In bad Latin and worse logic, the fake monks expose their own folly on every page. The satire struck the Cologne scholars who had hounded the humanist Reuchlin and his Hebrew studies. Learned Europe laughed, and the old school of theology never shook off the scorn. The work stands as the great humanist satire on the eve of the Reformation.
bashful-fifteen:
L. T. Meade published this school story with Cassell of New York in 1892. Meade, the most prolific girls' writer of her day, opens with curiosity and a new girl, then crowns a queen of the school. Ribbons and roses, the breaking in of a wild colt, and captivity set the early terms: a boarding school where reputations are made and unmade by small acts.

Irish Bridget, homesick at fifteen, frets over a posted letter and the postal order inside it, begging Janet not to mock the people she loves — Pat and Norah at home. Janet raises her delicate brows in well-acted astonishment. Meade writes the schoolgirl world in earnest: loyalty, snobbery, and kindness fought out in whispers, with bashfulness itself as the heroine's cross and cure.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-07-great:
John Lord gives the seventh Beacon Lights volume to great women, opening with Héloïse under the single heading Love. Her contents read as a romance outline. Extraordinary gifts, Abélard's genius and early triumphs, and mad infatuation lead to scandal. A secret marriage, its discovery, and separate convents close the tale. Lord retells the letters and her unconquered love without flinching.

Queens, saints, and court ladies follow in the same biographical manner. One duchess, whose story these pages tell, keeps her offices and palace apartments after favour cools. She is still addressed as a great person while envy gathers round her. Lord judges his heroines by character and influence, in the gallant, sermonising tone of the Victorian lecture hall, where a woman's life proved a civilisation's tone.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-09-europ:
John Lord's ninth Beacon Lights volume turns to the statesmen of Europe. Mirabeau opens it as the great voice of the French Revolution. The contents follow the fall of the old order step by step. Ruined finances, the Assembly of Notables, and the States-General come first. Then the Third Estate seizes power, the Bastille falls, and Mirabeau shows a strange wish to save the crown. Talleyrand and the seizure of Church lands close his tale.

Lord dwells on Talleyrand in a later talk. Cast out of the Church for his lack of faith, the bishop turned diplomat cared little for the ban. In London he charmed the highest circles with the shine of his talk and the bite of his wit. The Jacobins mistrusted him on his return, and he fled to England. Lord judges each statesman as an actor in a vast drama of revolt.
behind-the-arras-a-book-of-the-unseen:
Bliss Carman published this book of poems with Lamson, Wolffe of Boston in 1895, with designs by T. B. Meteyard. Its title names the theme: the unseen behind the arras of daily life. Contents move through The Moondial, The Face in the Stream, The Cruise of the Galleon, The Red Wolf, The Lodger, The Night Express, and Exit Anima, the soul's departure.

The lyrics keep one foot in the field and one in the spirit world. Apple blossom, orioles, and poppies do the seeing in one spring poem. Field-wise creatures — crickets and swallows — are called Brahmins of the universal grass, holier than the tiger-lilies they pierce past. Carman, Canada's lyric laureate of the nineties, writes nature as a veil: beautiful in itself, and always about to lift on something behind it.
bimbi-stories-for-children:
Bimbi, stories for children by Ouida, the pen name of Louise de la Ramee, gathers five tales written with a painter's eye for place. The longest and best known, The Nurnberg Stove, opens in Hall, a little town in Austria's Upper Inn valley. Ouida describes its green meadows, glacier fed river, latticed shop panes, and grand Gothic church before she ever introduces August, the boy who knows no other world.

August's treasure is a great porcelain stove, and the tale follows his fight to keep it when hard times press his family. Around it the collection sets The Ambitious Rose Tree, Lampblack, The Child of Urbino, and Findelkind, stories of plants, artists, and lost children across Italy and Germany. Ouida wrote for adults chiefly, but her children's tales keep her signature style: rich scenery, tender feeling, and beauty treated as a serious matter.
biographies-of-working-men:
Grant Allen's Biographies of Working Men, published in 1884, tells seven lives of men who rose from labour. Thomas Telford, the stonemason who became a great engineer, opens the volume. Allen begins with Telford's birth in a shepherd's cottage in Eskdale in 1757. His widowed mother raised him on her own ten fingers.

George Stephenson the engine-man and John Gibson the sculptor follow. William Herschel, once a bandsman, reached the stars as an astronomer. Jean François Millet the painter and James Garfield the canal boy turned president carry the theme abroad. Thomas Edward, a shoemaker naturalist, closes the set. Allen drew on earlier lives by Samuel Smiles and others. The book preaches energy and perseverance to working readers, Victorian self-help at its most earnest.
bonnie-prince-charlie-a-tale-of-fontenoy:
G. A. Henty's Bonnie Prince Charlie tells the Jacobite rising through the battles of Fontenoy and Culloden. The tale opens on a dull September evening in 1728, when Bailie Anderson's household sits down to supper above the shop, apprentices eyeing the food while grace drags on.

A knock at the door breaks the meal, and the old servant must peer through the grille before opening, since these are not times to admit a stranger lightly. From that domestic opening Henty builds toward the Young Pretender's cause, Highland campaigns and the disaster of Culloden. Young readers of historical adventure will find Henty's usual blend of domestic detail and battlefield action.
books-and-bookmen:
Andrew Lang's Books and Bookmen, printed by Longmans in 1887, opens with a verse dedication asking whether ladies can care for gossip of texts and bindings old. Chapters follow on Elzevir editions, curiosities of parish registers, the Rowfant library, Japanese bogie-books, and ghosts in the library. Literary forgeries and bibliomania in France get long treatments.

Lang retells how the Shakespeare Society was taken in by young William Henry Ireland's sham documents, with Boswell kneeling to kiss the relics. A bookman's purgatory and lady book-lovers round out the miscellany. The volume defined the amiable amateur tradition in English book collecting: learned, funny, and more interested in readers than in prices.
britannica-1911-aalen: Aalen is the subject of a short town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry sets the town in Württemberg, on the Kocher river at the foot of the Swabian Alps, east of Stuttgart, with rails to Ulm and Cannstatt. Its people are counted at ten thousand. Woollen and linen goods, ribbon looms, and tanneries employ the town, with large iron works near by. A statue of the poet Christian Schubart is noted. Aalen held free imperial city rank from 1360 until Württemberg took it in 1802.
britannica-1911-abdomen:
Abdomen receives a medical entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word, from Latin abdere, to hide, or from adeps, fat, names the belly region holding most digestive organs. Anatomy points onward to other articles; surgery takes the space here.

Exploratory laparotomy, opening the belly to find the fault by finger and hand, leads the argument. Holmes's line rules the case: you cannot tell a table's wood without lifting the cloth. Delay, the entry charges, once spoiled case after case as drug trials failed in medical wards. Prompt transfer to surgeons changed results day by day. Public trust grew as surgeons proved no reckless operators. Each organ's surgery sits with its anatomy elsewhere in the set, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-abraham-men: Abraham-men is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the name as a nickname for vagrants who infested Tudor England. The phrase stands as old as 1561. Such beggars pretended to be patients discharged from the Abraham ward at Bedlam. True discharged Bedlamites could roam and beg, wearing a badge. Gross abuse of that humane privilege bred the slang phrase to sham Abraham, the entry closes, fixing a bit of Tudor street language and the fraud that coined it.
britannica-1911-adam-of-bremen:
Adam of Bremen was a historian and geographer. He was probably born in Upper Saxony before 1045. Archbishop Adalbert likely invited him to Bremen. He arrived there about 1067. By 1069 he was a cathedral canon. He also mastered the cathedral school. A visit took him to Denmark's king Sweyn. After Adalbert died, Adam began his history. He finished the Historia about 1075.

Scope makes the work a primary authority. It covers the Hamburg-Bremen diocese fully. All North German and Baltic lands enter it. Scandinavian colonies appear as far as America. Vinland receives its earliest mention here. Russia, Kiev, and the Wends all feature. Trade at Jumne, Birka, and Novgorod is described. Adam gathered records and oral reports alike.
britannica-1911-adelaide-queen:
Adelaide, queen of Italy and empress, who lived from 931 to 999, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Rudolph the Second of Burgundy. When her father died in 937, her mother wed Hugh, king of Italy, and Adelaide was promised to his son Lothair. The marriage took place in 947.

After three sad years Lothair died, in November 950. His successor, Berengar, seized the young widow. He was wroth, it seems, that she would not wed his son and so shore up his claim to the throne. He held her close at Como for four months. She got free in August 951 and fled to Canossa. Otto, the German king, whose wife had died, had set his mind on a match with her and on the crown of Italy in her right.
britannica-1911-agen:
Agen is a city of south-western France, capital of the department of Lot-et-Garonne, 84 miles from Bordeaux by rail. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 18,640 people in 1906 and sets it by the Garonne and its side canal. A stone bridge, a foot suspension bridge, and a canal bridge cross the river there.

The cathedral of Saint Caprais mixes work from the 1100s to the 1500s, its oldest part a 12th century apse with three chapels. The museum holds fossils and Roman remains, and a statue honours the poet Jacques Jasmin, a son of the town. Agen markets the rich farm yield of its region: fattened poultry, prunes, cork, wine, and cattle. As Roman Aginnum it was capital of the Celtic Nitiobroges, and its bishopric dates from the 4th century.
britannica-1911-aiken:
Aiken, a city in South Carolina, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county-seat of Aiken county, seventeen miles east-north-east of Augusta, Georgia. Its population grew from 2,362 in 1890 to 3,911 in 1910. Railways and an electric line to Augusta serve the city, set about five hundred feet above sea level.

Fashionable winter visitors, chiefly Northerners, made Aiken's name. It sits in the state's famous sand-hill and pine-forest region, where dry, even temperatures and pine-scented air drew people seeking health and pleasure. The climate was said to help those with lung disease especially. Fine hotels, club houses, and cottages served the season, with golf, fox-hunting, polo, tennis, and shooting for sport. Cotton mills, lumber mills, and schools, including the Schofield Normal and Industrial School, round out the entry's picture.
britannica-1911-alhazen:
A boast about the Nile nearly wrecked Alhazen, the Arabian scholar of the eleventh century named Abu Ali Al-Hasan Ibn Alhasan. Born at Basra, he died at Cairo in 1038. He is not the Alhazen of a century before, who turned Ptolemy's Almagest into Arabic. This one had bragged he could build a machine to tame the floods, and the caliph Hakim called him to Egypt to do it.

The plan could not work, and fear of the caliph's wrath drove him to play the madman until Hakim died in 1021. His true field was optics, where no great finder had come since Ptolemy. Alhazen told why sun and moon look bigger near the skyline. He taught that sight does not come from rays shot from the eye. He also cracked the mirror puzzle: where on a curved mirror a ray from one point bounces to reach a second point.
britannica-1911-alien:
Who counts as a British subject, and who stays an alien? British law of the constitution takes up that question under a word drawn from the Latin alienus. An alien lacks the standing of a subject; in plain terms, a foreigner who forms ties with a state yet still owes loyalty to a ruler abroad. Much of the entry sorts out who falls on each side.

Birth inside British lands makes a subject, English law holds. A noted case in James I's reign ruled that Scots born before the crowns joined were aliens in England. Those born later were subjects, since loyalty runs to the king's own person. A child born overseas could claim the same standing through a British father or grandfather. The Naturalization Act of 1870 then swept away many bars, letting aliens own land and goods and pass them on as subjects could.
britannica-1911-almaden:
Mercury made Almadén famous. The Spanish town, also called Almadén del Azogue, sits in rough country in Ciudad Real province, west-south-west of its capital, and counted 7,375 people in 1900. Rome knew it as Sisapon, and Romans and Moors alike dug its mines.

The ore grows richer as shafts sink, and for ages the mines matched Idria's in South Austria as the world's most valued. That rank held until California's New Almaden deposits grew fast in the 1850s. Convict labour long did the digging, the underground air being foul; miners won freedom from military service after two years. Lead and sulphur also come from the ground nearby.
britannica-1911-aspen:
Aspen is a section of the poplar genus, covered in this 1911 Britannica article, with the common aspen of Europe taken as the type. It is a tall, fast growing tree with a slim trunk and grey bark that grows rough with age. Its round leaves have toothed edges and long, flat stalks, so the lightest breeze sets them moving.

That free motion gives the leaves their famed trembling, and their rubbing makes a rustling sound. The flowers come in March and April on hanging catkins, with male and female flowers on distinct trees. The tree grows in moist places across northern Europe and northern Britain, and its light, soft, tough wood serves coopers for pails and herring casks, and makers of trays and wooden shoes.
britannica-1911-auckland-william-eden:
William Eden, first Baron Auckland, was an English statesman born in seventeen forty five. He was the son of Sir Robert Eden of Windlestone Hall in Durham. Schooled at Eton and at Christ Church, Oxford, he was called to the bar in seventeen sixty eight. In seventeen seventy one he published a book on penal law. He won a name early as an authority on trade and finance.

In seventeen seventy two Auckland became an under secretary of state. He sat in parliament for New Woodstock and later for Heytesbury. He joined the board of trade and plantations in seventeen seventy six. Two years later he carried an act to improve the treatment of prisoners. He also sailed to North America with the earl of Carlisle. That mission sought to settle the dispute with the colonists and failed.
britannica-1911-bailen:
Bailén is a town of southern Spain in the province of Jaén, twenty-one miles north of Jaén city, with 7,420 people in 1900. It is probably the ancient Baecula, where Scipio the elder twice beat the Carthaginians, in 209 and 206 B.C.

Near it, too, was fought the great battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. Castile's Alphonso VIII crushed the Moors there. The chroniclers claimed 200,000 Moorish dead against twenty-five Christians. The entry dismisses that estimate as absurd. The town's lasting fame is the capitulation of Bailén in July 1808. The French general Dupont surrendered 17,000 men to the Spaniards there. Hard fighting ran for several days before it. It was the first severe blow France suffered in the Peninsular War.
britannica-1911-baillet-adrien:
Baillet, Adrien (1649-1706), was a French scholar and critic born at Neuville near Beauvais in Picardy, whose poor parents could afford only the village school. Friars at a nearby convent taught him Latin and brought him to the bishop of Beauvais's notice, winning him a full education at the seminary.

Ordained in 1676, Baillet became librarian in 1680 to Lamoignon, the Paris parlement's advocate-general, and catalogued that library in thirty-five handwritten volumes. The rest of his life was unbroken labour, five hours a day allowed for rest. His Judgments of the Learned on authors' chief works is his most celebrated book; his Life of Descartes mines sound sources, and his Lives of the Saints, critical on miracles, caused scandal. Praising Jansenists in the Judgments earned him the Jesuits' hatred.
britannica-1911-barmen:
Barmen is a town of Germany, in the Prussian Rhine province, in the district of Düsseldorf. Its growth was rapid: 19,030 people in 1816, 116,144 in 1890, and 156,148 in 1905. It lies just east of Elberfeld, with which it virtually forms one town, and stretches some four miles along the narrow valley of the river Wupper.

Twenty bridges cross the Wupper inside the town, and a suspended trolley line runs above the riverbed the whole length to Elberfeld. High wooded hills surround the streets. The 1911 Britannica entry lists nine Evangelical and two Roman Catholic churches, and a modern town hall. It also lists a Hall of Fame with statues of two emperors, a theatre, a picture gallery, and an ethnographical museum.
britannica-1911-batten:
Batten is a word with two distinct lives, set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. As a noun it is a form of baton, used in joinery for a board not more than seven inches broad or three thick. Such boards strengthen laths and other woodwork. On ship, a batten is a strip nailed to a mast to stop rubbing, or fixed over a tarpaulin on a hatchway to keep water out.

As a verb, batten has a different root. It is found in words of several Teutonic tongues meaning profit or gain, and it is kin to the English better and boot. To batten is to improve in condition, above all in the case of animals by feeding. From that sense it also means to feed greedily. In a figure, it means to thrive at another's cost.
britannica-1911-bautzen:
Bautzen, in Wendish Budissin, is a town of Saxony, Germany, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on a height above the right bank of the Spree, thirty-two miles east-north-east of Dresden, and is the capital of Saxon Upper Lusatia. Its people grew from 21,515 in 1890 to 29,412 in 1905. Walls ring the town, and old ramparts beyond them have been turned into walks. The cathedral of St Peter, from the 1400s, is shared: Protestants and Catholics both use it, split by an iron screen.

Scars and trade share the entry. The town was already standing when Henry the Fowler conquered Lusatia in 928, and it grew rich in part on pilgrims to a relic of St Peter. It suffered in the Hussite wars and worse in the Thirty Years' War. A battle of 1813 bears its name. Its trades run from woollens to leather, paper, and cigars.
britannica-1911-ben:
Ben, from an Old English word meaning “within,” is the inner room in the Scots phrase “a but and a ben.” Such a house has only one outer door, so the inner room is reached through the outer one. The outer room is the but, from a word meaning “without.”

Put together, “a but and a ben” first meant a living room and a sleeping room under one roof. From there the phrase widened to mean the whole dwelling, a cottage as such. The entry is a short word note, tracing how two plain room names grew into a fixed Scots expression for a small home.
britannica-1911-berchtesgaden:
Berchtesgaden is a town of Germany set high on the south-eastern edge of Bavaria, 1,700 feet above the sea. It lies on the southern slope of the Untersberg, six miles from Reichenhall by rail, and counted 10,046 people in 1900. Beauty of setting is its first claim on the visitor.

Rock-salt mines, worked as early as 1174, made the town’s living for centuries. Toys and small goods of wood, horn and ivory are its other famous products. Three old churches stand in the town, the early Gothic abbey church with its Romanesque cloister chief among them. The district was once its own church principality, founded in 1100 and secularised in 1803.
britannica-1911-bergen:
Bergen is a city and seaport of Norway, a county by itself on the west coast at about the latitude of the Shetlands. It counted 72,179 people in 1900. The town lies at the head of the broad Byfjord, partly on the rocky Nordnaes point between the Vaagen harbour and the Puddefjord.

Rain is Bergen’s weather mark: seventy-four inches a year on average, feeding lush growth on the steep hills. Timber ships and fishing smacks crowd the harbour, and Strandgaden, the main street, runs along it to the market square. King Olaf Kyrre founded the town, then called Björgvin, about 1070–1075. It is the birthplace of Holberg, Welhaven, the painter Dahl and Ole Bull, and now ranks first among Norwegian ship-owning ports.
britannica-1911-bertrand-henri-gratien:
Henri Gratien Bertrand (1773–1844), a French general, was born at Châteauroux. He had just finished his studies when the Revolution broke out. He joined the army as a volunteer. In Egypt Napoleon made him colonel in 1798, then brigadier-general. After Austerlitz he became Napoleon's aide-de-camp. From then on his life stayed bound to the emperor's. Napoleon trusted him fully and made him grand marshal of the court in 1813.

The 1911 Britannica entry marks his key services in brief. He directed the bridge building for the Danube crossing at Wagram in 1809. His action after Leipzig in 1813 saved the army from full destruction. He followed Napoleon to Elba, then to Waterloo, then to St Helena. In 1840 he was chosen to bring Napoleon's remains back to France. His fidelity made his name popular in France.
britannica-1911-bingen:
Bingen is a German town in the grand-duchy of Hesse-Darmstadt, 15 miles north-west of Mainz. It stands on the left bank of the Rhine, facing Rüdesheim. The Nahe stream joins the Rhine at the town. A stone bridge of Roman origin crosses the Nahe near its mouth. The 1905 population was 9,950. Above the town stands the ruined castle of Klopp, on a fortress site of Drusus.

Higher still sits the chapel of St Roch, rebuilt in 1895 after a fire. Thousands of pilgrims gather there each August, the 1911 Britannica entry says. The town trades in wine, grain, and cattle. New quays handle a transit trade in coal and iron. Downstream lies the Bingerloch whirlpool. On a mid-stream rock rises the Mäuseturm, where legend says mice ate Bishop Hatto in 969.
britannica-1911-bitumen:
Bitumen was the Roman name for the natural hydrocarbons, since classical Latin had no word petroleum. In its widest sense it covers the whole range of those substances. Natural gas stands at the light end of the family. Liquid petroleum grades follow, and solid asphalt closes the scale. Alberta-like solids such as albertite, gilsonite, elaterite, and ozokerite all fall under the name. The middle stuff, between asphalt and thin crude, is often called maltha.

The 1911 Britannica article groups the trade kinds under gas, petroleum, and asphalt. It sends readers to those heads for full treatment of each. Bible references to slime in Genesis are read as bitumen in the Vulgate. Herodotus is quoted on its early uses as well. The closing theory holds that solid kinds form as liquid petroleum escapes upward. Air and evaporation then thicken it in fissures and surface strata. Boverton Redwood signs the survey.
britannica-1911-blaikie-william-garden:
William Garden Blaikie (1820–1899) was a Scottish Free Church minister, editor, and social reformer. Born in Aberdeen, he studied at Marischal College and then under Thomas Chalmers at Edinburgh. He was among the 474 ministers who signed the deed of demission and left their livings at the Disruption.

He served the Free Church at Pilrig, between Edinburgh and Leith, from 1844 to 1868, and pushed better housing for working people. His book Better Days for Working People sold 60,000 copies, and model buildings rose at Pilrig through his work. He edited church magazines for years, raised £14,000 for the Waldensian churches, and wrote lives of Livingstone and Chalmers.
britannica-1911-blaubeuren:
Blaubeuren is a small town in Württemberg, Germany, 12 miles west of Ulm and joined to it by rail. It held 3114 people in 1900. The town sits 1600 feet up in a deep, wild valley of the Swabian Alps, partly ringed by old walls, and has two hospitals.

Its abbey church is the chief sight. Built in late Gothic style between 1465 and 1496, the choir holds fine carved stalls of the 1400s and a high altar with a triptych of 1496. Only the choir is still used for Protestant worship, while the nave serves as a school hall. The Benedictine abbey itself was founded in 1095 and, after the Reformation, became a school and then a Protestant training college for clergy.
britannica-1911-boieldieu-francois-adrie:
François Adrien Boieldieu (1775–1834) was a French composer of comic opera, famed for La Dame blanche. Born at Rouen, a cathedral organist's harsh pupil, he had two operas staged in his home city in 1795 and left for Paris the same year. Grand opera ruled there, and he lived at first by playing piano.

Work as accompanist to the singer Garat spread his songs through Paris drawing rooms, and stage success followed, with Le Calife de Bagdad in 1800. Fleeing a troubled marriage, he spent years at St Petersburg writing operas for the emperor. Back home he gave Jean de Paris in 1812, took a Conservatoire chair in 1817, and crowned his career with La Dame blanche in 1825, its libretto drawn in part from Scott.
britannica-1911-botzen:
Botzen, also Bozen or Bolzano, is a town in Austrian Tirol where the Talfer meets the Eisak, a little above its junction with the Adige. It stands 869 feet up on the Brenner railway, 58 miles south of the pass and 35 miles north of Trent. In 1900 it held 13,632 people, mainly German-speaking Catholics, though the Italian share was growing.

The entry calls it a Teutonic town in Italian surroundings and the busiest trading town of German Tirol. Its crossroads site, where the Brenner route from Germany meets the Swiss road down the upper Adige, brought a great transit trade and four large fairs a year. Its Gothic parish church of the 1300s and 1400s is praised, and a statue of 1889 honours the singer Walther von der Vogelweide, said to have been born nearby. Local wine is noted as early as the 600s.
britannica-1911-brixen:
Brixen, in Italian Bressanone, is a small city in the Austrian province of Tirol and chief town of its administrative district, with 5767 people in 1900. It sits in the Eisack valley where the Rienz joins that stream, on the Brenner railway 34 miles south-east of the pass and 24 miles north-east of Botzen.

Church rule gives the city its look: it is still a bishop's see, with an 18th-century cathedral, episcopal palace and seminary, twelve churches and five monasteries. The see was founded late in the 8th century at Saben above Klausen and moved to Brixen in 992. In 1027 the emperor Conrad II gave its bishops wide temporal powers, lost only to Austria in 1803. Walls rose in 1030, the first outbreak of the great peasants' revolt flared here in 1525, and the fortress of Franzensfeste guards the Brenner road nearby.
britannica-1911-brocken:
Brocken is a mountain of Germany in Prussian Saxony, the highest point of the Harz range at 3733 feet. A huge, bare, granite-strewn dome, it is the greatest height in north Germany and commands sweeping views in every direction. On clear days Magdeburg and the Elbe, the towers of Leipzig and the Thuringian forest can all be picked out from the top.

A mountain railway of 12 miles climbs from Dreiannen-Hohne, and two carriage roads come up from the Bodetal and Ilsenburg. Legend clings to the peak: long after Christianity reached the region it stayed a place of heathen worship. On Walpurgis night, the first of May, rites held there fed the belief that the devil and witches held their orgies on the summit. Country folk still hold it haunted that night, and Goethe fixed the fame in the Brocken scene of Faust.
britannica-1911-brown-charles-brockden:
Charles Brockden Brown lived from 1771 to 1810 and was an early American novelist. The Britannica life of 1911 opens in Philadelphia, where Quaker parents raised him. Frail and shy as a boy, he loved study above all else. His chief joy was to draw grand plans for ideal towns and halls.

That gift for bold design later shaped his tales of fiction. He first sketched a dream state in a tale called Carsol. The Dialogue of Alcuin in 1797 took up the rights of women. He drew strong hints from Godwin and from Mary Wollstonecraft. His later novels won note for plots built with great skill and care.
britannica-1911-bryant-william-cullen:
William Cullen Bryant (1794–1878) was an American poet and journalist. This 1911 Britannica biography gives his life at length. He was born at Cummington, Massachusetts, on 3 November 1794. His father was a country physician. Bryant had little formal schooling. He entered Williams College at sixteen. He left without a degree when family money ran short.

The article follows his twin careers in verse and journalism. His Poems appeared in 1821 and again in 1832. Later volumes include The Fountain and Thirty Poems. He also made blank-verse translations of Homer. His Iliad came out in 1870 and his Odyssey in 1871. The Poetical Works followed in 1876. The entry ranks him among the master poets of America. It calls him, in history, the first of them. His verse praises the divine mind seen in earth and sky.
britannica-1911-bushmen:
Bushmen is an entry on a people of South Africa in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. British and Dutch settlers at the Cape gave them that name. They often call themselves Saan, and one group name is Khuai. Other peoples call them Abatwa or Masarwa in their own tongues.

The entry treats them as the first known people of South Africa. Traces of their past reach north to the Nyasa and Tanganyika basins. It cites pierced stones used to weight digging sticks as one such trace. It also notes early claims of a link to Mongolian peoples. Those claims are shown as slight and based on face traits alone.
britannica-1911-calf-the-golden:
The golden calf was an image made by the Israelites in the desert. This 1911 Britannica article examines the story and its background. Moses had climbed the Mount of Yahweh to receive the Law. His long absence alarmed the people below. They clamoured for gods to lead them on. Aaron took their jewellery and made a molten calf from it. A festival was held around it.

Moses came down and stayed the full wrath of Yahweh. Still, 3000 men fell to the Levites' swords. The article then asks where calf worship came from. It rules out the Egyptian Apis, which was a living bull. Image worship was common among the Canaanites, it notes. Early Israel itself used images in worship without shame. Later writers, shaped by the Deuteronomic reform, condemned all such cults. The article notes that Elijah and Elisha never attacked the calf shrines.
britannica-1911-cameron-of-lochiel-sir-e:
Sir Ewen Cameron of Lochiel (1629-1719), a Scottish Highland chief, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of John Cameron and grandson of the head of the clan Cameron. His father died while he was an infant. He spent part of his youth with the Marquess of Argyll at Inveraray, then left about 1647 to take up his place as chief.

The article follows his long Royalist career. In 1653 he joined a rising for Charles the Second and, after its defeat, harried the forces of General Monk. Charles knighted him in 1681, and in 1689 he stood with Viscount Dundee at Killiecrankie. Too old to fight in the rising of 1715, he backed the Stuarts while his son led the Camerons in battle. Macaulay called him the Ulysses of the Highlands, and the entry stresses his vast strength of body.
britannica-1911-carmarthen:
Carmarthen is a town of Wales, county town of Carmarthenshire. Its Welsh name is Caerfyrddin. It stands on the right bank of the river Towy. The river is tidal and navigable for small craft there. Its population in 1901 was 10,025. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its role. Railways of two companies serve Carmarthen from several directions.

Works in the town make woollens and ropes. Tanneries also operate in Carmarthen. Its chief importance is as a market town, though. It serves a large and fertile district around it. The Saturday market is well attended each week. It shows scenes of modern Welsh agricultural life. The town holds the gaol for three Welsh counties. The lunatic asylum for the same three counties stands there too. The article then gives Carmarthen's long history as a borough.
britannica-1911-catechumen:
Catechumen is a church term for a person under instruction in the Christian faith, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. Such persons receive teaching in the principles of the religion with a view to baptism. The word comes from a Greek term for one instructed, from a verb meaning to teach orally. As soon as Christianity became a missionary religion, set arrangements for such teaching were found necessary.

At the beginning the Apostles themselves seem to have undertaken this duty in person. The instruction was in apparent fact given after baptism in that first age. The text cites the account in Acts, where those who received the word were baptised and then continued in the teaching of the Apostles. Luke addresses Theophilus as one who had been instructed in the things of the faith, a case the piece weighs in detail.
britannica-1911-cherchen:
Cherchen is a town of East Turkestan at the north foot of the Altyn-tagh, a range of the Kuen-lun, at 4,100 feet. The town spreads along channels drawn from the left side of the Cherchen-darya river. Its people numbered about 2,000 in 1900. The entry gives its place as 85 degrees 35 minutes east, on a river that starts in the Arka-tagh range.

Most of the entry follows the Cherchen-darya itself. The river flows north to the desert below Cherchen, then turns north-east through a wide bed lined with dense reeds. It ends by joining the Tarim at the lake of Kara-buran, after a course put at 500 to 600 miles. Falls, a broad delta, winter freezing and a basin of 6,000 to 7,000 square miles are all noted.
britannica-1911-chipping-campden:
Chipping Campden is the subject of a town entry in the 1911 Britannica. The town lies in Gloucestershire in England. It sits toward the north of the Cotswold hills. A rail line of the Great Western served the town. Its count in 1901 was just over fifteen hundred souls. Old houses show the town was once of more weight. A church with old brasses and grand tombs stands there.
