A ruined manor house and almshouses stand near the church. Campden House, also old, draws note in the entry. A tale links the town to a meet of Saxon kings. The first firm record comes in Domesday Book. Lords who held the manor are named in turn. Charters freed traders at its market from tolls. A grant set how fines for townsfolk should be capped. Notes on a town court and a clash in 1273 follow.
britannica-1911-christina-of-sweden:
Christina, queen of Sweden who lived from 1626 to 1689, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Stockholm in December 1626, she was the daughter of Gustavus Adolphus and Maria Eleonora of Brandenburg. Her father died when she was only six years old. She was taught mainly by the scholar Johannes Matthiae, in as masculine a way as possible. The great Oxenstjerna himself taught her politics.

Christina took the throne at eighteen, in December 1644. From her first day at the council board she impressed her veteran counsellors with her genius. Oxenstjerna said at fifteen that she was stout-hearted and of good understanding. Yet the article faults her inordinate pride and egoism. She showed contempt for public opinion and spent freely with no regard for the state's needs. Her poor treatment of the great chancellor sprang, it says, from jealousy of his fame.
britannica-1911-churching-of-women:
Churching of Women is the Christian ceremony of thanksgiving by mothers shortly after the birth of their children. It no doubt began in the Mosaic rule on purification in Leviticus, the entry says. In ancient times the ceremony was usual but not binding in England, while in the Greek and Roman Catholic Churches today it is imperative. No ancient form of service survives, and the English prayer book form dates only from the middle ages.

Custom set the fortieth day after confinement as the usual date, matching the presentment of Mary and the child Jesus at the Temple. A woman was thought unlucky if she left home before being churched, and services were sometimes said in private houses. Special churching seats, veils and churching cloths appear in parish records. Lighted tapers, offerings and rules on where the woman should kneel fill the detail of custom.
britannica-1911-churchwarden:
Churchwarden, in England, is the guardian or keeper of a church and the representative of the body of the parish. The name comes from the original duty of custody of the fabric and furniture of the church, fixed on parishioners in the 14th century. Churchwardens are always lay persons, yet in law they act as quasi-corporations, able to hold goods and bring actions for them. Resident householders are chiefly eligible, with some classes exempt or barred.

Choice is set by the 89th canon, by joint consent of minister and parishioners where possible, and otherwise one each. Local customs vary widely, from township choices in the north to vestry or manor appointments. Appointment usually falls in Easter week, after which each warden swears to execute the office faithfully. Duties cover service needs, offertory, order, seating, goods, repair of church and churchyard and presentment of offences.
britannica-1911-citizen: Citizen, in its root sense, names a person who lives in a city and holds rights there. The English word is a worn form of an old French word for a townsman. In England the term is still used first of persons with civic rights in a borough. A wider use has grown from the Latin word for a city state. In that use a citizen is a full member of a state, holding full national rights and owing loyalty to it. Republics use the word where monarchies use subject.
britannica-1911-cohen: Cohen is a Jewish family name. It comes from the Hebrew word for priest. The name points to descent from the ancient Hebrew priests. Many families that claim such descent do not bear the name, though. Other forms of the name are Cohn, Cowen and Kahn. The entry is very short and gives no more than that core claim and those variant forms. It closes with a reference to the Jewish Encyclopedia for fuller treatment.
britannica-1911-conshohocken:
Conshohocken is a borough in Montgomery County, Pennsylvania. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its site, mills, and growth. It stands on the Schuylkill River northwest of Philadelphia. Counts rose from about fifty-five hundred in 1890 to near seventy-five hundred in 1910.

Two rail lines served the borough and its mill trade. Cotton and wool mills stood beside rolling mills and steel works. Foundries, boiler shops, and tube works added heavy trade. Makers also turned out surgical tools and false stone. First settled about 1820, the place was called Matsons Ford at first. Its present name is an Indian word meaning pleasant valley. Across the river, West Conshohocken made carpets and wool goods.
britannica-1911-corwen:
Corwen, a market town in Merionethshire in Wales, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its name means the white choir. It stands on rail lines ten miles from Llangollen, through the vale of the Dee. Its people numbered 2,680 in 1901. The road built by Telford runs above the town and opens wide views of the Dee.

The article links the town to the last Welsh fight for freedom under Owen Glendower. His pew was shown by custom in the old church, and his knife, fork, and dagger were kept at a nearby house. His palace stood three miles off. The old British fort of Caer Drewyn, part of a chain of forts, was said to be the scene of his stand against Henry the Fourth. Hills ring the town on every side.
britannica-1911-covent-garden:
Covent Garden was once an open space north of the Strand in London. It now holds the chief flower, fruit and vegetable market of the capital. The ground was at first the convent garden of the abbey of Saint Peter at Westminster. That old use gave the place its name. No trace of the garden itself stays in the entry's tale.

In the first half of the 1600s Inigo Jones laid the site out as a square. A piazza ran along two of its sides. By 1656 the square was turning into a market for the same goods sold there now. A theatre has stood on the site since 1733. Covent Garden Theatre, built in 1858, is the chief seat of grand opera in London. Fire took its earlier houses in 1809 and in 1856. The entry is short and keeps to ground, square, market and stage.
britannica-1911-crossen:
The hosted text opens partway through its account of Crossen, in the middle of a sentence about the town's churches. What survives lists a modern school, a technical school for vine and fruit growing, and a dairy school. Manufactories of copper and brass ware and of cloth are named. The country round the town lives by fruit and grape growing. A brisk shipping trade, mainly in wine, fruit, and fish, is also recorded.

The closing history says Crossen was founded in 1005 and mattered in the middle ages as a crossing place on the Oder. It gained civic rights in 1232. For a time it was capital of a Silesian duchy. On the death of Barbara of Brandenburg, widow of the last duke, it passed to Brandenburg in 1482. In May 1886 a whirlwind devastated the town.
britannica-1911-cullen:
Cullen is a royal, municipal, and police burgh of Banffshire in Scotland, with 1,936 people in 1901. It stands on Cullen Bay, west of Banff and north-west of Aberdeen by rail. The Deskford Burn cuts it into Seatown, the older part, and Newtown, dating only from 1822. St Mary's church, a cross-shaped building, was founded by Robert Bruce, whose second wife died at Cullen. Rope and sail making, boat-building, brewing, and fishing employ the town.

The harbour, built between 1817 and 1834, counts among the best on that coast though wholly artificial. Cullen House, a seat of the earl of Seafield, stands a mile south and holds fine works of art. Ruins of Findlater Castle crown the cliffs two miles east. The entry closes with Portsoy, a thriving fishing town five miles east. Portsoy adds fish-curing, a distillery, and quarries of pink granite and marble to the district's trades.
britannica-1911-culloden:
Culloden is a bleak tract of moorland in Inverness-shire, Scotland, part of the north-east of Drummossie Muir. It lies about six miles east of Inverness by road. Its fame is the battle of 16 April 1746, by which the fate of the house of Stuart was decided. Highlanders more often call it the battle of Drummossie. About 1,000 clansmen lie in its trenches. Memorial stones of 1881 name the clans at the head of each trench.

A cairn twenty feet high marks the chief scene of the fight. The Cumberland Stone, a huge boulder, shows where the English commander stood. A mile north stands Culloden House, once the seat of Duncan Forbes of the Court of Session. The Culloden Papers, documents from 1625 to 1748, were found there in 1812 and published in 1815. South of the field, the plain of Clava holds stone circles, cairns, and other remains from before history.
britannica-1911-cuxhaven:
Cuxhaven, a seaport town of Germany, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It belongs to the state of Hamburg and sits at the west side of the mouth of the Elbe, 71 miles by rail from Hamburg. Its people numbered 6,898 in 1900. The harbour is good and safe, and ships held up in the Elbe by bad weather use it often.

The article notes a new harbour built in the eighteen-nineties, deep enough for large ships. The mail steamers of the Hamburg-American line made it their port, and the company moved part of its staff there in 1901. As a free port it stood outside the customs union. Coal, bricks, and timber came in, and fish went out. A fishing fleet had its own new harbour from 1892, and crowds from Hamburg came to bathe.
britannica-1911-darien:
Darien is a district covering the eastern part of the isthmus that joins Central and South America, lying mainly within Panama. Rodrigo Bastidas reconnoitred it in the first year of the sixteenth century, and Santa Maria la Antigua was its first settlement. In 1513 Balboa stood on a peak in Darien and saw the Pacific below him, and the narrow neck long seemed to promise a passage between the two oceans.

The first serious trade attempt was Scotland's. A company chartered in 1695, advised by William Paterson, planted a colony called New Caledonia in 1698 with 1200 settlers. Want, sickness and anarchy emptied it within a year, and a second expedition ended besieged by Spaniards and forced to capitulate. Only a handful of the settlers ever reached home.
britannica-1911-decatur-stephen:
Stephen Decatur, an American naval commander who lived from 1779 to 1820, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Sinnepuxent in Maryland, he entered the United States navy as a midshipman in 1798. He was made lieutenant a year later and served in the short war with France. In 1803 he held command of a ship in the Mediterranean.

In February 1804 he led a daring raid into the harbour of Tripoli. His aim was to burn an American frigate that had fallen into enemy hands. He succeeded and escaped under the fire of the shore guns, with only one man wounded. That exploit won him a captain's commission and a sword of honour from Congress. In the War of 1812 his ship captured a British warship after a desperate fight.
britannica-1911-emden:
Emden is a maritime town of Germany in the Prussian province of Hanover, near the mouth of the Ems, 49 miles north-west from Oldenburg by rail. Its population was 20,754 in 1905. The Ems once flowed beneath its walls but is now two miles away, joined to the town by a broad, deep canal. That canal splits into an inner dock harbour and an outer free port.

Canals cross the town and link it with most towns of East Friesland, whose trading capital it is. The entry notes its gabled medieval houses, giving it the look of an old Dutch rather than a German town. The Great Church, a large Gothic building finished in 1455, holds the tomb of Enno II, count of East Friesland. Emden trades in farm produce, live-stock, timber, coal, tea, and wine, and its deep-sea fishing fleet numbered 67 vessels in 1902.
britannica-1911-emmendingen:
Emmendingen is a town of Germany in the grand-duchy of Baden, close to the Black Forest, on the river Elz and the main railway from Mannheim to Constance. Its population is given as 6200. The town has a Protestant church with a fine spire and a Roman Catholic church. It also has a handsome town-hall and an old castle, now a hospital, once the home of the counts of Hochberg.

Spinning mills and tanneries work in Emmendingen, and its factories make photographic instruments, paper, machinery, and cigars. A large trade in timber and cattle is also carried on. The entry recalls Johann Georg Schlosser, husband of Goethe's sister Cornelia, who served here as bailiff for some years. Emmendingen was once the seat of the counts of Hochberg, a side branch of the margraves of Baden. It gained market rights in 1418 and town status, with walls, in 1590.
britannica-1911-enkhuizen:
Enkhuizen is a seaport of Holland on the Zuider Zee. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lingers on its old houses and churches. It stands northeast of Hoorn, with a ferry to Friesland. Its count in 1900 was about sixty-nine hundred.

Rich trade in the 1600s left the town its fine face. Houses of brick and stone bear carving and carved dates. A tower gate called the Dromedary still guards the harbor. One room in that tower once served as a prison. The South church shows a tall tower from the 1400s. The West church holds a carved screen and pulpit of rare skill. A quaint wooden bell house there dates from 1519. The town hall of 1688 keeps painted rooms and town records. Fishing, shipbuilding, and rope making give work today.
britannica-1911-enniskillen:
Enniskillen, a market town in County Fermanagh in Ireland, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county town, set on an island in the river that joins the upper and lower Lough Erne. It lies 116 miles north-west of Dublin by rail. The town fills the whole island, and two bridges join it to suburbs on each shore. Its district held 5,412 people in 1901.

The article lists a brewery, tanneries, and a small cutlery works, with a good trade in corn, pork, and flax. In 1689 the town beat a stronger force sent against it by James the Second. Part of its defenders were later formed into a regiment of horse that still bears the town's name. Water routes by the river, the loughs, and a canal give it wide reach, and the loughs hold trout and large pike.
britannica-1911-erard-sebastien:
Sébastien Érard (1752–1831) was a French maker of musical instruments, born at Strassburg on the 5th of April 1752. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his gift from his upholsterer father's workshop to a Paris harpsichord maker who dismissed him out of jealousy. By twenty-five he had his own shop and in 1780 built his first pianoforte, among the first made in France.

Orders flooded in, and with his brother Jean Baptiste he founded a piano works that became one of Europe's most famed. Driven to London by the Revolution, he set up a factory there too. In 1810 he brought out his double-movement harp, a great leap beyond all earlier harps. Back in Paris he crowned his work in 1823 with the model grand pianoforte using the double escapement. He died at Passy on the 5th of August 1831.
britannica-1911-essen:
Essen, a factory town in the German Rhine province, is described at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands north east of Dusseldorf on the main rail line to Berlin. Its count leapt from under nine thousand in 1849 to over two hundred thousand in 1905. Rail lines at its centre reach all the chief towns of the iron and coal fields.

The town looks gloomy, with narrow old streets of grey slate roofs. Its minster, from the tenth century, holds fine pictures and relics. Schools of many kinds, a theatre, and hospitals serve the town. All of Essen rests on the great Krupp iron and steel works. That firm spends vast sums on churches, schools, and clubs for its workers. The town began as the seat of a Benedictine nunnery. Its abbess ruled the town as a princess of the empire until 1803.
britannica-1911-esslingen:
Esslingen is a town in Württemberg, Germany, on the Neckar river near Stuttgart. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes old walls, towers, and thirteen suburbs around it. One suburb lies on an island in the river itself. An old citadel looks down on the town from a height.

Two churches draw special note for their age and craft. The Frauenkirche shows fine Gothic work and a tall spire. Saint Dionysius dates from the thirteenth century with a fine screen. Shops in town made cloth, gloves, machines, and wine for trade. The town won free city status in 1209 and joined Württemberg only in 1802.
britannica-1911-ettlingen:
Ettlingen is a German town in Baden on the Alb, on the Mannheim–Basel railway south of Karlsruhe. Its 1905 population was 8,040. Old walls and ditches still ring it, giving a medieval, picturesque air. Buildings include an old princely residence with grounds, one Evangelical and two Roman Catholic churches, and a former monastery. Roman remains survive, notably a Neptune sculpture built into the town-hall wall. Paper-making, spinning, weaving and machine building lead its trades.

Wine and fruit growing also support a good deal of trade. The first notice of Ettlingen dates from the 8th century. It became a town in 1227, when Frederick II gave it to the margrave of Baden. The French pillaged it in 1689. Near the town, Moreau beat the archduke Charles on 9 and 10 July 1796. The entry is a compact gazetteer notice of the town's fabric and past.
britannica-1911-eupen:
Eupen is a German town in the Prussian Rhine province. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica presents its trade and past. It sits in a fine valley where two streams meet. Rail links it with Aix-la-Chapelle, and its 1905 count was about fourteen thousand.

Cloth and buckskin mills gave the town its busy name. Net and glove works, soap works, dye works, and tanneries added jobs. Trade in cattle and dairy goods also ran strong. The town held Protestant and Catholic churches, a monastery, schools, and a hospital. As part of Limburg it was under Austria until 1801. It then passed to France, and in 1814 it came to Prussia.
britannica-1911-euskirchen: Euskirchen is a town of Germany in the Prussian Rhine province, and this short 1911 Britannica entry gives its setting and trades. It stands on a plateau east of the Eifel range, at a junction of railways from Cologne and Bonn, ten miles west of the latter city. Its people numbered 10,285 in 1905. The town has both an Evangelical and a Roman Catholic church. Its trades include cloth making, sugar making, and stocking making, besides breweries and tanneries.
britannica-1911-fa-hien:
Fa Hien, a Chinese monk and road writer at work from three ninety nine to four fourteen, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. His book is held as one of the first and best Chinese tales of India. He set out from the chief city of the Tsin realm. He passed the Great Wall and crossed the sand waste past it.

He calls that waste a home of foul fiends and hot winds. The sole marks for the road were the bones of the dead. No bird flew in the air and no beast walked the ground. At Khotan he saw a great feast of the faith. In lands later won by a new faith, he shows the old faith still strong. He reached India by a sheer drop of ten thousand cubits from wall like hills. The tale is a landmark of world travel.
britannica-1911-feltham-owen:
Owen Feltham, an English moralist who died in 1668, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Thomas Feltham of Mutford in Suffolk, and his birth year is given as 1602 or 1609. He is famous chiefly for the Resolves, one hundred short essays on divine, moral and political themes.

To later issues of the Resolves, Feltham added the Lusoria, a set of forty poems. Hardly anything is known of his life. The poet Randolph addressed a poem of compliment to him and became his friend. Feltham attacked Ben Jonson in an ode, then gave a flattering elegy to a memorial volume for him in 1638. He published notes on the Low Countries in 1652. He was a strict high churchman and a royalist. The entry grants that he lacks the elegance of Bacon, whom he copied, but finds charm in his imagery and true insight.
britannica-1911-fifth-monarchy-men:
Fifth Monarchy Men were a Puritan sect in England under Cromwell. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells their hope and their rising. They backed his rule as a step toward a fifth monarchy. Four great empires had passed, and Christ rule was to follow.

The sect sought to scrap all laws and institutions of the day. A plain code drawn from the law of Moses would replace them. Delay in that hope soured them against Cromwell fast. Arrests of their preachers drove the dream underground for years. After the king return a cooper led their last stroke. Thomas Venner band tried to seize London in January 1661. Most were killed or taken in the attempt itself. Venner and ten others died for treason that month.
britannica-1911-flamen:
A flamen was a Roman sacrificial priest. His name is taken from flare, to blow up the altar fire. Flamens served under the pontifex maximus, each consecrated to one god. The highest were the flamen Dialis, Martialis and Quirinalis, always chosen from the patricians. Their founding is credited to Numa. When the number rose from three to fifteen, those three were called maiores. The other twelve, lesser priests of lesser gods, were called minores and drawn from the plebs.

Flamens held office for life, yet neglect or an ill omen could force resignation. Their dress included the apex, a white conical cap, the laena mantle and a laurel wreath. The entry details the gear of the flamen Dialis, priest of Jupiter. It lists his white cap with olive branch and woollen thread, his heavy mantle woven by his wife, the sacrificial knife and a rod.
britannica-1911-flodden:
Flodden, or Flodden Field, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article on a famous battle. The field lies near the village of Branxton, in Northumberland, England. There the English and the Scots fought on the ninth of September 1513. A great Scottish army under King James the Fourth had crossed the border in August.

The earl of Surrey held the defence of the realm. King Henry the Eighth was away from England at the time. For the moment, Surrey had no settled force in the north. James wasted much precious time among the border castles. When Surrey came up at Wooler, his army matched the Scottish host in strength. That host was now much weakened by hardship and desertion. James had not advanced beyond Ford Castle. The English commander promptly sent in a challenge to battle. War readers get the stand-off that set up a king's last fight.
britannica-1911-fox-sir-stephen:
Sir Stephen Fox (1627-1716), English statesman, was born on 27 March 1627. He was the son of William Fox of Farley in Wiltshire, a yeoman farmer. At fifteen he got a place in the household of the earl of Northumberland. He then served the earl's brother, Lord Percy, and was with the royalist army at the battle of Worcester as Percy's deputy at the ordnance board. When Charles II fled to the continent, Fox went with the exiled court into its hardest years.

On Clarendon's advice, Fox was made manager of the royal household in exile. Clarendon praised his languages, clerkship, honesty and discretion. His skill in handling the tiny finances of the wandering court won him trust and promotion, and he ran several important missions. The entry follows the farmer's son who kept a king's purse in exile and rose high after the Restoration.
britannica-1911-fu-kien:
Fu-kien, formerly Min, is a south-eastern province of China, bounded by Cheh-kiang, Kwang-tung, and Kiang-si, with the sea to the east. It covers 53,480 square miles and holds an estimated 20,000,000 people. The capital is Fuchow Fu, and the province is cut into eleven prefectures. Ranges of the Nan-shan cross it from north-east to south-west.

The main river is the Min, formed by three streams joining near Yen-pʽing Fu and reaching the sea some 30 miles below Fuchow. Its upper course is narrow and full of rapids, fit only for small native boats. The soil is rich, the hills green and terraced, and the lead product is tea, the best being Bohea from the Wu-e Mountains. Open ports are Fuchow and Amoy, both opened in 1842, and Funing, opened in 1898. Salt, sugar, timber, and paper also figure in the trade.
britannica-1911-fussen: Füssen is a Bavarian town in Germany at the foot of the Alps on the Lech, 2500 feet above the sea, with some 4000 people. It has six Roman Catholic churches, a Franciscan monastery and a castle on a rocky height. Rope-making is an important industry of the town. The castle is remembered for the peace signed there on the 22nd of April 1745 between Maximilian III Joseph of Bavaria and Maria Theresa. Hohenschwangau castle stands two miles south-east, and Neuschwanstein, built by Louis II, a little to the north.
britannica-1911-gardiner-stephen:
Stephen Gardiner, who lived from about 1493 to 1555, was an English bishop. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica adds that he served as lord chancellor. He was a native of Bury Saint Edmunds, son of a cloth merchant. His father saw to it that he had a sound schooling. In 1511 the lad met Erasmus at Paris. At Cambridge he shone in the classics, above all in Greek. He then turned to canon and civil law.

In those subjects no one could dispute his lead. His gifts drew the notice of Cardinal Wolsey, who made him his secretary. In that post Gardiner learned foreign politics from the inside. By 1527 he was named a commissioner to treat with France.
britannica-1911-giessen:
Giessen is a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in Germany. It is the capital of the province of Upper Hesse. The town stands in a fair, rich valley where the Wieseck stream joins the Lahn river. Its count rose from 18,836 in 1885 to 29,149 in 1905.

The article puts the university at the heart of the town. That school was founded in 1607 by a landgrave of Hesse. It holds a large library, a plant garden, a star tower, and schools of medicine. Its chemistry rooms were led for years by Justus von Liebig, a famed name in that science. Cloth, machines, leather, candles, tobacco, and beer are made in the town. The old town keeps narrow, winding streets from its early days.
britannica-1911-girard-stephen:
Stephen Girard (1750-1831) was an American financier and philanthropist, founder of Girard College in Philadelphia. The 1911 Britannica entry has him born near Bordeaux on 20 May 1750, a sea captain's son with little schooling, who lost the sight of his right eye at eight. He traded to New Orleans and the West Indies before settling at Philadelphia in 1776.

His fleet grew, its ships named for French authors: Rousseau, Voltaire, Montesquieu. In 1810 he used about a million dollars held with the Barings to buy depreciated Bank of the United States stock, a move that steadied American credit in Europe. When the bank's charter lapsed he bought its building and opened the Bank of Stephen Girard in 1812. The entry closes with his great bequest: Girard College, a school for orphans run by trustees, with training partly industrial and partly preparing boys for college.
britannica-1911-glendower-owen:
Owen Glendower is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Glendower was the last man to claim the title of an independent prince of Wales. His fuller name was Owain ab Gruffydd, lord of Glyndyvrdwy in Merioneth. He came of good family, with two great houses in the north of Wales.

On both sides he claimed descent from the old Welsh princes. Born about 1359, he studied law at Westminster in London. He served as squire to the earl of Arundel and gave witness in a famous heraldry lawsuit. Later he served Henry of Bolingbroke, the future king of England. Welsh sympathy, though, lay with King Richard, Henry's rival. A personal quarrel also rankled, the entry begins to tell. Readers meet the trained lawyer and courtier who would raise Wales in revolt.
britannica-1911-golden:
Golden is a city in Colorado, county-seat of Jefferson county, on Clear Creek about 14 miles west by north of Denver. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 2,152 people in 1900 and 2,477 in 1910. It stands about 5,700 feet above the sea, and serves as a residential suburb of Denver.

Castle Rock rises 600 feet above the city, and Lookout Mountain, a natural park of 3,400 acres, lies to the west. In Golden stands the Colorado State School of Mines, opened in 1874, teaching mining and metallurgical engineering. Pottery, firebrick and tile come from local clays, and coal, copper and gold are found nearby. The first settlement was a gold camp of 1859, named for Tom Golden, a pioneer prospector. Golden was capital of Colorado Territory in 1862, though the offices sat there only in 1866-1867.
britannica-1911-goppingen:
Goppingen is a town of Germany, in the kingdom of Wurttemberg, on the right bank of the Fils, 22 miles east-south-east of Stuttgart. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 20,870 people in 1905. Its castle, built by Duke Christopher in the 16th century partly from Hohenstaufen stones, now houses public offices.

The town has two Evangelical churches, a Roman Catholic church, a synagogue, and classical and modern schools. Its manufactures are large: linen and woollen cloth, leather, glue, paper and toys, with machine shops and tanneries. Three miles north stand the ruins of Hohenstaufen castle. Goppingen belonged first to the Hohenstaufen house, passed to Wurttemberg in 1270, was walled in 1129, and was almost wholly rebuilt after a fire in 1782.
britannica-1911-gottingen:
Gottingen is a town of Germany, in the Prussian province of Hanover, in the broad, fertile valley of the Leine, 67 miles south of Hanover. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its population as 34,030 in 1905, up from 17,057 in 1875. The Leine canal parts the old town from the new, and tree-planted ramparts ring it as a promenade.

The town's fame is its university, the Georgia Augusta, founded by George II in 1734 and opened in 1737. It rose fast to a leading place, with 1,547 students in 1823. The entry notes the churches of St John and St James, the 14th-century town hall, and thriving trades: publishing, cloth, and mathematical and scientific instruments. The long article then gives the university's history in full, through its political troubles and famous teachers.
britannica-1911-gravamen: Gravamen is a term from Latin roots that mean to weigh down and heavy. In law it names a charge or wrong, and most of all the grave part of a charge. In England the word is used most in church cases. There it names a note sent from the lower house to the upper house of the church meet. Such a note sets out wrongs that call for fix, or breaks in church rule that need heed. The entry is a brief note from the nineteen eleven work.
britannica-1911-greifenhagen:
Greifenhagen is a town of Germany, in the Prussian province of Pomerania, on the Reglitz, 12 miles south-south-west of Stettin by rail. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 6,473 people in 1905. Its prosperity depends chiefly on agriculture, the entry says, and it has a considerable trade in cattle.

Felt making and saw mills are its other industries. The town was built in 1230 and raised to town rank and fortified about 1250. Its wars fill the rest of the notice. In the Thirty Years' War both imperialists and Swedes took it. In 1675 the Brandenburgers captured it, and in 1679 it came finally into their possession. The whole entry is a compact gazetteer paragraph: river, distance, population, the cattle trade, and a four-century outline of sieges.
britannica-1911-greisen:
Greisen, in the 1911 Britannica, is a rock made from granite by change. The hosted text opens part-way into the article, in the account of that change, so the entry's beginning does not survive in this record. What remains explains the process as pneumatolytic: vapours freed by cooling granite magma worked on the rock, probably while it was still hot.

The same change, white mica, quartz and tourmaline growing together, appears in sedimentary rocks around granite masses. Greisen stands close to schorl rock in make-up and origin, the entry says. Both often carry small shares of tin oxide, cassiterite, and are worked as tin ores. They occur in Cornwall, Saxony, Tasmania and other tin districts, though many greisens hold no tin. A table of analyses closes the piece. It shows fluorine and boron entering, and the alkalies falling, as Cornish granite became greisen.
britannica-1911-gretna-green:
Gretna Green is a village in the south-east of Dumfriesshire, Scotland, about nine miles north-north-west of Carlisle, near the river Sark, the border with England. The 1911 Britannica entry explains its notoriety. As the nearest village on the Scottish side, it was the resort of eloping couples who lacked their parents' consent.

Until 1754, clandestine marriages were commonly made in London's Fleet prison. Lord Hardwicke's act ended that, and couples crossed the border, where a simple declaration before witnesses sufficed. At Gretna the blacksmith usually performed the ceremony, though the toll-keeper or anyone else might. Fees ran from half a guinea upward, and as many as two hundred couples a year married at the toll-house. The traffic ended in practice in 1856, when the law required three weeks' residence in Scotland first.
britannica-1911-hainichen:
Hainichen, a town of Germany in the kingdom of Saxony, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Kleine Striegis, fifteen miles north east of Chemnitz, on the railway to Rosswein. The entry gives it 7,752 people in 1905. It has two Protestant churches, a park, and commercial and technical schools.

Hainichen is a place of considerable industry, and its chief manufacture is flannels, baize, and like fabrics. It may be called the centre of that industry in Germany, the entry says. The special whiteness and quality of its flannel are due to the nature of the water used in making it. Large dye works and bleaching works also stand in the town. Hainichen is the birthplace of Gellert, the writer. A bronze statue of him was set up in the market place in 1865.
britannica-1911-halesowen:
Halesowen is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a market town in Worcestershire, England. It stands about six and a half miles west-south-west of Birmingham, on a branch rail line. The count of 1901 gave it 4,057 people. It lies in pleasant country among the east foothills of the Lickey Hills, and it has large iron and steel works.

The church has rough Norman parts, and the poet William Shenstone lies in its yard, with a memorial inside. His love of landscape gardening shows in the near-by estate of the Leasowes, which was his own. The town has a grammar school founded in 1652. On the river Stour stand the slight ruins of an abbey of Early English date. The article also notes Cradley, two miles off, with its iron works, fire-clay works, and a large trade in nails and chains.
britannica-1911-hallowe-en:
Hallowe'en, or All Hallows Eve, falls on 31 October. It is the vigil of Hallowmas, or All Saints' Day. Its ceremonies long predate Christianity. Two traits marked the ancient festival. People lit bonfires on that night. They also believed ghosts and witches wandered then. The Druids held their autumn festival near 1 November. They lit fires for the Sun-god in harvest thanksgiving.

Druid belief gave the night its darker side. Saman, lord of death, summoned wicked souls that evening. Those souls had spent the year in animal bodies. Ireland still knew the night as the Vigil of Saman. Roman Pomona customs added nuts and apples. Apple-ducking and nut-roasting became standard sports. Highland fires survived in Scotland and Wales into recent years. Stones in the embers foretold who would die within the year. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hallowe'en entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hastings-warren:
Warren Hastings, first governor general of British India, born in seventeen thirty two, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in the hamlet of Churchill in Oxfordshire. His family had long been settled in a nearby village. His great grandfather had sold the old manor house.

His mother died a few days after his birth. His father drifted away and died in obscurity in the West Indies. The boy got the basics of schooling at a charity school in his village. At age eight an uncle in the customs took charge of him. After private schooling he went to Westminster. School fellows there included men who later held high posts. In seventeen forty nine his uncle died. A kinsman in the East India Company then sent him to seek his fortune in Bengal.
britannica-1911-havet-julien:
Julien Havet (1853–1893) was a French historian. He was born at Vitry-sur-Seine on 4 April 1853. Ernest Havet was his father. He showed remarkable aptitude for learning early. Pure rhetoric, though, held an aversion for him. The École des Chartes trained his critical faculty. He took first place entering and leaving that school. Historical method became his ruling passion there.

His thesis on the Norman Islands' guardians appeared in 1876. It rested wholly on original documents in London and the islands. Later research barely touched its conclusions. He then attacked Fustel de Coulanges' system on Frankish law. The Gallo-Romans, he showed, were conquered, not absorbed as equals. The Vrain Lucas forgeries drew him to questions of authenticity. Many short monographs ranged across varied subjects. His friends published his Mélanges in 1895.
britannica-1911-hawarden:
Hawarden is a market-town of Flintshire, North Wales. People pronounce its name Harden. Its Welsh name is Penarlâg. Chester lies six miles to the east. Its population in 1901 was 5,372. It stands on a height with an extensive prospect. Coal surrounds it, and clay beds lie near. Coarse earthenware and draining tiles are manufactured. Fire-clay bricks are another local product.

Hawarden castle stands in a fine wooded park. The present house was built in 1752 and Gothicised in 1814. An older castle of the same name stands nearby. William the Conqueror gave that castle to Hugh Lupus. Dafydd of Wales took it in 1282. Parliamentarians destroyed it in the Civil War. It passed from the Glynne family to W. E. Gladstone by marriage. St Deiniol church was restored in 1857 and 1878.
britannica-1911-hawes-stephen:
Stephen Hawes (fl. 1502–1521) was an English poet. He was probably a Suffolk native born about 1474. Oxford educated him, and he travelled widely. His accomplishments won him a court place on his return. By 1502 he was groom of the chamber to Henry VII. Poetry was his most excellent vein. He could repeat most English poets by heart. Lydgate was the master he acknowledged.

His capital work is The Passetyme of Pleasure. Wynkyn de Worde printed it in 1509. Its hero, Graunde Amour, seeks La Bel Pucel. Fame and her greyhounds, Grace and Governance, guide him. The poem allegorises man's life in seven-lined stanzas. Its sections borrow the machinery of romance. The knight's education through the seven sciences structures it. Martianus Capella's Marriage of Mercury and Philology underlies the design. Hawes died before 1530.
britannica-1911-hawker-robert-stephen:
Robert Stephen Hawker (1803–1875) was an English antiquary and poet. He was born at Stoke Damerel, Devonshire, on 3 December 1803. His father later became vicar of Stratton in Cornwall. Liskeard and Cheltenham grammar schools educated Robert. He matriculated at Pembroke College, Oxford, in 1823. The Newdigate prize for poetry came in 1827. In 1834 he became vicar of Morwenstow in Cornwall.

His parishioners were smugglers, wreckers and dissenters of many hues. He was a high churchman who ruled with a high hand. Yet his people loved him greatly. Stories of his eccentric sayings multiplied. The Quest of the Sangraal is his best poem. His Cornish Ballads gave the world the Trelawny refrain. He died at Plymouth on 15 August. Reception into the Roman Catholic Church preceded his death. That step aroused bitter newspaper controversy.
britannica-1911-hawtrey-edward-craven:
Edward Craven Hawtrey (1789–1862) was an English educationalist. He was born at Burnham on 7 May 1789. His father was the parish vicar. Eton and King's College, Cambridge, educated him. In 1814 he became an assistant master at Eton. Dr Keate was headmaster at that time. In 1834 Hawtrey himself became headmaster of Eton. His administration proved a vigorous one.

New buildings rose under him, including the school library. A sanatorium was built and the chapel restored. He closed the Old Christopher Inn. He suppressed the Montem custom of street begging. He founded the prize for English essay himself. The prince consort's language prizes were supposedly his suggestion. In 1852 he became provost of Eton. London called him the English Mezzofanti for his languages. He died on 27 January 1862.
britannica-1911-heathen:
Heathen is a term for people outside the Jewish and Christian faiths. It originally included Mahommedans as well. Modern usage usually restricts it to polytheistic races. That restriction now excludes Mahommedans. The word's derivation has been much debated. It is common to all Germanic languages. German Heide and Dutch heiden are its cognates. A Gothic word haiþi, meaning heath, is the usual source.

Ulfilas' Gothic Bible calls the Syrophoenician woman haiþno. The Vulgate there has gentilis. Heathen would thus mean people of the heath. That matches Latin paganus, people of the village district. Old worship lingered longest in country places. Bugge suggested an Armenian source instead, from the Greek ethnē. Gentilis in Latin meant tribesman, then foreigner. Church usage fixed it on non-Christian nations. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the heathen entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-helvetius-claude-adrien:
Claude Adrien Helvétius (1715–1771) was a French philosopher and littérateur. He was born in Paris in January 1715. His family of physicians bore the name Schweitzer originally. His grandfather introduced ipecacuanha to medicine. His father was first physician to Queen Marie Leczinska. Claude trained for finance but wrote verses in spare hours. At twenty-three the queen made him farmer-general. That post was worth 100,000 crowns a year.

Wealth let him enjoy life to the utmost. Ageing, he dreamed of more lasting distinction. Voltaire the poet and Montesquieu the philosopher spurred him. His poem Le Bonheur appeared after his death. His famous book De l'esprit came in 1758. It aimed to rival Montesquieu's Esprit des lois. It drew immediate attention and formidable opposition. He had already retired to a country estate. There he relieved the poor and encouraged agriculture and industry.
britannica-1911-hen:
Hen is a female bird, especially the female of the common fowl. Old English hæn is the feminine of hana, the male bird. German Hahn and Henne show the same correlation. Dutch haan and hen, Swedish hane and hönne, match too. The old English male name has disappeared entirely. Cock replaced it in ordinary speech. That word is probably onomatopoeic in origin. Its base kuk- or kik- also appears in chicken.

French coq and medieval Latin coccus carry the same base. The whole entry is a few lines of word history. Definition first, then Teutonic cognates, then the cock problem. Nothing about poultry keeping or breeds appears. It is one of the briefest entries in its band. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hen entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hildburghausen:
Hildburghausen is a town of Germany, in the duchy of Saxe-Meiningen, in a wide valley on the river Werra, 19 m. S.E. of Meiningen. Its population was 7,456 in 1905. Its chief buildings are a ducal palace of 1685–1695, now barracks, the old town hall, two Evangelical churches, a Roman Catholic church and a theatre.

A technical college occupies the rooms where Meyer's Bibliographisches Institut worked from 1828 until it left for Leipzig in 1874. Local trades include linen and cloth, toys, buttons, optical instruments, farm machines and condensed milk. In the 13th century the place belonged to the counts of Henneberg, then passed to Thuringia and Saxony. In 1683 it became the capital of a small principality, united to Saxe-Meiningen in 1826.
britannica-1911-hilden: Hilden is a town in the Prussian Rhine province, on the river Itter, 9 m. S.E. of Düsseldorf by rail. Its population was 13,946 in 1905. It has an Evangelical and a Roman Catholic church and a monument to the emperor William I. Its manufactures include silks, velvets and carpets, calico-printing, machinery and brick-making. The entry is a short gazetteer notice giving the town's place, size, churches and trades in a few lines.
britannica-1911-hohenstaufen:
Hohenstaufen takes its name from a village and ruined castle in Swabia, in the kingdom of Württemberg. The castle gave its name to a celebrated Swabian family. Its members were emperors or German kings from 1138 to 1208, and again from 1214 to 1254. The earliest known ancestor was Frederick, count of Büren (d. 1094), whose son built the castle and took its name.

That son, Frederick I, stood firm for the emperor Henry IV. Henry rewarded him with the dukedom of Swabia in 1079 and with his daughter Agnes in marriage. Yet Swabia was his only after twenty years of struggle. His son Frederick II, the One-eyed, held south-west Germany for Henry V with his brother Conrad. After failing to win the throne in 1125, Frederick submitted at Bamberg but kept his dukedom. In 1138 Conrad of Hohenstaufen was elected German king, followed in 1152 by Frederick Barbarossa.
britannica-1911-hooft-pieter-cornelissen:
Pieter Cornelissen Hooft (1581–1647) was a Dutch poet and historian, born at Amsterdam on the 16th of March 1581. His father was a leading citizen of Holland and for a time burgomaster of Amsterdam. At seventeen Hooft joined the chamber of rhetoric In Liefde bloeiende. Before it he produced his tragedy Achilles and Polyxena, printed only in 1614.

In June 1598 he left Holland for Paris, then went on to Venice, Florence and Rome, and in 1600 to Naples. He studied the best Italian writing deeply as he travelled. From Italy he sent home a fine letter in verse on his hopes for Dutch poetry. He came back through Germany after three and a half years away. The life follows the honours and works that made him the central figure of Dutch letters in his age.
britannica-1911-horten:
Horten is a seaport of Norway on the Christiania Fjord west bank. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It faces Moss across the fjord, south of Christiania by water and rail. Counts from nineteen hundred put its people at just under nine thousand.

Horten is joined in practice with Karl Johansvaern, its strong naval base. That base, guarded by strong forts, is the head place of the Norway fleet. An arsenal and ship building works stand at the base as well. The town setting on the fjord is praised as fine in the entry. Readers get a brief sketch of a small port built round sea defence.
britannica-1911-huningen:
Huningen is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Huningen is a town in Alsace Lorraine, on the left bank of the Rhine. It stands on a branch of a canal and north of Basel by rail. Its people numbered over three thousand at the census given. An iron rail bridge crosses the Rhine at the town. Its factories make silk, watches, chemicals, and cigars.

The article says Huningen is an old place that grew round a fort guarding the Rhine crossing. It was taken from imperial forces in 1634 and later passed by purchase to a French king. The fortress gave up to the Austrians in 1815, and its works were soon pulled down. In 1871 the town passed with its province to the German empire.
britannica-1911-innerleithen:
Innerleithen is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a small burgh and health resort in Peeblesshire, Scotland. It stands on Leithen Water, near where that stream joins the Tweed. The count of 1901 gave it 2,181 people. In old times it seems to have borne the name Hornehuntersland.

A son of Malcolm the Fourth drowned in a pool of the Tweed near the town in 1159. Its chief trade is the making of tweeds and fine yarns. That trade, and the fame of its mineral springs, raised the burgh late in the eighteenth century. The spa is said to be the Saint Ronan's Well of Scott's novel. Its salt waters help mild cases of indigestion and liver trouble. Old hill forts flank the town on both sides, relics of a much older settlement.
britannica-1911-jonson-ben:
Ben Jonson is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English dramatist. He lived from 1573 to 1637. He was born probably in Westminster in early 1573. By his own account, his grandfather was a gentleman from Carlisle. He thought that family came at first from Annandale. His arms bore three spindles, the device of the Johnstones. That fact confirms his claim of Border descent, the entry says.

Jonson told that he was born after his father's death. His father had suffered under Queen Mary in estate and person. In the end his father had turned minister of the church. Two years after the boy's birth, his mother married again. She is said to have loved him in a fierce, passionate way. The entry tells of one show of that fierce love. His schooling and stage career unfold from that home.
britannica-1911-kempen:
Kempen is a town in the Prussian Rhine Province, 40 miles north of Cologne by the railway to Zevenaar. Its people numbered 6319 in 1900. It has a monument to Thomas à Kempis, who was born there. Its industries are of fair size and count silk weaving, glass making, and the making of electrical plant.

Kempen belonged in the middle ages to the archbishopric of Cologne and gained civic rights in 1294. It is remembered as the scene of a victory won on the 17th of January 1642 by the French and Hessians over the Imperialists. The entry is a short town note: a birthplace of a famed devotional writer, a set of trades, a medieval grant of rights, and one battle of the Thirty Years' War.
britannica-1911-keshub-chunder-sen:
Keshub Chunder Sen lived from 1838 to 1884 and reformed religion in India. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Calcutta, where he was born in 1838. He came of a high caste family of that great city. At a Calcutta college he grew skilled in English letters and history. For a short time he clerked at the Bank of Bengal there.

He gave up that post to give his life to letters and thought. Hamilton, Blair, Cousin, Newman, and Emerson were his loved authors. Their works turned his eyes inward to his own soul and fate. Like many schooled Hindus, he had drifted from the folk forms of faith. Yet he held fast to what he took as its true spirit.
britannica-1911-kindergarten:
Kindergarten is a German word meaning garden of children. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica credits Friedrich Froebel with the name and the school behind it. His play school served children from age three to seven. Its aim was growth in body, mind, and moral sense through guided play.

Froebel held that young children need time with peers to grow for social life. He devised shared games and simple playthings he called gifts. Colored balls, blocks, tablets, and rings formed patterns in small hands. Songs, rhythm, sense training, and garden plots filled the day as well. Direct book lessons were kept out on purpose.
britannica-1911-king-te-chen:
King-tê Chên was a town in Kiang-si, China, famed as the chief seat of porcelain making in the empire, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes it. It stands, unwalled, on the south bank of the river Chang. Its streets are narrow and crowded, and its people were reckoned at a million, most of them at work in the porcelain factories. The trade had been the town's main business for centuries.

In the early eleventh century a works was founded there to make vases and art wares for the emperor, and the town took its present name from that reign. From Ming times a special magistrate watched over the factories and sent the imperial porcelain to Peking at set times. The entry counts three thousand furnaces, whose fires burn without pause and light the town at night like a blaze.
britannica-1911-kitzingen:
Kitzingen is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in Bavaria, Germany, on the river Main. The town lies 95 miles south east of Frankfurt by rail, where the lines to Passau, Wurzburg, and Schweinfurt meet. It held 8,489 people in 1900. A bridge 300 yards long joins it to its suburb Etwashausen on the left bank, and a rail bridge crosses the Main at the same point.

Within the old walls stand an Evangelical church, two Roman Catholic churches, two town museums, a town hall, a grammar school, and two old convents. The chief trades are brewing, cask making, and the making of cement and colours. Boats on the Main carry a large trade in wine, fruit, grain, and timber. A Benedictine abbey stood at Kitzingen in the eighth century, and the town later belonged to the bishopric of Wurzburg.
britannica-1911-knickerbocker-harmen-jan:
Harmen Jansen Knickerbocker (c. 1650–c. 1720) was a Dutch colonist of New Netherland, born at Wyhe in Overyssel, Holland. Before 1683 he settled near what is now Albany, New York. In 1704 he bought, through Harme Gansevoort, one-fourth of the land in Dutchess county near Red Hook that had been patented to Peter Schuyler in 1688. Schuyler later deeded lots in that share to Knickerbocker's seven children.

The family line runs on at the Schaghticoke estate, down to Harmen Knickerbocker (1779–1855), a lawyer who sat in Congress in 1809–1811 and in the New York Assembly in 1816. His courtly welcome at his manor earned him the name "the prince of Schaghticoke." Washington Irving borrowed his name for Diedrich Knickerbocker's History of New York (1809), and from that book the name Knickerbockers passed into wide use.
britannica-1911-krumen:
The Krumen, also called Kroomen, Krooboys, Krus or Croos, are a people of the west coast of Africa. Their villages run along the coast of Liberia from below Monrovia nearly to Cape Palmas. Their name was once wrongly derived from the English word "crew,". It more likely comes from Kraoh, the old name of one of their tribes. With kindred peoples such as the Grebo and Basa they number some 40,000.

The Krus proper live between the Sino river and Cape Palmas, in five chief villages. They are noted as skilled seamen and bold fishermen, a stout and strong-built race. They are described as honest, brave and proud, so set on freedom that they would starve rather than be taken, and they never traded in slaves. Their small commonwealths have hereditary chiefs who speak for them to strangers, while real rule rests with the elders.
britannica-1911-langton-stephen:
Stephen Langton (died 1228), cardinal and archbishop of Canterbury, won fame first as a scholar at Paris. English by birth, he rose there as a leading teacher of church learning, wrote large commentaries, and is linked with the splitting of the Bible into chapters. Friendship with Lothar of Segni, later Pope Innocent III, shaped all that followed.

Innocent made him a cardinal in 1206, then pushed his name when the Canterbury election fell into dispute. Set aside rival votes were followed by a fresh choice at Rome, and Langton was consecrated on 17 June 1207. King John shut out the Canterbury monks in anger. An interdict on England in 1208 and the king's own ban in 1209 followed, and only a threat of French invasion forced John to make peace.
britannica-1911-leandre-charles-lucien:
Charles Lucien Léandre, born in 1862, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica after a short tail from the town article before it. Léandre was a French caricaturist and painter from Champsecret in Orne. He studied painting under Bin and Cabanel. From 1887 he showed work at the Salon in Paris.

The article notes that he showed many portraits and genre pictures at the Salon. His wide fame, though, came from his comic drawings and caricatures. A series called the Gotha of the Sovereigns, printed in the journal Le Rire, made his name with the public. The short piece thus presents him as a sound painter whose drawings reached far more people than his canvases did.
britannica-1911-leiden:
Leiden, a city in South Holland, is drawn as a school town in the 1911 Britannica. It sits on the Old Rhine, south west of Haarlem by rail. Boats and steam trams link it to the Hague and the sea towns. Its folk count fell from a peak in past days to fifty six thousand in nineteen oh four. Two arms of the Rhine meet at its heart, crossed by tree lined canals.

An old round fort on a mound stands at that river meet. A park bears the name of the mayor who held the town in fifteen seventy four. A blast on a powder ship in eighteen oh seven made that open space. Churches hold the tombs of famed scholars of the town. Its college, set up in fifteen seventy five, rules its life still.
britannica-1911-lingen:
Lingen, a town in the Prussian province of Hanover in Germany, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Ems canal, 43 miles north-west of Munster by rail. Its people numbered 7,500. It held iron foundries, machine works, rail workshops, and a large trade in cattle. Its other trades were weaving, malting, and the making of cloth.

The article adds that Lingen was the seat of a university from 1685 to 1819. The county of Lingen, of which the town was the capital, was joined in the middle ages with a neighbouring county. It was split off in 1508, divided, then joined again in 1541. It passed in time to the emperor, to Spain, and to Maurice of Orange. After 1702 it went to Prussia, and in 1866 its lower part came back to Prussia from Hanover.
britannica-1911-llangollen:
Llangollen is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a market town and summer resort in Denbighshire, North Wales. The town stands in the valley of the Dee, nine miles from Wrexham, and its urban district held 3,303 people in 1901. A bridge of four arches from the fourteenth century crosses the Dee here, counted one of the seven wonders of Wales.

The church of St Collen holds a monument to the Ladies of Llangollen, Lady Eleanor Butler and Sarah Ponsonby, whose house, Plas Newydd, is now a museum. Above the town stand the ruins of Castell Dinas Bran, a fort of unknown date. Two miles away lies Valle Crucis Abbey, a Cistercian house founded about 1200 and dissolved in 1535, with the broken shaft of Eliseg's Pillar beside it. Local work spans linen and wool cloth, coal mines, brewing, and slate quarrying.
britannica-1911-lucas-van-leyden:
Lucas van Leyden, born about 1494 and dead in 1533, was a Dutch painter and engraver. The 1911 Britannica entry gives his first lessons to his father Huig Jacobsz at Leiden. He then entered the workshop of Cornelis Engelbrechtszen in the same town for training. Skill in glass design, copper engraving, and oil and distemper painting came fast.

At age twelve he painted a Legend of Saint Hubert for a dozen florins in pay. At fourteen he finished a plate of Mahomet and the monk Sergius story. At fifteen came nine plates for a Passion series of prints. The entry opens the brief life of a prodigy of the northern schools.
britannica-1911-margaret-queen-of-denmar:
Margaret, queen of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, who lived from 1353 to 1412, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. She was the daughter of Valdemar the Fourth of Denmark. At ten years old she was married to King Haakon the Sixth of Norway. After her father died in 1375, her first act was to secure the choice of her young son Olaf as king of Denmark.

Olaf died in 1387, having also succeeded his father in Norway. The next year Margaret, who had ruled both lands in his name, was chosen regent of Norway and Denmark. The entry praises her statecraft in winning Schleswig back from the Holstein counts. She returned it as a fief on terms so strict that the Danish crown gained all the advantage.
britannica-1911-marten:
Martens are small meat eating mammals of the north, described in a 1911 Britannica entry on the group. The name first fit the pine marten and now fits all kin in the same genus. They live across the north lands of both the Old World and the New World. One kind is even found as far south as Java in Asia.

Most time is spent in trees in woods and rocky ground, where they hunt birds, eggs, and small beasts. The female builds a nest of moss and dry leaves in a hollow tree for her young. The entry also stresses the fur trade, since skins from cold lands in winter fetch the best price.
britannica-1911-martensen-hans-lassen:
Hans Lassen Martensen, a Danish church leader born in eighteen hundred and eight, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Flensburg, he studied in Copenhagen and was ordained in the Danish Church. He rose step by step at the great school there. He taught church thought, then took higher posts, and served as court preacher too.

In eighteen fifty four he was made bishop of Seeland. Three great minds shaped his study, yet he kept a free mind of his own. He built a view of faith with a bent toward deep inward thought. His books cover the right way to live, the core truths of the faith, and the rite of baptism. He also wrote a sketch of the life of Jakob Boehme. The entry marks a calm, deep voice in the northern church.
britannica-1911-mary-i-queen:
Mary the First, queen of England from 1516 to 1558 by the years of her life, is the subject of a long life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Henry the Eighth and Catherine of Aragon. The entry recalls her grim name, Bloody Mary, earned by the burnings of her reign. She was born at Greenwich in February 1516.

She was a bright child who played the virginals at four for guests. At nine she answered envoys from Flanders in Latin with poise. Her mother taught her Latin herself and sought advice on her schooling. Her fate, though, was ruled by state deals from the cradle. At two she was promised in marriage to the heir of France. At six she was pledged to her cousin the emperor instead.
britannica-1911-matilda-queen:
Matilda, queen of England and empress, born in eleven hundred and two, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Henry the First of England by his first wife, also named Matilda. In eleven hundred and nine she was promised to the emperor elect, Henry the Fifth. She was sent to Germany, but the rite waited till eleven fourteen.

Her husband died after eleven years, and left her with no child. Both her brothers were dead too. So her father called her home to be named heir to England and Normandy. The great council swore to her, but under strong push. Their dislike of a female ruler grew when she wed Geoffrey of Anjou. When the old king died, England and Normandy took his nephew Stephen in her place. The fight that came next fills the rest of the tale.
britannica-1911-meiningen:
Meiningen, a town of Germany, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is the capital of the duchy of Saxe-Meiningen. It sits in forests on the right bank of the Werra river. Rail lines put it south of Eisenach. Its people numbered 15,989 in 1905.

The town consists of an old town and several handsome suburbs. Much of the old town has been rebuilt since a fire in 1874. The chief building is the Elisabethenburg, the old ducal palace. It holds several collections and was built mainly about 1680. Part of it is much older. Other buildings named are the Henneberger Haus, with its antiquities. The town church has twin towers. It was built by the emperor Henry the Second in the eleventh century. The theatre of Meiningen enjoyed a European reputation for many years. Its actors and scenic effects were famed from 1875 to 1890.
britannica-1911-meiringen:
Meiringen, the chief village of the upper Aar valley in Switzerland, is described in a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the canton of Bern at near two thousand feet, on the right bank of the Aar. Just over three thousand people lived there, all German speaking Protestants. Fires gutted much of the village three times over the years.

An old parish church stands in the village, with the ruins of a medieval castle above it. In summer guests crowd in, since many routes meet there. Roads and passes lead to Interlaken, Lucerne, and Grindelwald, among other places. Falls such as the Reichenbach drop down the slopes nearby. The great gorge cut by the Aar through a limestone wall is also noted. Old grants that passed the valley from the emperor to Bern are traced.
britannica-1911-memmingen:
Memmingen is a town of Germany in the kingdom of Bavaria. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on the Ach, a stream of the Iller. It lies 35 miles south west of Augsburg on the line to Ulm. Its count in 1905 was 11,618 souls in the town. Walls still ring part of it, with old gates and fine houses.

The Gothic church of St Martin holds 67 carved choir stalls. A town hall from about 1580 adds grace to its streets. Trade spans yarn, calico, wool goods, and thread in bulk. A large trade runs in hops, grown thick in the fields round. Cattle, wool, leather, and grain fill out its market days.
britannica-1911-menhaden:
Menhaden is a fish of high economic worth in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Few fishes of the United States matter more in trade. It goes by many local names, mossbunker among the most common. The name itself is a Narragansett word meaning fertilizer.

Native peoples and white settlers alike used the fish as manure. It is kin to the European shad and pilchard. Immense shoals of menhaden draw near the coast from Maine to Florida. In cold weather the northern shoals retire to deep water or southern seas. The fish runs about twelve inches long on average. It is too bony and oily for the table, but serves as bait for cod and mackerel. A large fleet works the fishery. Shore factories press out its oil for tanning and other uses. The refuse left behind makes a valuable guano for the fields.
britannica-1911-mercier-louis-sebastien:
Louis Sebastien Mercier is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Mercier was a French dramatist and writer of many kinds, born in Paris in 1740. He began his career with heroic epistles in verse. He soon decided that Boileau and Racine had ruined the French language.

The true poet, he held, was the man who wrote in prose. His best-known work, The Year 2440, appeared in 1770. It imagined the Paris of a distant future. His Tableau de Paris, issued through the 1780s, pictured the city of his own day. Other works cover drama, a new dictionary of words, and a history of France. He attacked French tragedy as a hollow copy of antique custom in pompous verse. In its place he urged a more human comedy. The entry presents a restless critic who helped clear the ground for new French writing.
britannica-1911-methven:
Methven is a village and parish in Perthshire, Scotland. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes its church, castle, and battle sites. It lies west of Perth on the Caledonian rail line. The parish count in 1901 was about seventeen hundred.

One aisle is all that is left of a church founded in 1433. Methven Castle, in part from 1680, stands in a park east of the village. A famed oak there spans eighteen feet around its trunk. Robert Bruce lost a battle to an English earl nearby in 1306. A public school on the English model opened in Glenalmond in 1847. Gladstone helped found that school, the first of its kind in Scotland. Montrose won his first battle over the Covenanters close by in 1644.
britannica-1911-milford-haven:
Milford Haven, a market town and sea port in Pembrokeshire, Wales, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the north shore of the famed harbour of the same name. Its count in nineteen hundred and one was five thousand one hundred and two, with a near hamlet counted in. A branch rail line of the South Wales system ends here.

The town has a pier and strong dock space. That space holds a dry dock six hundred feet long. It is the hub of a rich and still growing fish trade. A shore walk gives a fine view of the broad Haven, with its towns and forts spread out. The town itself is of modern growth. A hamlet once stood in its place. One keen man laid out the new town in seventeen ninety, and it rose from his plan.
britannica-1911-minute-men:
Minute Men is a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the militia men of the American War of Independence. The name came from their pledge to turn out for service at a minute's notice when they were called.

In Massachusetts the minute men were enrolled under an act of the provincial congress passed on the twenty-third of November 1774. In Boston alone they numbered sixteen thousand before the war broke out. The article closes by noting that the Americans who fought in the opening action at Lexington were minute men. The whole entry runs only a few lines, yet it fixes the facts a reader needs: who these men were, when they were enrolled, and where they first fought.
britannica-1911-moor-hen:
Moor Hen is a bird entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a shy water bird of ponds and slow streams in England. The bird is about the size of a small hen in the yard. Its back shows dark olive brown that looks black from afar.

The entry marks white tail plumes that flash as the bird swims off. A scarlet shield on its brow glows most in the spring of the year. A red band on its leg adds a second spot of bright hue. The bird hides at the least alarm and trusts its stealth more than flight. Yet it can fly far and well when pressed to take the air.
britannica-1911-moravian-brethren:
The Moravian Brethren were a Christian body founded in the east of Bohemia. The 1911 Britannica entry starts just after the death of John Huss, when his followers split into two camps and war broke out. One camp won terms from the pope and became the state church, while the more stern camp was crushed in battle.

The entry then shows how some of the beaten side held fast to the plain teaching of Huss. They stressed pure lives, set up small free groups in Moravia and Bohemia, and found a leader in Peter of Chelcic. He read the Sermon on the Mount in a strict sense, spoke against war and oaths, and urged true believers to leave the state church.
britannica-1911-morgarten:
Morgarten names the pasture slopes above the south end of Lake Aegeri in the Swiss canton of Zug. A 1911 Britannica entry ties the name for all time to one November day in 1315. On that shore a small Swiss force beat a large Austrian army marching on Schwyz. That win laid the base of Swiss liberty, the entry states at the start.

As the lake has shrunk since then, the true battle site is in dispute. Most place it near the Haselmatt Chapel, where the official monument now stands. Others hold for Schwyz ground near the old tower and battle chapel at Schornen. Old accounts of the fight are gathered in a Schwyz society volume.
britannica-1911-mulhausen:
Muelhausen, in French Mulhouse, is a town of Germany in Upper Alsace, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its cotton town character. It stands on the river Ill and the Rhine-Rhone canal, about fifty-six miles south of Strassburg. The old town, ringed by arms of the Ill, has narrow, crooked streets.

The entry says the town's chief interest is the making of cotton goods, introduced in 1746 and since prospered in the hands of a few rich, intermarried families. Woollens, machinery, chemicals, and hardware also count. It praises the makers' care for their workers, above all the model workers' town of some 1,200 dwellings founded in 1853, with baths, wash houses, and a library.
britannica-1911-nagyszeben:
Nagyszeben, also called Hermannstadt or Sibiu, is a town of Hungary in this 1911 Britannica place entry. It heads Szeben County in Transylvania, south east of Kolozsvar by rail. It sits high in the rich vale of the Cibin River. Alps of Transylvania ring it on all sides in a fine sweep. Its folk count for nineteen hundred was twenty six thousand seventy seven.

Most of its folk were Saxon Germans, with Rumanians next in count. Old German style homes give parts of town a past age air. A Gothic church holds a font cast in fourteen thirty eight. A palace holds Dutch school art and a large book hoard. Schools span law, church, and army posts, with cloth and soap works as its trades.
britannica-1911-neuhaldensleben: Neuhaldensleben is a town of Germany, in the province of Prussian Saxony, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the river Ohre, eighteen miles north-west of Magdeburg by rail, with 10,421 people in 1905. The entry notes an Evangelical church, an old mounted statue of Henry the Lion, and a gymnasium. Its busy trades include majolica and terra-cotta wares, machines, gloves, beer, malt, cheese, and sugar, and large pig markets are held in the town.
britannica-1911-neunkirchen:
Neunkirchen is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a town of Germany in the Prussian Rhine province, on the Blies river. The entry gives its population in nineteen hundred five. Its people were split almost evenly between Protestants and Roman Catholics.

Most of the entry deals with work and trade in the town. A huge iron foundry employed thousands of hands and made vast amounts of pig iron each year. Boiler works, saw mills, soap works, and a brewery also stood there. Coal mines around the town raised large amounts of coal each year. Churches, schools, and a ruined castle are also noted.
britannica-1911-neuquen:
Neuquen, an inland territory of Argentina on the Chilean border, is covered in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The Colorado and Limay rivers bound it. Mendoza lies to the north, and Rio Negro to the east and south. It covers over forty two thousand square miles.

Much of the land is hilly, with rich well watered valleys and good woods. The east holds large bare plains with salt beds and thin scrub. Long dry spells rule that part, and few folk settle there. Guanacos and hares are found in plenty. The Neuquen river joins the Limay to form the Rio Negro. A famed lake, near fifty miles long, lies in the high valleys.
britannica-1911-nordlingen:
Nördlingen is a town in Bavaria, Germany, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a compact gazetteer entry. The town stands on the Eger river, forty miles north of Augsburg by rail. It held 8,512 people in 1905. It was once a free imperial town, with a territory of thirty five square miles.

Walls and towers still ring the town from those free days. The Evangelical church of St George is a Gothic building of the fifteenth century. It holds paintings by Hans Schäufelein, a native of the town, and a tower 290 feet high. The late Gothic town hall keeps a store of pictures and old objects. Local work centres on linen goods, soap, malt, and farm tools. A brisk trade runs in cattle, grain, and geese.
britannica-1911-odenkirchen: Odenkirchen, a town of Germany in the Prussian Rhine province, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies twenty one miles by rail south west of Dusseldorf, at a junction of rail lines. The entry gives it 16,808 people in 1905. It has a Roman Catholic church, a Protestant church, a synagogue, and several schools. Its chief trades are spinning, weaving, tanning, and dyeing. It became a town in 1856.
britannica-1911-olen:
Olen, a half legendary Greek bard, seer, and writer of hymns, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is said to have been the first priest of Apollo. His birthplace was given as Lycia or the land of the Hyperboreans, both lands dear to that god. A Delphian poetess credited him with bringing Apollo's cult and inventing epic metre.

Many hymns, dance songs, and oracles in his name were kept at Delos. In them he sang of Opis and Arge, two maidens said to found Apollo's cult on that island. A hymn to Eileithyia told of the birth of Apollo and Artemis. His said Lycian birth backs the view that Apollo's cult came to Greece from Asia. His poems, the entry notes, were of the sacred kind. The entry cites Herodotus, Pausanias, and Callimachus as sources for him.
britannica-1911-orangemen:
Orangemen are members of the Orange Society, a body of Irish Protestants. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica centers the group in Ulster, with branches elsewhere. Their name honors King William III, Prince of Orange. They meet in lodges in the manner of a secret society.

Their famed toast honors William for saving them from popery and slavery. Drums, flags, and the words no surrender mark their public days. July dates tied to the Boyne and Aughrim are kept each year. Keeping Protestant rule was the founding aim, the entry says. That political spirit still defined the group when the entry was written.
britannica-1911-oxygen:
Oxygen is a gas and one of the base stuffs of the world, with a set mark and weight in the science of stuffs. It may first have been made in seventeen twenty-seven, but that maker did not know it was new. Priestley first told of its traits in print in seventeen seventy-four.

Scheele found it on his own a year on, and Lavoisier gave it the name it still bears. The name hints that it makes sour stuffs when things burn in it. The gas fills a chief share of the air and most of the weight of water. Plants give it off as they grow.
britannica-1911-paten: Paten names the flat plate that holds the bread or wafer in the Eucharist rite. The 1911 Britannica note gives the word roots in French and Latin for a flat dish. Most patens are round in shape. One rare square form from the seventh century sits in a Paris coin and medal room. The plate may bear a cut head of the Saviour or a ring of lobes at its heart.
britannica-1911-pen:
Pen is the subject of a tool entry in the 1911 Britannica. A pen is a tool for writing with ink or fluid. The word comes from a Latin word for feather. French and German words for it mean feather too. Yet the first tools for writing were not quills. The first tool was a sharp point of metal or bone. It cut marks in wax laid on wood boards.

A hollow reed stalk was the true old form of pen. Joints of bamboo served the same use in some lands. Quill pens are first named in works from the 600s. Quills came chiefly from the wings of geese. In 1809 a machine was made to cut quills into nibs. That step made the loose nib in a holder well known. Gold pens and hard tip pens then came in train.
britannica-1911-phillips-stephen:
Stephen Phillips is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a British poet and dramatist. He was born in 1868 at Somertown near Oxford. His father was a cleric at Peterborough Cathedral.
