Zeger Bernhard van Espen was a Belgian canonist, born at Louvain on 9 July 1646 and dead at Amersfoort on 2 October 1728. He soon taught canon law at Louvain University, teaching only six weeks each summer vacation on a decretal chapter of his choice. He resigned even that chair to devote himself wholly to study. Consulted by all classes for his profound learning, his famous Jus Canonicum Universum still stands despite just criticisms.

Van Espen borrowed considerably from predecessors, notably Thomassin, yet he set forth ancient Church discipline lucidly, lit obscure questions, and showed Belgium's special law with precision, an authority Benedict XIV recognized. In the Jansenist conflicts he denied that the right-and-fact distinction mattered on Jansen's condemned propositions. His backing for Utrecht's Jansenist bishop Steenoven, ordained without approval, brought his suspension by Mechlin's bishop.
celtic-tales-told-to-the-children:
Louey Chisholm's Celtic Tales Told to the Children retells old Irish and Scottish stories for young readers, with pictures by Katharine Cameron. Chisholm drew on Joyce's Old Celtic Romances, Cameron's Reliquae Celticae, O'Grady's Pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne, Hyde's Three Sorrows, and Fiona Macleod's Laughter of Peterkin.

Friends warned Chisholm that children would dislike tales so sad, or would ask what they were meant to teach. She answers that she tells them for their sheer beauty, expecting children to enjoy them as hundreds of Irish and Scottish children already have. Readers who love old tales of heroes, sorrows and enchantment will find this collection tender and faithful.
characters-from-the-histories-memoirs-of:
David Nichol Smith edited an Oxford anthology in 1918, gathering character portraits from seventeenth-century histories and memoirs. His opening essay traces the form itself. Beginnings, literary models, Clarendon, and other character writers get one section each. Historical notes support the texts throughout.

Clarendon dominates the collection, as he dominated the form. His Buckingham, Charles I, Strafford, Falkland, Hampden, and Pym all appear. Some sitters get several portraits. Bacon is drawn four times, by Jonson, Wilson, Fuller, and Rawley. Cromwell appears five times, including accounts by Baxter and by Lucy Hutchinson's husband's circle. The same face changes with each writer's loyalty. That contrast is the book's quiet lesson in reading history.
christmas-outside-of-eden:
Coningsby Dawson, author of Carry On, published a short Christmas fable with Dodd, Mead in 1922, illustrated by Eugene Francis Savage. Robins tell the story, he claims, huddling under holly each Christmas Eve. Their Christmas tale reaches back before Christ. It begins just outside Eden, within sight of its gold-locked doors, and explains the first laugh ever heard.

God gave the expelled Man and Woman no time to pack. The animals gather, puzzled and kind, around the exiles. A baby arrives, and no beast can name the small crying thing. The elephant, tobogganing down a snowy path on his tail, hears it plainly: baa-by, it says, asking to be called baby. The Woman agrees they were stupids not to understand their own child.
creatures-that-once-were-men:
Maxim Gorky's Creatures That Once Were Men presents his sketches of Russia's down-and-outers, introduced here by G K Chesterton. Chesterton praises Russian fiction's grim, analytical modernity and its pity for the fallen. The title story surveys a dosshouse kept near an eating-house, ruled by the ex-captain Aristid Kuvalda.

Kuvalda and his fellow lodgers, former teachers, officers, and merchants now begging or cadging, argue philosophy between drinks while the merchant Petunikoff builds across the way. Gorky knew this world from his own years of wandering and wrote it without sentimentality or contempt. His sympathy for people society discarded made his early reputation in Russia and abroad.
defenders-of-democracy-contributions-fro:
The Gift Book Committee of the Militia of Mercy edited this wartime anthology, a gift book of contributions from writers and public men of the allied nations. The contents open with messages, not essays: President Woodrow Wilson first, then Admiral Sims, commanding the American naval forces in European waters, and General Pershing of the Expeditionary Force. Lord Northcliffe, chairman of the British War Mission, supplies the introduction.

Theodore Roosevelt contributes an essay on essential service, and William Dean Howells a letter. Hermann Hagedorn asks how he can serve, and the contributions of writers follow from Britain, France, and the other allies as well as America. The book belongs to the First World War's literature of solidarity, made to be given. Its editor is a charitable committee, and the volume wears its purpose openly.
dick-sand-a-captain-at-fifteen:
A boy captain at sea fills Jules Verne's tale in this translation, first published by George Munro of New York in 1878. The A. L. Burt Company of New York issued this copy. A note at the front says it renders Un capitaine de quinze ans of the same year.

Dick Sand sails on the brig-schooner Pilgrim. A wreck, the survivors of the Waldeck, and a whale in sight fill the early chapters. When the captain is lost, Dick takes command at fifteen. The tale's second half turns on the African slave trade. Verne pauses to describe that trade as it stood, with men used as money in Egypt and Bornou, on a traveller's word. Peril at sea and on shore drives the plot.
divers-women:
Tales of women in home and church life fill Divers Women, by Pansy and Mrs C. M. Livingston. George Routledge and Sons of London issued it in the Pansy Books line, whose long list stands at the front. Sunday Fractures heads the contents, in four chapters on people who went up to the temple.

Those chapters take up folk who forgot the fourth commandment, the ever-listening ear, and false friends. New Nerves, Huldy, Vida, and How a Woman Was Converted to Missions follow as tales. Mrs Lewis' Book fills a long place in two parts. In one scene Mrs Brown goes to a meeting with her heart stirred, while Mrs Williams stays home sewing frills and lace on a daughter's dress. The tales press duty with a warm hand.
doe-osti-1677418-two-phase-cooling-for-h:
Kevin Bennion of the National Laboratory of the Rockies led this cooperative final report, CRADA number CRD-15-00592, issued in February 2026. The partner work concerned a planar inverter, a compact power unit, being built for John Deere. Its packed parts run hot, so the project tested cooling based on a fluid that boils as it takes up heat.

Modeling guided designs for an evaporator and an air cooled condenser that need no pump. Printed prototype parts were then built and tested in the lab. Tests showed the evaporator could carry the heat load and keep silicon transistor junction temperatures within limits. Condenser tests could not be run, because fluid leaked through the printed condenser walls.
doe-osti-17019144-performance-year-2-tec:
Year two technical report for OPEN COG Grid, a Lawrence Livermore project on open models and data sets for power grids, came out in September 2026. J. Peng, Le Xie, and colleagues study how new loads, above all cryptocurrency mining, behave on the Texas grid. Open, shared test systems are the project backbone.

One study built a transformer based model to forecast mining load over time. A second asked when Bitcoin miners cut use, testing how strongly power prices drive that choice in Texas. Later sections convert a synthetic Texas system for simulation, and describe added tools: a training data generator, a miner forecaster, a demand response decoder, and open data sets.
doe-osti-17032781-enhancement-of-steady-:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NEAMS-26/2 details major upgrades to computer models of heat pipe microreactors. Yinbin Miao, Yan Cao, Yiqi Yu, and colleagues link neutron behavior, heat flow, material stress, and the power conversion loop in one multiphysics model. Both steady running and changing conditions, called transients, are covered.

Work includes a full stress model for the graphite block that holds the core, with dose effects on graphite traits over the design life. A heat pipe model now treats trapped non condensable gas, which can hurt pipe performance. A secondary loop model was built alone, then coupled to the full core model. The KRUSTY test reactor serves as an early check case.
doe-osti-17120801-completeness-and-discr:
Roxana Bujack, Tomas Karella, Marco Cerezo, and Los Alamos colleagues settle a long standing conjecture about pattern fingerprints, in a report issued 1 October 2026. Moment invariants are numbers computed from a shape that stay fixed when the shape rotates, which makes them handy for recognition. Tensor contractions, one systematic way to build them, were long claimed to give a complete set.

Using classical invariant theory, the team proves the claim for three dimensional scalar moments. Every rotation and reflection invariant polynomial is a finite blend of complete contractions. A second result covers telling shapes apart: if two shapes share all contraction values, one common rotation or reflection maps one moment set onto the other. Choosing a short, independent list from the full family remains open work.
doe-osti-17197492-crada-nfe-22-09351-fin:
Kashif Nawaz, Joseph Rendall, and Jian Sun of Oak Ridge close out a CRADA on next generation refrigerants for heat pump water heaters, in a final report dated March 2026. Heat pump water heaters save energy over resistance models, but their working fluid matters for climate rules. New refrigerants with lower warming impact are replacing older ones, and each swap changes how the heater performs.

Phase II of the technical collaboration ran tests and analysis on candidate fluids in heater systems. Chapters state the project objectives and the benefit to the Energy Department Building Technologies Office. A technical discussion then covers the work in detail: setups, measures, and results. The report certifies the final state of the agreement, numbered NFE-22-09351.
doe-osti-2476958-brochure-on-the-2024-as:
A brochure with DOI 10.2172/2476958 sums up the 2024 Workshop on Energy-Efficient Computing for Science, held September 9 to 11, 2024. The Department of Energy's ASCR program convened the meeting, and Jeffrey Vetter, Rob Ross, Brad Aimone, and colleagues wrote the summary. Side workshops on analog and neuromorphic computing ran at the same time.

Those taking part warned that the power computing uses could soon cap what science can do, unless machines waste far less of it. Over three days they settled on five priority research directions. The list covers co-designing hardware for real workloads, new algorithms and software, and cheaper ways to move and store data. Each direction comes with key questions for the field. The brochure is the short public version of what the workshop found.
doe-osti-2572006-fundamental-studies-of-:
Final technical report DE-SC0021087, by Robert A. Fleming of Arkansas State University, tackles the dirt that coats solar panels. Dust and other particles settle on a module's cover glass and block light, and losses can pass 35 percent in bad cases. Scrubbing the glass clean costs water and labor. Anti-soiling coatings promise relief, but how they work at the surface level was poorly understood.

An instrumented chamber built for the project soils samples in a controlled way, using a library of representative dusts. Bare glass, standard antireflective coatings, and a commercial anti-soiling coating were compared as deposits formed and hardened into cemented layers. X-ray spectroscopy tracked the surface chemistry through the process. First-principles density functional calculations then modeled those spectra, pinning down which chemical changes the measurements were really showing.
doe-osti-2584203-v-int-automated-vulnera:
Final technical report for agreement DE-CR0000003, submitted July 21, 2025, presents V-INT, a vulnerability intelligence toolset for energy utilities. The University of Arkansas led, under Qinghua Li, with the University of Arkansas at Little Rock and two companies, Network Perception and Bastazo. The project ran September 2020 to September 2024. Its insight is simple: a vulnerability behind a firewall rule that blocks it is not an emergency, and operators drown in alerts that ignore that fact.

V-INT parses an organization's firewall policies into live network connectivity, matches asset inventories against known vulnerabilities through Bastazo's Spartan, and computes which flaws are actually reachable by an attacker. It then maps vulnerability-driven attack paths so operators can cut them deliberately. The toolset was integrated into both companies' commercial products, NP-View and Spartan. Five conference papers, talks, and a conference tutorial carried the results to the utility industry.
doe-osti-2584397-hybrid-powered-command-:
User guide NREL/TP-5R00-95154, by Bonnie Powell, walks fire managers through a cost-benefit calculator for hybrid powered command trailers. Wildfire incident command posts run on portable diesel: heating, cooling, cooking, showers, lights, and the computers that run the response. Rooftop solar and batteries can shave that fuel burn, if the math works for a camp's size and season. The tool exists to run that math before anyone buys hardware.

Two worked scenarios anchor the guide. One outfits command trailers with rooftop solar in a hybrid setup. The other uses a ground-mounted solar array. Inputs, calculations, and outputs are shown figure by figure, ending in estimated fuel cost savings. Fire camps are temporary cities, and their generators run around the clock. A guide that helps cut diesel use without risking the operation is a small, practical piece of decarbonization.
doe-osti-2586805-closeout-report-for-exp:
Charles Merrill Jenkins of the University of South Alabama wrote this closeout report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0022176. His group took part in Mu2e, an experiment searching for a muon converting directly into an electron, a process the standard model forbids. The physics department at South Alabama is small and teaching-heavy, with no graduate program, which shapes what the report can claim.

Jenkins attended collaboration meetings on the cosmic ray veto and the trigger and data acquisition systems. His technical work added the calorimeter system to a Phoebus-based alarm display, solving a channel-count problem by installing a newer Phoebus build. He also began a cosmic ray background study for the muon-to-positron channel using CORSIKA data and ROOT scripts. The report is candid about limits: late award notice and frozen funds kept the undergraduates he had lined up from being hired.
doe-osti-2589591-host-design-for-carbon-:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-11673R, by Jessica Rimsza, Brianna Addison, Nathan Bays, and co-authors, designs hosts for a new kind of carbon capture liquid. Porous liquids mix free-flowing liquid with cage-like molecules that hold empty pores. Carbon dioxide can enter those pores, be carried along, and later be released so the liquid can be reused.

Work focused on cages called porous organic cages and how their inner linkers behave. Models showed a hydroxide group on the linker can swing freely, which lets it interact directly with carbon dioxide at the pore window. Dissolving the cages may also free hydroxides tied up inside the solid, raising gas uptake over the solid form. The findings name a concrete design lever: linker motion at the window drives capture.
doe-osti-3000546-2024-aser-summary-annua:
Aaliya Casados, Alison Livesay, Leslie Hansen and a large Los Alamos team present the public summary of the laboratory's 2024 Annual Site Environmental Report. The report is LA-UR-25-29486 Revision 2, issued 9 December 2025. Los Alamos must account each year for its footprint on the land, air and water around it. This plain-language volume distils the full technical report for neighbours and the general reader.

Chapters track radiological monitoring, where public exposure from site operations has averaged about 1 millirem per year over the past decade, far under the 100-millirem public limit. Air emissions face a tighter 10-millirem cap. Other chapters cover groundwater protection, watershed quality with updated hundred-year floodplain lines, and ecosystem health. Wildlife sampling even checked PFAS chemicals in elk, deer and a mountain lion; most compounds went undetected, and found levels matched unpolluted sites in the literature.
doe-osti-3001105-safety-hazards-of-batte:
Bryan Wofford, Melissa Louie, Marina Miletic and Brian Ehrhart of Sandia examine a compound hazard in SAND2025-13581, printed October 2025: what happens when lithium battery storage sits next to hydrogen storage. Each technology fails dangerously alone. A battery in thermal runaway vents hot, flammable gas and can reach extreme temperatures; a hydrogen tank nearby carries a pressure relief device that heat can trigger, releasing its own fuel.

Chapters survey hydrogen tank designs and release behaviour, then battery types and their prevalence in storage installations. Incident and failure reviews ground the analysis, including how runaway temperatures interact with relief device opening. The point is spacing and layout: two clean-energy stores placed side by side can turn one failure into a chain. The report gives engineers and code writers a shared evidence base for judging safe separations and mitigations before such paired systems spread further.
doe-osti-3002160-impact-of-time-dependen:
Anthony Birri, K. C. Goetz, Jianwei Hu, N. Dianne Bull Ezell, and co-authors study reactor monitoring in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4157, dated September 2025. The task is core power synthesis: rebuilding a full picture of reactor power from a limited set of in-core sensors. Online control systems depend on that picture being right.

Using a model pressurized water reactor core, the team tested how time-changing physics affects the rebuild. Sensor response shifts as fuel burns, and the starting guess of the power pattern comes from neutron models. Ignoring burnup in that guess caused large errors in the synthesized power pattern. Fresh, once-burned, and twice-burned fuel bundles shift local power in ways the guess must track. The finding guides control design for operating reactors.
doe-osti-3004172-source-attribution-of-m:
Xiao-Ming Hu and Qingyu Wang of the University of Oklahoma report a field campaign in ARM report DOE/SC-ARM-25-027, dated November 2025. The campaign hunted the sources of methane spikes recorded at the Southern Great Plains observatory in Oklahoma. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and the region hosts oil and gas operations, farms, and wetlands that can all release it.

The team combined observations with plume simulations, building on their study of methane plumes during the morning boundary layer transition. Nighttime stability in the region traps emissions near the ground and amplifies the recorded peaks. Attributing a spike to a source type matters because mitigation differs by source. The short campaign report records the approach and findings for the ARM archive, where later researchers can pull the underlying data with full context.
doe-osti-3004256-nfe-24-10417-durability:
Praveen Cheekatamarla, Muneeshwaran Murugan, and Aly Elhefny deliver the final CRADA report for project NFE-24-10417, ORNL/TM-2025/4296, dated November 2025. The project aimed to keep vapor compression systems, the machines behind air conditioning and refrigeration, efficient over their whole service life. Dirty coils are a slow drain: dust buildup raises energy use year after year.

The team tested a centrifugal pre-cleaner that strips dust from incoming air before it reaches the coil. With the pre-cleaner, dust deposition fell and energy use ran lower than a dust-fouled baseline. Cooling towers fit the device best. In small residential systems, though, the pre-cleaner restricted airflow enough to offset gains. The authors recommend reshaping it to cut pressure loss, then trialing it in larger commercial systems.
doe-osti-3004272-performance-measurement:
Christopher Brumgard and Rick Mohr benchmark a storage system in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4264, dated October 2025. The system is DAOS, an object storage platform built for supercomputing centers. Programs can reach DAOS through several interfaces, and the wrong choice can waste a leadership machine's time. The tests ran on Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility resources.

Standard tools did the measuring: fio and ior for throughput, and the IO500 benchmark suite for ranking-style loads. The report compares the interfaces head to head so application teams can pick deliberately instead of by habit. Storage performance is invisible when it works and painful when it does not, especially at exascale. A short, factual benchmark record like this one becomes the reference the next team reaches for before a big run.
doe-osti-3007245-a-systems-framework-to-:
Final report for DOE award DE-SC0022987, from a Michigan State University team led by Erich Grotewold with Patrick Edger, covers three years of work on camelina, an oilseed crop suited to biofuel. The reporting period ran from September 2022 to August 2025. Camelina needs little fertilizer and shrugs off many stresses, but its modest seed yield holds back wider planting.

The team sequenced the genome of the widely used Suneson variety and built the first camelina pangenome, a combined view of genes across varieties. They also assembled a full collection of the crop's transcription factor genes and upgraded the CamRegBase knowledgebase with network tools. Drought experiments paired open-chromatin maps with gene activity data to pin down the switches that answer water stress. New promoters that switch genes on in chosen tissues came out of those regulatory maps.
doe-osti-3012790-qcd-theory-and-transver:
Ted C. Rogers of Old Dominion University wrote this final technical report for DOE grant DE-SC0018106 on QCD theory and transverse momentum dependent physics. Quantum chromodynamics describes the strong force binding quarks and gluons inside protons and neutrons. Transverse momentum dependent distributions, called TMDs, map how those particles move sideways inside a nucleon, along with their spin links and energy behavior.

Rogers worked on factorization theory, the rules for separating the parts of a collision calculation cleanly. His group assembled a hadron structure oriented TMD program across several published papers. It runs TMD evolution in the standard Collins-Soper-Sterman style while folding in limits from concrete models, effective field theories, and lattice QCD calculations. The report gathers the project's publications and tools for other theorists.
doe-osti-3012792-melter-tests-to-define-:
Keith S. Matlack and five colleagues at the Vitreous State Laboratory of The Catholic University of America wrote this report, VSL-14R3280-1, dated December 2014, for the Department of Energy Office of River Protection. The work supports Hanford's Waste Treatment Plant, which will melt low-activity waste, called LAW, into glass. Phase 2 tests worked out safe halide levels, chiefly chlorine and fluorine, in two waste streams.

The team ran crucible melts and continuously fed melter tests on the DM10 and DM100 systems. They checked how much halide the glass could hold and tested additives, including a vanadium oxide formulation, meant to suppress unwanted secondary phases in high-chlorine waste. The combined results feed the glass property models and the formulation algorithm used to set LAW concentration limits.
doe-osti-3013754-crcns21-computational-m:
Nitish Thakor of Johns Hopkins University led this final technical report for award DE-SC0022150, a US-German collaboration with the Technical University of Munich on multisensory integration in the upper limb. The project asked how the brain merges touch, force, and vision, with two payoffs in view: better prosthetic arms for amputees and better senses for humanoid robots. Human data in the report are de-identified under Johns Hopkins IRB oversight.

Amputee volunteers received electrical stimulation on their residual limbs while moving phantom hands, with EEG recording. Sensory feedback lit up sensorimotor and multisensory brain regions, which communicated dynamically during stimulation. Intact-limb studies added virtual reality motor training. The Munich team combined tactile and thermal sensing into one robot skin system.
doe-osti-3015066-state-technical-assista: Energy burden by utility territory in New Mexico is the subject of a short January 2025 slide brief by Vimont and Lopp. The state conservation division found the federal LEAD Tool's utility boundaries too imprecise for per-utility figures. The laboratory matched proprietary utility boundary files against census tracts, recording each tract's overlap share, then built a Python script that reruns the LEAD method on any boundary set. As a brief slide summary of a tool handover, it gives the problem and script design rather than final burden figures.
doe-osti-3017347-a-comprehensive-greenho:
Allegra Mayer of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this abbreviated final report, LLNL-TR-2012116, in February 2026, for project 24-LW-076. It gives a comprehensive greenhouse gas assessment of biomass-based carbon dioxide removal and storage, called BiCRS. BiCRS routes turn leftover biomass into forms that lock its carbon away, while capturing a high share of the carbon the biomass contains.

The assessment follows emissions across the full chain, not just the capture step. One finding is sharply practical: char amendments to soil behave differently by soil acidity. Nitrous oxide emissions from amendments run higher in higher-pH soils. Some chars cut nitrous oxide in low-pH soil compared with controls, yet methane is emitted from char in low-pH soil and consumed in other cases. Anyone claiming carbon removal credits from biomass gets a warning here: the soil decides part of the balance.
doe-osti-3018761-teleseismic-network-ass:
Stephen L Heck of Sandia applied a graph neural network to teleseismic association in SAND2026-16778, printed February 2026. The system is GENIE. Distant earthquakes and explosions send phases to stations worldwide, and someone must decide which detections belong to which event. GENIE treats detections as graph nodes. Its input features lean on backprojection: detections are projected onto trial source spots, and the stacks that build up reveal real events. Node data and the backprojection equations get full sections.

Training data were generated by computer, with metrics describing each dataset's difficulty. Worked examples show stacks at 32 stations with 81 arrivals, some associating 21 detections and some only 2. Results and a model comparison appendix close the report. The work was supported by NNSA defense nuclear nonproliferation research. For verification seismology, a learned associator that explains itself through backprojection stacks is a practical step forward.
doe-osti-3019926-impact-of-time-dependen:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4435 (Rev. 1), by Anthony Birri, K. C. Goetz, and Jianwei Hu, examines how fuel burnup and sensor wear change the accuracy of core power synthesis in a pressurized water reactor. Power synthesis rebuilds the core's power map from prior knowledge plus signals from in-core neutron detectors. The study covers standard low-enriched uranium fuel at 3 to 5 percent enrichment and higher-assay LEU+ fuel at 5 to 8 percent.

The team modeled a representative reactor core with Polaris and PARCS, used MCNP6 for detector response functions, and tracked isotope changes in detector emitters with ORIGEN. Rhodium and vanadium self-powered neutron detectors were compared as they degraded over time. A custom code then ran the point-based iterative synthesis method on the combined data. The results show how much trust operators can place in synthesized power maps late in a fuel cycle.
doe-osti-3020394-port-gamble-s-klallam-t:
A strategic energy plan prepared by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and Spark Northwest staff for the Port Gamble S'Klallam Tribe, dated December 2025, addresses an exposed position. The reservation sits at the end of the line in Kitsap County, Washington, reached by a single road and served by two power lines. Storms can cut power for days, and restoration reaches the Tribe last.

The Tribe's energy vision centers on resilience, self-reliance, and local capacity. One guiding target is keeping critical infrastructure running for seven days through a severe outage or natural hazard. The plan assesses energy infrastructure, efficiency options, and electric vehicles, with grant programs noted for vehicle and charging costs. It sequences renewable generation, battery storage, and workforce development so the community can sustain itself when the road or the lines go down.
doe-osti-3020895-making-an-s1g-self-pres:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory CRADA final report ORNL/TM-2026-4434, by Peter Wang and six co-authors, works with Smith-Root, Inc. on greener hardware for environmental DNA sampling. Crews filter river and lake water to capture DNA that fish and other species shed, detecting rare and endangered animals without catching them. Smith-Root's self-preserving filters dry the captured DNA automatically, saving field time and cutting contamination risk, but each filter is single-use plastic.

The project screened bio-based polymers and composites to replace the filter housings. Eight candidate materials were investigated, three for the top housing and five for the bottom. Thermal testing showed the bottom-housing options matched or beat the incumbent's heat stability. Two materials were identified for future development. The report weighs ease of processing and biodegradability alongside performance, aiming to keep the sampling advance without its growing waste stream.
doe-osti-3021818-advance-perovskite-sola:
University of Arizona final technical report for DOE Solar Energy Technologies Office award DE-EE0010238, led by Erin L. Ratcliff and submitted December 18, 2025, covers an October 2022 to March 2024 project on perovskite solar cell manufacturing. Perovskite layers are printed at high speed in roll-to-roll production, and defects formed during coating decide which cells perform and which fail. The project built a disposable, non-destructive electrochemical sensor to catch those defects in line.

Defect concentrations below 10^17 per cubic centimeter sit under the detection limits of many spectroscopic and electrical methods. The sensor uses redox probe chemistry, including 1,4-benzoquinone, to count donor defects in perovskite films such as a cesium-formamidinium composition. Measurements tracked a diffusion coefficient near 2.05 × 10^-9 square centimeters per second under stated scan conditions. The prototype targets quality, stability, and durability checks for an industry aiming at three-cent electricity by 2030.
doe-osti-3021935-a-comprehensive-greenho:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory full technical report LLNL-TR-2012095, by Allegra Mayer, dated March 2026, fills a gap in the accounting for biomass-based carbon removal. These technologies convert plant material into stored carbon. But their life cycle assessments have ignored what happens when byproducts like char and ash are spread on soils. The soils themselves can release or absorb carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide. The project, numbered 24-LW-076, measured those fluxes directly.

Incubation experiments amended two California grassland soils, from Hopland at pH 5.7 and Livermore at pH 9.0, with char and ash byproducts, using five replicates for most treatments. The team tracked soil carbon changes, microbial respiration, and methane and nitrous oxide fluxes against unamended controls. The resulting parameter ranges give life cycle analysts an empirical soil amendment component where previously there was a blank.
doe-osti-3024742-evaluation-of-ai-enable:
Sonali Sinha Roy, Harleen Kaur Sandhu, Angelica M Petrovic, Peter Anton Suyderhoud, Jake Rymer, and Kevin Marshall O'Rear of Idaho National Laboratory. They evaluate an AI-enabled version of documented safety analysis in INL/RPT-25-87369, Revision 1, dated March 2026. Nuclear facilities live inside huge safety documents, and drafting them is slow, expert work. The study asks how generative AI and linked data can speed the writing without loosening control.

The design grows in stages. Document sections pull facts from an external database through query syntax written into the section prompts. Knowledge graphs built in DeepLynx Nexus, using set ontologies and formal meanings, give the retrieval system better context. The third and most advanced stage generates the preliminary documented safety analysis through digital thread integration, connecting the Microsoft generative AI permitting accelerator.
doe-osti-3027549-update-on-model-specifi:
Jin Tan and Ningchao Gao of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory and Zerui Dong of OPAL-RT presented these slides on May 9, 2025, to a WECC model validation group. Their topic is model specifications for ternary pumped storage, a design whose separate turbine and pump, plus a hydraulic short-circuit mode, can generate and pump at the same time. Grid modelers need standard models before such plants join planning studies.

Background slides set the stakes. Interest in pumped storage revived in the late 2000s, and by the end of 2021 roughly 100 projects sat in the FERC development pipeline, most still at the preliminary permit stage. New projects are expected to sell capacity and grid services such as frequency regulation, not just peak energy. Block diagrams then lay out the hydraulic short-circuit mode, with governor, gate limits, and power distribution functions spelled out.
doe-osti-3029268-report-on-preliminary-d:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/LTR-2025/4157, by Stephen Taller, Drew Johnson, Caleb Massey, Yanli Wang, and six colleagues, lays out a test plan dated December 2025. The plan covers neutron irradiation of Alloy 709, a steel backed as the next advanced reactor structural alloy. Samples will go into two research reactors, the Advanced Test Reactor and the High Flux Isotope Reactor. The work supports the AMMT program and runs four years.

Hotter advanced reactors promise better efficiency but stress their materials more, so design data are needed. The campaign will build creep knockdown factors for the base alloy and its welds. Capsules cover doses of 1, 5, 2, and 10 displacements per atom at set heat levels from 400 to 800 degrees Celsius, across several heats and product forms.
doe-osti-3030361-report-on-preliminary-d: A709 got irradiation-planned again, and this DOE report details ATR and HFIR. The pages detail the preliminary findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The plan was experimental. The data were nuclear. The again were planned. The HFIR were ATR.
doe-osti-3362569-sparc-plans-for-a-new-c:
Nicolas E. Woolstenhulme, Mark R. Cole, Nicolas P. Martin, and colleagues from four laboratories plus the Nuclear Regulatory Commission plan a new critical experiment facility in report INL/RPT-25-84855, dated July 2025. Critical assemblies run a chain reaction at near-zero power to test nuclear physics models. Few such machines remain worldwide, and the survivors are small. Demand is back, driven by high-assay low-enriched uranium fuel for new reactors, which needs safety benchmarks at mid-range neutron energies.

The design, called SPARC, centers on a horizontal split table: two halves that slide together to reach criticality. A bigger future home, called LOTUS, will not be ready until well into the 2030s, so the table is built to move. Keeping it out of LOTUS near term also dodges that site heavier security costs for uranium fuel work.
doe-osti-3367412-3d-cloud-aerosol-precip:
ARM field campaign report DOE/SC-ARM-26-014 covers the 3D-CAPE-k cloud experiment at kennaook Cape Grim in Tasmania, June 2026. Alain Protat of Australia's Bureau of Meteorology led it, with Luis Ackermann, Robyn Schofield of Melbourne, and Gerald Mace of Utah. Cape Grim samples some of Earth's cleanest air, making it a baseline site for cloud and aerosol physics. The campaign adds scanning instruments to see clouds in three dimensions.

Planned deployments included the BASTA bistatic W-band radar, a scanning mini micropulse lidar, a vertically pointing depolarization lidar, and a multi-axis spectrometer, alongside the second ARM Mobile Facility. Scanning geometry multiplies chances to exactly collocate with the EarthCARE satellite's overpasses, complementing statistics from fixed instruments. The report records what was deployed and learned.
doe-osti-3375662-spartan-and-improve-com:
Atmospheric Radiation Measurement report DOE/SC-ARM-26-022, dated June 2026, is the interim account of SPICE, a side-by-side test of two air monitoring networks. Sandra M. L. Salazar, Connor Flynn, and Emily West of the University of Oklahoma wrote it. SPICE stands for the SPARTAN and IMPROVE Comparison Experiment. IMPROVE is the EPA network that tracks haze and fine particle mass at protected sites. SPARTAN is a global cousin built for remote, semi-autonomous posts.

The Oklahoma team runs a SPARTAN station of its own. To trust its readings, they parked it at the ARM Southern Great Plains site. An EPA-certified IMPROVE station, coded SOGP, sits at the same site. The two now sample the same air, day after day. Health stakes drive the care: fine particle harm turns on size, makeup, and how long people breathe them. This interim report logs the setup and early checks.
doe-osti-3377214-project-phase-1-report-:
Report NLR/TP-5700-100780, dated June 2026, closes phase one of a plan to cool data centers with stored cold. Josh McTigue of the National Laboratory of the Rockies heads a team from Berkeley Lab, the University of Chicago, Princeton, and the Energy Department's geothermal office. Data centers face cooling peaks on the hottest hours. Cold underground thermal energy storage banks chill in cheap hours and spends it at the peak. It asks how much peak load and cost the shift can cut.

Models pair the storage with growing data halls. Indoors, cold can idle the chillers at peak hours, freeing floor space. Outdoors, it trims dry coolers needed for extreme heat. Even so, space saved does not stop halls from crowding out IT gear. Under twelve percent grid growth, IT floor share falls to 54.4 percent by 2029 in a case. Phase one ends with those bounds for the design phase.
doe-osti-3377898-battery-energy-storage-:
Barbara O'Neill of the National Laboratory of the Rockies surveys licensing and permitting for battery energy storage systems in slides dated April 2026. Requirements differ by country and jurisdiction. But the deck groups them into broad categories most projects meet. These include safety standards such as fire prevention, siting and construction codes, and environmental conditions. They also include interconnection approval and a clear statement of the battery's role on the grid.

Environmental conditions can include a decommissioning plan, a post-life recycling plan, and water runoff permits. A case study from São Paulo, Brazil, shows a different payment logic. The regulator ANEEL invested 27 million dollars in the country's largest battery project. It was built because peak demand in Registro outgrew the transmission capacity. The system is paid five million dollars a year as a transmission asset.
doe-osti-3390984-evaluation-of-ai-enable:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-26-90824, dated March 2026, evaluates an AI-enabled route to the Documented Safety Analysis, the safety case every nuclear facility must write and defend. Nine authors are printed, led by Sonali Sinha Roy, Harleen Kaur Sandhu, and Nancy Gomez Dominguez. The work sits in the National Reactor Innovation Center's digital ecosystem work on generative AI for nuclear safety basis documents.

The case study uses one purpose-built tool, Microsoft's Generative AI for Permitting Solution Accelerator, to generate structured safety documentation from multiple sources. The verdict is measured: AI output needs improvement, but it acts as a force multiplier on large documents. The initial evaluation indicated the framework could cut DSA generation time by about half while producing an acceptable first draft for experts to improve and finalize. Systematic validation is urged before wider use.
doe-osti-3393364-cyber-informed-engineer:
Virginia Wright of Idaho National Laboratory and Venkatesh Venkataramanan of the National Laboratory of the Rockies present the Cyber-Informed Engineering Power Generation Guide in session slides dated May 7, 2026. The program is sponsored by the Department of Energy's Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response. The guide helps engineers understand cyber-induced effects. It helps them build fixes into design and operations.

The guide translates the general Cyber-Informed Engineering guide to eight generation technologies. They are natural gas, hydropower, nuclear, wind, solar, bioenergy, geothermal, and hydrogen. For each, key cyber challenges are named, and use cases suggest mitigations. The key takeaway is a division of labor. Security staff spot threats but cannot design engineering fixes. Engineers design fixes but may miss cyber risks. Consequence analysis therefore needs both. A Seattle City Light capstone on the Cedar Falls hydro project shows the method applied.
doe-osti-3401691-preliminary-assessment-:
Slides by Xiangkun Li of the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated July 2026, assess clean energy options for the Western State Bank Expo Center. Ford County asked for the study through an Expert Match technical help project. Solar panels, wind, and battery storage were all weighed for one public building.

Charts track hourly load, on-site generation, and power sent back to the grid. One finding puts average peak load cuts at 9.6 kilowatts per month for the option studied. Cost charts show how panel prices change the best system size. County staff can use the results to pick a system that saves money and rides through outages.
doe-osti-3409821-energy-transfer-in-lant:
Kenneth N. Raymond of the University of California, Berkeley led a Basic Energy Sciences project on energy transfer in lanthanide light-emitting complexes, under award DE-SC0016961. Juliana da Silva Padilha shares the evidence record. The grant ran from January 1, 2017 to October 31, 2023. The short hosted text supports a brief note.

Work focused on terbium and europium complexes and how ligands pass energy to the metal. X-ray tests at the Stanford lightsource showed edge shifts tied to that transfer. One complex showed a rise time of about 1.6 nanoseconds. Such timing facts guide design of brighter probes and sensors.
doe-osti-3409945-safeguarding-amines-fro:
Gary T. Rochelle of the University of Texas at Austin reports on guarding amine solvents from oxidation, under agreement DE-FE0031861, dated August 15, 2026. Amines such as piperazine scrub carbon dioxide from gas streams. Oxygen slowly breaks them down, raising cost and waste.

Lab studies and pilot plant work anchor the report. A baseline process called PZAS in the text sets the test frame. Past pilot work on the advanced stripper with piperazine feeds the energy analysis. Plant operators learn which guard steps slow solvent loss. Longer solvent life means cheaper capture and fewer chemical purchases.
doe-osti-3484653-strategic-biodeterrence:
Los Alamos document LA-UR-26-27612, by Ethan Romero-Severson and issued August 24, 2026, asks what biological deterrence can borrow from the nuclear age. Biological weapons differ from nuclear ones in ways that matter, the author argues. The paper builds a strategy frame from those gaps.

About 1,400 human pathogens are known, the text notes, with hundreds more for livestock and plants. One case covers a cult that tried seven biological attacks from 1990 to 1995 and failed each time. State programs can also stay secret despite bans. Deterrence built for missiles fits this threat poorly, the paper concludes.
doe-osti-3628757-aerodynamic-particle-si:
Brookhaven's instrument handbook DOE/SC-ARM-TR-343, dated August 2026, covers the Aerodynamic Particle Sizer. Ashish Singh, Delano Campos, and Tamanna Subba, all at Brookhaven, are the printed authors. The sizer sorts airborne particles by size as they pass through the device. It serves the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement sites that track aerosols in the air.

Early sections give the technical details and the measurement theory behind the readings. Later sections describe the data files, what each field means, and where to find them in ARM Data Discovery. Quality checks run at two levels. Lab staff test the unit on the bench, and field staff run daily checks on lights, flow, and pressure. Weekly checks confirm flow baselines and noise levels stay sound. A maintenance plan and history section close the book, which operators use to keep the data trustworthy.
doe-osti-3818600-market-analysis-of-tech:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-6A20-97680, dated September 2026, tracks technology trends in building envelope retrofits. Katie McMahon and Jack Mayernik are the printed authors. Sealing and insulating the shells of standing buildings cuts energy waste, yet uptake lags. The analysis maps the market, then sorts the drags on growth into technical, social, workforce, and money blocks.

One yardstick follows how fast each technology climbs the readiness scale. Smart windows took about twenty years to climb six steps. An early shop fitting then failed within two years, a warning that lab promise can fade in the field. Machine-applied envelope sealant sits far earlier on the same scale. Home and business retrofit costs are weighed apart. The report ends with an outlook for market, technology, and labour.
doe-osti-3883785-tex-chlorine-for-terrap:
Completion report for the TEX-Chlorine project, dated September 2026, records inspection of new salt plate components built for TerraPower work. Christopher Fitzgerald and Eric Aboud are the printed authors. The parts support a criticality experiment assembly catalogued as IER 630. Twenty-two lower encapsulation halves were procured for half-inch salt plates in a polyethylene-reflected setup. The aluminum shells, about fifteen inches across, pair with matching upper halves.

Los Alamos staff measured the hardware with standard gauges after delivery, checking each plate three times around its rim. Tables pair every specified dimension with its measured result, flagging the misses. Time ran short for the solid salt plates, so the fabricator's verified numbers stand in for those. The report is mostly those tables: page after page of serial numbers and readings. Its purpose is acceptance evidence, showing which parts conform before assembly.
doe-osti-3989582-preliminary-assessment-:
Xiangkun Li, Jordan Burns, and Dana-Marie Thomas of the National Laboratory of the Rockies give the small town of Greenville, Florida a first look at local energy choices. Their May 2026 report came through the Energy to Communities Expert Match program, which lends lab help to towns at no cost for about three months.

The study weighs on-site solar, wind, and storage for key town sites, among them the grocery store and the elementary school. For the school, one run found a solar array sized to match the site's full yearly use was the cheapest path, though the town could build in smaller steps. Tax credits change the math, so cases with and without them sit side by side. Town leaders get a clear first map of costs and gains before they commit to a full design.
dr-scudder-s-tales-for-little-readers-ab:
John Scudder, a missionary doctor, wrote simple tales for children about the peoples he called the heathen, in a book dated 1849. He says the Hindu parts rest on Duff, Dubois, and other writers. His preface is a plea: Christian parents should train their children to give money, prayer, and even their own lives to mission work.

Chapters march through Hindu dress, houses, food, marriage, funerals, caste, temples, and festivals. Strong pages describe the goddess Kali, with her red eyes, bloody girdle of hands, and dead bodies for earrings. Serpent worship, the Ganges, and self-tortures get chapters of their own. The book taught American and British children a stern, pitying view of India, and it shows how mission schools framed the wider world for young minds at home.
driven-back-to-eden:
E. P. Roe's Driven Back to Eden, prefaced from Cornwall-on-the-Hudson in August 1885, was written expressly for young people. Roe confesses he had never before attempted it, and that the tale appeared first as a serial in St. Nicholas magazine. The narrator states a problem: a city family suffocating in a tenement flat. New prospects open with Mr. Jones and a place in the country.

A voyage up the Hudson in March begins the family's Eden. Chapters teach chickens, maple sugar, raspberries, and early April gardening as the children learn them. Bobsey's peril, a thunderbolt, and berry-thieves supply the incidents. Roe, a horticulturist as well as a novelist, meant every task to be one real children could do. The book argues its title: honest work on real land drives a family back to paradise, one crop at a time.
eighteen-hundred-and-eleven:
Anna Laetitia Barbauld surveys a world at war in her poem Eighteen Hundred and Eleven, printed for J. Johnson and Company of London in 1812. The death drum still thunders from afar, she begins, and Britain feeds the fierce strife, bending by turns to hope and fear. Napoleon's colossal power bears down each fort of freedom in its course.

Verse follows armies across Europe. The sword, not the sickle, reaps the harvest now, and widowed mothers count sons who will not return. Barbauld then turns prophet. A later age, she writes, will wander London's splendid squares and climb crumbling turrets. Travellers will trace the city's ancient bound by scattered hamlets, and watch the Thames run idle through reeds and sedge. The poem is a bold, bleak forecast: empires fall, and Britain's turn will come. It angered many readers in its day.
elizabeth-and-her-german-garden:
Elizabeth von Arnim's Elizabeth and Her German Garden, first published anonymously in 1898, was Marie Annette Beauchamp's debut and a runaway success through printing after printing. The Gutenberg introduction, drawn from the illustrated Macmillan edition of 1900, explains her success and her cousinship to Katherine Mansfield. Elizabeth escapes to her husband's Pomeranian estate and its garden.

There she reads, plants, mocks the Man of Wrath, her husband, and endures amusing visitors and Russian guests who count seven marks a great sum for the journey home. The diary form mixes garden notes with quiet rebellion against German domestic duty. Its wit made Elizabeth famous and invented a genre of garden writing with a mind attached.
elsie-s-children:
Martha Finley closes her long series with Elsie's Children, a sequel to Elsie's Motherhood, first issued by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1877. Her preface is a farewell. Neither this nor any earlier volume, she says, was written at the request of personal friends, but to meet the demands of the public, Elsie's own friends and admirers.

The nursery at Viamede opens the tale. The little Travillas wait for their morning half hour with dear mamma, and Mammy comes in smiling, her apron thrown over a mystery for Vi's birthday. Later chapters grow graver, as children test their mother's faith against convent teaching. Isadore tells Vi that the sisters convinced her Mary may be called mother of God, and offers to show her something in secret. Finley ends the saga where she always stood: the mother's creed against the world's.
english-grammar-in-familiar-lectures-acc:
Samuel Kirkham teaches grammar by lecture in English Grammar in Familiar Lectures, here in a stereotype edition whose copyright entry dates to August 22, 1829. The eleventh edition, enlarged and improved, adds a compendium with a new order of parsing. A new system of punctuation and exercises in false syntax follow.

Kirkham builds from first principles: letters, syllables, then words as signs used by common consent. Pronouns get full treatment, with declensions of who, whose, and whom, and compound forms like whosoever. Philosophical grammar fills the notes, and a key answers the exercises. Kirkham aimed the book at schools and private learners. Generations of American schoolchildren parsed their sentences by his rules.
everlasting-pearl-one-of-china-s-women:
Johannsen's Everlasting Pearl tells the life of one Chinese woman through a missionary's eyes. Anna Magdalena Johannsen spent sixteen years as a missionary in China. The book first appeared in 1913, with a second impression in 1918. Walter B. Sloan wrote the preface.

Chapter headings trace Pearl's life from birth and infancy onward. Footbinding, engagement, and marriage fill the early chapters. Dark days, conflict, and persecution follow in the middle chapters. Later chapters turn to service, trial, and fruit from her labor. The first chapter opens in Kucheng, in Central China, with news of a daughter born to the Tu family. Illustrations show scenes such as the engagement document and Pearl as a bride.
excellent-women:
Various writers present Excellent Women, a set of short lives of notable Christian women. Each life is signed by its own author. James Macaulay wrote the lives of Elizabeth Fry and Rachel, Lady Russell. Other contributors include R. Lovett, J. P. Hobson, and Henry Johnson.

The contents list twelve women in all. Selina, Countess of Huntingdon, and Susanna Wesley appear early. Frances Ridley Havergal, Hannah More, and Mrs. Hemans follow. Madame Guyon, Ann Judson, and Mary Louisa Whately widen the range beyond Britain. Agnes Jones and Elizabeth, Duchess of Gordon, close the list. The Fry life opens with her Norwich birth on 21 June 1780. The volume honors faith shown through reform, writing, and mission work.
extract-from-captain-stormfield-s-visit-:
Mark Twain's Extract from Captain Stormfield's Visit to Heaven, published in 1909, was his last book and one he had drafted for decades. Captain Stormfield, a California sea captain, has been dead thirty years and racing through space like a comet when the story opens. He arrives at heaven's gate expecting trumpets, halos, and wings.

Heaven proves vaster and more bureaucratic than any church imagined: wings go to the wash, as a sly angel jokes, and saints from obscure planets outrank biblical celebrities. Twain satirizes earthly vanity while letting Stormfield's shrewd innocence carry the comedy. The tale's tenderness about ordinary souls surviving cosmic scale makes it more than a joke at religion's expense.
fathers-of-men:
Hornung's Fathers of Men is a school novel from the creator of Raffles. E. W. Hornung published it with Charles Scribner's Sons in February 1912. A list of his books fronts the volume, led by the Raffles series. The contents run past twenty-three chapters of school life.

Behind the Scenes and Change and Chance open the story. Very Raw Material and Settling In bring new boys to the school. Nicknames, Boy to Boy, and Likes and Dislikes map its society. A Merry Christmas and The Haunted House vary the terms. Sprawson's Masterpiece and The Fun of the Fair fill the middle. The Old Boys' Match looks back from later life. Hornung writes public school days with a grown man's hindsight.
five-months-on-a-german-raider-being-the:
Trayes tells of life as a prisoner at sea in Five Months on a German Raider, printed in 1919. Frederic George Trayes had been principal of the Royal Normal College at Bangkok. He was an Englishman captured by the German raider Wolf. His book bears his thanks to the Danish naval authorities, lighthouse keepers, and lifeboat men who helped him home.

The middle of the book is a litany of bad food. The prize ship Hitachi had carried ten thousand cases of Japanese canned crab to England. Much of it was saved and split between the Wolf and her prize. The prisoners were fed on it till they loathed it, with bully beef, beans, and dried fish for relief. Trayes keeps his good humor, and his tale is a rare inside view of a raider's long cruise.
freytag-debit-and-credit-soll-und-haben:
Young Anton Wohlfart leaves home to make his way in trade in Gustav Freytag's Debit and Credit, presented here in English. Soll und Haben, its German title, became the most famous German novel of the 1800s. A counting-house in Breslau becomes Anton's school for life, work, and character.

Honesty, hard work, and the moral worth of middle-class effort carry the story's values. Anton's rise runs parallel to the fall of flashier, emptier men around him. The novel was a publishing sensation that shaped Germany's image of itself for generations. Parts have dated, as Freytag's first readers' world has vanished. As a landmark of the realist novel, though, it still commands its shelf.
frobenius-atlantis-volksmarchen:
Leo Frobenius called his 1921 German gathering Atlantis, after his bold thesis. Folk tales and folk poetry from across Africa fill its rich pages. The great German Africanist hunted the oral wealth of many peoples.

Stories serve Frobenius as the memory of a whole continent speaking. He argues for Africa's deep cultural unity from the tales he gathered. Myths of kings, beasts, and first things crowd the treasure house. His method was romantic, sweeping, and often hotly debated by scholars. No reader can deny the sheer wealth of story he preserved in this volume. His Atlantis claim frames it, but the tales outlast the theory.
games-for-hallow-e-en:
Games for Hallow-e'en, by Mary E Blain and published at New York in 1912, is a party manual for the last night of October. Blain calls Hallow-e'en the most informal holiday of the year, a night for laughter, fun, and mystery, when fairies dance and ghosts, witches, devils, and elves wander. Young folks, and some who are not young, use its charms and spells to pry into the future.

The book starts with secrecy itself: invitations should be mysterious and guests bound to silence. A sample summons calls witches and choice spirits of darkness to high carnival at eight o'clock, in costume, prepared to test their fate. Pages of games, fortune telling devices, and decorations follow, drawn from folk custom and parlor practice. Blain writes for hosts who want the eerie without the dangerous, and her guide preserves how Americans played at haunting before the modern Halloween industry.
gerda-in-sweden:
Etta Blaisdell McDonald and Julia Dalrymple wrote Gerda in Sweden in 1910 for the Little People Everywhere series, which sent child heroes to many lands. Gerda and her twin Birger live in Sweden. A surprise box starts them on trips that show the country to young readers at home. The tall clock in their house seems to tick Ger-da, Ger-da.

The children sail on the North Star, cross the Arctic circle, and see the midnight sun. They visit Erik's home in Lapland, spend a day at the Skansen open-air museum, and pass through canal locks. Winter brings a carnival and Yule-tide feasts; summer ends with the Midsummer festival. Each chapter teaches a bit of Swedish life by story, which was the aim of the whole series.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Allen-ScottColu:
Paul Scott was a Washington columnist who wrote on national affairs, and this column takes up one of the assassination's loose ends: Lee Harvey Oswald's last letter. The letter bears an Irving, Texas postmark dated November 12, 1963, ten days before the killing.

Scott works over the mysteries surrounding that letter: where it was mailed, what it said, and how it fits the final days of Oswald's life. Such columns kept the case's unanswered questions in front of newspaper readers in the years after Dallas. The piece is press evidence of how early the doubts began, and how they were argued in public.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AllenJim_Jim_Al: nsia-AllenJim Jim Allen: the made public government document on Jim Allen, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the collection.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AllenWilliam_Wi: nsia-AllenWilliam William Allen: the made public government document on William Allen, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, of the files. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CasterWarren_Ca:
Two days before the assassination, Warren Caster, an executive connected with the Texas School Book Depository, brought two rifles into the building and showed them around. This essay argues that the Warren Commission avoided inquiring into those other rifles.

The essay builds on Caster's deposition of May 14, 1964, printed at volume 7, pages 386 to 388 of the hearings. In it he described buying the rifles and keeping them in the building. A second rifle story inside the sniper's building was an awkward fact, and the essay presses the commission's handling of it. It is research criticism in the classic form: one deposition, closely read.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ColemanLoren_Co:
Loren Coleman, a researcher of suicide patterns, prepared a presentation titled 'JFK Assassination-Related Suicides' for a suicidology conference on April 2, 1992. This request, dated February 14, 1992, asks Jerry Rose to publish an appeal for slides and photographs for it.

Jerry Rose edited The Third Decade, the research journal whose readers were the natural audience for such an appeal. That community kept photographs, clippings, and case files on the deaths that clustered around the assassination's witnesses and figures. Coleman's talk treated those deaths as a pattern to be studied rather than a mystery to be solved. The request is preserved as research correspondence at work.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIOswaldAsAgen: FBI Memorandum: Oswald as Agent - the heavily garbled FBI memo concerning allegations that Lee Harvey Oswald was an FBI agent. Damaged, but kept, complete, for researchers and readers. A US government document from the archive.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBISwearingenMW:
Freedom magazine, the Church of Scientology's journal, ran an article in its November-December 1984 issue on M. Wesley Swearingen. Swearingen was a former FBI agent who became a critic of the Bureau. The piece, titled Spyscam, covers the prosecution of an FBI agent for illegalities.

Scientology and the FBI were open adversaries, and the magazine wrote from that side of the fight. Even so, a former agent's case gave the article a factual spine: charges, a prosecution, a Bureau man in the dock. The piece preserves how the story was told by the Bureau's enemies.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FarringtonFenel:
A memo from Jim Garrison's office, passed through Mark Lake, records an interview at the Mexican Consulate in New Orleans. The district attorney's staff spoke with Consul General Ruben Gaxiola and a clerk, Teresa Jaruregui. Their subject was Mrs. Farrington's account of an Oswald visit to the consulate.

What Oswald did in Mexico in the fall of 1963 was a central question of the case. Garrison's investigators chased every report of his movements, including visits described by witnesses like Mrs. Farrington. The memo preserves her account as the consulate staff relayed it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Minutemen_Minut:
A book-length study of the paramilitary right in America stands behind this file. Its subjects are the Minutemen and the Ku Klux Klan, the armed groups of the 1960s right. Among its episodes: Robert Kennedy's proposed Justice Department investigation of the Minutemen. It also covers Congressman Henry Gonzalez urging the Warren Commission to look into possible Minutemen involvement in the Kennedy assassination.

The book treats the groups as a single problem of armed politics. It follows their members, their weapons, and the officials who wanted them investigated. For readers of the assassination files, its value is the overlap. The same names moved between paramilitary circles and the Oswald inquiry. This study maps that ground as its author found it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SenateInternalS:
John H. Averill reported for the Los Angeles Times on a rare Senate swipe at its own Internal Security Subcommittee. The subcommittee had been created 21 years earlier. Its charge was to investigate Communist activities and domestic subversion. Averill's headline is 'Senate Cools on Security,' and the story records the chamber turning on its own watchdog.

Internal Security was one of the Cold War's standing committees of suspicion, heir to the McCarthy years. A Senate willing to cut at it marked how far the climate had moved by the 1970s. The article preserves the vote of confidence that failed: colleagues, a budget, and a mission no longer assumed to be necessary. It is a small dated marker of the Cold War's domestic machinery winding down.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SpecialUnitSena: Someone who had read the book Special Unit Senator sat down on February 8, 1970, and wrote a letter about it to a man named Gary. The writer's name is not recorded. The letter gives one reader's judgment of the book soon after it appeared. It survives as a small piece of the reading and arguing that surrounded political books of that period.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StudentMobiliza: nsia-StudentMobilizationCommittee Student Mobilization Committee: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WarrenCommissio: CIA officers met with the Warren Commission on March 12, 1964, and the agency wrote a memorandum about the session. Chief Counsel J. Lee Rankin took part for the commission. The memo records how the spy agency presented itself to the body investigating President Kennedy's murder. Relations between the two were sensitive, and the paper shows both sides managing that contact in writing.
govdocs-archive_org-the-genesis-of-the-a: Rijad Kala's 2026 book, The Genesis of the Aerial Anomalies Phenomenon, asks where the modern UFO phenomenon began. Aerial anomalies is the newer term for sightings in the sky that witnesses and sensors cannot explain. Kala investigates the phenomenon's roots rather than a single case. The book joins a fast-growing shelf of serious-looking UFO studies written after governments began releasing their own files on the subject.
govdocs-archive_org-zenith-of-humanity-r: Rudolf John Gorsleben subtitled his book The Zenith of Humanity: The World Law of Three. Its pattern is becoming, being, and passing away, read as a law governing the world. Gorsleben was a rune mystic, and runes stand behind his cosmology of rise, height, and fall. The volume presents his system whole. It serves readers of runic esotericism and of the German occult writers who worked between the two world wars.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico_J: Newly released JFK files, according to this briefing-book page, detail close intelligence collaboration between the CIA and Mexico during the Kennedy years. Mexico City was one of the agency's largest stations, watching Cubans, Soviets, and Mexico's own left. The evidence supplied here is the headline alone, and the files themselves are not described. The subject is significant because the partnership ran both ways: Mexican security services gained support and training while the CIA gained a platform on America's southern border.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_mexico-ayotzinapa:
In September 2014, forty-three students from a teachers' college at Ayotzinapa were attacked in Iguala, Mexico, and forcibly disappeared; none has been found alive and the case remains unsolved. Ten years later, a National Security Archive posting marked the anniversary under the name the impunity cascade. It was built around senior analyst Kate Doyle's keynote speech at a University College London commemoration.

Impunity cascade names the pattern the case came to symbolize: one unpunished crime licensing the next, as investigations stall and officials escape blame. Doyle has worked the Ayotzinapa evidence for years, including records from Mexican military archives. The posting gives readers the anniversary argument in full. A decade without answers, it holds, is itself an outcome someone chose. Archives remain one of the few tools left to challenge it.
great-britain-and-her-queen:
Anne E. Keeling published Great Britain and Her Queen in a second edition, revised and enlarged, in 1897, the year of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee. Keeling had written a life of General Gordon. Her chapters begin with the girl queen and her kingdom, pass through storm and sunshine, and treat France and England, the Crimean War, and India.

Later chapters take up the beginnings of sorrows, the colonies, and the progress of mind and spirit. A last chapter carries the progress of the empire from 1887 to 1897. The tone is loyal and warm, the work of a subject who saw the reign as a great age. The book is now a window on how the Victorians praised themselves at their queen's feast, with Claremont and the queen's portrait among its pictures.
greybeards-at-play-literature-and-art-fo:
G. K. Chesterton published Greybeards at Play in 1900, when he was twenty-six and not yet famous. Its subtitle calls it literature and art for old gentlemen; its contents are rhymes and sketches by a very young one. He dedicates it to E. C. B., his friend Edmund Clerihew Bentley, in verses that recall how the two wore one hat and smoked one cigar, one at each end, through boyhood's storm and shower.

The rhymes are nonsense with a point, matched by Chesterton's own comic drawings. Old gentlemen, beasts, and moral tales are turned upside down in his early manner. The book is short and slight by design, a young man's holiday work. Yet the seeds of all his later writing are here: paradox, wonder at small things, and jokes that turn into arguments when no one is watching.
grillparzer-der-traum-ein-leben:
Rustan dreams of glory, and one night sleep shows him the whole life his ambition craves: power, crime, and ruin. Grillparzer's Der Traum ein Leben, given here in German, wakes him wiser than any sermon could. The verse drama follows Calderon's great model, Life Is a Dream, into Austrian theater.

A bridge, a murder, and a throne crowd the dream, each step upward paid for in guilt. Rustan wakes clutching his plain life like a treasure. Austria counts the play its great philosophical drama about ambition and illusion. The dream that teaches a man to live makes powerful theater still. Grillparzer's verse carries the vision with music and speed alike.
grillparzer-des-meeres-und-der-liebe-wel:
Every night Leander swims the Hellespont to reach Hero, and one stormy night the guiding lamp goes out. Grillparzer's Des Meeres und der Liebe Wellen, given here in German, gives the ancient myth of Hero and Leander the full tragic treatment. Its title joins the waves of the sea to the waves of love.

A priestess bound by vows and a youth bound by passion test fate once too often. Grillparzer builds the tragedy slowly, letting ritual, family, and the sea itself tighten the net. Passion and destiny share the stage with unusual equality. Austria's greatest dramatist found in this old story one of his purest subjects. The play remains a summit of German verse tragedy.
gritli-s-children:
Johanna Spyri, the Swiss author of Heidi, wrote Gritli's Children as a sequel tale of the children Gritli left behind. Louise Brooks translated it into English. The contents fall into two volumes. The first moves from a country house on the Rhine to the doctor's house at Buchberg and on to Oak-Ridge. The second reaches a new home, a fisherman's hut, and Rosemount. Aunty is in demand again, one chapter promises.

Gritli's children, among them Oscar and Emma, grow up under the care of kind kin and neighbors. Village school, journeys on the Rhine, and small plans and sorrows fill the pages. Spyri writes of Swiss life with her usual sunlit clarity. Grief is present, since the mother is gone, yet the tone is hopeful. The book carries Heidi's world on into a second generation.
henrik-ibsen:
Edmund Gosse wrote this life of Henrik Ibsen, the Norwegian playwright. Gosse follows Ibsen from childhood through his Bergen theater years. Later chapters trace the satires, the great prose plays, and the last years. Two closing chapters weigh the man's character and mind.

Gosse notes that the first full life came from Henrik Jaeger in 1888. He adds facts Ibsen himself gave on his early years. Plays are read as part of the life, not apart from it. Readers who know the dramas will find a clear map of how the work grew.
het-geheimzinnige-eiland-de-luchtschipbr:
Jules Verne's Mysterious Island appears here in a Dutch version, printed at Amsterdam in 1914. Gerard Keller translated from the twentieth French edition. This first part is named for the airship castaways. The book is in Dutch throughout.

A great storm in March 1865 drags a balloon far over the Pacific. Five travellers must throw all weight overboard to stay aloft. They come down on an unknown island with next to nothing. There they must build, hunt, and make tools from scratch. Dutch readers get Verne's famed tale of skill and grit in their own tongue.
his-heart-s-queen:
Mrs Georgie Sheldon wrote this popular romance, first copyrighted in 1890. Sheldon was a prolific teller of love tales for a wide public. The story turns on sisters, rank, and a great match. News spreads of Violet Huntington's coming marriage to the Earl of Sutherland.

Violet shrinks from gossip and keeps to her room at the hotel. She drives out daily with her betrothed and plays her part with care. His kindness is steady, but her heart's true state is the book's question. Readers get a lush, earnest romance of wealth, duty, and a bride ill at ease.
how-to-live-rules-for-healthful-living-b:
This health manual came from the Life Extension Institute of New York. Irving Fisher chaired its hygiene reference board. William H Taft chaired the institute's directors, and Eugene L Fisk directed its hygiene work. Its motto is blunt: prevent life-waste, upbuild national vitality.

Rules for air, food, work, and rest fill the chapters. Long tables grade common dishes by calories and cost. A sirloin steak and a baked apple custard sit side by side in its ledgers. The institute sold checks and counsel to a public newly keen on long life. Readers get early scientific health advice, measured to the last calorie.
in-defense-of-women:
H L Mencken published In Defense of Women in 1918, a paradoxical compliment arguing that women are cleverer, tougher, and more realistic than men. His contents march from the feminine mind and the maternal instinct through the war between the sexes to marriage, courtship, and the actual husband. The thing called intuition gets its own early chapter.

Mencken claims women see through male vanity, aesthetics, and honor with biological clarity, choosing husbands as coolly as generals choose ground. His chapter dissecting Havelock Ellis on the sons of old fathers shows the debunking method in miniature. The book offended feminists and gallants alike, which was the point; its epigrams still bite.
in-the-shadow-of-the-glen:
J. M. Synge wrote In the Shadow of the Glen as a play in one act, first performed in Dublin on October 8, 1903. The scene is the last cottage at the head of a long glen in County Wicklow. Dan Burke, a farmer, lies on a bed under a sheet as if dead. His wife Nora sets out whisky and cake for a wake.

A tramp knocks and is welcomed in from the great rain. Young herd Micheal Dara scorns the tramp's poor coat as tea is made. Talk of money, loneliness, and the dead man builds toward a sharp turn. Synge's Wicklow speech drives the brief play.
inferences-from-haunted-houses-and-haunt:
John William Harris drew inferences from haunted houses and haunted men in this 1901 book. He opens by noting how little interest psychical matters then drew. He quotes Sir William Crookes on thought passing from mind to mind without the senses. Miss Freer's account of a haunting at B---- House is cited at length.

Harris weighs hypnotism at a distance and pressure on the heart nerve as causes of alarm. A man twice attacked by hypnotists in a factory case is discussed. He asks whether fatal fainting can be made by changed heart beats. The book is an Edwardian inquiry into ghosts and mind power.
joanna-godden:
Joanna Godden is a novel by Sheila Kaye-Smith, published in 1921. It is divided into four parts: Shepherd's Hey, First Love, The Little Sister, and Last Love. A note warns that local names of places and people are used, but no living person is meant. The story is set in the marsh country where Sussex meets Kent.

The opening pages map three marshes inside a triangle of canal and coast. The Royal Military Canal runs from Hythe to Rye beside the Military Road. Romney Marsh, Dunge Marsh, and Walland Marsh lie between the canal and the Channel beaches. Kaye-Smith grounds her heroine's farming life in this flat, ditch-cut land before Joanna herself steps forward.
johnny-crow-s-garden:
Johnny Crow's Garden is a picture book in verse by L. Leslie Brooke, first issued in 1903. Brooke drew the pictures himself. He dedicates the book to his father's memory, since his father first told him of the garden. He also addresses his own boys, for whom he set the facts on record.

In the rhymes, Johnny Crow digs and sows until he makes a little garden. A lion visits in a green and yellow tie, and a rat wears a feather in his hat. A bear, poor thing, has nothing to wear at all. Animal after animal joins the fun in short, bouncing lines. Brooke's book became a nursery favorite for its pictures and its chant-like verse.
kathleen:
Kathleen is a novel by Christopher Morley, set in Oxford. Its device is a literary game: the Scorpions, a club of eight students, agree to write a serial story. Each man contributes a chapter in turn. Kenneth Forbes of Merton College holds one of the club's rooms in Fellows' Quadrangle.

That room, the book notes, sheltered Queen Henrietta Maria in the civil war year of 1643. Morley lingers over student life: cold tea, anchovy toast, and literary talk. The invented Kathleen of their serial draws the club's writers into rivalry and romance. Morley, himself an Oxford scholar, writes undergraduate Oxford with affectionate inside knowledge. The novel mixes campus comedy with the story the Scorpions are making up.
le-corbeau-the-raven:
Edgar Allan Poe's poem The Raven appears here in a famous French dress. Stéphane Mallarmé translated it as Le Corbeau. Édouard Manet supplied the illustrations for this Paris edition of 1875.

English and French texts stand together for the reader. The poem begins at a dreary midnight with a tired scholar. A tapping at his chamber door breaks his near sleep. French readers met Poe largely through such translations. This edition joins three major artists: poet, translator, and painter. Manet's stark black images suit Poe's midnight mood. Few poems exist in a more famous single-artist edition.
letters-to-his-children:
