Theodore Roosevelt wrote these letters to his children over more than twenty years. A few letters to friends and relatives about the children join them. He began when they were small and wrote until they were grown.

Whenever travel parted them, letters followed at once. The Spanish War, hunting trips, and school terms all prompted mail. Roosevelt's children were never out of his mind or heart, the editor says. Drawings, jokes, and animal tales fill many pages. The book shows a president as a tender, playful father. Many letters include small pen drawings for the children. Play, animals, and bedtime stories fill his pages home.
library-work-with-children:
Alice Isabel Hazeltine wrote this early manual on library service for children. Project Gutenberg issued it as one of its early electronic texts. The book grew out of American public library practice with young readers. Its subject is practical: how libraries should serve children well.

Hazeltine covers story hours, choosing books, and running a children's room. Her advice treats children as real readers with real needs. The manual helped shape American children's librarianship as a profession. Librarians still build on the foundation her generation laid down. Storytelling receives the same practical respect as cataloguing in her scheme. The children's room succeeds, she implies, when books meet young readers halfway.
life-and-public-services-of-john-quincy-:
William H. Seward wrote this life of John Quincy Adams. Adams was the sixth President of the United States. The book adds the eulogy Seward delivered before New York's legislature. A transcriber's glossary explains unfamiliar words like abjuration and abstemious.

Seward presents Adams's public services alongside his private character. The transcriber warns that the style is verbose but rewarding. Gems of character description repay the patient reader, he argues. The book also shows that political bickering changes little across centuries. His glossary also defines Aceldama, a place with dreadful associations. Seward's own eulogy gives the volume its public, ceremonial close.
little-folded-hands-prayers-for-children:
Anonymous compilers gathered these prayers for children from various sources. A revised edition presents morning prayers first. The opening prayer thanks God for keeping the child overnight. It asks the same keeping through the coming day.

Short rhymed prayers follow, numbered for daily use. One thanks the Lord for sleep and asks guidance till night. Children pray for forgiven sins and life near Jesus. The little book fits small hands and early devotions. Now I raise me up from sleep numbers among the rhymes. Each brief prayer ends with a simple Amen for children.
little-meg-s-children:
Hesba Stretton published this children's story with the Religious Tract Society. A 1905 London edition carries Harold Copping's frontispiece. Contents open with a chapter simply called Motherless. Little Meg herself becomes a mourner in chapter two.

Meg's cleaning day shows a child running a household. She plans a treat for her children, her younger siblings. A neighbor enters the story in chapter five. Stretton had written Jessica's First Prayer and Alone in London before. Jessica's First Prayer made Stretton's name among child readers. Pilgrim Street and No Place Like Home followed it successfully.
little-women:
Louisa May Alcott opens this novel with the March sisters playing pilgrims. A merry Christmas follows in chapter two. The Laurence boy enters the girls' world in chapter three. Burdens, neighborliness, and Beth's palace beautiful fill early chapters.

Amy's humiliation and Jo's meeting with Apollyon test the sisters. Meg goes to Vanity Fair while the family forms secret societies. Camp Laurence and castles in the air lighten the middle. Letters, dark days, and Amy's will deepen Part One's close. Beth's secret and tender troubles deepen Part Two considerably. The valley of the shadow closes Alcott's chapter list.
mae-madden:
Mae Madden is a sentimental novel by Mary Murdoch Mason. An introductory poem by Joaquin Miller opens the book. Before the story proper comes 'A Dream of Italy,' an allegory. Two souls parted before time began meet again at Venice.

By the blue Adriatic, under the lion of Venice, the lover finds her. She knows him not, though he has searched the world for her. This dream of fated love frames Mae Madden's own story. Mason writes in the earnest, flowery style of her day. Her romance pleased many readers in its time. It survives as a lush period piece of love and fate.
manual-of-the-mother-church-the-first-ch:
The Manual of the Mother Church sets the rules of Christian Science's chief church. This is the eighty-ninth edition of Mary Baker Eddy's handbook. Eddy founded the First Church of Christ, Scientist, in Boston. Copyrights on the manual run back to 1895.

An extract here insists the rules arose from no solemn conclave. They grew, Eddy wrote, from experience rather than dictation. The by-laws order officers, members, services, and discipline. They govern branch churches as well as the Boston mother church. Few religious bodies rest so much on one small rulebook. Students of American religion will find it a key document. It shows how Eddy built a lasting church order.
marching-men:
Marching Men is an early novel by Sherwood Anderson, dated 1917. He dedicated it, simply, to American workingmen. It opens in Coal Creek, Pennsylvania, at Nance McGregor's bake-shop. Uncle Charlie Wheeler laughs over the new baby's name, Norman.

Too soft and delicate for Coal Creek, declares Uncle Charlie. He rechristens the boy with a name that will stick: Beaut. Beaut McGregor grows up strong in the coal town's hard world. He dreams of order for the chaos of working life. In his vision, laboring men march like an army toward change. Anderson's brooding power already fills this strange, strong book.
marigold-garden:
Marigold Garden is a picture book of rhymes by Kate Greenaway. Frederick Warne published it in London and New York. Its title page promises pictures and rhymes by Greenaway herself. Few artists have ever been so loved by children and parents.

Greenaway's little figures wear the quaint dress she made famous. Sunbonnets, mob caps, and garden frocks fill her sunny pages. Short rhymes match the pictures verse by verse. Her children play in gardens much like the one named here. The book helped set the style of Victorian childhood. Marigold Garden remains a treasure of the nursery shelf.
memoir-of-jane-austen:
James Edward Austen-Leigh wrote A Memoir of Jane Austen, his aunt. Richard Bentley printed the second edition in 1871. His preface says the first was met with more favor than he hoped.

This edition adds letters, a piece of her child tales, and Lady Susan. It also prints the dropped chapter of Persuasion in full. The Watsons and a late, unfinished tale appear in part. Chapters trace her birth, Steventon life, Bath, Southampton, and Chawton in turn. Letters and remarks on her letter writing fill chapter three. Family memory, not mere praise, gives the book its lasting worth.
men-and-women:
Robert Browning's Men and Women gathers his dramatic monologues, poems spoken in the voices of other people. This edition carries an introduction and notes by Charlotte Porter and Helen A. Clarke. It follows the text published by Thomas Y. Crowell in 1898. The speakers range from Renaissance artists to bishops and physicians.

Fra Lippo Lippi defends his earthy painting, while Andrea del Sarto mourns his failed promise. A dying bishop orders his tomb, and Bishop Blougram argues about faith and doubt. Each poem lets one voice reveal a whole character through speech alone. The collection shows Browning's monologue form at its richest and most varied.
mr-dooley-in-the-hearts-of-his-countryme:
Finley Peter Dunne collected these Mr. Dooley sketches at Boston in 1899. Small, Maynard and Company printed three editions of ten thousand copies before publication. The pieces had run in the Chicago Journal in 1898 and 1899. Dunne's dedication ironically thanks the London publishers who reprinted Dooley without asking him.

He reserves his real dedication for the people of Archey Road, in Chicago's Bridgeport. There his Irish bartender-philosopher, Mr. Dooley, holds court for his friend Hennessy. Dooley's dialect monologues dissect politics, war, and fashion with barroom wisdom. The sketches made Dunne famous on both sides of the Atlantic.
music-talks-with-children:
Thomas Tapper wrote these talks on music for children, issued in 1898. Theodore Presser of Philadelphia published the book. A Wordsworth verse fronts it, praising the child's solemn thought. Tapper greets the children at home with a prayer to learn to live.

Chapters ask what the face tells and why we study music. Tones about us, listening, and thinking in tone follow. He treats music as a thing of the heart first. Classics come last, once ears are awake. The talks are short and warm, made to draw young readers toward sound with wonder, not fear.
my-first-visit-to-new-england-and-others:
William Dean Howells recalls his literary friends in this memoir volume. He meant for years to write of New England's great writers. For twenty-five years he lived near them and knew them well. The first paper tells of his first visit to New England.

Howells dates that paper to the early eighteen-nineties. He read it aloud to Harper's editor under willows at Magnolia. Later papers give first views of literary New York. He admits his memory, though strong, missed much he wished he had kept. The book is a dean of letters looking back, honest about what time kept and what it took.
my-summer-in-a-garden:
Charles Dudley Warner's garden papers open with a witty letter to Mr. Fields. The letter mocks introductions as flat pillars stuck on books. A mere letter, he says, is a footpath to a good viewpoint. From there readers may wander as they will.

Warner sends writers to the spider for a lesson in work. The spider works unseen and trusts the result, he jokes. The papers trace one summer among beds, weeds, and weather. A study of Calvin, a cat, joins the garden pieces. V1 dates the book to 1870 and calls it the beloved classic that made Warner's name in America.
nasa-tm-19680007769-possible-resonance-i:
Richard J. Drachman, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, tests a claimed effect in this January 1968 paper. A positron is the antimatter twin of an electron. Some had claimed that a positron flying at a hydrogen atom briefly sticks to it, just below the point where it can pair off as positronium.

Drachman first works out the pull between the pair with a rough method. That rough pass seems to show the sticking effect. A fuller method then adds terms the rough one left out, and the pull grows weaker. The effect fades away. He ends by calling the reported result a likely trick of the rough method.
nasa-tm-19690023997-variation-of-the-ion:
J. M. Grebowsky and N. K. Rahman of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this May 1969 preprint, X-621-69-225. They study how the ion temperature gradient varies along magnetic field lines in the outer plasmasphere. The plasmasphere is a doughnut of cold plasma trapped around Earth. Out there, hydrogen ions are the dominant positive charge carriers.

Using the equations of thermal diffusion, the pair explore how ion temperature changes along each field line. They show the gradient along the field depends only on one ratio. It compares how fast hydrogen ion density thins with height against the same measure for helium ions. Model temperature gradients are then worked out for that outer region and summarized.
nasa-tm-19720005136-empirical-expression:
David A Sagerser, Seymour Lieblein, and Richard P Krebs of the Lewis Research Center published these estimating formulas in December 1971. Early aircraft design needs quick engine sizes before detailed drawings exist. Their simplified equations give the length and weight of axial flow engine parts. The parts covered run from the fan and its duct to the turbine. Structure and accessories are included as well.

The equations came from matching lift and cruise engine data. VTOL aircraft, which rise straight up, drove the need for the study. The report checks its own math against real engines. Comparisons of actual and calculated total weights cover several typical engines. Designers could then size a power plant in hours, not weeks.
nasa-tm-19720016188-preliminary-experime:
Orlando A Gutierrez and James R Stone of the Lewis Research Center reported these noise experiments in May 1972, as NASA TM X-2553. Their models were target type thrust reversers for jet engines. A reverser throws engine thrust forward to slow a landing aircraft. Two target shapes were tested, a V gutter and a half cylinder. Both worked with round nozzles of two sizes. Reversers can add unwelcome noise at airports.

The team varied nozzle pressure across a working range. Spacing between the reverser and nozzle also changed between runs. Reverser orientation changed as well, to find quiet positions. Even the early data carried a warning. Under some settings, the reverser generated considerably more noise. Such results guide reverser design toward quieter operation.
new-discoveries-at-jamestown-site-of-the:
John L. Cotter and J. Paul Hudson wrote New Discoveries at Jamestown, issued in Washington in 1957. The National Park Service published it, under the Department of the Interior. Its subtitle calls Jamestown the site of the first successful English settlement in America. Copies sold for fifty cents.

Part one, called Exploration, reports what the ground yielded at the old town site. Sections cover churches, mansions, row houses, and single brick houses. Frame houses, workshops, brick walks, and drains follow. Ice pits, kilns, ironworking pits, and wells round out the finds. The book let visitors and scholars see the buried town take shape again.
notable-events-of-the-nineteenth-century:
John Clark Ridpath compiled and edited Notable Events of the Nineteenth Century for the Christian Herald in New York in 1896. The book formed one number of the Christian Herald Library series for 1896 to 1897. Its subtitle promises great deeds of men and nations, and the progress of the world, in short studies.

Ridpath's preface aims at a middle kind of reading for busy folk. Readers have enough heavy study, he says, and enough straw and chaff lightness too. Thoughtful short pieces for an unoccupied half hour are wanting, he argues. This volume supplies brief readings on large subjects, chosen from the century then closing.
number-seventeen:
Louis Tracy published Number Seventeen in 1915, opening with a chapter called The Outcome of Artistic Curiosity. Theatre crowds pour into drizzle outside Daly's, where all London has flocked for a musical comedy. A red faced commissionaire pockets sixpences as fast as he can summon cabs. Most playgoers hurry on foot toward tubes and omnibuses.

Francis Berrold Theydon hesitates whether to walk or risk a cab. A panting commissionaire promises him a taxi in half a minute. Theydon, a considerate person, steps aside to light a cigarette. An impetuous footman cannons into him, crying for a lady's car. Tracy sets a mystery in motion in a wet London crowd.
old-lady-mary-a-story-of-the-seen-and-th:
Margaret Oliphant wrote this tale of the seen and unseen. The title figure is very old and calm. She has lived through beauty, triumph, jealousy, and defeat. Now gentle habits make her quiet life feel endless. Oliphant argues that such calm makes death hard to accept.

Young people, she says, meet death with more ease. Middle age often longs for rest from its burdens. Old age clings to custom and mild comfort instead. The story follows Mary toward her final change. Oliphant writes with pity, insight, and ghostly suggestion. It is a thoughtful tale about aging and dying.
on-the-spanish-main-or-some-english-fora:
John Masefield wrote this history of buccaneers, first published in 1906. Methuen of London issued it with a map and pictures. The frontispiece shows Captain William Dampier in portrait. Chapter one follows Drake to the West Indies. His raids and secret harbor open the narrative.

English forays on the Isthmus of Darien form the core. Masefield describes the buccaneers and their hard sea life. He adds a short account of old ships and sailors. The metadata record lists the year as 1906. This entry duplicates another hosted copy of the same book. Both preserve Masefield's lively history of the Spanish Main.
orange-and-green: G. A. Henty's Orange and Green, dated 1888 in this edition, is a boys' adventure novel. Its subtitle is A Tale of the Boyne and Limerick. The hosted sample shows the table of contents only. A shipwreck opens the tale. Chapters then follow the siege and relief of Derry, the Boyne water, a first siege of Limerick, and Athlone. The book ends with Peace. No chapter text appears in the sample, so this note describes the scope from the contents page alone.
paradise-garden-the-satirical-narrative-: George Gibbs called Paradise Garden the satirical narrative of a great experiment. An epigraph from The Two Gentlemen of Verona frames it. No man is perfect, Shakespeare warns, without being tried and tutored in the world. The contents promise The Great Experiment, then Jerry, then Jerry Grows. Enter Eve and The Minx Returns follow. Jack Ballard Takes Charge comes later. The hosted sample shows the title pages, epigraph, and contents only. No chapter of Gibbs's satire appears, so this note follows the title and contents alone.
personal-poems-complete-volume-iv-of-the: The sample provided here shows only the front matter of the Personal Poems, the title page and contents of volume 4 of Whittier's works, with no poems visible. The contents list John Greenleaf Whittier's poems to and about people: memorials to Charles B. Storrs and Lucy Hooper, verses to Channing, Fredrika Bremer, and Charles Sumner, and famous pieces including Ichabod, The Lost Occasion, and To My Old Schoolmaster.
personal-recollections-of-birmingham-and:
Eliezer Edwards first published his Personal Recollections of Birmingham and Birmingham Men in the Birmingham Daily Mail, under the signature S.D.R. A note explains the sketches were written entirely from memory at first. For later pieces he owed facts and dates to others, and kept the title to show the connection of the series.

The revised book appeared at Birmingham in 1877. Contents begin with first impressions of Birmingham and the Bull Ring riots of 1839. Edwards came out from his incognito because the authorship was generally known. The sketches preserve a Victorian industrial city through one observant man's memory.
pictures-of-sweden:
Hans Christian Andersen, the Danish writer best known for his fairy tales, turned travel writer for an 1851 London volume on Sweden. He had already written The Improvisatore, and here he tours a country of canals, old towns, and northern legend.

His chapters move from the falls and works at Trollhatta to Kinnakulle, Vadstene, and Stockholm, with stops among the islands of the Skjargaards and at Upsala and Sala. Along the way he mixes plain description with tales, prison cells, beggar boys, a puppet showman, and a piece called The Mute Book. The result is part guidebook, part storybook, in his own wandering style.
plays-of-gods-and-men:
Lord Dunsany's Plays of Gods and Men gathers stage works by the Irish writer, in an edition prepared from the 1917 Unwin text. A note warns that later American printings changed small details and added a page of talk to one play. Dunsany mixes gods, kings, and prophets in far-off invented lands.

The volume opens with The Laughter of the Gods, a tragedy in three acts. King Karnos rules the jungle city of Thek, in a time like the decline of Babylon. Around him stand a prophet called Voice-of-the-Gods, three lords and their wives, sentries, and an executioner.
preliminary-announcement-list-of-members:
The Society for Pure English issued its first tract, a preliminary announcement and list of members, from the Clarendon Press in October 1919. The society had been founded in 1913 and was preparing its activities when war came in August 1914. The committee suspended proceedings until the Armistice, then met again and announced its first issues for 1919. The tract opens by disarming its own title: pure does not mean that words of foreign origin are impurities in English, quite the opposite.

What the society wanted, under founders who included the poet Robert Bridges, was care for the language's growth: good usage, clear meaning, and respect for English as a living instrument. The announcement handles finance, membership, and program in the driest committee prose, after the war, men of letters organized to mind the tongue. The tract series that followed became a small classic of English usage debate.
prince-hagen:
Upton Sinclair wrote Prince Hagen as a play that drags Wagner's Nibelungs into Gilded Age New York. The cast list sets the joke: Gerald Isman, a poet; Mimi, a Nibelung; Alberich, king of the Nibelungs. And his grandson Prince Hagen, set down among a railroad magnate, a coal baron, a lord of steel, a cotillon leader, and Mrs. Bagley-Willis, mistress of society. Act one moves from a tent in Quebec to the hall of state in Nibelheim, where the dwarf folk decide to try their luck above ground.

Two years later the scene is a Fifth Avenue library, then the conservatory of Prince Hagen's palace at the wind-up of his opening ball. Where the Nibelung prince, armed with the ring's gold, conquers society by its own rules. Sinclair's satire is a fable of capital: the gold's curse works on Fifth Avenue as on the Rhine.
raemaekers-cartoons-with-accompanying-no: Raemaekers' Cartoons was published at Garden City, New York, by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1916. It pairs the war cartoons of Louis Raemaekers with notes by well-known English writers. An appreciation from H. H. Asquith, prime minister of England, is added. Only the list of cartoons is shown. An introduction by Francis Stopford comes first. Then Christendom after Twenty Centuries appears. A Stable Peace by Eden Phillpotts follows. The Massacre of the Innocents comes next. Bernhardiism by Hilaire Belloc closes the list.
religious-reality-a-book-for-men:
A. E. J. Rawlinson, student of Christ Church, Oxford, and priest-in-charge of St. John the Evangelist, Wilton Road, wrote this book for men in 1918. The Bishop of Lichfield, to whom Rawlinson served as examining chaplain, supplies a preface. He calls it a book that is wanted.

Thoughtful men, the bishop writes, do not fear theology stated without conventions and hard terms. They want the problem of evil honestly faced, and Christian truth shown bearing on the real problems of life. Rawlinson had served as tutor at Keble College and as chaplain to the forces, and had known students, soldiers, and parish men at first hand.
saltykov-shchedrin-a-family-of-noblemen:
The Golovlyov family rots from within across three generations in Saltykov-Shchedrin's novel, presented here in English as A Family of Noblemen. Greed, spite, drunkenness, and hypocrisy do the slow work of destruction on a landed estate. At the center stands Porfiry, called the little Judas, whose oily talk smothers everyone near him.

Mikhail Saltykov-Shchedrin, Russia's most savage satirist, hated the gentry he anatomized with something like holy hatred. The comedy here is the darkest in Russian literature, laughter curdling into horror. This English selection introduces new readers to his corrosive genius. Few novels anywhere trace a family's moral collapse with such patience. It remains a book readers admire and slightly fear.
schnitzler-hands-around-reigen:
Ten dialogues link ten encounters in a chain that implicates a whole society in Schnitzler's Hands Around, the English title of Reigen. A prostitute pairs with a soldier, the soldier with a maid, and so upward through gentleman, wife, and count, until the circle closes. Each partner appears twice, once with the person below and once above.

Private printings in 1900 caused a scandal; productions were banned as obscene for years. Today the play reads as a brilliant anatomy of desire and class, its form as pointed as its content. Nobody in the chain escapes Schnitzler's level gaze. The roundelay structure has been imitated ever since, rarely with this economy. It remains the wittiest sad play about sex ever written in German.
schnitzler-the-road-to-the-open:
Cafes, concert halls, and drawing rooms of a glittering city carry Schnitzler's great Viennese novel The Road to the Open, presented here in English. A young composer moves through that world as it slides toward modernity, and toward the anti-Semitism that would help destroy it. The novel appeared in 1908, in an empire already trembling.

Love affairs, artistic ambition, and salon talk fill the foreground while history darkens behind them. Schnitzler writes both a love letter to old Vienna and a clear-eyed diagnosis of its doom. His hero's search for an open road becomes the city's own unasked question. The book stands as his largest canvas. Readers of Zweig and Roth will recognize the world, rendered here first.
side-lights-on-astronomy-and-kindred-fie:
Simon Newcomb gathered twenty-one essays and addresses on astronomy and kindred science in this volume. Contents open with unsolved problems of astronomy and the structure and extent of the universe. A photograph of the sun's corona, taken at Tripoli during the eclipse of August 30, 1905, stands among the pictures.

Newcomb treats telescope making, life in the universe, the weighing of planets, and the mariner's compass. Later pieces ask if men can make rain and weigh the flying machine's outlook. A leading American astronomer speaks here in plain terms, bringing deep questions within reach of keen lay readers.
sight-unseen:
Mary Roberts Rinehart tells this tale of a neighborhood club's trials in reaching the unseen world. A narrator who took part in the sittings makes the private record public at last. The aim, the narrator grants, is less to add proof than to chart the human mind's dark ground.

Analysts of the mind, the narrator argues, explain too much away as trickery with black silk threads and folding rods. Mind acting on mind stays unmapped, the narrator holds. Rinehart turns a seance circle into a mystery of fear and doubt, where each sitter's secrets press toward the light.
sister-carmen:
M. Corvus wrote this German tale, here in English by Kate Dykers for the Minerva Publishing Company of New York in 1891. Chapter one opens at dawn on Easter Sunday in a small Moravian village. Spring breeze stirs young grain while a lark climbs singing toward the light.

Villagers in plain dress walk through green fields to a woodland graveyard, where great lindens spread bare branches over the graves. An immense stone cross stands at the center. Trumpets and voices will mark the resurrection there. Faith, village custom, and a sister's calling shape a tale steeped in Moravian piety.
six-women:
Victoria Cross published this set of tales with Mitchell Kennerley in New York and dedicated it to two friends, with memories of the East. A list of her earlier books includes Anna Lombard and Life's Shop Window. Chapter one finds Hamilton walking a hot street in a listless, hopeless mood.

White bullocks drag creaking wooden carts through clouds of dust while flies swarm in yellow sunshine. Heat, thirst, and aching eyes weigh less on Hamilton than a deep nausea of life itself. Cross sets six women's tales in colonial heat and longing, written in her lush, daring manner.
sketches-in-lavender-blue-and-green:
Jerome K. Jerome published these tales with J. W. Arrowsmith at Bristol in 1920. Jerome had won fame with Three Men in a Boat and The Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow. Contents open with Reginald Blake, financier and cad, then an item of fashionable intelligence and Blase Billy.

Later tales treat a man who would manage, a man of habit, an absent-minded man, and Dick Dunkerman's cat. A nursery rhyme about lavender blue fronts the set and gives it a name. Jerome mixes humor with quiet pathos, in the mellow manner of his later story work.
sketches-of-young-gentlemen:
Sketches of Young Gentlemen opens with a mock dedication to the young ladies of the United Kingdom, Wales, Guernsey, Jersey, Alderney, and Sark. The writer poses as their true friend and admirer. His stated aim is to answer a work called Sketches of Young Ladies, written by Quiz and drawn by Phiz.

The dedication builds a comic charge sheet against Quiz. It says his book libels young ladies, classes them as animals, and calls them hard names in its preface. It also claims Quiz must have broken some trust to learn what he printed. The joke form lets the writer defend women while sorting young men into types of his own.
stickeen:
John Muir published Stickeen in 1909 and dedicated the small book to Helen Muir, calling it an icy storm-story for a lover of wildness. The title names his dog companion, whose courage and loyalty during hard travel in cold country form the heart of the tale.

Facing the story stands a poem by J. G. Holland addressed to his own dog, Blanco, which wonders at the narrow gap between a dog's soul and a man's. That pairing sets the tone. Muir's short narrative honors a small dog's devotion under harsh weather. It has stayed one of his best-loved pieces of nature writing. Young and old readers alike keep returning to it.
stories-from-hans-andersen:
Stories from Hans Andersen, printed at London by Hodder and Stoughton, pairs the Danish tale-teller's work with illustrations by Edmund Dulac. The list of plates points to two tales given special pride of place: The Snow Queen and The Nightingale.

The plate captions sketch the scenes Dulac chose. A boy stands delighted with a mirror he has made. A queen flies through streets on winter nights. An old woman comes out of a house. Crowds cry out that something is gold. For The Nightingale they mark the poor fisherman lying still to listen, and courtiers taking water into their mouths to copy the bird's song. Dulac's rich plates shape how readers meet these tales.
stories-to-tell-to-children:
Sara Cone Bryant gathered Stories to Tell to Children for parents and teachers who read aloud. The front matter gives counsel to the story-teller, a set of stories marked for reproduction by young listeners, and a piece on story-telling in the teaching of English.

The tales themselves mix old favorites and folk stories from many lands. They give The Little Red Hen and The Gingerbread Man. They give The Country Mouse and the City Mouse. They close with Brother Rabbit fooling the whale and the elephant. The Boy Who Cried Wolf, The Frog King, The Elves and the Shoemaker, and The Nightingale stand beside jackal tales from India and the story of how Moses was saved.
t-mann-der-kleine-herr-friedemann-novell:
Mann's first book of stories, Der kleine Herr Friedemann, gathers his youthful novellas in German. The title piece follows a deformed little man whose carefully built peace collapses when love finally arrives too late. Disappointment and self-mastery, Mann's early obsessions, govern the collection throughout.

These early works already show the master's themes in crystalline form: the outsider, the artist, and the solid bourgeois world watching both. Buddenbrooks was still ahead of him, yet the voice is unmistakable. Stories of renunciation and sudden feeling alternate like held breaths. Where the great career began is exactly what this volume documents. German readers meet the young Mann testing every instrument he would later master.
tales-and-novels-volume-10-helen:
Helen, Volume X of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels in ten volumes with engravings on steel, printed in 1857, closes the set with her last novel. The contents divide Helen itself into volumes, the first taking a long list of numbered chapters in the pages at hand.

Edgeworth wrote Helen late, as the story of a young woman whose horror of falsehood is tested by the small, kind lies of the fashionable world she moves in. A friend's secret tests Helen hard. Keeping it costs Helen her own candor. It draws her toward the very duplicity she hates. The novel turns on one question. Can truth be recovered after it has once been bent? The ten-volume set thus ends with its author's most inward study of female friendship and reputation.
ten-thousand-dreams-interpreted-or-what-: Ten Thousand Dreams Interpreted is credited to Gustavus Hindman Miller. It is also called What's in a Dream. A third title calls it Dreams, Their Scientific and Practical Interpretations. No page of the dream book itself is present here. The Project Gutenberg wrapper stands first. It is dated May 1997. It gives notes on rights and reuse. It names Miller's book and its file number. Its own gift appeals then follow.
the-adventures-of-mr-verdant-green: Cuthbert Bede wrote The Adventures of Mr. Verdant Green. A front note explains how this copy was made. It was matched to the first printings of 1853, 1854, and 1857. Heads and a frontispiece came from a later printing of about 1923. The note lists small shifts among those early printings. Spelling shifts in spots. One word in Part One shifts as well. The note recalls the frontispiece line from Swift. It calls the book a college joke to cure the dumps.
the-amateur-garden: Only the front pages appear for George W. Cable's The Amateur Garden, an illustrated New York book from Charles Scribner's Sons, copyrighted and published in 1914. Its contents promise six essays: My Own Acre, The American Garden, Where to Plant What, The Cottage Gardens of Northampton, The Private Garden's Public Value, and The Midwinter Gardens of New Orleans. A caption under the front picture calls one tree Barrie's elm and another Felix Adler's hemlock, both in the author's study garden.
the-angel-adjutant-of-twice-born-men:
Minnie L. Carpenter wrote this life of Staff-Captain Kate Lee of the Salvation Army, with an introduction by General Bramwell Booth and a foreword by Commander Evangeline Booth. Booth's own opening note calls the book an intimate and living picture of Lee. Her fine character and restless labor, he says, bore rare fruit.

Booth uses the life to argue a broad point: the Army's women officers have proved themselves fit for all the work of Christian service. Long denied a public voice, women in the movement have matched their brethren as teachers and as rulers in the kingdom. Lee's story stands as his chief proof, told by one close to the work.
the-arctic-queen:
A long poem in parts, The Arctic Queen is dedicated to Dr. Elisha Kent Kane, commander of the Grinnell Expedition in search of Sir John Franklin. The dedication praises Kane's enterprise, courage, and heroic self-devotion, and calls him discoverer of the open polar sea. No author's name is printed on the pages shown.

Part First seats its queen, Oene, on an everlasting throne built at the steady center of the world. She waits for the middle hour of night to call her court. Her fair island sits in an ocean of lasting calm, ringed by the Frigid Zone like a silvery wall of snow. The verse dwells on pearls, pale light, and a realm defended from all storm and sudden change.
the-aspirations-of-jean-servien:
Anatole France's tale, turned into English by Alfred Allinson, begins in a back-shop in the Rue Notre-Dame des Champs in Paris. Jean Servien is born there to a bookbinder who works for the religious houses. Jean is a small, weak child, and his mother nurses him as she sews books sheet by sheet with the curved needle of the trade.

One day, crossing the shop with the baby at her breast, she slips on boards damp with paste. To guard the child she throws up an arm and strikes her own breast hard on the corner of the iron press. An abscess forms, heals, then breaks open again, and a low fever keeps her to her bed, singing her big hopes for her son in a hot whisper.
the-book-of-joyous-children: James Whitcomb Riley wrote The Book of Joyous Children, put out in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1902, with art by J. W. Vawter. The book is a set of rhymes. Riley gave it to Joel Chandler Harris. His gift verse praises Harris for keeping the fresh heart of youth through a life of toil and stress. It says Harris's laugh, as young folk hear it, seems their own.
the-brethren:
H. Rider Haggard wrote The Brethren, a tale of knights and the Holy Land. Its chapters start by the Waters of Death Creek, then name Sir Andrew D'Arcy and the knighting of the brethren. Late chapters bring a combat on a bridge, the Sultan Saladin, Ascalon, Jerusalem, and Saint Rosamund.

A dedication letter, dated on board R.M.S. Mongolia, May 12, 1904, and sent to Ella, plays with what might have been. The gallant brethren might have quarreled over Rosamund, Haggard muses, and had their long swords at each other's throats. Rosamund might have failed in her hour of trial and missed her saintly crown. Masouda, too, might have made a far other sacrifice for her fierce love.
the-burgess-animal-book-for-children:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Burgess Animal Book for Children. He dedicated it to the cause of wild life in America, and to the mammals, many of them in grave threat of being wiped out. A preface says the warm welcome of his Bird Book, and many letters asking about the habits of American mammals, led to this book. Burgess is plain about his bounds. He makes no try at sub-species; that is for the scientist.

He aims at the larger groups, orders and families, so that chief kinds may be known and their habits grasped. Yet he claims care for truth in the smallest details: no claim stands that two or more known naturalists have not backed. Drawings by Louis Agassiz Fuertes, in color and in black and white, were made for the book.
the-burgess-bird-book-for-children:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Burgess Bird Book for Children. The dedication gives the book to America's children and its birds alike. Its hope is to strengthen the love and friendship between them. A preface says the book was written to fill a clear need. Booksellers and others had pressed him, feeling the lack of a good first guide to bird life for little children. It is not a rival to the fine books on birds, he says, but a help beside them.

His chief aim is to interest the small child in the feathered friends he is most likely to see. The book is meant as both a story book and a sound handbook. Louis Agassiz Fuertes made drawings in full color for it, so true to life, Burgess says, that study of them lets any one name the species shown.
the-call-of-the-twentieth-century-an-add:
David Starr Jordan wrote The Call of the Twentieth Century: An Address to Young Men, dated 1903. Jordan was Chancellor of Leland Stanford Junior University, and he gave the address to Vernon Lyman Kellogg. A framed verse at the front speaks of the afterself: the man you ought to be, waiting in the twenties and thirties of the new century. His body, brain, and soul are in your boyish hands, it says.

The address itself begins with the rush of energy of the new century, greater than any century has shown before. Let us see what work it has to do, and what manner of men it will demand. The same joys and sorrows, the same marrying, work and play, wisdom and folly, will fill this one too. The question is what the boy of the century will leave for the man he is to become.
the-children:
A set of essays on children, transcribed from the 1911 John Lane edition, opens with a piece called Fellow Travellers with a Bird. The contents range widely: children in midwinter, children in burlesque, authorship, letters, illness, and the young children. Each piece watches childhood at close range rather than teaching about it from a distance.

The first essay warns that no one can predict a living child. Blackbirds do not repeat the same phrases year by year, and children keep no appointments with adult expectation. They meet the watcher at another place, after failing him where he waited. As an example, a girl of four dictates a letter to a distant cousin, hoping the cousin enjoys herself with her loving dolls. The essays prize such small, unforced moments as the true record of childhood, and treat adult notes and prior experience as poor guides.
the-curious-case-of-lady-purbeck-a-scand: The Curious Case of Lady Purbeck, a scandal of the 1600s, was published by Longmans, Green in 1909. No author is named. The page credits the writer of lives of Sir Kenelm Digby and King James II, and of a life of a prig. The contents trace Sir Edward Coke, his marriage to Lady Elizabeth Hatton, and the rivalry of Coke and Bacon. Then comes Coke's bid to win favor by offering his daughter to Sir John Villiers. Only the title page and part of the contents are present here.
the-curly-haired-hen: A. Vimar supplied both text and pictures for The Curly-Haired Hen, translated by Nora K. Hills. Its contents list ten chapters opening at Mother Etienne's farm. They move through A Mother's Devotion, Yollande's Trousseau, Father Gusson's Secret, and Sir Booum's Circus. A close called Triumph of the Ointment ends the list. A picture caption shows Yollande emerging from her shroud. Only the title page and contents are present here, apart from the heading of Chapter I.
the-devil-s-garden:
W. B. Maxwell, author of In Cotton Wool and Mrs. Thompson, published The Devil's Garden in Indianapolis with the Bobbs-Merrill Company in 1914. An epigraph warns that the Devil plays in a man's mind like a wanton child in a garden, choking paths, uprooting tender plants, and trampling buds meant for the Master.

Chapter I opens in a village post office. The postmaster, Mr. Dale, stares at an official envelope just shaken from a mailbag onto the sorting-table, addressed to himself. His heart beats quicker, keeping time with the clerks' stampers, as he wonders whether the envelope holds his fate. Sorting ends, letters stand arranged by the postmen's bags, and at five fifty-six, up to time as usual, he strikes a bell and sends his lads out on the first delivery.
the-dollar-hen:
Milo M. Hastings wrote The Dollar Hen, printed at Syracuse in 1911, after work at the Kansas Experiment Station and on a federal poultry study. His preface argues that a man could read every poultry book of his day and still miss the plain facts that make the trade pay. Medicine once hid the worth of fresh air the same way, he says.

Hastings writes for profit, not show birds. He covers costs, feed, housing, and markets with a business eye. The book helped shift hen keeping from a yard hobby to a planned trade.
the-dragon-and-the-raven: G. A. Henty's The Dragon and the Raven; or, The Days of King Alfred is dated 1885 in its front pages. Only a title page and contents list are present here. The chapters run from The Fugitives and The Battle of Kesteven through The Massacre at Croyland. They end with the Isle of Athelney and the siege of Paris. The tale's own pages do not follow.
the-duke-s-children:
Anthony Trollope's novel The Duke's Children first ran in All the Year Round in 1879 and 1880, and its contents open with grief: When the Duchess Was Dead. Lady Mary Palliser, Francis Oliphant Tregear, and Major Tifto enter next, with chapters on the Derby, a new member for Silverbridge, and the Duke in his study.

The widowed Duke of Omnium must face children who choose love against his plans. A horse race fix, a rich American girl, and stern letters drive the plot. Trollope closes his Palliser series with this tale of pride and softening.
the-empire-of-russia-from-the-remotest-p:
John S. C. Abbott's The Empire of Russia, printed at Boston in 1859 in his Monarchies of Continental Europe set, runs from the remotest periods to the present time. In his preface Abbott says the world is too busy for vast tomes of battle detail and court intrigue. He aims to trace Russia's path from infancy to the present hour in clear, plain lines.

Russia's wild, strange career, he holds, needs no fancy to grip a reader. He leans on Karamzin, the famed Russian historian, without clogging pages with notes. Swift lives and wars fill the tale.
the-eternal-maiden:
T. Everett Harré's The Eternal Maiden, a novel printed at New York in 1913, opens in a mythic prelude. Long ages back, darkness held the frozen world, its waters locked and no beast astir. Men had risen like willows from the ice, yet lived as if dead: they did not speak, hunt, eat, or die. Then the Great Spirit set a strong man on earth to wake them.

The book is set in memory of Edgar Wilson Riddell, a friend lost young. Arctic myth and a doomed love shape Harré's tale of the far North and its first peoples.
the-fair-haven:
Samuel Butler wrote The Fair Haven under the mask of a dead author, John Pickard Owen, whose life opens the book in a memoir by his brother. This 1913 London edition adds an introduction by R. A. Streatfeild.

The work defends the miracles in the life of Jesus against two foes at once: doubters who call them myth, and church defenders whose weak methods do harm. Chapters take up Strauss and his dream theory of the Gospels, the change in Paul's life, and Paul's own words as proof. Butler's satire hides inside a grave, earnest form, which is the joke and the point.
the-faith-of-men: Only the old Project Gutenberg header is present here, before the text of the book itself begins. It names The Faith of Men by Jack London, taken from the 1919 William Heinemann edition, and gives the book's release data. No title page, contents list, or story text can be read in what is present, so nothing about the tales inside can be stated from this front matter alone.
the-fifteen-comforts-of-matrimony-respon:
The Fifteen Comforts of Matrimony, printed at London in 1706, is a verse satire given to bachelors and widowers. It calls itself a looking glass for all who have entered the married state.

The first comfort sets the joke: man is born free, then sets his heart on a girl and is undone. New-wed bliss soon fades. The wife grows proud and scolding, wants rich things, and finds fault with her keep. In the old broadside style, each comfort adds a fresh woe, warning young men that wedlock's sweets turn sour fast. The humor is rough, one-sided, and of its age.

A bold answer piece of 1706 replies to a paper on the comforts of whoring, and speaks in the voice of the women it defends. The title page gives the speakers as whores and bawds, answering back in print.

The preface says the women resent the attack on their trade and mock the author as a bashful fool, a spent old man, or a woman hater. They vow to keep their calling though disease be their daily share. Street speech, threats, and coarse jokes fill the reply. Such pamphlet wars show how low print of the day fought insult with louder insult.
the-firm-of-nucingen:
Honore de Balzac wrote The Firm of Nucingen as a tale of Paris finance, turned into English by James Waring. He gives the work to Madame Zulma Carraud and links it to his tale of Cesar Birotteau.

The tale is told as talk overheard through the thin wall of a private dining room in a Paris restaurant. Four young men of no clear means but fine living hold forth next door. Through their chat, the rise of the banker Nucingen unfolds: wealth built on planned crashes that ruin small holders. Balzac sets the honest fall of Birotteau against Nucingen's cold, rich fraud.
the-first-blast-of-the-trumpet-against-t:
John Knox wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women in 1558, a fierce tract against the rule of women. This copy is the 1878 printing edited by Edward Arber.

The preface scolds godly preachers, then in exile, for their silence while a woman ruled. Knox holds that a woman's reign over men is a monster in nature and against God's law. He answers claims that such views stir revolt or bring risk on readers. Aimed at the queens of his day, the blast made Knox foes for life and still shows the hard edge of reform-age faith.
the-friendships-of-women:
William Rounseville Alger wrote The Friendships of Women, printed at Boston in 1868, to test a common claim of his day. The book grew, he says, from work on a broad history of friendship.

Alger found few tales of deep friendship among women in his search, and heard it said that strong blocks in their nature made such bonds rare and weak. He kept digging, and the heap of cases grew past one chapter into a book of its own. With tales from history and verse, he argues that women form bonds as deep, true, and lasting as any between men.
the-frontiersmen:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote The Frontiersmen as a set of tales of the Tennessee frontier, printed in 1904. Six tales make up the book, with notes at the end.

The first tale, The Linguister, opens inside a small stockade where Peninnah Penelope Anne Mivane looks out of a blockhouse port-hole. Her world is no wider than the fort's yard, yet it has known battle and bloody death. Craddock, author of In the Tennessee Mountains, writes of Cherokee and settler folk, captive girls, bewitched ball sticks, and grandfathers who stir up storms on the wild edge of the young republic.
the-good-shepherd-a-life-of-christ-for-c: The Good Shepherd is a life of Christ for children. Fleming H. Revell Company printed it in New York, Chicago, and Toronto. No author is named in what is present here. That is front matter only. It gives the title page, a contents list, and a list of pictures. The contents run from Why Jesus Came and Jesus Is Born in Bethlehem, through John the Baptist and the prodigal son. They end with The Last Days in Jerusalem and The Crucifixion and the Resurrection. Songs and prayers close the book.
the-heroes-or-greek-fairy-tales-for-my-c:
Charles Kingsley wrote The Heroes, or Greek Fairy Tales for My Children, shown in a London edition from Macmillan and Co. dated 1889. Kingsley dedicates the book to his children Rose, Maurice, and Mary as a little present of old Greek fairy tales. A preface speaks straight to young readers.

Kingsley tells the children that some have heard of the old Greeks already, and that all will hear more as they grow. Boys, he says, may spend much time reading Greek books at school. The preface frames the tales as a first, friendly meeting with Greek story, given by a father before harder study begins.
the-hidden-children:
Robert W. Chambers wrote The Hidden Children, dated 1914, and he dedicates the book to his mother, crediting her wisdom, sympathy, and teaching. An author's preface insists that no undue liberties with history were attempted in the romance. Few figures, he says, are purely imagined, and fiction only sugar-coats a solid pill of fact.

Chambers traces a dark trail from burning Poundridge town to Catharines-town, across what he calls the bloody archives of the nation. He honors the League of the Iroquois, the Great Peace formed to impose peace, and the peoples of the Long House. Place names across the region, he argues, keep that memory alive in beauty.
the-hoyden: Mrs. Hungerford wrote this novel in 1894. Her dates are printed here as 1855 to 1897. The Tauchnitz Collection of British Authors carries this edition, made for English readers on the continent. Only the publisher's front matter is present here. The story itself does not appear. A Scotsman review survives in it, calling the tale clever, sprightly, fresh, sunshiny, and delightful. A list of her other Tauchnitz titles follows. They include Molly Bawn, Portia, Phyllis, and Faith and Unfaith. Several of her books ran to two volumes, like this one.
the-last-leaf-observations-during-sevent:
James Kendall Hosmer published his recollections in 1912 under a title borrowed from Oliver Wendell Holmes poem about old age. Hosmer answers the joke directly. He argues that men who saw great actors face to face and joined epoch making events hold ground the young cannot claim.

His observations span seventy-five years of men and events in America and Europe. Some pieces first ran in the Atlantic Monthly and in Boston and New York papers. Hosmer writes as a participant who hopes to totter across his panorama without doddering, retouching old sketches for a new audience.
the-last-of-the-plainsmen:
Zane Grey traveled in spring 1907 with Buffalo Jones, and his prefatory note introduces the old plainsman to readers. Jones was born on the Illinois prairie sixty-two years earlier and spent his life pursuing wild animals. His passion was to capture beasts alive, not kill them.

Jones once supplied buffalo meat to plains caravans, then smashed his rifle and vowed to save the bison. Grey promises color from yellow crags, deep canyons, and giant pines north of the Grand Canyon. He also promises a portrait of a strange, remarkable man at home on a desert plateau.
the-learned-women: Moliere wrote his comedy Les Femmes Savantes, and Charles Heron Wall translated it into English prose with short introductions and notes. Only the title page and cast list are present here, naming honest bourgeois Chrysale, his wife Philaminte, their daughters Armande and Henriette, pedantic Trissotin, and learned Vadius. Wall note on the first performance gives a date that conflicts with Moliere lifetime, so it is best left aside. The dialogue mocking pretentious learning does not appear in this record.
the-lovels-of-arden: The Lovels of Arden, by M. E. Braddon and dated 1871 in its heading, appears here in a cheap uniform edition of Miss Braddon's novels. The title page credits only the author of Lady Audley's Secret, Aurora Floyd, Vixen, and Ishmael. Only that title page, publisher's praise, and the start of the contents are present here, so the novel does not appear. The contents shown begin with Coming Home, Beginning the World, Father and Daughter, and Clarissa Is "Taken Up." The edition's notices call Braddon the queen of the circulating libraries.
the-man-in-lower-ten: Mary Roberts Rinehart's The Man in Lower Ten appears with only its title page, a contents list, and the first line of chapter one. The novel does not appear beyond that line. The thirty-one chapters promise a railway mystery. Titles include I Go to Pittsburg, A Torn Telegram, Numbers Seven and Nine, and The Woman in the Next Car. The Girl in Blue, A Fine Gold Chain, The Trap-Door, The Cinematograph, and Alison's Story follow. The opening line tells us that McKnight is taking over the criminal work.
the-mide-wiwin-or-grand-medicine-society: W. J. Hoffman wrote The Midewiwin, or Grand Medicine Society of the Ojibwa, an ethnological study. Its title page and partial contents are all that is present here, so the study itself does not appear. The contents promise an introduction, a section on shamans, and an account of the society and its lodge, the midewigan. Degrees follow, beginning with preparatory instruction for the first degree. A transcriber's note explains the macrons and breves used for Ojibwa vowels and notes that song music accompanies the fuller version.
the-midnight-queen:
May Agnes Fleming's novel The Midnight Queen opens in a London consumed by plague. Thousands die daily, grass grows in the streets, and the living can scarcely bury the dead. Coffin-makers and pest-cart drivers hold the only busy trades. Almost every house bears the red cross and the words 'Lord have mercy on us.' Watchmen with halberds guard the stricken houses while the few people abroad shrink from each other.

Fleming's contents promise a sorceress, a dead bride, a court page, and a dwarf by a ruin. Her chapters move through a masque, an execution, a dungeon, and a plague-pit before asking what was behind the mask. Bodies fall dead on the sidewalk and lie until the dead-cart rattles up, Fleming writes, in the mocking sunlight. Readers get sensation fiction staged in the great pestilence's emptied streets.
the-monster-men:
Edgar Rice Burroughs's novel The Monster Men lists seventeen chapters before Chapter 1, The Rift, begins. Titles such as Beauty and the Beast, The Soul of Number 13, Into Savage Borneo, and Man or Monster? sketch its direction. The opening scene is grim and secretive from the first line.

A man drops the last fragment of a dismembered body into a small vat of nitric acid meant to destroy evidence that could hang him. He collapses at his great teak desk, shaking, dry-eyed, and sweating as sobs rack him. Footsteps on the stair to his workshop bring him terrified to his feet, staring at the locked and bolted door. The gentle knock, when it comes, carries a girl's sweet voice calling Daddy.
the-new-magdalen:
Wilkie Collins's The New Magdalen is dedicated to the memory of Charles Allston Collins, dated April 9, 1873. A preamble fixes the first scene precisely. The place is France, the time autumn 1870, during the war between France and Germany. Captain Arnault of the French army, two surgeons from opposing ambulances, the nurse Mercy Merrick, and the travelling lady Grace Roseberry are the persons named.

Chapter I, The Two Women, opens on a dark night of pouring rain near the village of Lagrange, hard by the German frontier. French and German skirmishing parties met by accident there, and the French, for once, got the better of it after the great German victory of Weissenbourg. Captain Arnault sits alone in the miller's cottage, reading intercepted dispatches by a tallow candle while the wounded rest in the kitchen.
the-nuts-a-christmas-story-for-my-childr:
Georg Ebers wrote The Nuts as a Christmas story for his children and grandchildren. The tale is told inside a household scene: a wounded colonel, nursed back to health in the family home, rests in grandfather's chair each afternoon. The doctor allows him three pipes a day and no more than half an hour of talking at a time.

The children gather at twilight because his stories always hold them, and he often stops at the most gripping point. He favors six-year-old Hermy, who once cried at a stern look from him. Having lost his own wife, son, and daughter, the colonel finds comfort among the children.
the-parent-s-assistant-or-stories-for-ch:
Maria Edgeworth wrote The Parent's Assistant, or Stories for Children, shown here in the 1891 Routledge edition from London, with illustrations by F. A. Fraser. Her preface, addressed to parents, opens with Dr. Johnson's praise of Dr. Watts for stooping to write for children. Edgeworth says writing for children is no easy task.

She explains that the stories rest on careful notes of real children's talk and behavior, kept over years. Justice, truth, and humanity, she insists, belong to no rank and must be taught to the young of every station. A line from Pope stands on the title page: as the twig is bent, the tree is inclined. A second record carries the same edition and preface.
the-poisoned-pen: Arthur B. Reeve's The Poisoned Pen reaches this record through an old Project Gutenberg header, numbered Etext 1923 and dated October 1999. Only that header is present here, so the stories themselves do not appear. It gives the title and author's name before the usual Gutenberg notices. No contents, title page, or chapter text can be seen in what is present. A sibling record of the same title carries a fuller opening, with the Craig Kennedy series contents and the start of the first story.
the-port-of-missing-men: Meredith Nicholson's The Port of Missing Men was published by the Bobbs-Merrill Company at Indianapolis under a January 1907 copyright, with illustrations by Clarence F. Rutherford. Here only the title pages, dedication, and a frontispiece poem appear, so the novel itself is absent. A motto from Malory has Sir Pellinore doffing his armour before a midnight adventure. The book is dedicated to Herman Kountze's memory. The poem, The Shining Road, invites a sweetheart to ride beyond the city's bound toward a golden light past the dawn.
the-railway-children:
E. Nesbit dedicates her story to her son Paul Bland, whose knowledge of railways shelters her own ignorance, then introduces three suburban children who were not railway children to begin with. Roberta, Peter, and Phyllis live in a red-brick villa with every modern convenience.

Their mother plays and reads with them instead of paying dull calls, which makes the coming change sharper. Contents promise coal-mines, an old gentleman, prisoners, saviours of a train, and a terrible secret. The book remains a model of children's adventure writing because danger and kindness share the same country station world.
the-raven: Edgar Allan Poe's famous poem appears in a Harper and Brothers edition of 1884, illustrated by Gustave Dore with comment by Edmund C. Stedman. A list of illustrations names engravers and quotes the midnight opening lines about pondering over forgotten lore. Here only the title pages and opening of the illustration list are present, so the poem itself does not appear.
the-rectory-children: Mrs. Molesworth's story for young readers was issued at London by Macmillan in 1897 with illustrations by Walter Crane and dedicated to her niece and god-daughter. Contents begin in a parlour behind a shop, meet some young ladies, present a trying child, and give Biddy new thoughts before Celestina appears and a window in a wall draws attention. Here only the title pages, dedication, and opening of the contents list are present, so the children's story itself does not appear.
the-rival-heirs-being-the-third-and-last: Rev. A. D. Crake closes his Aescendune chronicles here. A third and last tale completes the set. Its chapter list opens in an Anglo-Saxon hall. A black and dark night follows. A wedding joins the hawk and the dove. Norman pages and a greenwood fray come next. Revelations, frustration, and a woodland hunt follow. Coals of fire and a guide lead toward restoration. Retribution ends the plot's movement. An English heir takes possession near the close. Only the title page and chapter list are present here.
the-secret-garden:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's The Secret Garden lists twenty-seven chapters in its contents. Early headings promise Mistress Mary quite contrary and a crossing of the moor. Martha, a cry in the corridor, and a key to the garden follow. Dickon, a robin who showed the way, and Colin all appear. Magic and a curtain come near the end, with a final chapter in the garden.

Chapter one is titled There Is No One Left. Mary Lennox arrives to live with her uncle at Misselthwaite Manor. Everybody called her the most disagreeable-looking child ever seen, Burnett writes, and agrees it was true. Thin face, thin body, and thin light hair are her marks, with a sour expression over all. India, her birthplace, had yellowed her face and kept her always ill, the opening explains.
the-stories-mother-nature-told-her-child:
Jane Andrews, author of Seven Little Sisters, wrote these nature stories for children, issued in illustrated editions dated 1888 and 1894. A contents list promises many tales. They cover amber beads, Indian corn, and water-lilies. Sea-life, frost giants, and tadpoles follow. Golden-rod and asters close the list. The first story then begins with a question. Does the reader know Mother Nature? God has entrusted her with the care of all living things.

Andrews personifies nature as a storytelling mother whose children learn how the world works through her tales. Some tales give the talk of village trees. Others follow the carrying trade of winds and waters. One peeks into one of God's storehouses. Each turns simple natural facts into bedtime lessons.
the-story-hour-a-book-for-the-home-and-t: Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora A. Smith compiled this story collection for the home and the kindergarten, opening with a Froebel motto on ears and hearts opening to the storyteller. Only the title page and contents are present here. The contents show an introduction and preface. The stories include The Oriole's Nest. Moufflou, adapted from Ouida, follows. The Babes in the Wood and a story of Christmas come next. The first Thanksgiving day appears too. George Washington tales in two parts close the list. The stories themselves do not appear.
the-surprising-adventures-of-baron-munch:
Rudolph Erich Raspe's Baron tells his marvellous travels in a volume whose 1895 edition carries a learned introduction on imaginary voyages. The introduction sorts imaginary voyages into types. The three great types were all created in England, it observes. Utopia serves the philosophical kind. Robinson Crusoe serves the edifying kind. Gulliver's Travels serves the satirical kind. Munchausen adds a fourth type. It is the wildly lying kind. It came at the end of the eighteenth century.

The Baron's notoriety is universal and his name proverbial, the introduction argues, though the learned condemned the work as worthless. It first appeared in London in 1785. The form was a slim pamphlet of forty-nine small pages. The Critical Review noticed it as a satire. It mocked bold parliamentary assertions. A second edition was printed at Oxford in 1786. It recommended the tales to country gentlemen. They could repeat them after a hunt.
the-survivors-of-the-chancellor-diary-of:
Jules Verne tells this shipwreck tale as the diary of J. R. Kazallon, a passenger on the Chancellor, and a companion record carries an editor's introduction to the same work. The diary opens at Charleston on September 27, 1869. At high tide the ship leaves the Battery quay. Captain Huntly commands her. She doubles Fort Sumter. By seven in the evening she stands free on the wide Atlantic.

Kazallon describes his ship proudly. She is a fine three-master of 900 tons, square-rigged. The Liverpool firm of Laird Brothers owns her. She is copper-sheathed and teak-decked. She is registered first class. She is making her third voyage between Charleston and Liverpool. He then explains that no direct steamship service ran between South Carolina and Great Britain, so travellers chose between New York and New Orleans sailings, but fate decided otherwise for him.
the-tale-of-balen:
Algernon Charles Swinburne retells the old wild tale of Balen in verse, published by Chatto and Windus in London in 1896. A dedication poem to his mother is dated March 24, 1896. He lays his hope, heart, and self before her in song. He hopes the remade tale will live through one springtide of strong April suns.

The poem itself then opens in hawthorn-time. The heart grows light there. The world turns sweet to ear and eye. Birds and glad thoughts take wing in the verse. Heather kindles toward the light. Whin burns like frankincense and flame. Swinburne's dense music sets the Arthurian story of Balen in a blaze of spring imagery.
the-tale-of-henrietta-hen: Henrietta Hen, by Arthur Scott Bailey, appeared in 1921 in his Slumber-Town Tales series, with drawings by Harry L. Smith. This record holds the title page and contents only, leaving Henrietta's story itself unread. Nine chapters are listed, beginning with her fine family and moving through wet feet, a swimmer, a capture by Mr. Crow, and a warning delivered to the rooster. A later chapter calls her haughty, so readers can guess at her proud character even without the pages that follow.
the-tale-of-tom-kitten:
Beatrix Potter's Tom Kitten was first published by Frederick Warne in 1907 and dedicated to all Pickles, especially those on her garden wall. Three little kittens, Mittens, Tom Kitten, and Moppet, tumble about the doorstep and play in the dust. Their mother, Mrs. Tabitha Twitchit, expects fine company to tea one day. She brings the kittens inside, to be washed and dressed before the guests arrive.

First she scrubs their faces, then she brushes their fur, dressing each kitten in clean clothes. Anyone who knows kittens can guess how long the good outfits last outdoors. Potter turns a mother's careful preparations into a comedy of dignity lost, and children enjoy watching tidy plans fall apart in the garden.
the-three-jovial-huntsmen:
Randolph Caldecott's Three Jovial Huntsmen, one of his celebrated picture books from Frederick Warne, sings of three huntsmen who go a-hunting with horns blowing. The verses run in broad dialect, with the refrain 'Look ye there!' after every discovery. One huntsman warns the others to mind their eyes and keep their noses right in the wind. Then the first thing they find is a tattered boggart in a field, and they leave it behind.

The joke builds as the three disagree over everything they meet: one calls the boggart a gentleman-farmer who has lost his way. Caldecott's pictures carry much of the comedy, with the huntsmen's solemn confidence mocked at every turn. It is a nursery favourite built from a folk song, valued for rhythm, dialect, and drawings that generations of children have pored over.
the-tree-of-heaven:
May Sinclair's Tree of Heaven, dated 1918, opens in its first part, called Peace, with Frances Harrison sitting in her garden. She rests under the tree her husband calls an ash, though the local people call it a tree of Heaven. The children keep her from dozing away the afternoon: Dorothy, Michael, and Nicholas are going to a party, and Nicky, for whom it is the first, is beside himself with excitement. Baby John, too young for parties, rides furiously on Mary-Nanna's knee to a singing game.

Frances describes the party for the third time: dancing, a Magic Lantern, a Funny Man, and Rosalind's cake with eight pink candles. Nine-year-old Dorothy laughs at Nicky, and his mother kisses him each time. Sinclair's family idyll, dated by its title Peace, stands knowingly on the edge of the war that will take these children.
the-two-noble-kinsmen: The Two Noble Kinsmen, credited on its title page to Mr. John Fletcher and Mr. William Shakspeare, is presented here through a contents list and the opening of its dramatis personae. The scenes run from Athens before a temple and Thebes's court, through prison rooms and forests, to the temples of Mars, Venus, and Diana and a block prepared for combat. The personae begin with Arcite and Palamon, cousins and nephews of Creon, King of Thebes. No line of their rivalry for Emilia appears here.
the-veiled-lady-and-other-men-and-women:
F. Hopkinson Smith heads his story collection with The Veiled Lady of Stamboul and adds ten more tales. A letter to readers admits the title may mislead, since the veiled houri is only one figure among many between the covers. One Venetian beauty, whose love affairs unsettled a quarter of the city, also appears.

Smith's letter ranges over the cast with affection: a motherly nurse, a plucky New England girl, a prim spinster comforted by a boarder, and rough sea-dogs kind to other dogs. Brave men make derricks of their arms, club swells chase adventure, and gay Bohemians taste everything. Story titles include Loretta of the Shipyards, A Coat of Red Lead, and Captain Joe and the Susie Ann.
the-ways-of-men:
Eliot Gregory, writing as An Idler, published The Ways of Men with Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1900. He dedicates the essays to Edith Wharton, quoting lines about her mild reproof and golden praise. Chapter one, Uncle Sam, begins with a governor at this century's birth who loved classical names.

That governor's ardour scattered Utica, Syracuse, and Ithaca across the map, raising trolley-car towns instead of historic pomp. He also christened a city Troy and its hill Mount Ida, little dreaming a youth on those slopes would give his name to the republic itself. Gregory then introduces two brothers, Ebenezer and Samuel, who walked from New York and set up a brickyard near Perry Street, Troy.
the-woman-who-toils-being-the-experience: Front matter alone is present for The Woman Who Toils, published by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1903. Mrs. John Van Vorst and Marie Van Vorst wrote it together. Its subtitle promises the experiences of two gentlewomen as factory girls. Photographs show one writer dressed for a pickle factory. The other is shown at work in a shoe factory. The sisters dedicate the book to Mark Twain.
topsy-turvy-land-arabia-pictured-for-chi: Samuel M. Zwemer and Amy E. Zwemer pictured Arabia for children in a book published by Fleming H. Revell in 1902, at New York, Chicago, and Toronto. They dedicated it at Bahrein, Arabia, to boys and girls helping to turn the world upside down. Contents begin by asking why Arabia is topsy-turvy land, on page fifteen. The dedication and opening contents are what is given in this record, giving the book's missionary purpose and child audience. The Zwemers' chapters on Arabian life themselves do not appear here.
treatise-on-parents-and-children: Bernard Shaw's Treatise on Parents and Children survives here as its full table of contents. The headings run from Trailing Clouds of Glory and The Child is Father to the Man to School, Taboo in Schools, and Children's Rights and Duties. Later headings cover children's happiness, earning a living, and the conflict of wills. The list ends with reforming society before reforming ourselves. Only the contents page is present here, so the essays themselves do not appear. Even the headings show Shaw attacking the schooling of his day.
troublesome-comforts-a-story-for-childre:
Geraldine Robertson Glasgow's Troublesome Comforts, a story for children from Thomas Nelson and Sons, opens in a stuffy third-class carriage at Liverpool Street Station. Mrs. Beauchamp looks wistfully at her husband on the platform. Behind her the carriage overflows with children, paper parcels, and packages held by straps.

The ticket collector cannot make the nurse's count come right: five halves, two wholes, a dog, and a bicycle. Susie, Dick, and Amy are named, the baby is in arms, and Tommy has vanished. He is under the seat, Dick announces, and crawls out covered in dust, quite unashamed. A seaside holiday begins in cheerful family chaos.
twelve-men:
Theodore Dreiser's Twelve Men, dated 1919, profiles a dozen men who marked his life. The contents name Peter, a doer of the word, his brother Paul, a country doctor, and Culhane the solid man. A mayor and his people, village feudists, and a man called the Mighty Rourke fill out the list.

The first portrait, Peter, opens with a claim about character. In any group, Dreiser writes, Peter stood out as deliciously and irrefutably different, an oasis in American intellectual dreariness. Dreiser met him at St. Louis in 1892, in the art department of the Globe-Democrat. Peter's spiritual freedom, facing nature unafraid, anchors the whole gallery of sketches.
val-d-arno-ten-lectures-on-the-tuscan-ar: John Ruskin's Val d'Arno offers ten lectures on the Tuscan art that came just before the Florentine year of victories. Pages present here hold the lecture list and a list of plates, so the lectures themselves are not shown. Titles move from Nicholas the Pisan and John the Pisan through heraldic subjects like Shield and Apron and Parted per Pale, to the Tyrrhene Sea and the Fleur de Lys. Plates promise Pisano's pulpit, the fountain of Perugia, the door of the Pisa baptistery, and scenes of St. John.
vendetta-a-story-of-one-forgotten: Marie Corelli, author of Ardath, Thelma, and A Romance of Two Worlds, wrote Vendetta, or A Story of One Forgotten. Pages present here give the title page and a contents list that names a preface and thirty-four numbered chapters with no titles given, so the story itself is not shown. Nothing in these pages names the forgotten one or the wrong that drives the revenge. Readers learn only the book's frame: a long novel in thirty-four chapters, built on a single buried life and the vengeance it seeks.
war-in-the-garden-of-eden: Kermit Roosevelt wrote War in the Garden of Eden about his service in Mesopotamia. The book came out at New York in 1919. He had served as a captain in the British forces, and then in the American field artillery. He dedicated the book to the memory of his father. Pages present here hold the title page, contents, and picture list only, so his narrative is not shown. Contents promise the Tigris front and patrols among the ruins of Babylon. Fights on the Kurdish and Persian fronts follow.
what-great-men-have-said-about-women:
E. Haldeman-Julius edited What Great Men Have Said About Women as number 77 in his Ten Cent Pocket Series. The little book came from Girard, Kansas. It gathers short quotes on women from famed male writers. Shakespeare leads the set, with lines drawn from several of his plays.

One quote praises a woman's eye as a teacher of beauty, from Love's Labour's Lost. Much Ado About Nothing adds a softer image of a life entering a man's thoughts. Other lines say kindness wins love more than looks do. Gifts, one verse warns, can move a woman's mind when words fail. Readers get a pocket set of old praise, wit, and bias.
when-we-dead-awaken:
Henrik Ibsen wrote When We Dead Awaken, his last play, in a version by William Archer. Archer's introduction tells how the play broke Ibsen's steady two-year rhythm. Fans expected a new work in 1898, but Christmas brought no word of one. Ibsen was past seventy, and the gap looked like a bad sign.

Archer met Ibsen at the new National Theatre in Christiania in September of the next year. Ibsen said he was at work on a new play, and planned to name it a dramatic epilogue. He wrote it in fever and haste, as if death stood behind him. The play came out just before Christmas 1899. An aging sculptor and a lost love face what their lives have cost.
ximenez-historias-origen:
Francisco Ximénez was a Dominican friar in Guatemala in the early 1700s. His Histories of the Origin of the Indians reached print in an 1857 edition. Carl Scherzer edited the old manuscript for its first wide release.

Inside stands Ximénez's Spanish version of the Popol Vuh itself. That text is the great creation epic of the Maya peoples. No European version of the epic had appeared before his work. His manuscript kept the story safe while conquest tried to erase it. The book that saved the Maya Bible still anchors study of it today. Without Ximénez, the epic might have vanished for good.
